descs.en: She saw through the guard nobody else noticed. He has spent ten years making people disappear, and now he wants to disappear with her.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
At a government reception on Battery Hill, sixty guards stand at the doors and look at the guests. One of them doesn’t. He watches a single man for forty-one minutes, and the only person in the building who notices is Serafina Song, there on a staff pass to inspect a red Lancia, in her sister’s dress and her own boots.

She walks across the ballroom and tells him he isn’t a guard. She’s right. Qin Haozhen has spent ten years making people disappear for a state that doesn’t put its name on doors, and nobody has ever looked at him before.

She finds his name with one bribed caterer. She asks him for a race, not a date. And a man who sleeps four hours a night in any bed in any country falls asleep in the passenger seat of her thirty-year-old car at three in the morning, and keeps coming back.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Serafina walked out of her engagement dinner between the soup and the fish in The Woman Who Sets the Price, and then turned up at her sister’s wedding in Milan with oil on her boots. I always wanted to know who could keep up with her.

The answer turned out to be the most forgettable man in the room. Haozhen is not a good man at the start of this book, and it doesn’t pretend he is. It’s about a man finding out he’s allowed to want something, starting with an egg sandwich, and a woman who decides every single morning whether she can live with the truth about him, and keeps deciding yes.

The racing is as real as I could make it: braking markers, tyre temperatures, driver changes, telemetry in four coloured lines. The spy work stays at the level of a story. And yes, the car really can do two hundred miles an hour. He did the brakes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a fast, funny book, but it has some hard moments:

• A state operative’s work, including abductions and killings, mostly off the page and remembered (What He Does for Work, The Target Has a Family, Chen Si Brokers a Truce)

• A man taken from his family in front of his young son (The Target Has a Family)

• Trauma, depression and silence after a mission (He Comes Home Wrong)

• A cruel parent and a family’s financial collapse (The Song Family Opposes the Match)

• Threats against family members and surveillance (A File on the Workbench)

• A car chase, gunfire, a gunshot wound and a burning car (Shoot the Tyres), and a fever (The Safe House in the Mountains)

• Wound stitching without a doctor (The First Time He Bleeds in Her Garage)

• A serious racing crash, intensive care and a long recovery from concussion (The Needle, Hospital, Night Two, She Drives Again)

• Illegal street racing throughout Volume One

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Nonna — Serafina’s red 1992 Lancia Delta HF Integrale, named after their grandmother.
Gilded — Team AURELIA’s matte black race car, number 7, with AURELIA in gold on the bonnet.
Nobody — The getaway car: a grey 2006 Toyota Crown estate with wooden-bead seat covers and an engine it should never have had.
Two Hundred — A burnt-out 1991 endurance prototype, bought for scrap.
The garage — Under the railway bridge in the industrial district. Trains every eleven minutes.
Granny Shum’s — The Saturday street races by the paint works: the long straight, the S-bends, the lamp posts round the gas works.
The Needle — The hairpin at the end of the back straight at the circuit in the north.
The Eleventh — The Bureau Haozhen worked for, in a building with no name on it.
Brake on the marker — Braking exactly at the board, to the metre.
Telemetry — The car’s data: speed, throttle, brake and steering, a thousand times a second.

chapters.title: The Guard Nobody Else Noticed
chapters.desc: A government reception on Battery Hill, a car with a forged chassis plate, and the only guard in the building who never once looked at the guests.
chapters.epigraph: “Everyone in that room was looking at somebody. He was the only one looking at the right person.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
The dress was her sister’s, and it was too short, because everything of Aurelia’s was too short on Serafina. It stopped two fingers above the top of her boots. She had considered borrowing shoes as well and decided that there were limits to what a person should do for a Lancia.

The Residence on Battery Hill had been built by people who wanted the harbour to know they were watching it. White columns, a lawn that went down in terraces to a black iron fence, and at the top, a ballroom with eleven chandeliers and four hundred guests in it, every one of them the kind of person whose name was checked twice at the gate. The Autumn Reception. A delegation from the capital, three consuls, the men who owned the container terminals, and their wives in silk the colour of expensive fruit.

Serafina had been checked twice at the gate as well. Her pass said VEHICLE SPECIALIST — LOT 9 and had a photograph of her that the auction house had taken against a white wall that morning. In it she looked like someone who had been arrested.

“You have forty minutes with the car before the bidding,” the auction woman had told her, walking fast in heels across the gravel of the service yard. “Don’t touch the paintwork. Don’t sit in it. Don’t talk to the guests.”

“I never talk to guests,” Serafina said. “They talk to me. Then they ask me to fix their son’s Porsche for free.”

The auction woman had not laughed. That was fine. Serafina had not come to be liked.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lot 9 was in a glass pavilion at the end of the east terrace, lit from below like a jewel in a case. A 1974 Lancia Stratos HF Stradale, red, low, short as a sneeze, a wedge of a car that had won the world rally championship three years running and still looked as though it had been drawn by a boy in the back of a maths lesson. Signor Bassi, who was eighty-one and had known her grandmother in Milan and lived now in a flat above Lake Como with eleven cars and a parrot, was going to bid for it by telephone at ten o’clock. He had paid Serafina eight thousand euros to look at it first.

“If your grandmother were alive she would do it for nothing,” he had said on the phone. “But she would also tell me I was a fool to want it. So. Eight thousand. And tell me the truth.”

She lay on her back on the pavilion floor in her sister’s dress with a torch in her teeth and looked at the truth.

The truth was on the chassis plate, riveted to the frame behind the front left wheel. It was the right shape. It had the right number. And the rivets were wrong. Too clean, too round, the heads slightly too domed for anything that had come out of a factory in Turin in 1974. Someone had drilled out the old plate and put a new one in, very carefully, and then aged the paint around it with something that smelled faintly of tea.

She took a photograph. She took four. She rolled out from under the car and sat up, and brushed the dust off Aurelia’s dress, and that was when she saw him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was standing by the east service door.

There were sixty guards in the building. She had counted them coming in, because counting things was a habit she had got from her sister and could not give back. They wore dark suits and earpieces with coiled clear tubes, and they stood at doors and at the edges of rooms and looked at the guests the way guards looked at guests: a long sweep across the room, a pause on anyone who moved too fast, a sweep back. Bored, mostly. One of them by the bar had been looking at the canapés for ten minutes with real longing.

This one wasn’t looking at the guests.

He was looking at one guest. A tall fair man in a grey suit by the third chandelier, holding a glass of champagne he had not drunk, talking to a woman from one of the consulates. The guard’s eyes went to the fair man and stayed there. Not staring. Nothing so obvious. He looked at the door, at the floor, at the edge of the carpet, and every time, his eyes came back to the same place, the way a needle comes back to north.

Serafina got up off the pavilion floor and went to stand at the glass and watch him watching.

He was thirty, or a little less. Medium height, medium build, a dark suit that fitted well enough to be forgettable. A face that would have been handsome on anyone who wanted it to be, and on him was simply a face, the kind you looked at in a lift and could not describe to the police five minutes later. Short dark hair. A small notch at the end of his left eyebrow, like a pen that had skipped.

His earpiece tube was too clean. The others had gone faintly yellow with wear. His was new. And his shoes were wrong. The other guards wore thick rubber soles for standing all night. He wore black leather oxfords, polished, resoled with something thin and grippy, the shoes of a man who expected to run on marble.

At nine twenty-two a waiter dropped a tray of glasses by the orchestra.

Half the room jumped. The guards by the bar turned their whole bodies toward the noise. The man by the east door did not turn at all. He didn’t even look. But his right hand came up off his left wrist, a few centimetres, toward the inside of his jacket, where there was nothing, and stopped, and went back down.

Serafina felt it in her stomach, the way she felt a car beginning to step out at the rear a quarter of a second before it happened.

“Oh,” she said out loud, to the glass. “Oh, you’re not a guard at all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went over.

She should not have. She knew that even as she was crossing the terrace, the way she always knew, a beat too late, that the gap she was going for was too small. She went anyway. She went in her sister’s dress and her own boots, with oil on her thumb and the torch still in her hand, through two hundred people who did not see her because she was staff, and stopped beside him at the east service door.

“Good evening,” she said.

He looked at a point just above her left shoulder.

“Madam. This door is for staff.”

“I’m staff.” She showed him her pass. “Vehicle specialist. Lot nine. The red car. It’s a fake, by the way, or at least the part of it that says it isn’t. Don’t tell anyone, I haven’t told my client yet.”

“Please step away from the door, madam.”

His voice was low and level and completely without accent. It sounded like the voice on a train announcing the next station. She found that she wanted, very badly, to hear it say something it hadn’t planned to.

“You’ve been watching the Belgian for forty-one minutes,” Serafina said.

Nothing moved in his face. That was what told her. A real guard would have frowned, or laughed, or said what Belgian. He didn’t do any of those things. He went on looking at the space above her shoulder with an expression of polite, total absence, and the absence was so complete that it was its own kind of answer.

“I don’t know what you mean,” he said.

“The tall one. Third chandelier. Champagne he isn’t drinking. He’s been here since eight forty-five and you’ve looked at him every eleven seconds since. I timed it.” She tilted her head. “Everyone else in this room is looking at somebody. The consul’s wife is looking at the consul’s assistant. The shipping men are looking at the delegation. The guards are looking at the prawns. You’re the only one looking at the right person.”

Then, for the first time, he looked at her.

It was not a long look. Two seconds, perhaps. But it went all the way in, the way a torch goes into an engine bay, and she had the strange certain feeling that in those two seconds he had seen the scar on her hand and the oil on her thumb and the boots under the dress and the fact that her pulse was going faster than it should, and filed all of it somewhere, neatly, in order.

His eyes were very dark, and much less absent than his face.

“Madam,” he said. “You should go back to your car.”

“It isn’t my car. I’d never buy a car with a forged plate.”

“Then you should go back to someone else’s car.” A pause, so slight she nearly missed it. “And you should stop timing people.”

“Why? Is it rude?”

“It’s noticeable,” he said.

Behind her, the orchestra started something by Strauss. Over his shoulder, by the third chandelier, the tall fair man put down his untouched glass, kissed the consulate woman on both cheeks, and began to walk, without hurrying, toward the main doors.

The guard’s eyes went with him.

“Excuse me,” he said, and stepped past her through the service door, and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told Signor Bassi the truth at nine fifty-five, on the phone, standing in the service yard among the catering vans.

“The car’s real. The plate isn’t. Someone swapped it, probably in the eighties, probably to sell a crashed one as a clean one. It’ll still be worth a lot. Just not what they’re asking.”

“So I should not buy it.”

“You should buy it for forty per cent less, from the man who’ll still own it at eleven o’clock when nobody bids.”

Signor Bassi laughed, the old dry Milanese laugh she remembered from her grandmother’s parties. “You are wasted on engines, cara.”

“Everyone says that,” said Serafina, “and they’re all wrong.” She rang off, and looked up.

The staff car park was behind the vans. Most of the cars in it were ordinary: delivery vans, waiters’ scooters, the auction house’s white Mercedes. At the far end, under the one lamp that didn’t work, there was a grey estate car with its engine running and no lights on.

It was a big plain car, the kind taxi firms bought by the dozen. But it sat too low on its springs for an empty estate. Something heavy in the doors, she thought. Something heavy in the floor. Her eyes went to its number plate without her asking them to and took it, the way they always took number plates, and kept it.

The rear door opened. The guard from the east service door came out of the dark between the vans with the tall fair man walking beside him, close, as if they were old friends leaving a party early. The fair man’s face was very white. The guard had a hand on his elbow. He was not holding it hard. He didn’t have to.

The fair man got into the back. The guard closed the door, quietly, and walked round to the driver’s side, and stopped.

He looked across the car park at her.

Forty metres, under a broken lamp, at night. She was standing between two catering vans in a black dress with a phone in her hand. She did not move, and neither did he, and she understood, quite clearly and without any fear at all, which surprised her, that she was looking at something she was not supposed to have seen.

He inclined his head. Very slightly. As if she had held a door for him.

Then he got in, and the grey car rolled out of the gate with its lights off, and turned them on at the bottom of the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, on page nine of the business section, there was a paragraph about a Belgian logistics consultant called Lucien Marchal, who had attended the Autumn Reception on Battery Hill and left the city on an early flight for reasons his office declined to discuss.

Serafina read it twice, standing up in her garage, eating cold fried rice from the pan.

Then she wrote the number plate of a grey estate car on the whiteboard above the workbench, in red marker, very large, where she would have to look at it every day.

“What’s that?” said Big Wu, coming in under the shutter with the doughnuts.

“A guard,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove for three hours.

North, out of the city, on the old road and then the new one, the man in the back silent under a black cotton hood, his breathing loud and fast and then, after the first hour, slower, the way they always slowed, when they understood that nobody was going to hit them yet. At a petrol station at the edge of the province two men in a white van were waiting. Qin Haozhen handed over a man, a phone and a passport, and signed nothing, and got back into the grey car alone at ten past three in the morning, and sat with his hands on the wheel.

He did not think about the man in the hood. He had learned, a long time ago, at eighteen, not to think about them afterwards. There was a room in his head where they went, and he kept the door shut, and it was very quiet in there.

He thought about boots.

Black leather, with the heels worn down on the outside, the way a driver’s heels wore from working the pedals. Under a dress that didn’t fit her. Oil on her thumb. A scar on the back of her right hand, old and shiny. A voice that was much too loud for a staff entrance and did not care.

You’re the only one looking at the right person.

Ten years, he had been standing at doors. In capitals, in embassies, at receptions like this one, in fourteen countries. He was good at it. The best, Director Duan said, though she said it the way someone says it about a tool. He was good at it because he was nobody. People’s eyes slid off him like rain off a windscreen. In ten years nobody had ever walked across a room to tell him what he was.

He sat in the dark at the petrol station with the engine ticking as it cooled and found, with something like alarm, that he was trying to remember exactly what she had said about the red car.

He started the engine. He drove home.

He did not sleep, but that was not new.

chapters.title: Serafina Finds Out His Name
chapters.desc: It takes her three weeks, a leasing company that doesn’t exist, and one bribed caterer. Then he turns up under her shutter at two in the morning to ask her to stop.
chapters.epigraph: “A car tells you everything about the man who drives it. His just told me to mind my own business.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
The number plate on the whiteboard belonged to a leasing company called Silver Line Fleet Solutions, which had an office on the fourth floor of an office block by the old ferry piers that had been knocked down in 2019.

“It’s not real,” said Mouse.

She said it to Serafina, at the far end of the workbench, without looking up from her three screens. Mouse was twenty-two and had a ring through the side of her nose and had not said a word to Big Wu in four years. She would talk to Serafina and, since a few weeks in 2019, in single words, to Aurelia. That was the whole list.

“The plate’s real,” said Serafina. “I saw it.”

“The plate’s real. The company isn’t.” Mouse turned a screen round. “Registered to a man who died in 2011. Insurance paid by a bank in the capital. No fines. No parking tickets. Not one, in four years.” She looked up at last, small and pale and worried. “Nobody has no parking tickets, Sera.”

“He does,” said Serafina, and wrote it on the whiteboard under the plate. No parking tickets.

Big Wu, under Gilded with his legs sticking out, said, “You’re writing things about a man on the wall now. That’s how it starts. My cousin did that. Now she’s married to a dentist.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The security firm that had staffed the Autumn Reception was called Harbour Guard Services, and it had sixty men on its list for the night, and their supervisor, a tired man with a moustache, was very happy to tell Serafina so on the phone, because she said she was from the auction house and had found a set of keys.

“Fifty-nine,” he said, after a while. “I had fifty-nine. The sixtieth was from the delegation. Their own man. Came with their paperwork. East service door.” He paused. “I didn’t see his face, to be honest. Never thought about it. Why?”

“No reason,” said Serafina. “The keys are probably his.”

She put the phone down and wrote Delegation’s own man on the whiteboard and stood looking at it with her arms folded, tapping one fingernail against her front teeth, which was what she did when an engine made a noise she couldn’t place.

A train went over the bridge. Everything on the shelves shook. A spanner fell into a bucket.

“Leave it,” said Mr. Kwok, from the camping stove, where he was frying garlic in a wok big enough to bath a child in. He was seventy-one and had driven a taxi in this city for forty years, and he had opinions about most things, and they were usually right. “A man who comes with the delegation’s paperwork and leaves with a Belgian in his back seat. That’s not a man you write on a wall. That’s a man you forget you ever saw.”

“I can’t forget him.”

“Try harder,” said Mr. Kwok, and added chilli.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not try harder.

What she did, in the second week, was go and see Auntie Chu.

Auntie Chu owned Golden Spoon Catering, which had done the food at the Autumn Reception and at every government party in the city for twenty years, and she had three refrigerated vans, and all three of them had brakes that made a noise like a cat being sat on. Serafina had heard them in the service yard on Battery Hill. You did not forget a noise like that.

“Free,” said Serafina, in the yard behind the Golden Spoon kitchens in the old market district, with her head under the bonnet of the first van. “All three. Pads, discs, fluid. And I’ll do the rattle in the second one’s gearbox, which you haven’t noticed yet but you will on the flyover in about a month.”

Auntie Chu stood over her in a white apron with her arms folded. She was small and round and had been in charge of very large kitchens for a very long time.

“What do you want?”

“The sign-in sheet. From the Reception. Staff and security, at the service door. You keep everything. I saw the clipboard.”

“That sheet is government business.”

“It’s a clipboard,” said Serafina. “And I’ll throw in a crate of Chinotto. The real stuff. From Italy. My sister gets it.”

Auntie Chu looked at her for a while. She had the look of a woman who had been offered bribes by consuls and had turned down better ones.

“The bitter orange,” she said. “With the little bottles.”

“Twenty-four little bottles.”

Auntie Chu went inside, and came out four minutes later with a photocopy and a phone.

“He signed in at two minutes past seven,” she said. “East door. I remember him, because he was the only one who didn’t eat. Everyone eats my prawns. The consuls eat my prawns. The delegation ate my prawns with their hands. He stood at the door all night and ate nothing.” She sniffed. “A man who won’t eat a prawn is hiding something.”

On the photocopy, in a column of sixty careless signatures, there was a single line of small, square, exact handwriting. Each letter separate, like something typed.

Qin H. East service. 19:02.

Serafina looked at it until the letters stopped being letters.

“And this,” said Auntie Chu, holding out the phone. “My nephew. He takes photographs of the staff for the company page. He thinks it’s good for morale.” On the screen, there was a photograph of the service corridor at seven in the evening: four waiters with trays, grinning, and behind them, slightly out of focus, a man in a dark suit at a door, looking at the camera without any expression at all.

“He made my nephew delete it,” said Auntie Chu. “Very politely. My nephew deleted it. He didn’t know it went to the cloud.”

“Send it to me,” said Serafina.

“Do the gearbox first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the grey car on a Tuesday, at ten past one in the morning, on the fourth level of the multi-storey by the ferry pier.

She had been looking for eight nights. Not cleverly. She had simply driven Nonna, slowly, through every car park on the harbour side of the city between midnight and three, because it was the kind of car you kept at the harbour if you needed to leave by sea or by road in a hurry, and because she didn’t sleep much anyway. Nonna was a red 1992 Lancia Delta Integrale with three hundred thousand kilometres on her and a gearbox Serafina had rebuilt four times, and she was named after their grandmother because she was old, Italian, and had never once in her life done what she was told.

The grey estate was parked nose-out in a corner bay, under a camera that had been turned to face the wall.

Serafina did not touch it. She crouched by the rear wheel with her torch, the way you’d crouch by a sleeping dog, and looked through the spokes at the brakes.

Then she sat back on her heels and laughed out loud in the empty car park, because they were terrible.

She wrote the note on the back of a parts receipt, against Nonna’s roof.

Your rear pads are down to about three millimetres and the discs are blue. You’re carrying four hundred kilos in the doors and floor that this car was never built for, and on the first long hill with someone behind you, you’re going to cook them. Then you’ll have no brakes. Then you’ll have a problem. I can fix it.

She thought about how to sign it. Then she wrote Lot 9, and the address of the garage under the railway bridge, and folded it once, and put it under his wiper.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came two nights later.

She was alone. Big Wu had gone home to his mother’s at ten, and Mouse had left at midnight with her headphones on, and Mr. Kwok had gone at six, as he always did, because he said a man of his age needed to see the evening news to be sure he was still alive. Serafina was on her back under Gilded with a lamp, chasing a hydraulic leak she had been chasing for a week, with the radio on low and the shutter half up because the fumes got bad.

A train went over. When the noise had gone, the radio was off.

She hadn’t turned it off.

She lay very still on the creeper and looked at the underside of her car and listened. Nothing. The drip of the leak. The tick of the lamp. A dog somewhere down the street of shuttered workshops. And something else, something she could not have named, that was simply the feeling of not being alone any more.

“You’re very good at that,” she said, to the gearbox. “Standing in places. Is it a course?”

“Yes,” said a voice by the shutter.

She rolled out.

He was standing just inside the door, under the edge of the half-raised shutter, with the street light behind him. He wasn’t in a suit. Dark trousers, a black jumper, a plain dark jacket, all of it the kind of thing you’d see on a thousand men in this city and never look at twice. His hands were empty and in plain view, and she understood that this was on purpose too, a courtesy, the way you hold your hands out to a horse.

He was holding her note between two fingers.

“You left this on a car,” he said, “that you shouldn’t know about.”

“You drove off in it,” said Serafina, “with a man you shouldn’t have had.” She sat up on the creeper and wiped her hands on the rag at her waist. “Was he all right? The Belgian?”

He didn’t answer that. She hadn’t expected him to. He looked round the garage instead, slowly, once, in the way she’d seen him look round the ballroom: the shutter, the side door to the alley, the stairs up to the loft, the window over the workbench, the fire extinguisher, the whiteboard. His eyes stopped on the whiteboard. On the number plate in red marker, very large, and underneath it, No parking tickets, and Delegation’s own man, and Doesn’t eat prawns.

Something happened at the corner of his mouth. It was not a smile. It was a smile’s distant relation, from the countryside, who had never been to the city.

“Doesn’t eat prawns,” he said.

“Auntie Chu says a man who won’t eat a prawn is hiding something.”

“I’m allergic.”

“Are you?”

“No,” he said.

A train was coming. She could feel it in the concrete before she heard it. He felt it too, she saw: his weight changed, very slightly, toward the side door. Then it went over, and the whole garage shook, and the spanner fell into the bucket again, and he didn’t move at all.

“I came to ask you to stop,” he said, when it had passed. “Looking. Asking caterers. Driving round car parks in a red Lancia at one in the morning. You’ll be noticed.”

“By who?”

“By people who are less polite than me.”

“You’re not very polite,” said Serafina. “You turned my radio off.”

“It was a long song.” He folded the note and put it in his pocket, carefully, as though it were something he meant to keep. “Will you stop?”

“Tell me your name.”

He looked at her. The same look as at the east service door, all the way in, two seconds, three. She sat on the creeper with oil to her elbows and let him do it, and looked straight back, and did not blink, and this time she thought she saw something move behind it, far back, like a light in a house you’d thought was empty.

“Qin Haozhen,” he said.

She hadn’t thought he would. She had expected a lie, a good one, and she had been ready to be impressed by it.

“That’s your real name?”

“Yes.”

“Why tell me?”

“Because you’d have found it.” He said it simply, without flattery, as a fact about the weather. “And I’d rather you heard it from me than from someone who’d want to know why you were asking.”

Serafina got up off the creeper. She was tall, and in her boots she was nearly level with him. She held out her hand, then looked at it, black to the wrist, and wiped it on her overalls, which made no difference, and held it out again.

“Serafina Song,” she said.

“I know. I read your pass.”

“That was three weeks ago.”

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen, and shook her hand.

His was warm and dry and very clean, and he did not let go of hers quite as soon as he should have, and when he did, he looked at his palm, at the oil on it, as if he wasn’t sure what to do with it.

“Now,” said Serafina, “the brakes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He let her do them.

She would think about that afterwards, a lot. That a man who signed in at doors in handwriting like type, and drove cars registered to the dead, had stood in her garage at half past two in the morning and handed her his keys.

He brought the grey car round and backed it in under the shutter, perfectly, in one movement, with about a hand’s width to spare on either side, and she put it on the lift and took the wheels off and showed him. The rear discs, blue and scored. The pads, nearly metal. The calipers, standard, built for a family estate, being asked to stop a small tank.

“You need bigger discs. Vented, front and back. Four-pot calipers. Pads that like heat. A fluid that doesn’t boil.” She ran her thumb along the scoring. “Whoever looks after this for you is either very lazy or wants you to crash.”

“The motor pool,” he said.

“Then the motor pool wants you to crash.”

“Possibly,” said Qin Haozhen, and she laughed, and then looked at him, because he hadn’t been joking, and he looked back at her with no expression at all, and she laughed again, harder, because it was the most frightening thing anyone had ever said to her in her own garage and she found she didn’t care.

She did the rears that night, with what she had. He stood by the workbench and watched. Not her face. Her hands. The whole time. When she dropped a pin he had picked it up before it stopped rolling. When she reached without looking for the torque wrench it was in her hand.

“You’ve done this before,” she said.

“No.”

“Then how did you know what I wanted?”

“You looked at it,” he said, “four minutes ago. Before you started the second side. You always look at the next thing before you need it.”

She stopped with the wrench on the bolt and turned round.

He was leaning on her workbench under her whiteboard, in his forgettable jacket, with oil on one palm, looking at her as though she were the only thing in the room worth the trouble of watching. She’d been looked at a lot in her life. By her mother, mostly, measuring. By men at street races who wanted her car or her number. By the photographers at the circuit. Nobody had ever looked at her like that, as though they had been taking notes for weeks and found the notes inadequate.

“Stop it,” she said.

“Stop what?”

“Noticing things about me. It’s my job to notice things about you.”

“Then we have a problem,” said Qin Haozhen, and that was the closest thing to a smile she would get out of him for nearly a month.

✦ ✦ ✦

He left at ten past four. She heard the grey car go down the street of shuttered workshops, and at the corner, where it always caught, she heard him brake, and the new pads bit clean and quiet, the way they should.

In the morning, Big Wu came in under the shutter with the doughnuts and stopped, and looked at the floor by the lift, and crouched, and touched a small dark patch on the concrete with one enormous finger.

“Brake dust,” he said. “Not ours.” He looked up at her. “You did a job last night.”

“I did a job.”

“For who?”

Serafina took a doughnut. She went to the whiteboard, and picked up the red marker, and above the number plate, in her own large, untidy capitals, she wrote a name.

Mr. Kwok came in at nine with the shopping and stood in front of it for a while, holding a bag of pak choi.

“Does he eat,” he said finally, “or is he still hiding something?”

“Both,” said Serafina.

And from the far end of the workbench, without looking up from her screens, Mouse said, very quietly, to nobody but Serafina, “He made the camera in the car park face the wall, you know. Before you got there. He knew you were coming.”

chapters.title: A Race, Not a Date
chapters.desc: Granny Shum’s Saturday meet, four kilometres of factory road, and a grey estate car everyone laughs at. He accepts. He loses on purpose. She knows.
chapters.epigraph: “A circuit is a circuit and a road is a road, and I’m not giving up the road for anybody.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
He came back for the front brakes on the Thursday, and again on the Friday, because the calipers she had ordered from Stuttgart came in a box with the wrong brackets and she spent half the night swearing at them in Italian.

“What does that one mean?” he asked, from the workbench.

“It means the man who packed this box should be buried in it.” She threw the bracket into the bin. “With his mother.”

“And the one before?”

“That one you don’t want to know.”

He didn’t say anything. But he wrote something down, in a small black notebook he kept in his inside pocket, in his square, separate letters, and she had the feeling that she was being added to a file, and found she didn’t mind.

By Friday night he had stopped standing by the door. He stood by the workbench now, or sat on the stool by the kettle, or once, for twenty minutes, held the lamp for her under the car without being asked, angled exactly where she needed it, and when his arm must have been aching he didn’t move it at all. He drank hot water from her second mug, the plain one. He would not take coffee. He would not take Mr. Kwok’s leftover noodles, which were in the fridge in a plastic box with a note on the lid that said ANYONE BUT BIG WU. He did not talk about himself, not once, not a word, and every time she came near a question he moved out of its way so smoothly that she only noticed afterwards, the way you only notice a car’s suspension when it’s bad.

At three in the morning she tightened the last bolt and dropped the car off the lift and slapped the bonnet.

“Done,” she said. “Now you owe me.”

“How much?”

“Not money.” She wiped her hands. “A race.”

He looked at her.

“Not a date,” said Serafina. “I don’t do dates. Dates are two people sitting still, being polite at each other over soup. A race. Tomorrow night. Three o’clock. You in this, me in Nonna. Factory roads, out past the paint works.” She grinned. “Unless you’re scared.”

“Street racing,” said Qin Haozhen, “carries three years now.”

“I know. They changed the law in the spring of 2019. My mother sent me a copy.” She leaned on the bonnet of his grey car. “I have a national licence and a team and my sister’s name on my race car and a sponsor in every second shop on Harbour Road, and I still go to Granny Shum’s on a Saturday, because a circuit is a circuit and a road is a road and I’m not giving up the road for anybody. Are you coming or not?”

He was quiet. She watched him think. He did it without moving his face at all, which she had begun to find very interesting, the way she found a sealed gearbox interesting.

“If I come,” he said, “there’ll be people there with phones.”

“There are always people with phones.”

“I don’t photograph well.”

“You don’t photograph at all,” said Serafina. “Auntie Chu’s nephew had to dig you out of the cloud.” She held out her hand, palm up, for the keys to his own car, which she still had in her pocket. “Three o’clock. Bring the taxi.”

He put his hand into hers. Not the keys. His hand, flat on her palm, for a second, warm, and she nearly dropped it from surprise. Then he took his keys out of her other hand, which she hadn’t noticed him reaching for, and stepped back.

“Three o’clock,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum ran the Saturday meet from a folding chair at the junction by the paint works, with a thermos of chrysanthemum tea and a blanket over her knees and a police scanner on a string round her neck like a crucifix.

She was eighty, or said she was. Her husband had raced on these roads in the seventies, in a Datsun with no doors, and died of something ordinary in his bed in 2005, and she had kept the Saturdays going out of what she called respect and everyone else called spite. She had spotters at the four junctions with walkie-talkies. She had a granddaughter who dropped the scarf. She had a rule, painted on a piece of hardboard tied to the lamp post beside her chair: NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING. Serafina had been coming since she was nineteen, the week after she left the house on the Peak. On her first night, Granny Shum had looked at her for a long time and said, “Rich girl. You’ll crash by Christmas,” and on Christmas Eve, when Serafina had won four races in a row in a Fiat she had built from two dead ones, Granny Shum had given her a clementine and said nothing else ever again about rich girls.

“Who’s the taxi?” said Granny Shum, at a quarter to three.

The grey estate car had come down the road from the gas works with its lights off and parked at the end of the line, behind a purple Nissan with a wing the size of a dining table and a boy in a hoodie standing on its roof filming himself. Forty people were standing about in the floodlight from the paint works. Every one of them turned to look at the grey car, and somebody laughed, and then a lot of people laughed.

“A friend,” said Serafina.

“He drives a taxi?”

“He drives something that looks like a taxi.”

Granny Shum turned her head and looked at the man getting out of it. He had a dark jacket on and a black cap pulled low, and he stood beside his car with his hands in his pockets and his head down, so that the boy on the Nissan, panning his phone along the line, got a cap and a shoulder and nothing at all.

Granny Shum drank her tea. “He’s not a friend. Friends don’t stand like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like they know where the police are going to come from,” said Granny Shum, and turned up her scanner.

✦ ✦ ✦

The route was four kilometres and twenty metres, and Serafina could have driven it in her sleep and once, in 2018, very nearly had. Off the line at the paint works. The long straight down past the container yard, six hundred metres, where the cars that had big engines and nothing else always got ahead. Left at the fish-ball factory. The S-bends between the warehouses, tight and blind, where the cars that had big engines and nothing else always went into the wall. The long right-hander round the gas works, under the two old gasholders, with a lamp post at every fifty metres, where you braked at the third lamp post if you were sensible and the fourth if you were Serafina. Then back up the service road to the line.

“One run,” said Granny Shum’s granddaughter, a bored girl of sixteen with purple nails, standing between the two cars with the white scarf. “No contact. If the scanner goes, you go home. You know the rules.”

“He doesn’t,” said Serafina, through Nonna’s open window.

The granddaughter looked at the grey car. In the driver’s seat, he had taken off his cap. He was sitting with both hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, which nobody did, and his seat was much further forward than a man of his height should have needed, and he was looking straight ahead through the windscreen as though there were nobody around him at all.

“No contact,” the granddaughter said to him.

“No contact,” said Qin Haozhen.

The scarf went up.

Serafina put Nonna in first and brought the revs up to five thousand and held them, and felt the car shake under her like a dog on a lead, and looked once to her left. Through two windows and a metre of cold night air, he looked back.

The scarf came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nonna went off the line like something fired.

All four wheels, no slip, the way she’d built her; the turbo coming in at the top of second with that long rising whistle that always made the back of Serafina’s neck go hot. She was half a car ahead by the end of the paint works and a whole car ahead by the container yard, and she looked in the mirror expecting to see the grey estate dropping back, the way every heavy car dropped back on the straight.

It wasn’t dropping back.

It was there. A length behind her, exactly a length, sitting in her mirror like it had been painted on, and it stayed there all the way down the straight, through third and fourth, at a speed that a family estate with four hundred kilos in its doors had no business reaching.

“What,” said Serafina, out loud, to the mirror, “is in that thing?”

Left at the fish-ball factory. She braked late and turned in hard and felt Nonna’s rear go light and caught it, and came out of the corner sideways on purpose with her foot flat, and in the mirror, in the orange light, the grey car took the same corner as if it were on rails. No slide. No drama. Just turned, cleanly, the weight of it set down exactly where it needed to be, and came out still a length behind her.

The S-bends. Left, right, left, the warehouse walls a hand’s width from her mirrors, the cones of her headlights bouncing off corrugated iron. She went through them as fast as she had ever gone through them, faster than in 2018, faster than the night she won four in a row in the Fiat, and when she came out onto the gas works straight he was still there. Closer, now. Half a length. She could see his face through her rear window in the glow of his dashboard. He looked like a man filling in a tax return.

She started laughing. She couldn’t help it. She laughed all the way down to the gas works with her foot flat to the floor and her hands loose on the wheel and the gasholders coming up black against the orange sky, because nobody had ever done this to her, nobody had ever simply sat on her bumper through the S-bends as if it were nothing, and it was the most fun she’d had in a car in a year.

The lamp posts came. First. Second.

And in her mirror, at the second lamp post, a full lamp post before anybody sensible would brake, the grey car’s brake lights came on.

Red. Clean. Perfectly timed. Too early by fifty metres.

She went to the fourth lamp post, the way she always did, and braked, and turned in, and went round the gas works with the back of the car hanging out and the tyres howling, and by the time she came onto the service road he was three lengths back, and he stayed there, politely, all the way up to the line.

Four tenths of a second. That was what Granny Shum’s granddaughter’s stopwatch said. Four tenths.

The crowd went mad. People banged on Nonna’s roof. The boy on the Nissan was shouting something about the taxi. Somebody gave Serafina a can of beer, and she took it and didn’t drink it and got out of the car and walked straight down the line, through all of them, to the grey estate, where he was standing by the driver’s door with his cap back on.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You lifted at the gas works,” she said.

“I didn’t.”

“Your brake lights came on at the second lamp post.” She stood in front of him and jabbed a finger at his chest, not quite touching. “Nobody brakes at the second lamp post. Mr. Kwok brakes at the third, and he’s seventy-one and drives a transporter. You were on my bumper through the S-bends in a car that weighs as much as a bus, and you braked at the second lamp post.”

He looked at her from under the cap. In the floodlight from the paint works his face was all shadow and planes, and completely calm.

“You were happy,” he said.

That stopped her.

“What?”

“Through the S-bends. You were laughing. I could see you in your mirror.” He said it as plainly as he’d said the motor pool, as a fact. “If I’d passed you at the gas works, you’d have stopped.”

She stared at him.

All round them people were shouting and laughing and revving engines and the boy on the Nissan was filming everything and Granny Shum’s scanner was crackling with somebody’s lost dog in the next district, and Serafina stood in front of a man in a black cap who had just told her that he had lost a race on purpose so that she would go on laughing, and she couldn’t think of a single thing to say, in any of her three languages.

“That,” she said finally, “is the most insulting thing a man has ever done to me.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not.”

“No,” he agreed.

“There were people filming,” she said slowly. “If you’d won, they’d have filmed the man who beat Serafina Song in a taxi. That’s it, isn’t it. You can’t be filmed winning.”

“That too,” said Qin Haozhen.

She looked at him for a moment longer. Then she laughed again, she couldn’t help it, short and incredulous, and put her hands on her hips.

“Rematch,” she said.

“Serafina—”

“Somewhere with nobody filming. Somewhere you can’t lose on purpose without me seeing every tenth of it on a screen. And you drive like yourself. Not like a man in a taxi. Like whatever it is you actually are.” She lifted her chin. “Or you never come in my garage again.”

He was quiet.

“And if I do drive like myself,” he said, “and you don’t like it?”

“Then at least I’ll know what you’re like.”

At the junction behind them, Granny Shum’s scanner said something sharp and official, and Granny Shum stood up out of her folding chair, and blew a whistle she kept for the purpose, and forty people and eleven cars began to vanish into the industrial district the way water goes into sand.

He opened his car door.

“Saturday,” he said. “The circuit in the north has a track day on the tenth. I’ll book it.”

“How do you know it has a track day?”

“I checked,” said Qin Haozhen, “on Thursday,” and got in, and the grey car slid away down the road toward the gas works with its lights off, and was gone before the first blue light came round the corner by the paint factory.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the bonnet of Nonna, under her windscreen wiper, there was a folded piece of paper.

It was her own note. The parts receipt from the car park by the ferry pier: Your rear pads are down to about three millimetres. He’d kept it. He had kept it in his pocket for ten days and brought it to a street race and put it back under her wiper while she was walking down the line to shout at him.

Under her signature, in small, square, separate letters, he had written a phone number.

And under that, one more line.

You brake at the fourth lamp post because you like the noise the tyres make. It’s a beautiful noise. It costs you a tenth.

chapters.title: Rematch
chapters.desc: A track day at the circuit in the north, one red Lancia, two drivers and Mouse with a stopwatch. This time he drives like himself. She has never been happier.
chapters.epigraph: “He drove like someone signing his name. No flourishes. Every letter exactly where it belonged.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
The circuit in the north of the province was four point six kilometres of grey tarmac laid across a valley that used to grow rice, with a grandstand at one end that held eleven thousand people and, on the second Saturday of December, held a man selling noodles and nobody else.

Track days were not races. Serafina explained this to him in the paddock at eight in the morning, with her breath smoking in the cold, while Big Wu unloaded Nonna from the transporter and Mr. Kwok set up the camping stove under the awning and Mouse sat on an upturned crate with a laptop and a cable plugged into a transponder the size of a matchbox.

“Nobody races. It’s against the rules. You go out, you drive, you come in. You only overtake on the straights, and only if the person in front waves you by.” She pulled her helmet bag out of the van. “Forty cars. Mostly dentists in Porsches. Very slow, very rich, very angry when you go past them.”

“And us?”

“We’re not racing either,” said Serafina. “We’re timing.”

She had thought about it all week. Two cars wouldn’t do. Two cars meant his car or hers, armour or turbo, and an argument at the end about whose car had done the work. One car. The same car. Five flying laps each, timed to the hundredth by a girl who didn’t speak to anyone and couldn’t be bribed. The best lap wins.

“Nonna,” she said, and patted the red roof. “You drive mine. I drive mine. Mouse times us. Then we both know.”

He looked at the Lancia for a while. It was thirty years old and the paint on the roof was going pink at the edges. The rear arches were wider than the factory had ever made them, because Serafina had made them wider. There was a dent in the driver’s door from the night in 2020 she’d been pushed into a lamp post by a boy in a Subaru, and she had never fixed it, because the boy had paid for it in other ways.

“She’s very old,” he said.

“So’s the Pope,” said Serafina. “Get in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went first.

She did it partly to show him the circuit and partly, if she was honest, to show off. She did her out lap gently, warming the tyres, talking him through it over the intercom she had wired into both helmets: here’s the first corner, it’s a long right, you brake at the hundred board, you’ll think it’s too early and it isn’t. Here are the esses, don’t use the kerbs on the second one, they’ll throw you. Here’s the long back straight, nine hundred metres, you’ll see two hundred on the clock if you’re brave. And this, at the end of it, under the advertising bridge, is the Needle.

“The Needle?”

“The hairpin. Hundred and eighty degrees, first gear in a race car, second in this. It’s called the Needle because you have to thread it.” She was coming down the back straight as she said it, at a hundred and ninety, and the hairpin was rushing up at them, a tight grey loop under a bridge with a gravel trap behind it and a wall of tyres behind the gravel. “Everybody’s first time, they brake too late and go straight on into the gravel. Second time they brake too early and look stupid. Third time—”

She braked. Hard, on the marker, Nonna’s nose diving, the tyres just at the edge of their grip, and she came down two gears with her heel on the throttle to match the revs, and turned in, and the car rotated round its own centre like a dancer on one foot, and they came out the other side with the back of it wagging and her laughing.

“Third time you thread it,” she said.

He didn’t say anything over the intercom. She glanced across. He was sitting very still in the passenger seat with his hands loose on his knees, watching the track. Not holding on. Every passenger she had ever had held on.

She did her five laps. Her best was a 1:58.41, which Mouse read out over the radio in a flat whisper, and which was good, very good for a thirty-year-old Lancia on road tyres. She came into the pit lane with her heart going and stopped by the awning and pulled off her helmet, and her hair was standing up in spikes, and she turned to him.

“Well?”

“You lift a fraction at the top of the esses,” he said. “On the second lap and the fourth. Not on the third. I think it’s when the sun gets in your eyes.”

She stared at him.

“Out,” said Serafina. “Your turn.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took off his watch first.

She saw him do it. He undid the steel strap and took it off and laid it face down on the camping table under the awning, beside Mr. Kwok’s wok, very precisely, the way you’d put something down that you meant to come back for. Then he put on her spare helmet, and climbed into the driver’s seat, and moved it forward two notches, and adjusted both mirrors, and sat for ten seconds with his hands on the wheel at a quarter to three and his eyes closed.

“Is he praying?” said Big Wu.

“He’s reading,” said Mouse. She didn’t say it to Big Wu. She said it to the laptop. But Big Wu heard it, and looked at her, and closed his mouth.

Serafina got in the passenger seat and did up the harness and plugged in the intercom.

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

“You don’t want to know anything else? The braking points? The kerbs?”

“You told me on your laps,” said Qin Haozhen, and put the car in first.

✦ ✦ ✦

She would try, afterwards, to describe it to Aurelia, and fail.

It wasn’t that he was fast, though he was. It wasn’t the sound of it, though Nonna had never in her life made that sound: the engine held right at the top of its range, never over, never under, the turbo singing one long note from one end of the straight to the other. It was that there was nothing extra. Every driver she had ever sat beside, herself included, put something into a car that the car didn’t need. A twitch of the wheel. A stab at the brakes. A little flourish on the way out of a corner to feel the back go. He put in nothing. He turned the wheel exactly as far as it needed to turn. He braked exactly as hard as the tyres could take and not a gram harder, and let the brakes off in one long smooth line as the car turned in, so that the weight moved across it like water tipped carefully from one cup into another.

On the second lap he was quicker than her through the esses.

On the third lap he went down the back straight at two hundred and three kilometres an hour, which was faster than she had ever made Nonna go, and she said, “Madonna,” out loud into her helmet, and he didn’t reply. He braked for the Needle at the same marker she had used, to the metre, and came down the gears, and the car went round the hairpin so neatly that she didn’t feel it rotate at all. It was simply pointing one way, and then it was pointing the other.

She looked at him across the cockpit.

Through the visor she could see his eyes, and they were not absent any more. They were wide awake. They were more alive than she had ever seen anything be. And at the corner of his mouth, under the chin strap, there was the smile’s distant relation from the countryside, only it had come to the city now, and found a flat, and was thinking of staying.

He was enjoying himself.

She understood all at once that he might not have done that in a long time, and something went through her that was not to do with speed at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Same,” said Mouse.

She said it to Serafina, in the paddock, when they had come in and pulled off their helmets, and she turned the laptop round to show her. Two columns. Five laps each. At the bottom of each, in red, a best lap.

1:58.41.

1:58.41.

“To the hundredth,” said Mouse. “Same.”

Serafina looked at the screen. Then at him, standing by the car with her spare helmet under his arm and his hair flattened on one side and his face back to its usual calm, except that it wasn’t quite, it had a colour in it she hadn’t seen.

“You did that on purpose,” she said.

“No.”

“You matched my time to the hundredth on purpose. So nobody won.”

“I couldn’t do that if I wanted to,” said Qin Haozhen. “Nobody could. Ask Mouse.”

Serafina looked at Mouse. Mouse looked at the laptop and shook her head, once, very slightly, which from Mouse was a speech.

Serafina started laughing.

She laughed so hard she had to sit down on the transporter ramp. Big Wu looked at her as if she had gone mad. Mr. Kwok said, from the wok, that it was the cold, it went to people’s heads, he had seen it in 1983 at the Lunar New Year market. And Qin Haozhen stood in the paddock and watched her laugh, and she saw him do it, and she thought that if a man could look at someone the way he was looking at her and still say he was only a guard, then he was the worst liar in the province.

“Again,” she said, when she could breathe.

“Again?”

“We’ve got the track till four. Five more each. Then five more. Then we do it in the dark if they’ll let us.” She stood up. “I’m not going home with a draw.”

He picked up his watch from the camping table. He looked at it. He didn’t put it back on.

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove until the light went.

Lap after lap, taking turns, the cold December sun going across the valley and down behind the grandstand, the dentists in their Porsches going home one by one until it was just them and the noodle man and a bored marshal at the Needle in an orange coat. They got faster. Both of them. He taught her the thing at the top of the esses, which was the sun, and she taught him to use a little more kerb at the long right, and by three o’clock they were trading tenths, then hundredths, and the laptop was full of red numbers and Mouse had started, very quietly, to giggle.

At half past three he beat her by six hundredths.

At a quarter to four she beat him by two.

At four o’clock the marshal waved the chequered flag at them from his post with an expression of great weariness, and they came into the pit lane for the last time with the brakes glowing and the engine ticking and the tyres giving off a smell like burnt sugar, and Big Wu crouched by the front left with the probe and said, “Ninety-four,” and then, “I’m going to get the van,” and walked away very fast, and took Mr. Kwok with him, and Mouse too, by the sleeve, which Mouse allowed.

The paddock was empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got out of the car first.

She stood in the cold blue light under the awning with her helmet in her hands and her race suit unzipped to the waist, the sleeves tied round her middle, in a black vest with steam coming off her shoulders, and she was so happy she didn’t know what to do with her hands.

He got out the other side. He came round the bonnet, slowly. He was holding her spare helmet. His hair was flat on one side and sticking up on the other and his face was flushed and his eyes were very dark, and the engine was ticking between them as it cooled, tick, tick, like a clock somebody had wound too far.

“Well,” said Serafina. “Now I know what you’re like.”

“And?”

She put her helmet down on Nonna’s roof. Then she took his out of his hands and put that down too, beside hers.

“You’re the best driver I’ve ever sat next to,” she said. “And you haven’t been happy in about ten years, have you.”

He didn’t answer.

He didn’t have to. It was in his face, for a second, before he put it away. Something old and very tired and surprised, as if she’d opened a door in a house he’d been living in for years and shown him a room he didn’t know was there.

She kissed him.

She did it the way she took corners, which was later than was sensible and harder than she needed to. She took a handful of his jacket and pulled, and he came, and she kissed him in the empty paddock with the engine ticking and her helmet on the roof and the noodle man packing up his cart forty metres away, and for one second he didn’t move at all, and she thought, oh no, I’ve got it wrong.

Then his hands came up.

One at her jaw, warm, his thumb under her ear. The other at the small of her back, where her race suit was tied round her waist, flat and spread and holding her there. And he kissed her back like a man who had read about it in a manual and decided, if he was going to do it at all, to do it properly. Slow. Very thorough. Taking his time over it, as though there were a right way and he meant to find it, and every time she thought he’d found it he went on looking. Her back met the side of the car. The metal was warm from the engine. She made a noise she would deny to her grave, and he heard it, and she felt him smile against her mouth, a real one this time, and that was so much worse than anything else that her knees went.

“You,” she said, when he let her breathe, “are a menace.”

“Is that one of the Italian words?”

“No. That one’s in English.” She was holding on to his jacket with both hands. She didn’t remember deciding to. “You took your watch off.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He looked down at her. His thumb moved once along her jaw, very lightly, as if he were checking that it was there.

“I didn’t want to know what time it was,” said Qin Haozhen.

Behind them, the transporter came round the end of the paddock with its headlights on and Big Wu leaning on the horn, two long blasts and a short one, for no reason at all except that he could, and Mr. Kwok in the passenger seat with his hands over his eyes, and Mouse in the back with her face in her sleeve, shoulders shaking, not making a sound.

chapters.title: 3 A.M., Passenger Seat
chapters.desc: He sleeps about four hours a night, in any bed, in any country. Then one night after Granny Shum’s, in the passenger seat of a thirty-year-old Lancia, he sleeps for two hours and eleven minutes.
chapters.epigraph: “In ten years I’ve never sat in a car I wasn’t driving or guarding.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
He came at strange hours after the track day.

Never in daylight. Never when Big Wu or Mouse or Mr. Kwok were there, at first, although that changed. He came at one in the morning, or half past four, or once at a quarter to six with the sky going grey over the railway bridge, and he stood under the half-raised shutter until she noticed him, and she always noticed him, because the garage felt different when he was in it, the way a room feels different when someone has opened a window.

Sometimes he stayed ten minutes. Sometimes three hours. He held lamps. He passed her spanners before she asked for them. He drank hot water from the plain mug, which was his now; she had written HIS on it in marker and he had looked at it for a while and then turned it round so the writing faced the wall. And he kissed her, against workbenches and under the lift and once, memorably, on the bonnet of Gilded, until Serafina was so dizzy she put a socket wrench in the fridge.

He did not sleep. She noticed that in the second week.

He came in at two with his eyes perfectly clear and left at five with them perfectly clear, and the next night he came in at one and they were the same, and she began to count the hours, the way she counted everything, and the hours didn’t add up.

“When do you sleep?” she asked him, on the Thursday before Christmas.

He was sitting on the stool by the kettle with a carburettor from a 1971 Alfa in his lap, because she’d given it to him to clean, and he was cleaning it the way he did everything, slowly and completely, as if he’d been asked to defuse it.

“I sleep.”

“How much?”

He thought about it. She could see him deciding whether to answer, and then deciding that he would, and that was new, and she held very still so as not to frighten it off.

“Four hours,” he said. “Sometimes three.”

“A night?”

“A night.”

“For how long?”

“Since I was eighteen.”

She put down her spanner.

“That’s ten years,” said Serafina. “Of four hours.”

“You get used to it.”

“No, you don’t. You get used to being tired. That’s different. I’ve seen men drive tired. They brake late and think they braked on time.” She looked at him across the garage. “You don’t brake late. You never brake late. So you’re the kind of tired where you’ve forgotten what the other thing feels like.”

He didn’t say anything. He went on cleaning the carburettor.

But a little later, when she wasn’t looking, he said, “In hotels I sleep in the chair by the door. In my flat I sleep on top of the covers, in my clothes. I don’t sleep on planes. I don’t sleep in cars. In ten years I’ve never sat in a car I wasn’t driving or guarding.” He turned a jet over in his fingers. “It isn’t a choice. It’s just how it is.”

“Everything’s a choice,” said Serafina.

“Not that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she took him to Granny Shum’s in Nonna, in the passenger seat.

He didn’t want to go. He said so, very reasonably, in the garage at two o’clock: that there would be phones, that it would be better if he waited somewhere, that he could watch from the gas works. She said he could watch from her passenger seat or not at all, and got in, and started the engine, and waited, and after a while he got in beside her and did up his belt and put his cap on and pulled it down, and she pulled out under the railway bridge with a grin she didn’t bother to hide.

She raced three times that night. A boy in a white Honda who cried afterwards, which was against the rules, and Granny Shum made him stand by the lamp post until he stopped. A man in a Mitsubishi she had beaten nine times and who kept coming back, out of what he called loyalty. And a woman in an old BMW who was very good, actually good, who got past her in the S-bends and held her off round the gas works and lost by half a car at the line only because Serafina went to the fifth lamp post, which nobody had ever done, and nearly took the car into the gasholder fence.

“Fifth,” said Granny Shum, from her chair, at the end. She was holding out a clementine. “That was stupid.”

“It worked.”

“Stupid things work until they don’t.” Granny Shum looked past her, through Nonna’s open window, at the passenger seat. “And your taxi friend went to sleep.”

Serafina turned round.

He was asleep.

He was sitting exactly as he had been sitting all night, upright, belt on, cap down, hands loose in his lap, and somewhere between the fifth lamp post and the finish line his head had tipped sideways onto the window and stayed there. His mouth was a little open. His face, under the brim of the cap, had gone completely smooth. Not calm, the way it was calm in the garage; that was a calm he made. This was the other thing. The thing he’d forgotten.

“He’s been asleep since the gas works,” said Granny Shum. “I watched him go. Like a light. Through a fifth-lamp-post braking zone. I’ve seen dead men less relaxed.” She drank her tea. “Go on. Before the police come and wake him up.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t take him home.

She didn’t know where home was, for one thing. For another, she was afraid that if she stopped the car he’d wake.

So she drove.

She drove Nonna down out of the industrial district at three in the morning, gently, the way Mr. Kwok drove, with no hard braking and no sudden turns, the turbo never coming on, the engine burbling in third. Along the harbour road past the container terminals, where the cranes stood up over the water like enormous patient animals. Over the old bridge. Through the tunnel under the harbour and out the other side and round the long empty loop of the coast road, the sea black on one side and the city on the other, every window lit, every tower, and the ferries going back and forth across the dark water like slow lamps. Round again. Over the bridge. Through the tunnel. She drove the way you’d rock something.

He didn’t wake.

At one point, on the coast road, his head slid off the window and onto her shoulder.

She kept both hands on the wheel. She drove for twenty minutes with the weight of his head on her shoulder and his breath, slow and even, warm through her jacket, and the cap knocked crooked, and she did not move her shoulder by a millimetre, not on the corners, not at the lights, and she thought that this was harder than the fifth lamp post. Much harder. She thought that if she could do this she could do anything.

At ten past five he woke up.

He did it the way she imagined soldiers woke, all at once, his whole body going from nothing to everything in the space of a breath. His head came up off her shoulder. His hand went to the door, and then to his jacket, and then stopped, and she saw him take it in: the car, the coast road, the grey light coming up over the sea, her.

“I slept,” he said.

He said it the way a man might say I’ve been shot. Very carefully, as though he wasn’t yet sure how bad it was.

“Two hours and eleven minutes,” said Serafina. “I timed it.”

“I don’t sleep in cars.”

“You do in mine.”

He sat back. He looked out of the window at the sea for a long time. He took his cap off and turned it round in his hands. And then he did something she would remember all her life: he put his head back against the headrest and closed his eyes again, on purpose, and let out a breath that seemed to come from somewhere very deep and very old, as if he’d been holding it in since he was eighteen.

“Why,” he said, without opening his eyes, “does it work in this car?”

Serafina drove for a while before she answered.

“Because you know how I drive,” she said. “You’ve sat behind me through the S-bends. You’ve sat beside me through the Needle. You know I won’t crash. Not with you in it.” She swallowed. “You trust how I drive. That’s all it is.”

He opened his eyes and turned his head and looked at her.

“That isn’t all it is,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, she picked him up.

It became a thing they did, without either of them deciding it. Two or three nights a week, at three in the morning, a text, or no text: she would simply be outside, in Nonna, at the corner of whatever street he told her, and he would get in, and she would drive. Sometimes they talked. Mostly they didn’t. Sometimes she went to Granny Shum’s and raced and he slept through it, which became a joke in the industrial district; the boy in the white Honda said he’d lost to a woman whose own passenger couldn’t stay awake for her. Mostly she just drove the long loop. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. He slept with his head on the window, or on her shoulder, and she drove until the sky went grey.

She did his car as well. She didn’t ask. The next time he left the grey estate in her garage she rebuilt the front suspension, because she had felt it wallow on the track day, and replaced the shocks, and corner-weighted it on her scales so that it sat level at last, and when he drove it away she heard him take the first corner at the end of the street and stop, and reverse back, and get out and stand by the shutter.

“What did you do?”

“It was falling over. It doesn’t fall over now.”

He looked at her for a while.

“Thank you,” he said, and she realised, from the way he said it, that nobody had ever done anything for his car that wasn’t on a form.

✦ ✦ ✦

On New Year’s Eve, he didn’t sleep.

She had driven him out to the lay-by on the coast road above the harbour, where people went to watch the fireworks, but late, so that by the time they got there every space was taken and she had to park Nonna half on the grass with two wheels in a ditch, which he pointed out, and she ignored. They sat on the bonnet in their coats. The engine was warm under them. Below them, the whole harbour was lit, the towers and the ferries and the long bridge, and the water black and glittering, and at midnight it all went up at once: gold and red and white, great slow chrysanthemums of fire opening over the water, and the sound arriving a second late, rolling up the hill, like something enormous clearing its throat.

She watched them. He watched her.

She could feel him doing it. She turned her head.

“You’re supposed to look at the fireworks.”

“I’ve seen fireworks,” said Qin Haozhen. “In nine countries. From roofs, mostly. I was usually watching someone else.” The gold came down over the water and lit his face. “This is the first time I’ve watched the person I wanted to.”

She didn’t have an answer to that. So she kissed him instead, on the bonnet of a car with two wheels in a ditch, with the sky going off like a war over the harbour, and he pulled her into his lap without seeming to move at all, and she sat there with her knees either side of him and her hands in his hair and his coat open round both of them, kissing him in the noise and the light until she couldn’t tell which was the fireworks and which was her pulse. He kissed her neck, under her jaw, slow, the place where her pulse was, and stayed there, as though he were counting it. She laughed, breathless, into his hair.

“What,” she said, much later, when the last of the smoke was drifting out over the water and the cars on the coast road had started to leave, “do you want? For next year?”

He was quiet.

“I don’t know,” he said. “I don’t think I know how.”

“How to what?”

“Want things.” He said it simply, without self-pity, the way he said everything. “They tell you where to stand. They tell you what to eat, when. Where to sleep, which chair. For ten years I’ve wanted the job done and the car to start. I don’t think I’ve wanted anything else since I was a boy.”

She sat back in his lap and looked at him.

“Then start small,” said Serafina. “Want a sandwich.”

The smile came, the real one. She had seen it twice now. She thought she would build a whole garage to keep it in.

“A sandwich,” he said.

“A good one. With the egg. From the place under the flyover. That’s next year. Then when you’ve got the hang of it, you can want something bigger.”

He looked at her, in the dark, in the smell of gunpowder drifting up from the harbour.

“I want this,” he said.

He said it carefully, the way he’d said I slept, as though he’d found something in his pocket he didn’t remember putting there and wasn’t sure if he was allowed to keep.

“This,” said Serafina. “The car? The ditch?”

“The passenger seat,” said Qin Haozhen. “You driving. Three in the morning.” His hand moved on her back, slowly, under her coat. “I’d like that for next year. If it’s not too big.”

She had to look away, at the water, for a second, before she could answer him.

“It’s not too big,” she said. “Get in. I’ll drive.”

chapters.title: What He Does for Work
chapters.desc: A Belgian family reports a missing father. She lays the whole thing out on the workbench like a diagnosis, one part at a time, and waits for him to say she’s wrong. He doesn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
It was Mouse who found it.

Mouse had been looking. Serafina hadn’t asked her to and would never have asked her to; it was one of the things Mouse simply did, in the hours after midnight at the end of the workbench with her headphones on, the way other people did crosswords. She looked into things. Engines, mostly, and wiring, and once, in 2020, the man in the Subaru who had pushed Nonna into a lamp post, about whom she had found a number of facts that the man had paid a great deal to keep quiet. She looked, and she said nothing, and then one day she turned a screen round.

On the second Saturday in January, at eleven in the morning, she turned a screen round.

It was a Belgian newspaper. Serafina couldn’t read Flemish, but she could read a photograph, and she could read a name. A tall fair man in a grey suit, smiling, at what looked like a wedding. Lucien Marchal (46). And under the photograph, a smaller one, of a woman with her hand over her mouth, and two teenage boys standing behind her on a doorstep.

“His family,” said Mouse. “In Antwerp. They reported him missing in October. The paper there only ran it last week, when the police gave up. He was supposed to fly home on the twenty-third of October. His ticket was used. He wasn’t on the plane.” She looked at Serafina with her small worried face. “The police here say he left the city. The police there say he never arrived.”

Serafina looked at the woman with her hand over her mouth for a long time.

“Print it,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She laid it out on the workbench.

She did it the way she did a diagnosis, when a car came in that nobody else had been able to fix. You didn’t guess. You didn’t go with your stomach, although your stomach was usually right. You took every symptom and you laid it out in order on the bench, every noise and leak and warning light and strange smell, and you looked at all of them together until they stopped being separate things and turned into one thing. Then you knew.

She used parts. She was in that kind of mood.

A spark plug, for the number plate. Registered to a dead man. No parking tickets, not one, in four years.

A brake pad, for the delegation’s paperwork. The sixtieth man. East service door.

A shoe, one of his old ones, from the night he’d stood in a puddle by the shutter and she’d given him a pair of Big Wu’s boots and he’d left his oxfords to dry by the kettle and forgotten them. Black leather. Resoled thin. For running on marble.

A shock absorber, for the four hundred kilos in the doors and floor. Steel plate. Somebody had been worried about bullets.

A torch, for his right hand at nine twenty-two, going toward his jacket where there was nothing.

A clementine, for four hours’ sleep a night since he was eighteen.

A firework casing she had picked up out of the ditch on New Year’s morning and kept in her jacket without knowing why. For nine countries’ fireworks, from roofs, watching someone else.

And at the end of the row, in the middle of the bench, the printed photograph of a woman on a doorstep in Antwerp with her hand over her mouth.

She stood back and looked at it.

Big Wu came in from the alley with a crate of oil and stopped and looked too. He put the crate down very slowly. He didn’t say anything. After a minute he went and found Mr. Kwok, who was buying vegetables, and took him for lunch somewhere a long way away, and didn’t come back until four.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at two in the morning.

She heard the grey car at the end of the street, and the pads biting clean at the corner, the ones she’d fitted. She heard him park. She heard the side door from the alley, which he used now, because he said the shutter was too loud. She didn’t turn round. She was sitting on the stool by the kettle, his stool, with her back to the door and her hands round the mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST MECHANIC, which had gone cold an hour ago.

He came in. He stopped.

She knew exactly where he was looking. She had put it all under the work lamp so he would see it from the door.

The garage was very quiet. Somewhere down the line a train was coming; she could feel it beginning in the floor.

“I’m going to tell you what I think,” said Serafina, still not turning round. “And you’re going to tell me if I’ve got it wrong. All right?”

“All right.”

She told him.

She went down the bench, part by part, in the same voice she used to tell a customer what was wrong with his gearbox, flat and exact and not unkind. The plate. The paperwork. The shoes. The steel in the doors. The hand at nine twenty-two. The sleep. The roofs. She got up off the stool while she was doing it and walked along the bench, and touched each thing as she came to it, and he stood by the door and listened and didn’t move.

At the end she picked up the photograph.

“You don’t guard people,” she said. “You take them. For somebody. Somebody with a delegation, and paperwork, and a bank in the capital that pays your insurance. You stand at a door in a building full of people until the one you want goes outside, and then you walk him to a car with his arm in your hand, as if you’re friends, and you drive away with him. And his family in Antwerp is in the newspapers in January because he never came home.” She turned round at last and held up the photograph. “That’s what you do for work.”

The train went over.

Everything shook. The parts on the bench rattled in their row. The clementine rolled, very slowly, off the end and onto the floor, and neither of them looked at it.

He didn’t say she was wrong.

He stood by the side door in his forgettable jacket with the light from the work lamp on half his face, and looked at her, and his face did not do any of the things a guilty face does. It didn’t harden. It didn’t fall. It didn’t look away. It simply stayed open, the way it had in the paddock at the circuit, the way it did in her passenger seat, and that was worse, much worse, than if he’d lied.

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had thought she was ready for it. She had sat on his stool for three hours getting ready for it.

She found that she wasn’t.
