“Do you kill them?” She heard her own voice go up and couldn’t stop it. “Do you—when you take them. Do you kill them?”

“Sometimes.”

“The Belgian?”

“No.” He said it at once. “I drove him to a petrol station at the edge of the province and gave him to two men in a van. He was alive. He’ll be alive now, I think. Somewhere he doesn’t want to be, answering questions.” A pause. “I don’t know what he did. I’m not told. Most of the time I’m not told.”

“And you don’t ask.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I was eighteen,” he said, “and they’d told me since I was sixteen that the asking was someone else’s job.” He looked at the woman in the photograph in her hand. “And because when you’ve done it once without asking, it gets very hard to start.”

Serafina put the photograph down. Her hands were shaking. She put them in her pockets so that he wouldn’t see, and knew that he’d seen.

“How many?” she said.

He didn’t answer.

“How many people, Haozhen?”

“I know the number,” he said. “I know every one of them. Names, dates, where, what they were wearing. I don’t forget them. That’s the one thing I never let myself do.” He was very still. “I won’t tell you tonight.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’d hear it tonight,” said Qin Haozhen, “in this voice, standing up, with that photograph on your bench, and you’d never be able to hear it any other way.” He drew a breath. “Ask me again. In a year. If you still want to know, I’ll tell you all of it. I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked him to go.

She did it badly. She would be ashamed of it afterwards: that she couldn’t look at him, that she said it to the bench. “I think you should go.” Like a woman in a film. Like her mother, ending a phone call. She hated it as it came out of her mouth and she said it anyway, because the woman in Antwerp had her hand over her mouth, and there were two boys behind her, and Serafina could not, that night, make the man in her garage and the man who had walked Lucien Marchal to a car into two different people. She tried. She stood there and tried, with her hands in her pockets, and she could not do it.

He didn’t argue.

That was the worst of it. He didn’t ask her to understand, or say he’d been following orders, or tell her she was being naive about the world. She had braced for all of those. She’d have had something to push against. He just looked at her for a moment longer, and then nodded, once, as if she’d told him the time.

He went to the kettle. He picked up the plain mug, his, with HIS on it in her marker, which he had turned to face the wall. He turned it back round. So that the writing faced the room.

Then he put it down, very carefully, exactly where it had been.

“If you tell anyone about this,” he said, at the side door, with his back to her.

She went cold all over.

“Then what?”

He turned his head.

“Then nothing,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’d make sure nobody touched you for it. That’s what I was going to say.” He looked at her across the garage, across the row of parts on the bench and the clementine on the floor. “Lock this door after me. And the shutter. You leave the shutter up at night. You shouldn’t.”

He went.

She heard the grey car start in the alley. She heard it go down the street of shuttered workshops, slowly, and brake at the corner, clean, and turn, and then she couldn’t hear it any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t lock the door.

She sat down on the concrete floor in the middle of the garage with her back against Gilded’s front wheel and her knees up and her arms round them, and the trains went over, every eleven minutes, the whole building shaking round her like a car on a bad road. She counted them. She had nothing else to count. Six. Seven. At the eighth, she picked the clementine up off the floor and peeled it and didn’t eat it.

At half past four she got up and got into Nonna and drove the loop.

Bridge. Tunnel. Coast road. Gently, the way she’d been driving it for three weeks. No hard braking. No turbo. The engine burbling in third and the ferries going back and forth across the dark water.

She’d forgotten. She’d driven it so many times with him in the seat beside her that her body had learned it that way, and on the coast road, at the place where his head always slid off the window onto her shoulder, she found that she had dropped her right shoulder a fraction, the way she did, to catch it.

There was nobody there.

She pulled into the lay-by above the harbour, where the fireworks had been, and turned off the engine, and sat in the dark with both hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, the way he held it, and cried until the sky went grey over the water. She didn’t hold back any of it, because there was no one in the passenger seat to hear.

chapters.title: She Should Run
chapters.desc: Four days. Any sensible woman would run, and she knows exactly how. Instead she turns up outside his flat at six in the morning with two egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to run. I’m the one people run with.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
She knew how to run. That was the thing.

She had known since she was nineteen. In the industrial district, among the shuttered workshops and the street races and the men who rebuilt engines for cash, there were people who built cars for other people who needed to stop existing. Plain cars, mostly. Cars that looked like nothing, with false floors and two sets of plates and engines that didn’t match the paperwork. There was a man under the flyover by the fish market who could make you a passport in four days. There was a woman in the Walled City who rented rooms by the week and never wrote anything down. Serafina had fixed their cars. She had driven, twice, for people she would not name, through the night to the border with someone lying under a blanket in the back. She had told Aurelia so once, at a wedding in Milan, by a fountain, and meant it.

She could go. She could be gone by Thursday. A new name, a new garage somewhere nobody had heard of Team AURELIA, and no one would ever stand by her shutter at two in the morning with their hands in plain view again.

She thought about it for four days.

She thought about it on Sunday, lying on the mattress in the loft above the garage listening to the trains. She thought about it on Monday under Gilded, getting nothing done. She thought about it on Tuesday when Aurelia rang from the boutique to talk about the new season’s livery, and Serafina said “Yes” and “Fine” and “Gold, obviously,” until Aurelia stopped and said, “Sera. What’s wrong,” in the voice from when they were small, and Serafina said, “Nothing. An engine,” and Aurelia didn’t believe her and didn’t push, which was new, and which Serafina suspected was Chen Si’s influence.

And on Tuesday night, at nine, while Mr. Kwok was washing the wok in the sink by the back door, she said, without meaning to:

“Mr. Kwok. In forty years. Did you ever drive someone who’d done something terrible?”

He went on washing the wok.

“Every night,” he said.

She looked at him.

“Forty years. Night shift, mostly. You think the people in the back of a taxi at three in the morning are going home from the opera?” He rinsed the wok and turned it over on the rack. “Men who’d hit their wives. Men who’d stolen from their brothers. A man in 1991 who got in at the hospital with blood on his cuffs and gave me the address of a police station and sat there the whole way with his hands like this.” He held them out, flat, palms up, on his knees. “I never asked him what he’d done. I asked him if he wanted the radio on.”

“Did he?”

“He wanted the news.” Mr. Kwok dried his hands. “I’ll tell you what forty years taught me, since you’re asking and you never ask. It’s never the question of what they did. Everybody in the back of a cab has done something. The question is what they’re going to do next. Where they’ve asked you to take them.” He hung the towel on the hook. “Your guard. Where’s he asking you to take him?”

Serafina didn’t answer.

“Thought so,” said Mr. Kwok, and put on his coat, and went home to see the news.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mouse had his address. Of course Mouse had his address.

“It’s above a laundry,” Mouse said, very quietly, at half past five on Wednesday morning, when Serafina came down the stairs from the loft dressed and with her keys in her hand and found Mouse still at the end of the bench, where she had been all night. “In the old harbour streets. Behind the market. Second floor, the window with no curtain.” She hesitated. “He doesn’t have anything in it. I looked at the electricity. He uses less than the laundry’s cat.”

“How do you know how much a cat uses?”

“The cat has a heated bed,” said Mouse, and turned back to her screens.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stopped at the place under the flyover on the way.

It was a metal stall under the concrete, with a corrugated roof and three plastic tables and an old man who had been making egg sandwiches since before the flyover was built. Thick white bread, toasted on a grill, butter, and an omelette folded so soft it was nearly custard, with a slice of ham that nobody asked about. Serafina had been eating them since she was nineteen. She bought two. She bought two cups of milk tea, very sweet, in plastic bags with straws, the way the old man did them. Then she drove to the old harbour streets behind the market and parked Nonna across the road from a laundry with its shutters still down, under a window on the second floor with no curtain, at six in the morning, and leaned on the bonnet in the cold, and waited.

At six eleven the street door beside the laundry opened.

He came out the way she’d known he would. Not straight out. He stood just inside the door for a second, in the dark, and she watched him look: up the street, down the street, the parked cars, the windows opposite, the alley by the market. Thoroughly. Without moving his head very much. And his eyes came across the road and found a red Lancia, and a woman leaning on its bonnet with two plastic bags of milk tea hanging off one finger, and stopped.

He didn’t move for a moment.

Then he crossed the road. Not fast. He stopped a metre away from her, in the grey light, in his dark jacket, with his hands at his sides, and looked at her face as though he was reading it for damage.

“You should have run,” he said.

“I know.”

“You know how. You’ve driven people.”

“Twice.”

“Then why are you here?”

Serafina held out one of the sandwiches. It was in a paper bag going translucent with butter.

“You wanted a sandwich,” she said. “For this year. From the place under the flyover. With the egg.” She swallowed. “It’s January. I thought you’d better start.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate on Nonna’s bonnet, because the laundry wasn’t open and there was nowhere else.

He ate like he did everything, slowly and completely, with his full attention, as though the sandwich had been put in front of him for evaluation. Halfway through he stopped and looked at it.

“This is very good,” he said.

“I know.”

“I didn’t know they were this good.”

“You’ve never had one?”

“I’ve walked past that stall,” said Qin Haozhen, “probably sixty times. I’ve never stopped.” He looked at the sandwich for a moment longer. Then he went on eating it.

She waited until he’d finished. She drank her milk tea, which was too sweet and perfect. A woman came and unlocked the laundry shutter and rolled it up with a long screech and looked at them, the two of them sitting on a red car at six in the morning, and went inside, and came back out with a cat in her arms, a fat grey one, to look at them again.

“I’ve got rules,” said Serafina.

He turned his head.

“Three. Maybe four. You don’t have to agree to them. But if you don’t, I’m going to drive off and you can eat the sandwiches from now on by yourself.” She held up one finger. “One. You don’t lie to me. I know you don’t, already. Keep not doing it. If you can’t tell me something, say I can’t tell you that. I’d rather have that than anything made up.”

“Yes.”

“Two. You never bring it into my garage. Not the job. Not a gun. Not a person. Not a file. My garage is mine. Big Wu’s done two prison sentences and he won’t talk about either of them and I’ve never once asked, because the garage is where you don’t have to. That’s yours too. But only if you leave the rest outside.”

“Yes.”

“Three. If you’re going to be gone, you tell me. You don’t have to say where. You don’t have to say for what. Just I’ll be gone, and roughly how long, so I don’t stand by the shutter at two in the morning wondering if I’m ever going to hear the brakes at the corner.”

He was quiet on that one.

“Yes,” he said. “I’ll always tell you. If I can.”

“If you can?”

“Sometimes they don’t tell me until I’m in the car.”

She looked at him. He looked back. It was the open look, the one that didn’t do any of the things a guilty face did, and she thought, this is going to be the whole of it, isn’t it. Him telling me the truth, and me deciding every day whether I can stand it.

“Then you tell me from the car,” she said.

“All right.”

“And four.” Her voice came out rougher than she’d meant. “If you ever want out. Of all of it. You tell me first. Before anyone. Before you’ve worked it out, before you’ve got a plan, before you’ve even said it to yourself properly. You come to the garage and you say Sera, I want out, and I’ll have the car outside.”

He went completely still.

“Serafina,” he said.

“I know what I’m saying.”

“You don’t. You don’t know what you’re offering. You don’t know who they are.”

“I know they’ve got a bank in the capital and a delegation and men in a white van at a petrol station. I know they’d be very angry.” She set her milk tea down on the bonnet. “I’m not going to run, Haozhen. I thought about it for four days. I could have been gone by Thursday. But I’ve been watching people run since I was nineteen, and I’ve driven them, and I know what I am. I’m not the one who runs.” She looked at him. “I’m the one people run with.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything for so long that the laundry woman put the cat down and went inside.

Then he did something she didn’t expect. He took her right hand, the one with the old shiny burn across the back, and turned it over in both of his, palm up, and looked at it, the way he’d looked at the oil on his own palm the first night. He ran his thumb along a cut across the base of her fingers that was still healing from a bracket on Monday.

“The first time I didn’t ask,” he said, “I was eighteen. It was a man in a hotel in the capital. He was a teacher. They said he’d written something. I didn’t read it.” He was still looking at her hand. “I’ve never told anybody that. Not a priest. Not a doctor. They make you see a doctor, every year, and you tell the doctor you sleep fine.” His thumb moved on her palm. “I don’t know what you’re doing, Sera. I don’t know why you’re here.”

It was the first time he’d called her Sera.

She found that she couldn’t speak, so she didn’t. She leaned in and kissed him instead, on the bonnet of her car, in the grey morning in the old harbour streets, with the sesame from the bread still on his lower lip. She wiped it off with her thumb first. Then she kissed the place where it had been, slow, until he made a sound in his throat, a low, surprised sound, and his hand came up to the back of her neck and held on.

Across the road, the laundry woman had come back out to look, and was standing in the doorway with her arms folded, and when Serafina finally sat back, breathless, she called across the street, “About time! He’s been living up there two years and never once brought anyone home!”

He closed his eyes.

“She knows you,” said Serafina, delighted.

“She knows my electricity,” said Qin Haozhen. “Her cat has a heated bed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday it was Lunar New Year’s Eve, and Mr. Kwok cooked.

He did it every year, in the garage, for whoever was there: a reunion dinner on two trestle tables pushed together under the hanging lamp, with a tablecloth he brought from home and chairs borrowed from the noodle shop at the end of the street, because, he said, a team was a family whether it liked it or not, and families ate together on New Year’s Eve, even ones with criminal records. Big Wu’s mother came, tiny and fierce, and sat at the head of the table and told everyone what to eat. Mouse came, and sat at the end, and ate four bowls of rice without speaking. Serafina wore a red jumper that Aurelia had sent over by courier with a note that said For luck. Wear it, or I’ll know.

At seven o’clock the side door from the alley opened.

He came in with a net bag of mandarins, and stopped just inside the door, looking at the trestle tables and the tablecloth and the borrowed chairs and Big Wu’s mother at the head of the table, as if he’d walked into the wrong building.

Big Wu got up. He was very large and he took his time about it. He crossed the garage and looked down at the net bag in Qin Haozhen’s hand, and counted.

“Eight,” he said.

“Eight,” said Qin Haozhen.

“Not four.”

“I asked,” said Qin Haozhen, “at the market. The man said you never bring four. And you never bring an odd number. And you never bring the ones with no leaves.”

Big Wu looked at the mandarins. Every one of them had two green leaves still on its stem.

Then he took the bag, and turned round, and carried it to the table, and put it down in front of his mother, and said, “Ma. This is the guard,” and pulled out the chair beside his own, and pointed at it.

Serafina, at the stove with Mr. Kwok, put her face in her hands.

“Is he crying?” Mr. Kwok asked her, under his breath. “Big Wu? Is that what that is?”

“I think it’s the onions,” said Serafina, who was.

chapters.title: The First Time He Bleeds in Her Garage
chapters.desc: Valentine’s night. He said eight o’clock, with dinner. He comes at ten to one with the dinner, cold, and a knife cut down his left forearm, because a Bureau doctor would write it down. She stitches him with fishing line and swears in three languages.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule two doesn’t cover blood. Sit down before you fall on my car.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
She did not do Valentine’s Day. She had told him so, very clearly, on the Sunday.

“It’s a florists’ holiday,” she said. “And a restaurant holiday. And a jewellers’ holiday. My sister sells eleven per cent of her year in the first two weeks of February, and she lights a candle to Saint Valentine in her workshop every year as a joke and I don’t think it’s a joke any more. I don’t need flowers. I don’t need dinner in a restaurant with a man playing the violin at me. I don’t do dates.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “You told me in November.”

“Good.”

“I’ll come at eight,” he said, “with dinner.”

She opened her mouth.

“Not a date,” he said. “Dinner. In the garage. From the dumpling place you like by the tram depot, the one with the chilli oil. I’ll bring the good vinegar.” He looked at her. “You eat standing up at the workbench every night anyway. I’ll stand up with you.”

She thought about it.

“Pork and chive,” she said. “Not the cabbage ones.”

“Not the cabbage ones,” he agreed, and wrote it down.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight he didn’t come.

At nine he didn’t come. She had been under Nonna since seven doing a clutch she didn’t need to do, so that she would be busy when he came, and at nine she rolled out and looked at her phone. Nothing. At ten there was nothing. At a quarter past ten she found she was standing at the shutter, which she had left half up again in spite of what he’d said, looking down the street of shuttered workshops toward the corner where his brakes always bit. She went back inside and was furious with herself.

At eleven, her phone buzzed.

Haozhen: Late. I’m sorry. In the car. Coming.

Rule three. From the car. She looked at the four words for a while and then went back under Nonna and finished the clutch, which now she did need to do, because she’d taken it apart.

At ten to one she heard the brakes at the corner.

They didn’t bite clean. They bit late, and hard, and a little crooked, and she was out from under the car and on her feet before the grey estate had stopped in the alley, because she knew every noise his car made now, and that one was wrong.

✦ ✦ ✦

The side door opened.

He came in holding a plastic bag from the dumpling place by the tram depot. He was holding it in his right hand. His left arm was folded against his chest, inside his jacket, and the left sleeve of the jacket was black and wet from the elbow to the cuff, and it was dripping. Not much. Steadily. A drop every few seconds onto her concrete floor, very dark under the work lamp.

He stopped just inside the door.

“I’m breaking rule two,” he said. “I’m sorry. I couldn’t go to the doctor.”

She had been angry since eight. She had stopped being angry at some point in the last three seconds and she couldn’t have said when.

“What happened?”

“A knife. In a stairwell.” He said it as he would have said a puncture. “It isn’t deep. It’s long. I’ve stopped most of it. But if I go to the Bureau’s doctor it’s on a form, and the form goes to a desk, and someone at that desk asks why a man who was supposed to be watching a door in a stairwell was close enough to someone to get cut.” He looked at the bag in his hand. “I brought the dumplings. They’re cold.”

“You brought the—” Serafina stared at him. “You’ve been stabbed and you stopped for dumplings?”

“I’d ordered them,” said Qin Haozhen. “At seven. They were waiting.” A pause. “Pork and chive. Not the cabbage.”

She crossed the garage. She took the bag out of his hand and put it on the bench without looking at it. Then she took him by his good arm and walked him to the stool by the kettle and sat him on it, and he let her, which frightened her more than the blood.

“Rule two doesn’t cover blood,” she said. “Sit down before you fall on my car.”

“I am sitting.”

“Then stay sitting. Jacket. Off.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cut was down the outside of his left forearm, from just below the elbow almost to the wrist. Long and clean and gaping a little at the middle, where it was deepest. He had wrapped it tight in something, a scarf, she thought, grey wool, not his, and the wool was soaked through. When she unwound it he didn’t make a sound, but the muscle in his jaw went tight and stayed tight.

She looked at it under the work lamp and made herself breathe. She had seen cuts. You couldn’t work on engines your whole life and not see cuts. She’d seen Big Wu open his palm to the bone on a bonnet catch and tape it shut with gaffer tape and finish the job. She’d done her own, on her forearms, many times, small ones. She had never stitched anyone in her life.

“It needs stitching,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I can’t stitch.”

“You can,” said Qin Haozhen. “You do the wiring on the dashboard of a thirty-year-old Lancia with tweezers. I’ve watched you.” He was looking at her face, not his arm. “Wash it out first. Boiled water, cooled, lots of it, until there’s nothing in it but me. Then fishing line, if you’ve got it. Boil it. Boil a needle. Clean it with whatever you’ve got that’s strongest. Then just close it, one stitch at a time, about the width of your little fingernail apart. Tie each one off. Don’t pull them too tight.” He paused. “I’ll tell you if it’s wrong.”

“You’ve done this.”

“Twice. On myself.” A breath. “It’s easier when someone else does it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Kwok kept his fishing things in a red metal box under the workbench, because on Sundays he went to the breakwater at the end of the container terminal and caught nothing and was very happy about it. Serafina found the line, clear nylon, the light one. She found a needle in Mouse’s drawer, where Mouse kept everything, and bent it into a curve with two pairs of pliers. She boiled them both in the saucepan on the camping stove for five minutes, by the clock on her phone, while he sat on the stool with the arm held out over a clean rag and watched her.

The strongest thing she had was Big Wu’s emergency bottle, which was a Scotch whisky he had been given in 2017 and was saving for a death. She poured it over her own hands, and over the needle, and then, while he looked at her, over the cut.

He made a noise then. Short. Through his teeth.

“Porca miseria,” said Serafina, “scusa, scusa—”

“It’s fine.”

“It’s not fine, you’re bleeding on my floor, I’ve just poured a dead man’s whisky on you—”

“Is Big Wu dead?”

“He’s saving it for when he is,” said Serafina, and picked up the needle, and her hands were shaking so badly she couldn’t hold it, and she put it down again.

He didn’t say anything. He reached out with his good hand and took her right wrist, gently, and held it. Just held it, his thumb on the inside of her wrist where her pulse was going like a piston, until it slowed.

“One at a time,” he said. “Like a wiring loom.”

She picked up the needle.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did it in fourteen stitches.

She swore through every one of them. In Italian, mostly, the Milanese kind, the kind her grandmother had used at watchmakers. In Cantonese, the industrial-district kind, at the fishing line when it wouldn’t knot. And in English, at him, very quietly, every time she pushed the needle through and his jaw went tight. She called him an idiot and a lunatic and a man who stopped for dumplings with a knife wound, and a stairwell, what kind of man went into a stairwell, and she told him that if he died in her garage she would tell everyone in the industrial district that he’d been killed by a dumpling, and he sat on the stool with his arm on the rag and his eyes on her face and didn’t once look down at what she was doing.

“Why aren’t you looking?”

“I’m looking at what I want to,” said Qin Haozhen.

The eighth stitch went wrong. She pulled too tight and the edge of the skin puckered and she said something in Cantonese that would have made Granny Shum put down her tea. He said, “Leave it. It’s fine,” and she said, “It is not fine, it’ll leave a mark,” and he said, “Sera. I’ve got a lot of marks. That’ll be the only one somebody put there to help.”

She had to stop for a second, after that. She sat back on her heels on the concrete with the bloody needle in her fingers and the lamp in her eyes, and didn’t look at him until she could.

Then she did the other six.

✦ ✦ ✦

When it was done she dressed it with clean gauze from the first-aid kit Big Wu kept in the van and a crepe bandage, wound round firm, and taped it, and sat back.

It was half past two. A train went over. The garage shook. The bloody rag and the empty whisky bottle and the saucepan and the bent needle were all on the floor round the stool, like the aftermath of a very small war.

He looked down at his arm for the first time.

“That’s good,” he said. “That’s better than mine.”

“Shut up.”

“It is.”

His shirt was ruined. The left sleeve was stiff with blood up to the shoulder. She told him to take it off, because she’d find him one of Big Wu’s T-shirts, and he took it off with his good hand, slowly, and she stopped with Big Wu’s T-shirt halfway out of the locker and looked at him.

She’d known there’d be scars. You didn’t do what he did for ten years and come out clean. She had not known there would be so many, or that they would all be so neat. A short white line under his right collarbone. A round pucker low on his left side, old. Three faint parallel marks across his ribs, like a fork. A long thin one down his back she could only see the start of. Each one healed flat and pale, like a sentence somebody had written very carefully and then crossed out.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were going to count them.”

She was. She put Big Wu’s T-shirt down on the bench. She walked across the garage to the stool. He was sitting with his bandaged arm on his knee, bare to the waist under the work lamp, looking up at her, and she stood between his knees and put her hand flat on his chest, over the short white line under the collarbone, and felt his heart going under it, much faster than it had been while she was stitching him.

“I don’t want to count them,” said Serafina. “I want to know which ones still hurt.”

He looked up at her. His eyes were very dark.

“None of them,” he said. “Until tonight.”

She kissed him.

He made the low surprised sound in his throat again, the one from outside the laundry, and his good hand came up to her waist and found the gap between her vest and her overalls and stayed there, warm, flat, spread on her bare back. She kissed him slowly, because he’d lost blood and because she wanted to, both hands on his face, his jaw rough under her palms, his mouth opening under hers, the taste of the whisky still on him from where she’d splashed it. He pulled her closer by the waist. She went. She went until she was standing pressed between his knees and his face was against her collarbone and he was breathing hard against her skin, and she had her fingers in his hair, and she could feel him trembling, very faintly, all through, like an engine at the edge of its limit.

Then she felt something warm on her hip and looked down.

He was bleeding through the gauze.

“No,” said Serafina, and took his face in both hands and held it away from her. “No. Absolutely not.”

“It’s fine.”

“It’s leaking. You’re leaking on my overalls. You’ve got fourteen stitches put in by a woman who’s never stitched anything but a seat cover.” She was laughing, and breathless, and her face was burning. “Not tonight. You’ll bleed on my car.”

He looked up at her with his hair wrecked and his mouth red and an expression she had never seen on him, a kind of dazed, offended disbelief, and she laughed harder.

“You’re a menace,” she told him. “I’ve said this before.”

“In English,” he said, a little hoarse. “You said it in English.”

“I’ll learn it in Mandarin,” said Serafina, “so you understand,” and went to get the clean gauze.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let him drive home.

She looked at the grey estate in the alley while he was putting on Big Wu’s T-shirt, which came down nearly to his knees. There was a hole in the driver’s door. Small and neat and round, about level with where his hip would be, with a bright ring of torn paint round it. When she put her finger in it, she touched steel. The armour in the door had stopped whatever had made it.

She stood in the alley for a while with her finger in the hole.

Then she came back in and took his keys off the bench, and put them in her pocket.

“You’re sleeping here,” she said.

“Where?” He looked up the stairs at the loft.

“Not there. Not tonight. You’d bleed on that as well.”

She opened Nonna’s passenger door.

He looked at it. He looked at her. And then he got in, slowly, in Big Wu’s T-shirt, with his arm across his chest, and put the seat back two notches, and she got in the driver’s side and pulled the door to, and they sat in the red Lancia in the middle of the garage under the hanging lamp with the engine off and the dumplings cold on the bench, and she reached across and pulled the blanket off the back seat and put it over him.

“Happy Valentine’s Day,” she said. “This isn’t a date.”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. His eyes were already closing. “It’s much better than a date.”

He was asleep before the next train. She sat beside him in the driver’s seat and ate four cold pork and chive dumplings with her fingers, with the good vinegar, and didn’t take her eyes off the bandage until the sky through the high window had gone from black to grey, and the gauze stayed white all the way through.

chapters.title: Twelve Days and a Postcard
chapters.desc: “I’ll be gone. Maybe two weeks.” No calls. A pre-season test that nearly ends in the tyre wall at the Needle. A sister who notices everything. Then, on the twelfth day, a postcard with no words on it at all.
chapters.epigraph: “When you can tell me, tell me. That’s how it works in my house.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
She took the stitches out on the Friday, ten days after she’d put them in.

He sat on the stool by the kettle with his sleeve rolled up and his arm on the clean rag, and she sat on an upturned crate in front of him with Mouse’s tweezers and a pair of nail scissors she had boiled in the saucepan, and snipped each knot and drew each stitch out, one at a time, slowly, all fourteen. The cut had closed into a long pink line, puckered at the eighth stitch where she’d pulled too tight. She ran her thumb down it when she’d finished.

“It’s ugly,” she said.

“It’s yours,” said Qin Haozhen. “I like it.”

She kept her thumb on it.

“You’re going somewhere,” she said.

He didn’t ask how she knew. He had stopped asking that in January.

“Sunday,” he said. “I’ll be gone. Maybe two weeks. Maybe a little more.” He looked at her thumb on his arm. “I can’t tell you where.”

“Rule three.”

He nodded.

“Can you ring?”

“No.”

“Text?”

“No.” He was quiet. “There won’t be a phone that’s mine. If I could, I would. You know I would.”

She did know. That was the worst part. She sat on the crate with her hand on his arm and looked at the long pink line she’d made, and thought of fourteen countries and roofs and stairwells, and a hole in a car door with steel at the bottom of it.

“Come back,” she said, “with that arm. I want to see it heal.”

“I’ll come back,” said Qin Haozhen, “with the arm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning he left his grey car in her garage, because, he said, they’d be giving him another one, and he’d rather this one were somewhere he knew it would be looked after. He left his keys on the bench beside the kettle. He left the plain mug with HIS on it, facing the room.

He kissed her at the side door at six in the morning, in the alley, with the dustcarts going past at the end of the street. It was a long kiss and a careful one, as if he were memorising something. Then he walked to the corner, and turned, and was gone, and she stood in the alley until the dustcarts had finished and the sun had come up over the railway bridge.

That was Day Nothing. She didn’t count it. Day One was Monday.

✦ ✦ ✦

She counted. Of course she counted.

Day Two, she rebuilt his grey car’s gearbox, which didn’t need it. Day Three, she did the same to Nonna’s. Day Four, Big Wu took a spanner out of her hand and said, “Go to bed,” and she said she wasn’t tired, and he said, “You’ve put that bolt in and taken it out four times,” and she looked down and it was true.

Day Five, Mouse turned a screen round, without being asked, and showed her a page of numbers that meant nothing, and said very quietly, “There’s been nothing. On anything. No news, no reports, no names.” She paused. “That’s good, I think. When it’s bad there’s always something.”

“How do you know?”

Mouse looked at her screens.

“I looked,” she said, “in January. At what happens when it’s bad.”

Day Six. Day Seven. Mr. Kwok made her lunch every day and stood over her until she ate it. On Day Seven he made her the noodles he made for people when someone had died, with the long life in them, and she ate them and didn’t say anything, and he didn’t either, and when she’d finished he took the bowl away and patted her once on the top of her head, which he had never done before in four years.

At night she drove the loop. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. Alone. She kept forgetting and dropping her shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Day Six, Saturday the fourth of March, it was the pre-season test at the circuit in the north.

Every team in the series came, all twenty-two cars, for two days of practice before the season opened in April. It mattered. It was where you found out if the winter’s work had been any good, and where the sponsors came to see their logos on the cars for the first time, and where people who might give you money stood in the pit lane with their arms folded and watched how fast you went.

Aurelia came at ten in a cream coat with fur at the collar and dark glasses and a coffee, with Lily from the boutique behind her carrying a portfolio of the new livery proofs. She came into the pit garage and looked at Gilded, matte black, the gold AURELIA on the bonnet freshly painted, and said, “It’s crooked,” and Serafina said, “It is not,” and Big Wu got the tape measure out, and it was crooked by four millimetres, and Aurelia took her glasses off and looked at her sister.

“Sera,” she said. “What’s wrong.”

“Nothing. It’s four millimetres.”

“You’ve never in your life let anything be four millimetres out.” Aurelia put her coffee down on the tyre rack. “You’ve been looking at your phone like it owes you money.”

“I haven’t.”

“You’ve looked at it eleven times since I came in.” Aurelia didn’t smile. “I counted.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon session, on her ninth lap, Serafina lifted at the top of the esses.

The sun. She knew it was the sun; he had told her it was the sun, in December, and she had fixed it, and for three months she hadn’t done it once. She did it now. She came over the crest with the sun full in her visor and her foot came up a fraction off the throttle without her asking it to, and the car went light, and she caught it, and she was so angry with herself that she went down the back straight two hundred metres later at two hundred and forty-one kilometres an hour without having decided to, and braked for the Needle ten metres late.

Ten metres. In a race car, at that speed, ten metres was the whole game.

She felt the front tyres go. That long sickening slither, like stepping on a stair that isn’t there. The car wouldn’t turn. She came off the brakes to get the steering back and the car went straight on, off the tarmac, across the kerb with a bang that went up through her spine, into the gravel trap, and the gravel took it, the way gravel was meant to, grabbing at the wheels, slowing it, and the tyre wall came up at her, red and white, enormous, and she thought, very clearly and calmly, well, he’ll have to come back now, to see this—

The car stopped.

A metre from the tyres. Less. She could see the bolts in the conveyor belt that held them together.

She sat in the gravel with her hands on the wheel and her heart going so hard she could hear it inside her helmet, and the red flag went out all round the circuit, and the marshals came running with their extinguishers, and she put her head down on the steering wheel and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu didn’t speak to her for an hour.

He got the car back on the truck and into the garage and went over every centimetre of it with a torch, and there was gravel in everything, in the radiator ducts and the wheel arches and the undertray, and a crack in the splitter that would cost four thousand to replace, and he didn’t say one word the whole time. Mouse sat at the laptop with the data from the crash on the screen, the speed trace going up and up and then the brake trace, a fraction late, and then the steering angle doing something wild, and she didn’t say anything either. Mr. Kwok made tea.

At five, when the session was over and the pit lane was emptying, Aurelia came and sat on the tyre stack beside her sister, in her cream coat, among the gravel and the oil, and didn’t say anything for a while.

“Are you hurt?” she said finally.

“No.”

“You went off at the Needle. You never go off at the Needle. You told me in 2019 it was the only corner on earth you trusted.”

Serafina didn’t answer.

“I’m not going to ask who he is,” said Aurelia.

Serafina turned her head and looked at her.

“You think I don’t know what this looks like?” Aurelia’s voice was very dry. “I’ve spent four years married to a man who leaves at three in the morning and comes back at six smelling of the docks and says it’s handled, and means it. I know what the phone looks like. I know the face.” She looked at the cracked splitter on the floor. “I’m not going to ask. When you can tell me, tell me. That’s how it works in my house. We say I can’t tell you that yet, and the other one waits.”

“And if I never can?”

Aurelia was quiet.

“Then I’ll pay for the splitter,” she said, “and wait anyway.”

Serafina put her head on her sister’s shoulder. Aurelia smelled of the boutique, of polishing rouge and something French, and of coffee, and she let her sister’s head stay there, oil and all, in her cream coat, and didn’t move, the way nobody in their family had ever let anyone’s head stay anywhere, until Big Wu came over and said that the van was loaded and if anyone wanted a lift back to the city they’d better stop crying on the tyres.

“Nobody’s crying,” said Aurelia.

“Course not,” said Big Wu, and gave Serafina his handkerchief anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Day Seven. Day Eight. Day Nine.

She didn’t drive at all on Day Nine. She sat in his grey car in the garage with the door open and her feet on the dashboard and looked at the small round hole in the driver’s door, which she had not yet filled, because she didn’t want to fill it until he could see.

Day Ten. Day Eleven.

On the morning of Day Twelve, Friday the tenth of March, the post came at ten as it always did. A tyre catalogue. A gas bill. A letter from the series about the splitter. And a postcard.

It had been posted from somewhere she couldn’t read. The stamp was foreign and the postmark was smudged and the address, on the right-hand side, was hers, the garage under the railway bridge, in small, square, separate letters. The same hand as the caterer’s clipboard.

There was nothing else written on it. Not a word.

She turned it over.

It was an old photograph, hand-tinted, in colours that had never existed: the banking at Monza. The great concrete curve of the old oval, tilted up like a wall against a too-blue sky, with a single silver car from the fifties going round it, high up at the top, leaning in, impossible, the way she’d seen it once when she was nine years old, standing at the bottom of the banking in the rain with Nonna’s hand in hers.

She had told him that. At three in the morning, on the coast road, in January, when he was supposed to be asleep and wasn’t. She’d told him about the day Nonna took her to the old banking at Monza, which they didn’t race on any more, and let her walk on it, and how steep it was, and how she had tried to run up it and slid down and grazed both knees and Nonna had laughed and said, That’s where the brave ones went, cara. Round the top. Where it’s steepest. Never at the bottom.

He’d remembered. He had found, somewhere in whatever country he was in, a postcard of a place he had never seen, because a woman had mentioned it once at three in the morning, and he had written nothing on it, because there was nothing he was allowed to write.

It said everything.

Alive. Thinking of you. The brave ones go round the top.

Big Wu came in with the doughnuts and found her sitting on the floor by the post with the postcard in both hands, and stopped, and looked at it over her shoulder, and grunted.

“Monza,” he said. “Did he go to Italy?”

“I don’t know,” said Serafina, and laughed, wetly, with her face in the postcard. “I don’t know where he went. I don’t care where he went.”

She put it on the whiteboard. In the middle. Over the number plate, which she wiped off for the first time since October.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past two that night, she was lying on the mattress in the loft with the window open, not sleeping, listening to the trains.

She heard the car before she heard the brakes. It wasn’t his grey estate; that was still downstairs. It was something else, something with a diesel engine and a loose exhaust bracket, a taxi or a hire car, coming down the street of shuttered workshops much too slowly.

It stopped at the corner.

Then she heard footsteps. And then, at the bottom of the stairs, in the dark garage, she heard somebody stop by the kettle and pick up a mug, and put it down again, very carefully, exactly where it had been.

She was down the stairs before she knew she’d moved.

chapters.title: The Ring Was in the Glovebox
chapters.desc: She only wanted the tyre gauge. He had a plan in four parts and a speech he’d practised for eleven days. She says yes before he gets to part two. Then the coast road, the engine ticking, and the loft over the tracks, where they count trains.
chapters.epigraph: “I had a plan. It had four parts. You were supposed to let me finish.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
He was standing by the kettle in the dark with the plain mug in his hand.

He’d lost weight. That was the first thing she saw, before anything, before she’d reached the bottom stair: twelve days, and his face had gone thinner, sharper at the cheekbones, the shadows under his eyes gone from grey to nearly black. He was in clothes she had never seen, a brown jacket with a hood, jeans, cheap trainers, like a man who’d bought everything at an airport. He smelled of aeroplanes and somewhere cold.

He put the mug down.

She didn’t say anything. She crossed the garage and walked straight into him and put her arms round him under the brown jacket and held on, hard, with her face in his neck, and he made a sound she had never heard from him. Not the low surprised one. Something lower, much older, that seemed to come up out of the floor.

His arms came round her. Both of them. He held her so tight she couldn’t breathe and didn’t want to.

“The arm,” she said, into his neck.

“It’s here.”

“Show me.”

He let her go just far enough to push his left sleeve up, and held his forearm out under the dim light from the street, and there it was. Her long pink line. Paler now. Healing. The pucker at the eighth stitch.

She ran her thumb down it. Then she bent her head and kissed it, the whole length, from the elbow to the wrist, slowly, while he stood there in the dark garage and let her and didn’t breathe.

“You came back with it,” she said.

“I said I would.”

“You said maybe two weeks.”

“It was twelve days.” His voice wasn’t steady. She’d never heard his voice not be steady. “I counted.”

“So did I,” said Serafina, and laughed, and found she was crying, and didn’t care.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove him the loop. Of course she did.

He was asleep before the tunnel. She had known he would be. He’d slept, she guessed, perhaps fifteen hours in twelve days, in chairs by doors in rooms she would never see, and he went down in her passenger seat like a building being demolished, all at once, from the bottom. His head went onto her shoulder at the bridge and stayed there. She drove until seven in the morning, round and round, the ferries and the cranes and the long coast road, and the sun came up over the water and lit the side of his face, and he didn’t move, and neither did her shoulder.

When she pulled back in under the railway bridge he woke up, all at once, the soldier way, and looked at her.

“How long?”

“Four hours and six minutes.”

He closed his eyes again.

“That’s the longest,” he said, “since I was eighteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept again in the afternoon, upstairs, on the mattress in the loft, on top of the blankets in his airport clothes, while she was downstairs finishing his car.

She’d rebuilt the grey estate’s gearbox on Day Two, for something to do. Now she put it back together properly, and filled the bullet hole in the driver’s door at last, because he’d seen it, and sanded it, and primed it, and at four o’clock, when he came down the stairs with his hair flattened on one side and a crease from the blanket on his cheek, she was standing by the car with the keys.

“Test drive,” she said.

“Now?”

“The gearbox needs bedding in. And you need waking up. Get in.”

He got in. The passenger side. She noticed that he did it without thinking any more, the way you’d put on your own coat. She got in behind the wheel and moved the seat back four notches and adjusted his mirrors, which he watched with an expression of real pain, and then she leaned across him to the glovebox.

“Tyre gauge,” she said. “You keep one in here. I saw it in November.”

“Sera—”

She had the glovebox open.

The tyre gauge was there. A black one, cheap, from a petrol station. And beside it, pushed into the corner behind the car’s handbook, there was a small box. Old. Dark red leather, worn pale at the corners, with a brass clasp, the kind of box that had been opened and closed a great many times by a great many people over a very long time.

She stopped with her hand on the gauge.

Beside her, in the passenger seat, Qin Haozhen had gone completely still. Not the calm stillness. The other kind. The kind she’d seen at the east service door when a tray of glasses hit the floor.

“That’s not,” he said. “I was going to.”

She took the box out of the glovebox. She held it in her oily palm and looked at it, and then at him.

He had closed his eyes.

“I had a plan,” said Qin Haozhen. His voice was very level, which was how she knew. “It had four parts. The first part was the coast road, the lay-by, at three in the morning, because that’s where you asked me what I wanted, at New Year. The second part was what I was going to say. I’ve had eleven days to practise it. I practised it on a ferry. In a stairwell. In a hotel room on the floor by the door. It was quite long, and it had reasons in it, in order, and it began with the fact that I don’t know how to want things and that you said start small, and then it explained, carefully, that I’d tried, and this was the smallest thing I could find that was still true—”

“Yes,” said Serafina.

He opened his eyes.

“—and the third part was the ring, and the fourth part was an apology, in advance, for what I am, and the fact that you’d be marrying into a life with stairwells in it—”

“Yes,” said Serafina again, louder.

“You were supposed to let me finish.”

“I’m not letting you finish.” She had both hands round the little red box and she was laughing and her eyes were burning. “You can finish later. You can finish at the lay-by, you can finish every night for the rest of your life if you want, I’ll sit there and listen to the whole thing with the reasons in order. But I’m saying yes now, Haozhen. Before part two. I’m saying yes in a car in my garage with a tyre gauge in my hand, because if you think I’m waiting until three in the morning to say it you’ve learned nothing about how I drive.”

He stared at her.

Then he put his face in his hands, in the passenger seat of his own car, and his shoulders shook, and she thought for a terrible second that he was crying, and then she realised that he was laughing. Silently, helplessly, into his palms, the way a man laughs who has not done it in years and has forgotten where it goes.

“Open it,” he said, muffled.

She opened it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a ring from before the war. She knew that at once, before anything; she’d grown up in a family that bought jewellery the way other families bought bread, and she knew old gold when she saw it. Yellow gold, gone soft and warm with age, worn thin on one side where some woman’s other finger had rubbed against it for forty years. A plain band rising to a small square setting, four claws, and in the setting a single stone.

Red. Not pink, not purple. Red the way blood is red, or brake lights, or a 1992 Lancia Delta Integrale with its paint going pink at the edges.

“It’s the colour of your car,” said Qin Haozhen.

She couldn’t speak.

“There was a pawnshop,” he said. “In a city by a river. I can’t tell you its name. I walked past it every day on the way to—on the way. On the second day I went in. The man said it came from a family that left in a hurry, a long time ago. He said the stone was old and the woman who’d worn it had worked with her hands, because of how the band was worn.” He looked at the ring in her palm. “I don’t know anything about rings. I know that it’s red and someone wore it for a long time doing something difficult, and kept it on.”

Serafina took it out of the box.

It was too small for her ring finger. She’d known it would be; her hands were her father’s hands, long and bony, a mechanic’s hands with scars on the knuckles. It went on her little finger. It sat there, red and old and perfect, between the burn on the back of her hand and a fresh nick from a hose clamp.

“Aurelia,” she said, “is going to have opinions about the size.”

“I know.”

“She’ll want to resize it.”

“Let her,” said Qin Haozhen. “Just don’t let her make it new.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove the coast road with the ring on her little finger.

Not gently. Not the loop. She took the grey estate out from under the railway bridge in the last of the afternoon light and up onto the coast road and put her foot down, the way she never did with him in the car, the way she did at Granny Shum’s, and the new gearbox snicked through third and fourth like a knife through butter, and she took the long bends above the harbour flat, the steel in the doors leaning on the springs, the sea going by on the left gold and enormous, and she shouted. Wordlessly. Out of the open window. At the sea, at the sky, at the ferries.

He didn’t tell her to slow down. He sat in the passenger seat with his hand braced on the dashboard, laughing, actually laughing, out loud now, so she could hear it over the engine, and she thought that she would drive a car into the sea for that sound and not regret it.

She came back down into the industrial district at seven, in the dusk, and pulled in under the railway bridge so fast the tyres squealed on the concrete, and stopped, and pulled the handbrake, and turned off the engine.

The engine ticked.

Tick. Tick. The metal cooling in the dark garage, like a clock wound too far.

She turned in her seat. He was already looking at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She climbed over the gearstick.

It wasn’t graceful. Nothing about it was graceful; she banged her knee on the handbrake and swore and he caught her by the hips and pulled her the rest of the way and she landed in his lap, in the passenger seat of his own car, with her knees either side of him and her head bumping the roof and both of them laughing so hard they couldn’t kiss, and then they could, and then they weren’t laughing at all.

He kissed her like the paddock in December. Slow, thorough, as though there were a right way and he meant to find it. She didn’t let him. She kissed him back fast and hard, the way she’d driven the coast road, the way she took the fourth lamp post, and she felt him try to slow it, to take control of it, and she wouldn’t give it to him. She took his face in both hands and held it and kissed him until his breath went ragged, until his hands on her hips weren’t steady any more, until he made that low old sound again, against her mouth, the one that came up out of the floor. The windows were fogging. Her elbow hit the horn and it blared in the empty garage and neither of them stopped.

“Sera,” he said, against her throat. “Sera, the gearstick—”

“I know where the gearstick is.”

“It’s in my—”

“I know,” said Serafina, and pulled his jacket off his shoulders, the airport one, and threw it into the back seat, and got her hands under his shirt, flat on his bare back, on the long thin scar she’d only ever seen the start of, and felt his whole body jolt under her palms like a car going over a kerb.

He caught her wrists. Gently. He held them, and looked up at her in the fogged dark with his hair wrecked and his eyes almost black, and he was breathing as if he’d run up a flight of stairs.

“I’m trained,” he said, unsteadily, “to keep control. Of everything. Always. In every room.”

“I know.”

“I can’t,” said Qin Haozhen. “With you. I can’t keep it.”

She leaned down until her forehead was on his.

“Then don’t,” she said. “Let me have it. Just for tonight. Let me drive.”

He let go of her wrists.

✦ ✦ ✦

They made it to the loft eventually. She was never sure, afterwards, how. There were the stairs, and his shirt on the third one, and her vest on the landing, and her boots, which took a very long time and which he knelt on the top step to unlace for her while she sat on the edge of the mattress and laughed at him, and then stopped laughing, because of the way he did it. One lace at a time. His hands slow and sure on her ankles, as though they had all night. Then they did have all night, and there was nothing between them but the dark and the window open onto the railway, and his mouth on the inside of her knee, then higher, slow, and her hands in his hair, and the long breath she let out when he finally came up and over her, his weight on his arms, looking down at her as if he’d been waiting at a door for her for ten years and it had just opened.

She pulled him down.

She didn’t let him be careful. That was the whole of it, if she’d had to describe it, and she would never have to, because she’d never tell anyone, not even Aurelia, who would ask. He was careful the way he was careful with everything, and she wouldn’t let him be. She rolled him over onto the blankets and pinned his wrists and kissed him until he forgot to be, until she felt it go out of him, all of it, ten years of doors and stairwells and chairs by the door, and what was left under it was a man who laughed into her shoulder and said her name like something he’d found and held her as if the building were coming down.

The first train went over at nine minutes past ten.

The whole loft shook. The window rattled in its frame. The mattress trembled under them like a car at the line, and she laughed, breathless, into his neck, and felt him laughing too.

“That’s one,” she said.

“You’re counting.”

“I count everything.” She lifted her head and looked down at him in the orange light from the tracks. “Don’t you?”

His hands were on her back. His face, under her, was open in a way she had never seen any face be. Not calm. Not absent. Nothing put away.

“Not tonight,” said Qin Haozhen. “Tonight you can do it for both of us.”

She counted six.

At some point after the sixth, very late, with the window still open and the blanket kicked onto the floor and the red ring on her little finger catching the light from the railway every time a train went by, he finished his speech. All four parts. In order, with the reasons, in the dark, his mouth against her hair, while she lay with her head on his chest and listened to every word, and didn’t interrupt him once.

He was asleep before the seventh train.

She stayed awake for it, and the eighth, and the ninth, with her hand flat on his chest, and felt him sleep in a bed for the first time in ten years without a chair, without a door, without his clothes on, and he didn’t wake when the building shook. Not once.

chapters.title: Qin Haozhen Has Never Planned a Party
chapters.desc: He has stood at the door of eleven weddings and never once been inside one. Now he has a notebook, a run sheet for an engagement drinks timed to the minute, a form to fill in for the Bureau, and a fiancée who has just bought a burnt-out race car for scrap.
chapters.epigraph: “If I report it, she’s a fact. If I hide it, she’s a weakness.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
“Eleven,” he said.

“Eleven what?”

“Weddings.” He was sitting on the stool by the kettle with his black notebook open on his knee, on the Sunday after the glovebox, with the plain mug of hot water in his other hand. “I’ve been to eleven. In six countries. A minister’s daughter. A banker’s son. Two ambassadors. A man who ran a port.” He turned a page. “I stood at the door at every one. I’ve never been inside.”

Serafina was under Gilded. She rolled out on the creeper and looked up at him, upside down.

“Never?”

“Not once. I know how they end. Somebody drinks too much and somebody’s uncle makes a speech and the bride’s mother cries in the car park. I know where the fire exits are at the Harbour Hotel.” He looked at the notebook. “I don’t know what happens in the middle.”

“The middle’s the good bit.”

“I assumed,” said Qin Haozhen, “that it must be.” And he wrote something down.

She sat up on the creeper to see. At the top of the page, in his small square letters, underlined twice, it said WEDDING. Under it, a column. Date. Venue. Guests (number). Guests (who). Food. Her family?? My mother. Clothes. Rings (hers: resize, not new). Music. What happens in the middle.

And at the bottom, on its own, circled: Ask Mr. Kwok.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Kwok, asked, put down his wok.

He had been waiting, it turned out, for somebody to ask him this question for thirty years. His own daughter had married in a registry office in Vancouver in 1994 in jeans, and he had never recovered. He pulled out the stool beside the kettle and sat on it and put his hands on his knees, like a man about to give evidence.

“Nine courses,” he said. “Not eight. Not ten. Nine.”

Qin Haozhen wrote 9.

“The suckling pig first. Red skin, for luck, the whole thing, on a board, and the groom cuts it. The shark fin, no, not any more, we don’t do that now, my wife would come back from the grave. So the crab claw. Then the scallops with the green vegetable. Then the chicken, whole, with the head on, so the marriage has a beginning and an end. Then the fish. Whole. Head and tail. You never turn it over. If anybody turns it over you tell them to get out.” He held up a finger. “Then the noodles, long, for long life. Then the fried rice. Then the red bean soup. Then the little buns shaped like peaches, for the old people. Ten to a table. Round tables. Never square.” He paused. “Then the toasts. You go round every table with her and drink. Every one. You don’t sit down until you’ve done every table.”

“How many tables?”

“Depends how many people love you,” said Mr. Kwok, and looked at him for a long moment, and picked up his wok again. “Start counting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu’s advice was shorter.

“Don’t let her mother near it,” he said, from under the transporter.

“I’ve never met her mother.”

“Good,” said Big Wu. “Keep it that way. I’ve heard about her mother. Everyone in the industrial district has heard about her mother. She had a man following Sera for two years.” He rolled out from under the transporter and sat up and looked at Qin Haozhen, very seriously, with oil on his face. “You find that man. If he’s still at it. You find him and you explain things to him.”

“He stopped in 2019,” said Qin Haozhen. “Her brother-in-law spoke to him.”

Big Wu stared.

“How do you know that?”

Qin Haozhen didn’t answer. He wrote something in his notebook instead, and Big Wu, after a moment, lay back down on the creeper and rolled under the transporter again, and said from under it, in a different voice, “Right. Course you know that.”

Mouse didn’t give any advice. But that night, on the end of the workbench, beside the kettle, there was a printed sheet of paper. It had a table on it with forty rows. The rows were numbered. Most of them were empty. In the first seven, in Mouse’s tiny handwriting, it said: Big Wu. Big Wu’s ma. Mr. Kwok. Me. Aurelia. Aurelia’s husband. Granny Shum (she won’t come but ask).

At the top it said GUESTS (WHO).

He looked at it.

Then he put it in his notebook, folded once, very carefully, at the page that said WEDDING.

✦ ✦ ✦

The date was the problem.

“Autumn,” she said, on the coast road, at three in the morning. “October. When it’s cool. Before the rain.”

He didn’t answer.

She looked across. He wasn’t asleep. He was looking out of the passenger window at the dark water, and his face had gone the way it went when he was reading a room.

“I can’t give you a date,” he said.

“Because of them.”

“Because they give me a date. A week before. Sometimes a day.” He was quiet. “If I tell you October the fourteenth and they put me on a plane on the twelfth, then you’re standing in a room with nine courses and a whole fish and no groom. And your mother in the car park.”

“I don’t care about the fish.”

“I do,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve stood at the door of eleven weddings. I’m not going to miss the middle of my own.”

She drove for a while.

“Then we don’t set a date,” said Serafina. “We set a when. When it’s safe. When you can stand in a room for nine courses and nobody’s going to ring you. Whenever that is.” She glanced at him. “I don’t need a party, Hao. I need you at the end of an aisle that isn’t in a stairwell. Everything else is extra.”

It was the first time she had called him Hao. She hadn’t planned to. It had come out of her on the coast road the way the turbo came in at the top of second, by itself, with a whistle.

He turned his head from the window and looked at her.

“Say that again,” he said.

“What?”

“You know what.”

She didn’t. She smiled at the windscreen instead, and put her foot down, just a little, so the turbo came in, and didn’t say it again until the tunnel.

✦ ✦ ✦

He filled in the form on the Thursday.

She found it on the workbench, in the morning, next to the kettle, where he’d left it while he went to get the egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover, which he now did on his own, every Thursday, as if it were a duty. It was two pages. Printed. A crest at the top she didn’t recognise, a seal with something stylised on it, and a reference number, and a title.

NOTIFICATION OF CHANGE IN PERSONAL CIRCUMSTANCES.

Under Nature of change, in his square letters, it said Engagement to be married. Under Name of other party it said SONG Serafina. Under Occupation of other party: Racing driver. Mechanic. Under Known associations of other party, it said Song family (Milan, the Peak). Sister married to CHEN Si. And then, a line below, very small: No relevant concerns.

She was still holding it when he came in.

“You’re telling them,” she said.

He put the sandwiches down. He looked at the form in her hands.

“Yes.”

“You’re telling the people with the white van at the petrol station that you’re marrying me. With my name. In capitals.”

“Yes.”

“Why would you do that?”

He took his time. He took the form out of her hands, gently, and smoothed it flat on the bench, and looked at it.

“Because they’ll know anyway,” he said. “In a month, or six. Someone will see the ring. Someone will see me at the circuit. They watch everyone. They watch the people who watch everyone.” He touched the place where her name was. “If I report it, you’re a fact. You’re on a form, in a drawer, no relevant concerns. A fact is boring. Nobody looks at a fact twice.” He looked at her. “If I hide it, and they find it, you’re a secret. And a secret they find is a weakness. And they look at weaknesses very carefully, Sera. For years.”

She looked at the form. No relevant concerns.

“I don’t like it,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’d rather they didn’t know I existed.”

“So would I,” said Qin Haozhen. “But you walked across a ballroom on Battery Hill in your sister’s dress and told me what I was. You were never going to be someone who didn’t exist.” He folded the form in three and put it in an envelope. “This is the next best thing. It makes you boring.”

“I’m not boring.”

“No,” he agreed. “That’s why I have to lie about it on page two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The engagement drinks were on the second Saturday in April, and he planned them like an operation.

She found the run sheet afterwards, in his notebook. It was a single page. 19:00 Arrivals (side door; shutter down). 19:04 Drinks (Chinotto for Mouse, beer for Big Wu, Big Wu’s ma: brandy, small). 19:10 Mr. Kwok’s food, served. 19:25 Toast (me; 40 seconds). 19:26 Ring shown to guests. 19:30 Aurelia arrives (late; she will be late). 19:45 Cake. 20:30 Guests leave. Contingencies: (1) Big Wu cries. (2) Rain. (3) Granny Shum.

It went wrong at 19:02, when Big Wu’s mother arrived early with a whole roast duck under her arm in a plastic bag and announced that she would be in charge of the food, and Mr. Kwok, who had been planning the food for a week, said that over his dead body she would, and Big Wu’s mother, who was eighty-three and the height of a fire hydrant, said that could be arranged.

It went wrong again at 19:04, when Granny Shum came. Nobody had thought she would come. She came in through the side door on the arm of her bored granddaughter, with her folding chair and her thermos and her scanner round her neck, and set the chair up in the middle of the garage floor, and sat in it, and said, “Where’s the taxi,” and when Qin Haozhen came to stand in front of her she looked up at him and then handed him a clementine and said, “You’ll do.”

And at 19:25, when he stood up to make his toast, forty seconds, he had timed it, a train went over the railway bridge, and the whole garage shook, and the spanner fell into the bucket, and in the noise he stood there with his beer raised and his mouth open, and waited for it to pass, very patiently, and when it had passed he’d forgotten every word.

Everyone looked at him.

Serafina, beside him, felt him go still.

He looked round the garage. At the trestle table with Big Wu’s mother’s duck on it and Mr. Kwok’s nine dishes, because Mr. Kwok had done nine anyway. At Big Wu, already crying, contingency one. At Mouse, at the end of the bench, with her Chinotto. At Granny Shum in her folding chair. At the whiteboard with the postcard of the Monza banking in the middle of it.

“I had a speech,” he said. “It was forty seconds.”

“We’ll wait,” said Granny Shum.

“I’ve forgotten it.” He was quiet. “I’ve stood at the door of eleven weddings and I always wondered what happened in the middle. I think this is it.” He lifted the beer a little higher. “To the middle.”

There was a silence.

Then Big Wu said, “To the middle,” thickly, and drank, and so did everyone, and Mr. Kwok said it was a terrible speech and the best one he’d heard since 1994, and Aurelia came in through the side door at 19:31, one minute after the run sheet said she would, in gold, alone, because Chen Si was in Rotterdam, with a box of pastries from the Milanese bakery on Harbour Road, and said, “What did I miss,” and nobody could tell her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car arrived on the Monday.

It came on the back of a flatbed lorry from a salvage auction in the port, under a tarpaulin, and the driver backed it in under the shutter and tipped it off onto the concrete with a noise like a bin lorry dropping a skip, and drove away very fast before anyone could ask him to take it back.

They stood round it.

It wasn’t a car. It had been a car once. Now it was a shell: a long, low, flat carbon tub, black and blistered, with the remains of a bodywork that swept back over where the wheels had been into a tail like a shark’s. No engine. No wheels. No glass. The cockpit was a burnt hollow. Something had melted across the nose and set again in a frozen dribble.

“What,” said Big Wu, “is that.”

“A 1991 endurance prototype,” said Serafina. She was walking round it with her hands in her pockets and her face shining. “Built for Le Mans. For the long straight. The old ones did four hundred an hour on it before they put the chicanes in, in 1990. This one came the year after and still did three-fifty. This one was in a museum warehouse that burned down in 2009. Nobody wanted it. I got it for nine thousand. That’s the scrap price for the carbon.”

“It’s a coffin,” said Big Wu.

“It’s a car.”

“It’s a coffin that used to be a car.”

Qin Haozhen didn’t say anything. He was crouched by the nose, where the melted thing was, looking at it closely, the way he’d looked at the rivets on the forged chassis plate in October. Then he looked up at her.

“What are you going to do with it?”

“Make it go two hundred miles an hour,” said Serafina.

“Three hundred and twenty-two kilometres,” said Qin Haozhen.

“Two hundred miles an hour,” said Serafina firmly. “It sounds better in miles. Everything fast sounds better in miles. Nonna used to say it.” She crouched down beside him by the burnt nose and put her hand on the carbon, flat, the way you’d put your hand on a horse. “She took me to Monza. I told you. The brave ones went round the top, she said, where it’s steepest. When I was nine I asked her what the fastest anyone had ever gone was, and she said, in miles, because she was being dramatic, two hundred miles an hour, cara. That’s the top. So.” She shrugged. “That’s the top. I want to go there. Once. In something I built.”

He looked at her, in the noise of the trains.

Then he took out his notebook, and opened it, not at the page that said WEDDING but at a new one, and wrote something at the top of it, and underlined it twice.

She leaned over to read it.

Two hundred.

And under it, in smaller letters, as if it were just another item on a list:

Find out how.

chapters.title: Aurelia Finds Out Who Pays for the Racing Team
chapters.desc: A splitter that was already paid for. A gearbox from Germany nobody ordered on her account. A company with one director and ten years of salary behind it. Two sisters, one table at Da Gianni, and a lunch the whole restaurant will remember.
chapters.epigraph: “Your sister pays because she couldn’t go with you. I paid because I might not be able to stay.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
Aurelia did the team’s books on the first Friday of every quarter, at two in the morning, at her bench in the workshop behind the boutique on Harbour Road, with a pencil behind her ear and a cup of cold coffee and Enzo’s radio playing opera very quietly in the dark.

She had done it since December 2019, since the night in the garage under the railway bridge when she’d found clause fourteen of a tyre contract and rebuilt the sponsorship deck before dawn. She did it because she was good at it, and because nobody else would, and because it was the only part of her sister’s life that Serafina let her touch without arguing. Every invoice. Every part. Every entry fee and hotel bill and tank of fuel. She knew what Team AURELIA had spent on tyres in the third quarter of 2021 to the cent, and why, and whether they’d been overcharged, which they had, and she had rung the tyre company about it herself.

So she noticed the splitter.

Four thousand two hundred, from the March test, when Sera had gone into the gravel at the Needle. Aurelia had said she’d pay. She’d meant it. She had the invoice in front of her, from the carbon shop in the north, and she went to pay it, and found it stamped PAID IN FULL, on the eighth of March, two days before she’d even seen it.

Not by her.

She sat back. She took the pencil from behind her ear.

Then she went back through the quarter, line by line, the way she’d once gone through four ledgers at a basement table in the old town, and found the rest.

✦ ✦ ✦

“A gearbox,” she said, at Da Gianni, at one o’clock on Saturday, at the table by the window. “Sequential. From the people in Germany you’ve been begging for since 2021. Thirty-eight thousand. Paid on the first of April, direct to the supplier. A full set of brakes, discs and calipers, both axles, eleven thousand. The new engine in the transporter, which Mr. Kwok has been praying for, nine thousand four hundred. And my splitter.”

Serafina, opposite her, had stopped with a forkful of risotto halfway to her mouth.

“Your splitter?”

“I said I’d pay for it. It was paid already. On the eighth of March.” Aurelia laid four invoices on the white tablecloth between the bread basket and the olive oil, side by side, the way she laid out stones. “Sixty-two thousand six hundred, in a quarter. Not from me. Not from any sponsor on the deck. From a company called Northgate Services, which has one director, no employees, no website, no office, and an address in a building in the capital that turns out to be a post box.”

“I don’t know who that is.”

“I know you don’t. I could see from your face before I’d finished the word gearbox.” Aurelia picked up her wine. “So I asked Qian.”

“Chen Si’s Qian?”

“There is only one Qian.” Aurelia drank. “He took a day and a half and ate four antacids and came back with a name.”

She put a fifth piece of paper on the tablecloth. It was a single printed page. A bank statement, from a state bank in the capital, a salary account. Ten years of it, in columns, on one page, because it was so simple. A deposit on the twenty-fifth of every month since June 2012. The same amount, give or take a little for promotions. And almost nothing going out. Rent on a flat above a laundry, every month. A transfer, every month, to an account in a mining town in the north. A dentist, once, in 2017. And then, this spring, four enormous withdrawals, in a row, to Northgate Services.

At the top, the account holder’s name.

Serafina put her fork down.

“He did what,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant had been quite full. Da Gianni was always quite full at Saturday lunch: bankers, mostly, and women who had been shopping on Harbour Road, and a long table of Italian businessmen near the back celebrating something. It got much quieter, very quickly, when Serafina Song stood up out of her chair and said, at a volume she normally kept for the pit wall, “He paid for my GEARBOX?”

“Sit down,” said Aurelia.

“With his salary?”

“Sera. Sit down. The man at the next table has stopped chewing.”

“I don’t care about the man at the next table!” Serafina did not sit down. She stood beside the window in her leather jacket with the bank statement in her hand and her face going red. “Ten years! He’s had that money ten years! He doesn’t spend anything! He lives above a laundry! He doesn’t have curtains! Mouse says he uses less electricity than the cat!”

“What cat?”

“The laundry’s cat! It has a heated bed!” Serafina waved the statement. “And he took it out, all of it, a quarter of it, and he gave it to a post box in the capital, so the post box could buy me a gearbox, and he didn’t tell me—”

“I know exactly how that feels,” said Aurelia. “Sit down. I’ll explain it to you.”

Serafina looked at her.

Aurelia looked back, over the rim of her glass, with an expression Serafina had not seen since a night in October 2019, in a garage under a railway bridge, when the two of them had stood over a folder of receipts from a bank in Luxembourg.

Serafina sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I didn’t tell you either,” said Aurelia. “For two years. Do you remember why?”

“Because I’d have stopped taking it.”

“Because you’d have stopped taking it.” Aurelia set down her glass. “And because I couldn’t go with you. I stood at the top of the stairs and watched you walk out of that house and I didn’t say a word, and the money was the only brave thing I knew how to do. I’ve told you this.” She tapped the bank statement. “So. Ask yourself why a man who has never spent a cent on himself in ten years would spend a quarter of all of it on you, in one spring, without saying anything.”

Serafina didn’t answer.

“I’ll tell you what I think,” said Aurelia. “And you’ll tell me if I’m wrong.” She folded her hands on the tablecloth. “I think he isn’t sure he can stay.”

The long table of Italian businessmen at the back had gone back to their celebration. The man at the next table had started chewing again. Outside the window, Harbour Road went by in the April sun, trams and shoppers and the gold letters over the door of number eighteen, two hundred metres away.

“I think,” said Aurelia, “that he’s in some kind of work where people don’t always get to stay, and he knows it, and he’s done the sum. And he wanted the car to keep running whatever happened to him.” She looked at her sister. “That’s what I’d do. That’s what I did do, in a way. Chen Si would do the same. Zhao would buy you a tank.”

“I don’t want a tank.”

“Nobody wants a tank, Sera. That isn’t the point of a tank.” Aurelia reached across the table. “Now give me your hand. The left one. I’ve been looking at that ring for a week and you keep putting it in your pocket.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at it for a long time.

She took a loupe out of her handbag, the small gold one she kept for clients who thought they could fool her, and held her sister’s hand flat on the white tablecloth with the ring on its little finger and bent over it, the way their grandmother had bent over a watch in Geneva in 1968 and argued for two hours about a balance cock. Serafina sat with her hand out and her face still red and watched her.
