“Yellow gold,” said Aurelia, to the loupe. “Eighteen carat. Handmade, not cast, you can see the file marks inside the shank. Probably 1930s. The band’s worn thin on the side toward the middle finger. Whoever wore it worked with her hands. A seamstress, maybe. Something with a lot of small movements.” She turned the hand very slightly toward the window. “The stone’s a ruby. Not glass, not synthetic. Old cut. Burmese, I think, from the colour. They call it pigeon’s blood.” She was quiet for a moment. “It’s a very good stone, Sera.”

“Is it?”

“It’s a very good stone that he paid about a third too much for, to a man in a pawnshop who saw him coming.” Aurelia lowered the loupe. Something had happened to her face. “He didn’t haggle. He didn’t know how much it was worth. He just saw that it was red.”

“He said it was the colour of my car.”

Aurelia looked at her.

Then, at the table by the window in Da Gianni, in front of the bankers and the shoppers and the long table of Italians, Aurelia Chen put the loupe down and laughed out loud, the bark, the one from the balcony, and wiped her eyes with her napkin.

“I like him,” she said. “Oh, God help me. I like him.”

“You’ve met him once. For an hour. He forgot his speech.”

“That was plenty. He overpaid for a ruby because it was the colour of a thirty-year-old Lancia.” Aurelia picked up her wine again. “I’ll resize it. Properly. For your ring finger.”

“Not new,” said Serafina. “He said don’t make it new.”

“Of course not new. I’m not a barbarian.” Aurelia looked at the ring again. “I’ll open the shank at the back and put in a piece of the same gold, from the same period. I’ve got some, from Nonna’s earrings, the last of them. You won’t see the join. Enzo won’t see the join.” She paused. “What does he do?”

“Security.”

Aurelia looked at her sister over the rim of her glass.

“Security,” she said.

“Chen Si,” said Aurelia, “is going to want to have him to dinner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at two in the morning. Of course he did.

She was waiting for him. She was sitting on the bonnet of Gilded in the middle of the garage, under the hanging lamp, with the five pieces of paper from Da Gianni laid out beside her on the matte black paint in a row. The splitter. The gearbox. The brakes. The transporter’s engine. And the bank statement.

He came in through the side door. He stopped.

He looked at the row of paper. Then at her face. She saw him read it, the way he read rooms, and she saw him get to the end, and she saw him understand, and she saw him not try to get out of it.

“Your sister,” he said.

“My sister. And Qian, with four antacids.”

He closed the side door behind him. He stood with his back to it.

“You needed a gearbox,” he said.

“I’ve needed a gearbox since 2021.”

“Yes. The old one was going. Big Wu said so. In January. You were going to lose third at the first race in April and you’d have gone into the wall at the long right on the second lap. I heard it on the track day. The noise in third.”

“With your salary, Haozhen.”

“I never spent it. I didn’t have anything to spend it on.” He said it simply. “I didn’t want anything. I told you. For ten years I didn’t want anything. And then I did, and it was a gearbox, and I could get it.” A pause. “It’s the first thing I’ve bought in ten years that wasn’t on a form.”

She slid off the bonnet. She walked across the garage to him and stood in front of him, and he looked at her and didn’t move.

“Aurelia thinks you’re not sure you can stay,” she said.

He was quiet. A train went over. The garage shook round them.

“Your sister pays because she couldn’t go with you,” said Qin Haozhen, when it had passed. “I paid because I might not be able to stay. I wanted the car to keep running. Whatever happens. I wanted to know that if one day I don’t come back from a stairwell, you’ll still have third gear at the long right.” His voice didn’t change at all. “I didn’t tell you because you’d have asked me why. And then I’d have had to say it. Like this.”

She hit him.

Not hard. She hit him on the chest with the flat of her hand, once, and then again, and then she took a fistful of his jacket in both hands and held on, the way she’d held on in the paddock in December, and put her forehead against his collarbone.

“You don’t get to buy me a gearbox in case you die,” she said into his jacket. “That’s not a thing. You don’t get to do that.”

“All right.”

“You come back from every stairwell. That’s the deal. That’s the whole deal.”

“All right,” said Qin Haozhen. His hand was on the back of her head. “I’ll come back from every stairwell.”

“And no more secret money.”

“No more secret money.”

“You put your name on it,” said Serafina. “If you’re paying, you put your name on it. Like Aurelia did. Gold, on the bonnet, where everyone can see.”

He went still under her hands.

“I can’t put my name on a car, Sera.”

She lifted her head. She knew. She’d known before she said it. She looked at him in the light from the hanging lamp, his face very close, very tired, very careful, and she thought of a form in an envelope that said no relevant concerns, and a man whose eyes slid off cameras.

“No,” she said. “I know you can’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, Big Wu found a sticker on Gilded.

It was on the driver’s door, low down, just above the sill, where you’d only see it if you were crouching to check the tyre pressures. Small. The size of a thumbnail. Cut out of grey vinyl, very carefully, with a craft knife, by somebody who had sat up very late doing it at the end of the workbench with Mouse’s magnifying lamp.

It was the shape of a plain estate car. The kind taxi firms bought by the dozen.

Big Wu crouched and looked at it. Then he went and got the clear lacquer, the good stuff, and gave it three coats, so that it would stay on through anything.

chapters.title: Two Professionals at One Table
chapters.desc: The forty-fourth floor. Chen Si cooks. Aurelia gives back the ruby, resized with the last of their grandmother’s gold. And on the balcony after dinner, two men who are very good at the same things recognise each other without either of them saying what they are.
chapters.epigraph: “In my house we have a sentence for it. ‘I can’t tell you that yet.’ You’ll find it saves a great deal of furniture.” — Chen Si
chapters.content:
“He’ll sit facing the door,” said Serafina, in the lift.

“What?”

“Chen Si. He’ll sit facing the door. So will you. You’ll both go for the same chair and one of you will have to sit with your back to the room, and I want to watch.”

The lift went up the Coastal High-Rise like a held breath. Forty-four floors, the numbers going by in white on a little black screen. He stood beside her in a dark suit, the forgettable one, and a white shirt, and no tie, and he had shaved twice; she’d heard the razor go at six and again at seven. He was holding a bottle of wine he had chosen at a shop on Harbour Road after forty minutes and a conversation with the owner that Serafina had watched through the window and would remember for the rest of her life.

“I won’t fight him for a chair,” he said.

“You will. You won’t even know you’re doing it.”

He looked at the numbers going by.

“I’ve read about him,” he said. “That’s all. There’s a file.”

“On Chen Si?”

“There’s a file on everybody who matters in this city.” He was quiet. “His is very thick and says very little. That’s the mark of someone who’s good.”

“And yours?”

“Mine’s thin,” said Qin Haozhen, “and says nothing at all.”

The lift stopped. The doors opened onto a corridor with one door at the end of it, and in the door, holding it open, there was a small, tired, kind-faced man in glasses with a packet of antacids in his top pocket, who looked at Haozhen for a full three seconds without blinking.

“Mr. Qin,” said Qian. “Welcome. You don’t exist.”

“Thank you,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat facing the door.

So did Chen Si. They did it at the same time, from opposite ends of the long table by the window, with the whole harbour lit up behind the glass. Both of them pulled out the chair that let them see the door to the corridor and the door to the kitchen and the reflection of both in the window, and both of them stopped, with their hands on the chair backs, and looked at each other down the length of the table.

Aurelia, at the kitchen counter with a glass of wine, said “Oh, for heaven’s sake,” under her breath.

Serafina, beside her, was so happy she had to bite her lip.

There was a pause of perhaps a second and a half.

Then Chen Si inclined his head, very slightly, as if conceding a point in a negotiation he had expected to lose, and moved round to the side of the table, and sat with his back to the window and the harbour, and only the reflection to watch the door by. Haozhen sat where he was. He did not look triumphant. He looked, if anything, mildly apologetic.

“Thank you,” he said.

“You’re a guest,” said Chen Si. “And she’d have made us flip a coin.” He picked up the wine Haozhen had brought and turned the label to the light. “This is good. The man on Harbour Road?”

“Yes.”

“He doesn’t sell this one to people he doesn’t like.”

“He asked me a lot of questions,” said Qin Haozhen. “I answered them.”

Chen Si looked at him across the table for a moment, and Serafina saw something in his face she had only seen once before, at the circuit in the north in December 2019, when her sister had sat in the front row in every piece of gold she owned: a look of quiet, absorbed attention, as if he were committing something to memory.

“I’ll open it,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

He cooked. Aurelia had told her he would. Braised beef with star anise and dried tangerine peel, done since the afternoon until it fell apart at a look; greens with garlic; a soup with lotus root; rice. No fish.

“I was told,” said Chen Si, putting the beef on the table, “in red ink, on a piece of my own paper, no fish. Underlined.”

“She hates fish,” said Aurelia.

“I’ve noticed,” said Haozhen.

Serafina looked at him.

“You’ve never seen me not eat fish.”

“At the reunion dinner. Mr. Kwok made a whole one. You put rice over your piece so he wouldn’t see you hadn’t eaten it, and gave it to Big Wu’s mother when she wasn’t looking.” He picked up his chopsticks. “Big Wu’s mother saw. She didn’t say anything. She ate it.”

Aurelia put down her glass and looked at her sister’s fiancé for a long moment.

“How long have you been watching my sister?” she said.

“Since the twenty-second of October,” said Qin Haozhen, “at nine twenty-two.”

It went quiet at the table. Not uncomfortable. Just quiet, the four of them and the harbour.

Then Aurelia laughed, the bark, and said, “Oh, he’s as bad as you,” to her husband, and Chen Si said, “Worse. I didn’t know the minute,” and served the beef.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the beef, Aurelia gave back the ring.

She’d brought it in a box from the boutique, a plain cream one with AURELIA on the lid in gold, and she put it on the table in front of Serafina between the soup bowls and, for once in her life, didn’t say anything at all. Serafina opened it.

The ruby sat in its old claws, red as a brake light. The band looked exactly as it had. She turned it to the light from the harbour and looked for the join where Aurelia had opened the shank and put in new gold, and she couldn’t find it. She looked again.

“It’s there,” said Aurelia. “Inside. At the back. Four millimetres.” She was looking at her own hands. “It’s Nonna’s. The last of the earrings. The ones she wore to Geneva.”

Serafina couldn’t say anything.

She took the ring out. She held it out to the man beside her, across the corner of the table, on her open palm, the way she’d held out her hand to Chen Si once, at a circuit, covered in oil and champagne.

He looked at it. Then at her.

Then he took it, and took her left hand, and put the ring on her ring finger, where it went on easily and stopped where it should, and sat there as though it had always been there, between the old burn on the back of her right hand and nothing at all on her left, and he didn’t let go of her hand afterwards. He kept it, under the edge of the table, in his, on his knee.

Under the table, Serafina found his ankle with her boot, and stayed there.

Across the table, Aurelia had picked up her wine and was looking out at the harbour very hard.

“Lia,” said Serafina.

“Don’t,” said Aurelia. “Don’t say anything. If you say anything I’ll cry on my own tablecloth, and Chen Si will never let me forget it.”

“I won’t,” said Chen Si. “I’ll write it in the margin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten, Chen Si took him out onto the balcony.

He did it without saying anything; he simply picked up the bottle of wine, and two glasses, and went to the long glass door, and looked back, and Haozhen got up and followed him. The sisters stayed inside on the long grey sofa with their feet tucked under them and their heads together, Serafina talking very fast and Aurelia looking at the ruby, and neither of them pretended not to watch the balcony through the glass.

“Look at them,” said Serafina.

“I’m looking.”

“They’re standing exactly the same. Look. Both of them. Back to the wall. Facing the door.”

“There’s no door,” said Aurelia. “It’s a balcony. On the forty-fourth floor.”

“They’re facing where a door would be,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

The balcony was narrow and long and went round the corner of the building, and forty-four floors below it the harbour lay black and glittering, and the wind came up off the water and moved Chen Si’s hair.

He poured two glasses. He held one out. Haozhen took it, and didn’t drink, and Chen Si noticed, and didn’t drink his either, and they stood with the glasses in their hands like two men holding something for someone else.

“The Eleventh,” said Chen Si.

He said it to the harbour, pleasantly, the way you’d remark on the weather.

Haozhen didn’t move.

“I can’t tell you that,” he said.

“You just did,” said Chen Si. “By how long you took to say it.” He turned the glass slowly in his fingers. “I’ve met three of you. In twelve years. One at a port in 2014, posing as a customs officer. One at a funeral. One at a hotel in the capital, at a breakfast, holding a teapot.” He looked at the water. “You stand the same. All three of you stood the same. Weight on the back foot. Hands where people can see them. Looking at the space just past whoever’s talking.” A pause. “The teapot one was very good. You’re better.”

“Thank you.”

“It wasn’t a compliment,” said Chen Si. “It was a description.” He was quiet for a moment. “I read about your kind before I’d met one. At sixteen. In a cell. They had a file on my father. They had a file on me. I was sixteen and someone had decided I was worth a file.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve read it.”

Chen Si turned his head and looked at him.

It was not a long look. But Haozhen felt it go through him the way he knew his own went through people, and he let it, and didn’t put anything in the way.

“Block C,” said Chen Si.

“Block C. The riot. The bed slat. The drain.” Haozhen looked at the glass in his hand. “It’s three pages. It says you and another boy went into the drain in the snow and came out the other side. It doesn’t say how.” He paused. “It doesn’t say much about the other boy. A surname. Wang. Nobody ever found a Wang.”

Chen Si was quiet.

“No,” he said finally. “Nobody would have.” He looked at the water. “It was the first name we could think of in the snow.”

They stood on the balcony and looked at the harbour. Inside, behind the glass, Serafina said something and Aurelia laughed, the bark, and put her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Does she know?” said Chen Si.

“Yes.”

“All of it?”

Haozhen didn’t answer at once.

“No,” he said. “She knows what I am. She guessed it. She laid it out on her workbench with car parts, in January, in order, and I told her she was right.” He looked at the wine. “She doesn’t know the number. I told her to ask me again in a year.”

“And if she asks?”

“I’ll tell her.”

“All of it.”

“All of it,” said Qin Haozhen. “Names. Dates. What they were wearing.”

Chen Si turned his glass round once more, slowly, in the wind.

“In my house,” he said, “there’s a contract. Eleven pages. My wife wrote it in red ink. Clause three says neither of us will lie to the other, about anything. And there’s a sentence we use, when the truth is something we can’t say yet.” He looked at Haozhen. “I can’t tell you that yet. You say it, and the other one waits. And then one day you can, and you do.” A pause. “You’ll find it saves a great deal of furniture.”

“She has a rule,” said Qin Haozhen. “It’s rule one. It’s the same.”

“Of course it is,” said Chen Si. “They had the same grandmother.”

He took a card out of his inside pocket. Cream. Heavy. Nothing on it but a telephone number, written by hand in black ink.

“If you ever need a door,” he said, and held it out. “Not a car. She’ll be the car. A door.”

Haozhen took it. He looked at it. He put it in his own inside pocket, against his chest, where he kept the notebook.

“And if anything ever comes to her through you,” said Chen Si, in exactly the same pleasant voice, looking out at the water, “anything at all, from anyone in the capital, I will know about it before you do. And I won’t be polite.”

“Good,” said Qin Haozhen.

Chen Si glanced at him.

“Good,” said Haozhen again. “I’d rather there were two of us.”

Something moved at the corner of Chen Si’s mouth.

Then, at last, both of them drank, at the same moment, as if a signal had passed between them that nobody else could see.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He’s very good,” said Haozhen, in the lift, going down.

Serafina was leaning against the mirrored wall with her left hand held up in front of her face, turning it, so the ruby caught the light. She had been doing it since they’d left the flat.

“At what?”

“Everything I’m good at.”

“Is that a problem?”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. He looked at her in the mirror, at the ring, at her face. “It’s a relief. He’d have found me anyway. Now he knows I’m not hiding.”

The lift was at thirty. Twenty-nine. She pushed herself off the mirrored wall and took two steps across it and kissed him, hard, with her left hand on his jaw and the ring cold against his skin, and he made the low sound in his throat and backed her into the mirror on the other side, and they kissed all the way down from twenty-nine to the lobby, past twenty and fifteen and the floor where the lift always lurched, his hands at her waist and hers in his hair and her laugh going into his mouth every time the lift jolted.

The doors opened on the ground floor.

Qian was standing in the lobby with his coat on and his car keys in his hand, waiting to go home.

He looked at them for three seconds without blinking.

Then he took the packet of antacids out of his top pocket, and took two, and walked past them into the lift, and pressed the button for forty-four, and said, as the doors closed, very mildly, “Congratulations, Miss Song. He still doesn’t exist,” and was gone.

chapters.title: Director Duan Sends Congratulations
chapters.desc: A tea house in the old town, a red scarf that has been on the needles since 2012, and a woman who never raises her voice. She has read his form. She knows about the braised beef. Her wedding present is a silver pen with a number engraved on it.
chapters.epigraph: “We look after our families, Haozhen. You know that. It’s in the training.” — Director Duan Qiuyan
chapters.content:
The tea house was on the second floor of a building in the old town that had been a pawnshop, then a printing works, then a pawnshop again, and was now called the Pavilion of Clear Springs, though there was no spring and nothing in it was clear. You went up a narrow wooden stair from a lane that smelled of dried fish. At the top there were twelve tables and a man who boiled water in a copper kettle and never looked at anyone’s face.

She was at the back, by the window with the bamboo blind half down. She was always at the back.

Director Duan Qiuyan was fifty-five. She had a neat grey bob and reading glasses on a chain round her neck and a grey cardigan with a hole at one elbow that she had darned in a slightly different grey, and she was knitting. She was always knitting. The same scarf. Red wool, ribbed, on two bamboo needles, and it had been on those needles the day she walked into the commandant’s office at the State Military Academy in June 2012 and asked to see the eighteen-year-old who never hesitated. It was perhaps two metres long now. It had never, as far as anyone knew, been finished.

“Sit,” she said, without looking up. “I’ve ordered for you. Hot water. You still don’t drink tea.”

He sat. Facing the door, by the reflection in the window. She had left him that chair. She always did.

“Director.”

“Haozhen.” The needles clicked. “Congratulations.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had the form.

She took it out of a canvas shopping bag on the floor beside her chair, between a bag of oranges and the wool, and laid it on the table between the teacups, smoothed flat. His form. His square letters. NOTIFICATION OF CHANGE IN PERSONAL CIRCUMSTANCES. Engagement to be married. SONG Serafina. Racing driver. Mechanic.

“No relevant concerns,” she read aloud, and looked at him over the top of her glasses. “You wrote that.”

“Yes.”

“In your own hand.”

“Yes.”

“You know, I thought about framing it.” The needles went on. “Ten years, I’ve had your forms. Change of address, twice. Dentist, once. Annual medical, sleeping well, every year, which is a lie and the doctor knows it’s a lie and writes it down anyway because you’re very convincing. And then this.” She tapped it with the end of a needle. “Engagement. I read it on the train. A woman across the aisle asked me if I’d had good news.”

He didn’t say anything.

“I’m pleased for you,” said Director Duan. She said it gently. She said everything gently. In ten years he had never once heard her raise her voice, and he had seen her end a man’s career, and a man’s marriage, and once, in a hotel in a country he would not name, a man. “Truly. I’m pleased. I’ve always worried about you. You know that. You were the youngest I ever took. You never had anything. You’d sleep in a chair outside a door for a week and come back and fill in the form and never complain.” The needles clicked. “I used to think, one day that boy will find something, and I’ll have to decide what to do about it.”

“And have you?”

“Decided?” She looked up. “Of course. Last night. On the train.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew everything. He had known she would. It still went into him like cold water.

She didn’t list it. She was too good to list it. She mentioned it, the way you’d mention the weather, between rows, while the man with the copper kettle came and filled their cups and went away again.

“Team AURELIA,” she said. “Second in the series last year, I think, on a very small budget. A new gearbox this spring. Sequential. German.” A row. “I’m told she still goes to the industrial district on Saturdays. To an old woman with a folding chair. They changed the law about that, didn’t they, in 2019? Three years.” Another row. “And you had dinner on the forty-fourth floor of the Coastal High-Rise. With Chen Si. Braised beef, I’m told. And you sat facing the door, and he let you.”

He held his cup of hot water and didn’t drink it.

“Chen Si,” said Director Duan, “has a very thick file.”

“I know.”

“And very little in it.”

“I know.”

“I’ve always rather admired him.” She turned the scarf on the needles and started back the other way. “His father had a very unpleasant time. Through no fault of his own. A vice-minister called Fu, I believe. Who is going to have a very unpleasant summer.” She smiled at the wool. “Things come round.”

He went very still.

“Don’t look like that,” said Director Duan. “It’s not us. It’s other people. We just read about it first.” The needles clicked. “My point is that your fiancée’s family is extremely interesting. That’s all. Her sister is married to a man who sits on the docks like a spider. Her parents are about to lose everything they own. And she races cars against the law on Saturday nights with an old woman with a scanner.” She looked at him over her glasses. “No relevant concerns.”

“She’s a mechanic,” said Qin Haozhen.

“She’s a lovely girl. I’ve seen the photographs. She has a very loud laugh.” Director Duan put down her knitting. For the first time she looked at him properly, with her hands still. “I’m not threatening her, Haozhen. I want to be clear. I don’t threaten people. You know that. It’s in the training. We look after our families.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She gave him the box at the end.

It was red lacquer, the size of a pencil case, with a gold clasp. She took it out of the canvas bag, from between the oranges, and set it on the table beside the form.

“For the wedding list,” she said. “When you have one. She’ll want to write thank-you notes. Brides always do.”

He opened it.

A fountain pen. Silver, heavy, beautifully made, the kind of thing you’d find in a glass case in the old shops on Harbour Road. It lay on red silk. And on the barrel, just below the clip, engraved very small and very neatly, there was a single numeral.

7.

Serafina’s racing number. The white 7 on the side of a matte black car with a gold name on its bonnet.

He looked at it for a long time.

“Thank you, Director,” he said.

“You’re welcome.” She picked up her knitting again. “Now. Lisbon.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She slid it across the table under the form. A plain grey folder, thin. He didn’t open it.

“June,” she said. “Mid-month. Four weeks, perhaps five. There’s a man there who took something of ours, in 2021, and has been living quite happily by the sea ever since, and the people upstairs would like it back. And him.” The needles clicked. “You’ll have Tianyi. He’s been asking for you. He says nobody else lets him have the window seat.”

He looked at the grey folder.

“What did he take?” he said.

The needles stopped.

It was a very small thing. A pause of perhaps half a second, a row left unfinished, the red wool lying still over the bamboo. In eleven years, he had never once asked her what anybody had taken, or done, or written, or said. He had taken the folder and read it and gone. She looked at him over the top of her glasses with an expression he had never seen on her, which was not anger, and not suspicion, but something much more careful: a kind of attention, the way you’d watch a dog you had raised from a puppy that had just, for the first time, looked at the door.

“Ledgers,” she said.

Then the needles started again.

“You never used to ask,” said Director Duan Qiuyan, gently, to the scarf.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t take the pen into the garage.

He left it in the grey car, in the glovebox, where the ring had been. He came in through the side door at eleven at night, when Big Wu and Mr. Kwok had gone home and Mouse was a shape at the end of the bench in the light of her screens, and Serafina was sitting on the floor by Gilded with a wheel off and a brake caliper in her lap.

She looked up and saw his face.

“Rule one,” she said. “What is it?”

He crouched down on the concrete in front of her. He took her left hand, with the ruby on it, oily, and held it.

“My director sends her congratulations,” he said.

“That’s nice.”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “It isn’t.”

He told her. All of it, because it was rule one and because he had decided on the stairs of the Pavilion of Clear Springs that he would. The form, on the table. No relevant concerns. The gearbox, German, sequential. Granny Shum’s, on Saturdays. Three years. The braised beef. He told her, carefully, exactly what Director Duan had said, word for word, in the order she’d said it, because he remembered everything, and he watched Serafina’s face go from puzzled to white to something he had seen once before, in a photograph Aurelia had told him about, on a mother’s face: cold and flat and furious.

“Show me the pen,” she said.

“It’s in the car.”

“Rule two. I know. Go and get it.”

He got it.

She held it under the work lamp, turning it. She found the 7 at once; of course she did, she’d painted it herself on the side of a car forty times. She looked at it.

“That’s a threat,” she said.

“Yes.”

“She said she doesn’t make threats.”

“She doesn’t,” said Qin Haozhen. “She gives presents.”

At the end of the workbench, very quietly, Mouse had taken her headphones off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina sat on the floor of her garage with a silver pen in one hand and a brake caliper in the other, and for a while she didn’t say anything at all. A train went over. The building shook. He knelt in front of her and waited, because he didn’t know what she would do and had learned, since October, that he never would.

Then she got up.

She walked to the workbench, to the pile of papers by the kettle that was the team’s paperwork, and dug through it, and pulled out a form. Three pages, printed, with the series logo at the top and a box at the bottom for a signature. The entry form for the Baizhang Pass hill climb on the eighteenth of June, in the mountains in the north of the province. Twelve point four kilometres. A hundred and fifty-six corners. She’d been putting off entering it for a month because Big Wu said it was a waste of tyres.

She unscrewed the cap of the silver pen.

“What are you doing?” he said.

“She’s watching,” said Serafina. “She said so. She’s got photographs. She knows I’ve got a loud laugh.” She smoothed the entry form flat on the bench under the lamp. “So she can watch me do this.”

She signed it. Serafina Song. Her big, untidy, fast signature, in the director’s silver pen, right across the box and out the other side of it, so that the S went over the line onto the table.

Then she capped the pen, very calmly, and handed it back to him.

“Send that to your director,” she said. “With a thank-you note. Tell her I’ve used her present. Tell her I’m racing up a mountain on the eighteenth of June, number seven, and she’s very welcome to watch.” She lifted her chin. “Tell her I’ll wave.”

He stood at the bench looking at her signature going off the edge of the form.

Then he started to laugh.

It wasn’t the helpless laugh from the glovebox. It was something else, lower and darker, a laugh that had a lot of fear in it and a lot of something else too, and he put his hand over his eyes while he did it, and when he took it away his eyes were wet.

“You’re going to get us both killed,” he said.

“Probably,” said Serafina. “Not this year.” She took his face in her oily hands. “When’s the plane?”

He went still.

“How did you know?”

“Because you came in through the side door and didn’t pick up your mug,” said Serafina. “You always pick up your mug. You only don’t when you’re going.”

He looked at her. She looked back.

“The twelfth,” he said. “Of June. Early.”

“Then I’ll drive you,” said Serafina. “Five in the morning. In Nonna.” She kissed him once, hard, on the mouth, with her hands on his face and the director’s pen in his pocket between them. “And you’ll be back to see me win the hill climb.”

“I don’t know if I’ll be back.”

“Then you’ll watch,” she said. “From wherever you are. Like her.”

At the end of the bench, Mouse put her headphones back on. But before she did, she reached out and took the hill-climb entry form off the bench, the one with the signature going off the edge, and scanned it, both sides, at the highest resolution her scanner would do, and saved it in a folder on her desktop that had no name.

chapters.title: Five A.M., Departures
chapters.desc: The last night before Lisbon, the loft, the trains. Then the airport road in the dark in a red Lancia, a brass tyre gauge he has to bring back, and three words through a car window that a traffic warden interrupts.
chapters.epigraph: “You have to bring it back. It’s the only one that reads true. I’ll need it for the hill climb.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
He didn’t sleep the night before. Neither did she. They didn’t pretend to.

It was a Sunday, and hot, the first properly hot night of the summer, and the loft over the garage held the heat of the day like an oven. She opened the window onto the railway as far as it would go and the air that came in smelled of hot iron and diesel and the jasmine growing wild on the fence by the tracks. They lay on the mattress with the sheet kicked off and the light from the railway coming in orange and going across the ceiling every time a train went by.

He had packed already. One bag, black, small, by the top of the stairs. She’d watched him do it, at eight, on the floor of the loft: four shirts, folded in a way she’d never seen anyone fold anything, flat and square like envelopes. Trousers. A washbag. A book he didn’t read. Nothing else. Nothing of his own. It had taken him six minutes.

“Is that all?”

“They give you the rest.”

“What rest?”

He didn’t answer. She hadn’t expected him to.

Now he lay on his back beside her with one arm under his head, looking at the ceiling, and she lay on her side, looking at him, with her hand flat on his chest over the short white scar under his collarbone, and felt his heart go, slow and even.

“Talk to me,” she said.

“About what?”

“Anything. Something you can tell me.” She moved her hand a little on his chest. “I want to have your voice. For the next however long.”

He was quiet for a while.

Then he told her about the mining town in the north. Not much. It came out of him slowly, in pieces, the way rust comes off a bolt. The two streets. The coal dust on everything, on the washing, on the windowsills, in the creases of his father’s knuckles that never came out. The noise the winding gear made at the pithead, a groan and a clank, every four minutes, all day and all night, so that when he went away to the academy at sixteen he couldn’t sleep for a month because it was too quiet.

“That’s why you like the trains,” she said.

He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her.

“I hadn’t thought of that,” he said.

“Every eleven minutes. Something big going over, making a noise, and the building shaking.” She smiled in the dark. “You sleep through the trains. You don’t sleep anywhere else.”

“I sleep in your car.”

“My car makes a noise too.”

He looked at her for a long moment in the orange light. Then he reached up and touched her face, her cheekbone, with two fingers, very lightly, the way he’d touched her jaw in the paddock to check that it was there.

“What else,” he said, “have you noticed about me that I don’t know?”

“Lots,” said Serafina. “I’ll tell you when you get back. One a day. It’ll take years.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, she climbed on top of him and made him stop talking.

Slowly. That was the difference, that night. Everything else between them had been fast, the coast road and the fourth lamp post and the gearstick, and that night she didn’t want fast. She wanted to remember it. She kissed him the way he kissed, for once, thorough and careful, taking her time over every part of it, his mouth and his jaw and the notch at the end of his eyebrow and the long pink line down his forearm, all fourteen stitches, one at a time, while the trains went over and he lay under her with his hands on her hips and his eyes closed and his breathing coming apart. When he tried to turn her over, she wouldn’t let him. When he said her name, she kissed it out of his mouth. It was very hot, and very quiet between the trains, and she could feel his heart under her palm going faster and faster and then not slowing down at all.

“Sera,” he said, at the end, into her hair, as if it were a question.

“I’m here.”

“I know,” he said, and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past four the alarm went.

They didn’t need it. They were both awake. She’d been lying with her head on his chest for an hour listening to him not sleep. He got up and dressed in the dark: one of the envelope shirts, grey trousers, the forgettable jacket. He went down the stairs. She heard him in the garage, by the kettle, and she heard him pick up the plain mug, and hold it, and put it down again, and she lay on the mattress for a second longer with her eyes shut and her fists closed.

Then she got up and got dressed and went down and started Nonna.

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was forty minutes away, out over the long bridge to the island where they’d built it on reclaimed land in the nineties, and at five in the morning on a Monday the road was empty. She drove it with the windows down and the warm air coming in and the sky going from black to a deep dirty purple over the sea, the lights of the bridge going by overhead one after another like something being counted.

She didn’t drive gently. She didn’t drive fast either. She drove the way she drove when she was thinking, which was exactly at the limit, perfectly smooth, never a gram more.

He sat in the passenger seat with his bag at his feet. He didn’t sleep.

Halfway across the bridge he looked in the wing mirror. Then again, four seconds later. Then again. She’d seen him do it a hundred times. Checking. The car behind. The car behind that. The lorry three hundred metres back. He did it the way other people breathed.

“Look at me,” said Serafina, “not the mirror.”

He turned his head.

“There’s nobody there. It’s five in the morning. There’s me, and a fish lorry, and the sea.” She didn’t take her eyes off the road. “You’ve got thirty more minutes of me. I want you looking at the right person.”

He looked at her for the rest of the bridge. She felt it the whole way, on the side of her face, like sun.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the turn-off for departures, she reached into the door pocket and took something out and held it out to him without looking.

“Here.”

He took it. It was a tyre-pressure gauge. Not the cheap black kind from the petrol station that had been in his glovebox. An old one, brass, round-faced, the size of a pocket watch, with a dial under a scratched glass and a short rubber hose and a needle that had been bent once and straightened. Her initials were scratched into the back with a nail. S.S. And under them, smaller, older, someone else’s. A.C.

“It was Nonna’s,” said Serafina. “She had it for her Alfa. In the sixties. Antonia Conti.” She swallowed. “She gave it to me when I was twelve and told me never to trust a tyre gauge that came from a petrol station.”

He turned it over in his fingers.

“Sera. I can’t take this.”

“You have to bring it back,” said Serafina. “That’s the point. It’s the only one that reads true. I’ll need it for the hill climb.” She glanced at him. “So you have to bring it back. Before the eighteenth, if you can. And if you can’t, after. But you bring it back.”

He held it in his palm and looked at it, at the bent needle and the scratched glass and the two sets of initials.

Then he put it in his inside pocket. The left one. Against his chest, beside Chen Si’s cream card and the black notebook.

“I’ll bring it back,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Departures was a long concrete lane under a concrete canopy, with a rail down the middle and signs every twenty metres that said NO WAITING, and at ten past five in the morning there were a few taxis and a coach and a traffic warden in a yellow vest with a whistle, a young man with the air of someone who had been looking forward to his whistle all night.

She pulled in. She didn’t turn off the engine.

He got out. He took his bag off the floor. He closed the door and stood on the pavement with the bag over his shoulder, and bent down to the open window, and looked at her.

She’d said she wouldn’t cry. She’d said it to herself in the loft, and again on the bridge, and again at the turn-off. She had her hands on the wheel at a quarter to three. She looked straight back at him.

“Go on, then,” she said. “You’ll miss it.”

He didn’t go.

He stood bent at her window with one hand on the roof of the car and his face very close, and the purple light coming in under the canopy, and the taxis going past behind him, and she saw him decide something. She saw it happen. She saw it go across his face the way she’d seen the smile go across it in the paddock in December, the first time.

“I love you,” said Qin Haozhen.

He said it quietly. Not carefully. Not like I slept, or I want this, testing whether he was allowed. He just said it, straight, through the window of a red Lancia at five in the morning under a sign that said NO WAITING, as though it were the simplest and most obvious fact he had ever reported.

She opened her mouth.

And the traffic warden blew his whistle. Very long, very loud, directly behind him, and shouted something about moving on, NO WAITING, that meant you, sir, and pointed at Nonna with his whole arm.

Haozhen straightened up. He looked at the warden. The warden, who was perhaps twenty-two, looked back at him, and something in Haozhen’s face made him take one step backward and lower his arm.

Then Haozhen looked back down at her through the window. Just once more. And stepped away from the car, and turned, and walked toward the sliding doors with his bag on his shoulder, not fast, not looking back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got out of the car.

She didn’t decide to. She was simply out of it, standing in the road in the departures lane with the door open and the engine running and the warden blowing his whistle again behind her, and the taxi drivers looking, and a family with a luggage trolley stopping dead on the pavement.

“QIN HAOZHEN,” she shouted.

He stopped. Ten metres away, at the sliding doors. He turned round.

She had a voice that was much too loud for a staff entrance and did not care. She had used it on pit walls and at Granny Shum’s and across a restaurant full of bankers on Harbour Road. She used it now, all of it, across the departures lane at ten past five in the morning.

“I LOVE YOU. YOU IDIOT. YOU SAID IT THROUGH A WINDOW. YOU COULDN’T WAIT TILL I’D PARKED? BRING BACK MY GAUGE.”

The family with the trolley had turned round to watch. The taxi drivers had stopped. The traffic warden had his whistle halfway to his mouth and had forgotten it was there.

And Qin Haozhen, a man whose eyes slid off cameras, who had stood unseen at the doors of eleven weddings in six countries, stood in front of the sliding doors at departures in full view of everyone and smiled at her. The real one. The whole thing. All the way across his face, in front of strangers, in the purple light, as though he didn’t care who saw.

He put his hand flat on his chest, on the left side, over the inside pocket. Over the gauge.

Then he went through the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove home over the long bridge with the sun coming up out of the sea on her right.

She didn’t cry until the middle of the bridge. Then she cried so hard she had to pull into the emergency lane and put the hazards on, and sat there with her forehead on the steering wheel while the fish lorries went past and shook the car, and she laughed in the middle of it, twice, because of the traffic warden’s face.

When she got back to the garage at a quarter past six, Mr. Kwok was already there. He was never there before nine. He was sitting on the stool by the kettle, in his cardigan, with a bag of egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover on the bench beside him, and when she came in under the shutter with her face all swollen he didn’t say anything at all. He just held one out.

“How did you know?” she said.

“He rang me,” said Mr. Kwok. “Last night. At eleven. He said he was going away and would I come in early, because you’d be back by a quarter past six and you shouldn’t have to come into an empty garage.” He looked at her. “He said you’d want the egg one. Not the ham.”

Serafina sat down on the floor with her back against the workbench and held the egg sandwich in both hands and didn’t eat it.

On the bench, the plain mug that said HIS was sitting exactly where he’d left it. Facing the room.

chapters.title: Baizhang Pass
chapters.desc: Twelve point four kilometres, a hundred and fifty-six corners, a rock wall on one side and nothing on the other. She sets her tyres without the gauge. Seven time zones away, in a hotel lobby at four in the morning, a night porter and a man with a brass gauge in his pocket watch her climb.
chapters.epigraph: “A hill climb is a race against a mountain. The mountain doesn’t care. That’s what makes it fair.” — Big Wu
chapters.content:
The Baizhang Pass climbed eleven hundred metres in twelve point four kilometres, from a village of tea sheds and noodle stalls at the bottom of the valley to a concrete car park at the top with a temple and a view of four provinces. The road had been cut into the side of the mountain in the 1960s by people who did not believe in guard rails. On the left, going up, there was rock. On the right, for most of the way, there was air.

One weekend a year, they closed it, and let people race up it, one at a time, against the clock.

“A hill climb,” said Big Wu, on the Saturday, in the paddock in the village car park, with his arms folded and his face like thunder, “is a race against a mountain. The mountain doesn’t care. That’s what makes it fair. That’s also what makes it stupid. There’s no run-off. There’s no gravel trap. If you go off at the Needle you sit in the gravel and cry on your sister. If you go off at the hundred and twelfth corner up there, you go off the mountain.” He looked at Gilded, matte black on the transporter, with the white 7 and the gold name and a small grey taxi on the driver’s door, just above the sill. “And we’re doing it in a car built for a circuit. On circuit tyres. In a field of specials built for nothing but this.”

“Yes,” said Serafina.

“Waste of tyres.”

“You said.”

“I’m saying it again,” said Big Wu, “so it’s on record,” and went to unload the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were forty-one entries, in nine classes. Most were locals: men from the provinces in old saloons with roll cages and stickers from their uncles’ garages, a woman from the city in a Lotus, two brothers in a pair of identical hatchbacks who had driven up from the coast and slept in their cars. And at the top of the list, as he had been at the top of it for nine of the last eleven years, there was Lau Kam-wing.

Lau was sixty-two. He had built his car himself, in a shed in the next valley, over thirty years. It wasn’t a car, really. It was a frame of steel tubes with a motorcycle engine bolted in the back, an open cockpit, four fat tyres and a wing on the back like an upturned table, and it weighed less than Lau did. It had been designed for exactly one thing, which was going up the Baizhang Pass faster than anything else in the world, and it was very good at it. The record was his. Six minutes, eleven point four seconds. Set in 2018.

“Nobody beats Old Lau in a circuit car,” said one of the brothers from the coast, at the noodle stall on Saturday night, to nobody in particular. “Can’t be done. Too heavy. Too wide. The corners up top are too tight.”

Serafina, at the next table, ate her noodles standing up.

“Can’t be done,” she said, “is what they said about the Needle in 2019.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She set her tyres on Sunday morning without the gauge.

She had known she would have to. She had known it at five in the morning on the departures lane, handing it over, and she’d done it anyway. Big Wu had a digital one, a good one, from the team’s kit, black plastic with a screen that read to two decimal places. She looked at it for a long time, at seven o’clock, crouched by the front left wheel in the cold mountain air with her breath smoking.

“It’s accurate,” said Big Wu. “I had it calibrated in March.”

“I know.”

“It’s more accurate than that old brass thing ever was.”

“I know,” said Serafina. “It’s not hers.”

She used it anyway. One point five two bar cold, on the fronts. One point four eight on the rears, a shade under what she ran at the circuit, because the temple car park was eleven hundred metres up and every gauge on the mountain would read a tenth higher by the time she got there. She wrote the numbers on her forearm in marker, the way Nonna used to write them on the back of her driving glove. Then she did a thing she hadn’t done since she was twelve, which was to put her bare palm flat on each tyre in turn, and hold it there, and close her eyes.

“What,” said Big Wu, “are you doing.”

“Feeling it.”

“You can’t feel point oh four of a bar.”

“Nonna could,” said Serafina, and stood up.

At eleven, before the second run, at the end of the paddock, on an upturned crate under the awning, Mouse had the laptop open and a cable running to the car. She wasn’t looking at the screen. She was looking at Serafina. When Serafina looked back, Mouse held up her own phone, without a word, and turned the screen round.

On it was the series’ live stream page. Under the video, a small grey number: the count of people watching.

Two hundred and eighty-one.

“It’s four in the morning in Lisbon,” said Mouse, very quietly.

Serafina looked at her.

“You don’t know he’s in Lisbon.”

“No,” said Mouse, and put the phone away. “I don’t know anything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel was on a steep street in the old part of the city, a narrow yellow building with green shutters and a lobby the size of a lift, and at four in the morning it was dark except for one lamp on the front desk and the glow of the guest computer in the corner.

The night porter was called Fernando. He was seventy, and had been a night porter for fifty years, in four hotels, and had seen everything that happened in a hotel lobby between midnight and six. He had seen the quiet Asian guest in room nine come down at ten to four and stand in the doorway of the lobby for a moment, looking at the street, before he crossed to the guest computer and sat down and typed something very carefully with two fingers. That was not unusual. Guests in room nine, over the years, had often come down at four in the morning to look at the street.

What was unusual was that he was watching a car race.

Fernando came round the desk with his coffee, slowly, in his slippers, and stood behind the guest’s chair. On the screen was a mountain road, steep and grey, cut into rock, with a drop on one side into green nothing. A car was coming up it. Black, low, with a gold word on the front, very fast, faster than Fernando had known a car could go up a road like that.

“Formula One?” said Fernando, in Portuguese.

“No,” said the guest, in Portuguese, without turning round. “A hill. In the mountains. On the other side of the world.”

“Who is driving?”

The guest didn’t answer at once. He had something in his left hand, Fernando saw, held against the desk beside the keyboard. A round brass thing, like a watch, with a short rubber tube. He was holding it the way Fernando’s mother used to hold her rosary.

“My fiancée,” said the guest.

Fernando put his coffee down on the desk. He pulled up the other chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first run had been at nine, local time. Two in the morning in Lisbon. He had watched that one alone, in the dark, with Tianyi asleep in the other bed in room nine with his mouth open and a stick of cinnamon gum still in his fist. Six minutes, fourteen point eight. Second, behind Lau. Three point four seconds behind, which on a mountain was a lifetime.

This was the second run. The last.

She went off the line at the bottom of the pass in the village with the tea sheds, and the stream cut to a camera on a pole, and he watched the black car go away up the first straight and into the trees, and he stopped breathing.

He knew the road. He had watched the first run nine times, between two and a quarter to four, frame by frame, every corner, until he knew where the camera posts were and where they weren’t, where the rock came out to the edge of the tarmac, where the drop was worst. He knew the twelve corners after the first bridge where she’d been cautious on the first run, because the tyres had been cold. He knew the long left-hander at the halfway point where she’d been perfect. He knew the hundred and twelfth corner, the tightest on the mountain, a hairpin with nothing on the outside but a white-painted rock and a view, where she had lost a second and a half to Lau.

He sat in the guest computer chair in a hotel lobby in Lisbon with his whole body gone cold and still, and watched.

She was faster through the twelve corners after the bridge. The tyres were warm this time. She’d done something with them; he could see it in how the car sat, a fraction lower at the front, biting. She was faster through the long left. She was faster through the cutting where the rock overhung the road and made a tunnel of shadow.

The split times came up in a box at the bottom of the screen. Green, for faster than Lau. Green. Green.

Fernando said something in Portuguese that was either a prayer or the opposite.

The hundred and twelfth corner. The camera on the outside of it, on the white rock. The black car came up the steep straight toward it, very fast, much too fast, he thought, much too late, she’s going to the fifth lamp post—

She braked. The car’s nose went down. The back of it stepped out, just a little, just enough, on purpose. And she went round the hairpin with the outside wheels on the very edge of the tarmac, a hand’s width from the white rock and the drop behind it, and came out the other side already accelerating, and the split came up in the box.

Green.

“Meu Deus,” said Fernando.

Haozhen found that his hand was locked round the brass gauge so tightly that the edge of the dial had cut into his palm.

✦ ✦ ✦

Six minutes, ten point nine.

Half a second under Lau’s record. The first time in the history of the Baizhang Pass that anything with a roof on it had won outright.

The stream cut to the top of the mountain, to the concrete car park by the temple, and there she was, getting out of the car. She took her helmet off. Her hair was standing up in spikes. Her face was red and wet and she was laughing, shouting something at Big Wu, who had picked her up off the ground, all of her, and was turning round in a circle with her held against his chest like a sack of rice. Mouse was jumping up and down. Mr. Kwok was holding a camping stove for some reason.

And behind them, getting out of his open-cockpit tube-frame special, sixty-two years old, Lau Kam-wing pulled off his helmet and stood looking at the black car for a moment. Then he walked over to it, and put his hand on its roof, flat, the way an old jockey touches the horse that has just beaten his, and held it there.

Then the camera found her face, close up. The commentators were saying something. She was being handed a microphone.

She didn’t take it. She looked past the man holding it, straight into the lens, and grinned, and waved. A big, stupid, unmistakable wave, her whole arm, above her head. Number seven. On top of a mountain. Waving.

Tell her I’ll wave.

Then she put two fingers to her lips. And then she held up her left hand to the camera. Palm out. With something red on the ring finger that caught the sun.

And she mouthed something. Three words. Slowly, so that anybody could read them.

Bring it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fernando, in the other chair, was crying. He was seventy years old and had seen everything that happened in a hotel lobby between midnight and six, and he was crying into his coffee.

“Your fiancée,” he said, in Portuguese.

“Yes.”

“She waved at you.”

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen. “And at someone else.”

Fernando didn’t ask who. Fifty years of night shifts. He got up and went round the desk in his slippers and came back with two small glasses and a bottle of something from under the counter, very old and very brown, and poured two, and pushed one along the desk.

“It is four in the morning,” said Haozhen.

“It is eleven in the morning,” said Fernando, “on the other side of the world. And she won.” He raised his glass. “To your fiancée.”

They drank. The guest from room nine drank all of it at once, the way you’d take medicine, and set the glass down, and sat looking at the screen, where it had gone back to the start of the stream, a black car at the bottom of a mountain, waiting.

He pressed play again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He watched it eleven times.

Fernando stayed for four of them. Then he went back to his desk, because a German couple came down at half past five with their suitcases for an early flight, and after that the street outside began to go grey, and a man went past with a cart of bread, and the first tram came groaning up the hill. Haozhen sat at the guest computer with the brass gauge in his fist and watched her climb the mountain over and over, and on the eleventh time, at the hundred and twelfth corner, when the back of the car stepped out on purpose and she held it a hand’s width from the drop, he found that he was laughing.

Quietly, alone, in a hotel lobby in Lisbon at six in the morning, with the target’s file upstairs on his bed and a man asleep in the other bed whom he’d trained beside at sixteen and who would wake at seven and want breakfast and the window seat and the details of a street, a house, a family, and a man who took ledgers.

He stopped laughing.

He looked down at the gauge in his hand. There was a small half-moon cut in his palm from the edge of the dial, and a little blood. He wiped it on his trousers. He looked at the two sets of initials on the back. S.S. A.C.

“Fernando,” he said.

The night porter looked up from the desk.

“If I asked you,” said the guest from room nine, “to keep something for me. In your desk. For a few weeks. And if I didn’t come back for it, to post it to an address on the other side of the world.” He held out the brass gauge. “Would you?”

Fernando looked at it. Then at the man holding it.

“No,” he said, in Portuguese. “I would not.” He shook his head slowly. “You will keep it in your pocket. And you will take it back to her yourself. She asked you. On the television. In front of everybody.” He picked up his coffee. “I saw her. I would not like to be the man who posted it.”

Haozhen looked at him.

Then he put the gauge back in his inside pocket, the left one, against his chest. And went upstairs to room nine, where Tianyi was just waking up, stretching, reaching for the cinnamon gum on the bedside table, and saying, in Mandarin, with a yawn, “You’re up early. Couldn’t sleep?”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “I slept fine.”

It was the first lie he had ever told Tianyi. He noticed it, and filed it, and went to stand at the window, where the street went down the hill toward the river, and a yellow house with blue tiles stood on the corner with a boy’s bicycle leaning against its door.

chapters.title: The Target Has a Family
chapters.desc: Lisbon. A yellow house with blue tiles, a man who waters geraniums, a woman who works nights at the hospital, and a boy of eleven who has been trying all summer to do thirty-two keepy-ups against the wall. The mission that cracks him.
chapters.epigraph: “Not in front of the house. Please. That’s my son’s window.” — Gong Ruiming
chapters.content:
The yellow house stood on the corner where the street turned down toward the river. Three storeys, narrow, with green shutters and a front faced in blue and white tiles, old ones, some of them cracked, a pattern of ships. There were geraniums in a window box on the first floor. There was a bicycle against the door, a boy’s, blue, with a bell that didn’t work and a football wedged in the basket.

He had been watching it for twenty-three days.

The room they’d taken was on the third floor of a guesthouse across the street and two doors up, with a window that looked down at an angle onto the front door and the side wall and a small paved square where the street widened. Tianyi had the window seat. Tianyi always had the window seat. He sat in it with his feet up on the sill and a pair of binoculars on the windowsill and a packet of cinnamon gum in his shirt pocket and told jokes, very quietly, in Mandarin, for twelve hours at a time.

Haozhen sat in the chair by the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man’s name was Gong Ruiming.

He was forty-six. He had worked for nine years in the accounts section of a building in the capital that did not appear on any map, and in the spring of 2021 he had walked out of it on a Friday afternoon with a briefcase and never walked back in, and seven weeks later he had been in Lisbon, teaching mathematics to the children of diplomats at a language school by the river, under a different surname. He had married a Portuguese nurse called Ana, who worked nights at the big hospital on the hill. They had a son. Tomás. Eleven. Ana’s from before, the file said, though the boy called Gong Pai, and Gong walked him to football every Saturday morning at nine with his hand on the back of the boy’s neck, and stood on the touchline in a raincoat, even when it wasn’t raining, and shouted.

Gong watered the geraniums at seven every evening. He put the bins out at eleven on Saturday night. He liked a custard tart from the bakery at the bottom of the street with his coffee and he always gave the last bite to the bakery’s dog.

And Tomás practised keepy-ups against the side wall of the house, every evening, after dinner, in the small paved square, for an hour, until his mother leaned out of the first-floor window and called him in.

He was trying to get to thirty-two. Haozhen didn’t know why thirty-two. Some boy at school, perhaps. Some player. He had got to thirty-one on the ninth day, and stopped, and stood in the square with the ball under his foot, and shouted something up at the window in Portuguese that made his mother laugh. Since then he had not got past twenty-six.

Haozhen counted, every evening, from the chair by the door. He couldn’t see the boy from the chair. He could hear the ball. The flat soft slap of it against the boy’s foot, his knee, his foot again. He counted under his breath without meaning to.

“You’re counting,” said Tianyi, on the fourteenth day, from the window seat.

“No.”

“Twenty-two. Twenty-three.” Tianyi didn’t turn round. “He’s going to drop it at twenty-four. He always drops it on the even numbers after twenty. He gets excited.” The ball hit the cobbles. Tianyi chewed his gum. “Twenty-four.”

Haozhen said nothing.

“You’ve changed,” said Tianyi pleasantly, to the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi knew. Of course he knew.

They had come into the State Military Academy in the same intake, at sixteen, in September 2010, and slept in the same dormitory of forty boys under the same leaking roof, and been taken out of it by the same woman with the same red scarf on her needles. Tianyi was a year older. He laughed easily, and often, and with his whole face, and he was the best shot Haozhen had ever seen, and he had sat in more window seats in more cities than anyone in the section, telling jokes for twelve hours at a time, and then done his job, and then come home and told jokes about that.

“The Director told us at the section dinner in April,” he said, on the sixteenth day, with his feet on the sill. “Stood up at the end with her glass. Haozhen is getting married. Half the section didn’t believe her. The other half thought it was a code.” He grinned at the window. “I knew it was true. She had the face she has when she’s been surprised and doesn’t like it.”

“You never said.”

“I was waiting for you to.” Tianyi shifted the binoculars. “A racing driver. That’s very good, Haozhen. That’s the best thing I’ve ever heard. You, who drives like a hearse.”

“I don’t drive like a hearse.”

“You drive like a very fast hearse,” said Tianyi. “With great respect for the deceased.” He chewed for a moment. “Is she pretty?”

Haozhen didn’t answer.

Tianyi laughed. Quietly, delighted, into his shoulder.

“Oh, she is,” he said. “Look at you. Oh, Haozhen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He asked on the twentieth day.

“What did he take?”

Tianyi, at the window, turned his head and looked at him. It was the first time in twenty days he had turned his whole head from the street.

“Ledgers,” he said. “Accounts. Nine years of who paid who, for what, in the building with no map.” He looked back out of the window. “Upstairs wants them back. And they want to know who he’s shown them to. That’s why it’s both. Him and the books.”

“Has he shown them to anyone?”

“I don’t know. I’m not told.” Tianyi chewed. “Does it matter?”

Haozhen didn’t answer that either.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ledgers were in a locker at the railway station by the river. Tianyi found the key on the twenty-first day, in a biscuit tin on top of a wardrobe, while Gong was at the language school and Ana was asleep in the back bedroom after her night shift and Tomás was at football. He was in and out of the house in four minutes. Haozhen stood on the corner and watched the street.

They opened the locker on the twenty-second day.

There were four of them. Old-fashioned, hardbacked, grey cloth, the kind of ledger you could still buy in the capital in stationery shops that hadn’t changed since the eighties. Columns of dates and figures and initials in a small, neat, accountant’s hand. Haozhen turned the pages standing in front of the open locker, in the echoing station, while Tianyi watched the concourse.

He didn’t mean to read anything. He wasn’t supposed to read anything. He was supposed to put them in the bag.

He read one line.

It was halfway down a page in the third ledger, in the spring of 2020. A date, a figure, a company name he didn’t recognise, and in the column for authorisation, two initials, very small. D.Q.Y. And in the column at the far right, where the other entries said section or upstairs or the number of a department, this one said, in the same small hand, underlined:

Private.

He closed the ledger.

He put all four in the bag. He did it slowly, squaring the corners, and Tianyi, watching the concourse, didn’t see his face. He filed it. He put it in the room in his head where he put things, and shut the door.

But it was a different room. It wasn’t the room where the people went. He noticed that, and filed that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

The twenty-third day was a Saturday.

Gong walked Tomás to football at nine. He stood on the touchline in his raincoat and shouted. He bought a custard tart at the bottom of the street and gave the last bite to the bakery’s dog. At seven he watered the geraniums. At eight there was dinner; they could see the three of them through the first-floor window, at the table, Ana in her nurse’s tunic because she was on nights again, Tomás talking with his mouth full, Gong laughing.

At half past eight Tomás came down to the square with the ball.

Haozhen sat in the chair by the door and counted.

Nineteen. Twenty. Twenty-one. The flat soft slap of it. Twenty-two. Twenty-three. Twenty-four, and the ball didn’t drop. Twenty-five. Twenty-six. Haozhen found that he had stood up out of the chair. Twenty-seven. Twenty-eight. Tianyi, at the window, had stopped chewing. Twenty-nine. Thirty.

Thirty-one.

The ball hit the cobbles.

Down in the square the boy shouted something, furious and laughing at once, and kicked the ball against the wall, and from the first-floor window his mother leaned out and said something back, and his father’s voice came from somewhere inside, and the boy stood in the square in the evening light with his hands on his hips and his face turned up to the window.

“Thirty-one,” said Tianyi, quietly. “Again.”

Haozhen sat back down.

At nine Ana left for the hospital. She kissed the boy in the doorway. She kissed Gong on the step. She walked down the hill toward the tram stop with her bag over her shoulder.

At eleven Gong put out the bins.

✦ ✦ ✦

The street was empty. It was always empty at eleven on a Saturday. Gong came out of the front door in his slippers with two black bags, one in each hand, and carried them to the bins on the corner, by the bakery, and put them in, and turned round.

Haozhen was standing on the pavement between him and his front door.

He had come down the stairs of the guesthouse and across the street without a sound and he was standing there in his dark jacket with his hands at his sides, where people could see them, and he said, in Mandarin, the man’s real name.

“Gong Ruiming.”

Gong stopped.

He didn’t run. Haozhen had known he wouldn’t; you could tell, after ten years, who would run, and Gong was not a man who ran. He was a man who had walked out of a building on a Friday afternoon with a briefcase and known, every day since, that one evening someone would be standing on the pavement saying his name. He stood by the bins in his slippers with his hands empty and looked at Haozhen, and Haozhen saw him understand all of it at once: the jacket, the hands, the car that had just pulled up at the corner with its engine running and Tianyi at the wheel.

“Yes,” said Gong. “All right.”

He said it in Mandarin. His accent was from the capital. It had gone soft at the edges in two years by the sea.

“Not in front of the house,” he said. “Please.” He looked up, past Haozhen’s shoulder, at the first floor. “That’s my son’s window.”

“All right,” said Qin Haozhen.

They walked toward the car. Side by side. Close, as if they were friends leaving a party. Haozhen’s hand was on Gong’s elbow. He didn’t hold it hard. He didn’t have to.

They had gone four steps when the light came on in the first-floor window.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard the boy on the stairs.

Fast, barefoot, the slap of it on old wooden treads, and then the front door was open and Tomás was on the step in a T-shirt and pyjama shorts with the football under his arm, because he’d been lying in bed with it, Haozhen thought, he’d been lying in bed with it thinking about thirty-one, and he looked at his father walking away from the house toward a car at eleven at night with a strange man holding his elbow.

“Pai?”

Gong stopped. He didn’t turn all the way round. He turned his head.

“Vai para dentro, Tomás,” he said. Go inside. Gently. In the voice he used on the touchline. “É trabalho. Volto logo.” It’s work. I’ll be back soon.

The boy didn’t go inside.

He stood on the top step with the football under his arm and looked at Haozhen. Not at his father. At Haozhen. Straight at him, the way children look at things before they have learned not to, and Haozhen stood on the cobbles of a street in Lisbon with his hand on a man’s elbow and was seen.

He had been looked at by a great many people in ten years. Frightened ones. Angry ones. A teacher in a hotel in the capital at eighteen. A man in a hood at a petrol station. A woman across a car park on Battery Hill, without any fear at all.

He had never been looked at like this. As if he were the thing under the bed.

“Tomás,” said Gong again. “Por favor.”

Down the street, a light came on in another window. Then a woman’s voice from somewhere, calling a question.

Haozhen opened the rear door of the car. Gong got in. He did it without being pushed. He folded himself into the back seat and put his hands on his knees, palms up, flat, and looked straight ahead through the windscreen, and did not look at the house again.

Haozhen closed the door.

The football hit the car.

The boy had thrown it from the step, with both hands, as hard as he could. It bounced off the rear passenger window a hand’s width from Haozhen’s face with a flat hollow bang, and fell, and rolled away down the cobbles toward the river, into the gutter, and stopped against a drain.

Haozhen looked at it.

Then he walked round the car and got into the passenger seat, and Tianyi drove away down the hill, not fast, with the lights on, like anybody.

In the wing mirror, the boy was standing in the middle of the street in his pyjamas, in the light from the bakery, with his hands at his sides.

✦ ✦ ✦

Gong didn’t speak for half an hour. Then, on the long road out along the river toward the marina, he said, in Mandarin, from the back seat, quite conversationally:

“You have someone.”

Haozhen didn’t answer.

“You keep putting your hand on your pocket. The left one. Like something’s in it.” A pause. “I used to do that, the first year. With a photograph of the boy. In case I had to leave in a hurry.”

Tianyi glanced across at the passenger seat and back at the road.

“Then you know,” said Gong Ruiming, gently. “You know exactly what this is.”

Nobody said anything else all the way to the marina.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the marina, at ten to two, there was a boat, and two men on it who did not say their names, and Haozhen walked Gong down the pontoon in the dark with his hand on his elbow and gave him to them, and the bag of ledgers, and signed nothing, and walked back up the pontoon alone.

Halfway up the pontoon he stopped, and went to the edge, and was sick into the black water.

He hadn’t been sick since he was eighteen. Since the hotel in the capital. He knelt on the wet planks with his hands on the edge of the pontoon and was sick until there was nothing left, and then went on retching for a while longer, and the boat’s engine started behind him and went away out across the river toward the sea.

Tianyi was standing at the top of the pontoon when he got there. He held out a stick of cinnamon gum.

Haozhen took it.

“First time I’ve seen you do that,” said Tianyi. He wasn’t joking. For once in his life, he wasn’t joking. He looked at Haozhen’s face in the marina lights for a long time. “Haozhen. Are you all right?”

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

It was the second lie.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, on the way to the airport, he asked the taxi to go the long way. Up the hill. Past the yellow house with the blue tiles.

The geraniums needed watering. Nobody had watered them.

The boy was sitting on the front step in his school tracksuit with the football in his lap. Somebody had gone down to the drain and got it. He was holding it in both arms against his chest, the way Haozhen had held the brass gauge in the hotel lobby, and he was looking down the hill toward the river, at nothing, the way you look at a road somebody has gone down.

The taxi went past. The boy didn’t look up.

Haozhen put his hand flat on his chest, on the left side, on the inside pocket, and kept it there all the way to the airport, and all the way through the airport, and through two weeks of debriefing rooms in the capital, and most of the way home.

chapters.title: He Comes Home Wrong
chapters.desc: He comes in through the side door at four in the morning, gives her back the gauge, gets into the passenger seat of a car that isn’t going anywhere, and doesn’t speak for two days. She doesn’t make him. On the third night her sister rings about their father, and he finally tells her about a boy and a football.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to ask. I’m going to sit here. You talk when there’s something you can say.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
The text came on the Friday from a number she didn’t know.

Unknown: Back Saturday. Late. H.

Rule three. She read it standing at the workbench with a socket in her hand and Big Wu watching her from under the transporter, and she said “Saturday,” out loud, to nobody, and Big Wu said “Good,” and went back under the transporter, and neither of them said anything else about it all day, which was how she knew Big Wu had been worried too.

She waited up. Of course she did.

She heard the car at ten to four on Sunday morning. It wasn’t his grey estate, which was still in her garage with the bullet hole filled and primed. It was a taxi. It came down the street of shuttered workshops and stopped at the corner and she heard a door, and the taxi going away, and then nothing. She stood at the bottom of the loft stairs in the dark garage in her vest and shorts and listened to the nothing. Four minutes. Five. She was halfway to the side door to open it when it opened.

He came in.

He had the black bag over his shoulder. He was wearing one of the envelope shirts and the grey trousers and the forgettable jacket, and they were all clean and pressed, and he had shaved, and his hair was cut. He looked, under the dim light from the street, like a photograph of himself. Like the one Auntie Chu’s nephew had taken in the service corridor on Battery Hill, slightly out of focus, a man at a door with no expression at all.

He looked at her across the garage.

Then he came to her, and took her hand, and opened it, and put something in it, and closed her fingers round it.

Brass. Round. Warm from his chest.

“I brought it back,” he said.

His voice was perfectly level. It was the voice from the east service door. Please step away from the door, madam. She hadn’t heard it in months.

“Haozhen,” she said.

He let go of her hand. He walked past her, carefully, the way you’d walk past someone in a narrow corridor, to Nonna, parked in the middle of the garage under the hanging lamp. He opened the passenger door. He got in. He closed the door. He sat in the passenger seat of a car that wasn’t going anywhere with his hands on his knees and looked straight ahead through the windscreen at the whiteboard, at the postcard of the Monza banking, and didn’t move.

She stood in the middle of the garage with her grandmother’s tyre gauge in her fist.

Then she went and got the blanket off the back seat of his grey car, and opened Nonna’s driver’s door, and got in, and put the blanket over his knees, and sat beside him.

She didn’t ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t speak on Sunday.

He didn’t sleep either. That was what frightened her most. She had been so sure, all the way through the six weeks, all the way through the hill climb, that whatever happened, whatever he came back as, the passenger seat would work. It had always worked. She sat beside him from four until it got light and from when it got light until Big Wu came in at nine, and he sat with his eyes open, looking at the whiteboard, and his breathing never changed. Not once. Not the long slow breath that meant he was going down.

Big Wu came in under the shutter with the doughnuts and stopped.

He looked at the red Lancia in the middle of the floor. At Serafina in the driver’s seat in her vest with her bare feet up on the dashboard. At the man in the passenger seat.

Big Wu had done two prison sentences, and would never say for what. He looked at Haozhen’s face through the windscreen, and Serafina saw him recognise something in it, and saw his own face change, close up, the way a door closes.

He didn’t say anything. He put the doughnuts on the bench. He went out again.

At eleven he came back with a pot of soup from his mother, wrapped in a towel, still hot. Pork bone and old cucumber, the one she made for people coming out of hospital. He put it on the camping stove. He put two bowls beside it. He went and stood in front of Nonna’s passenger window for a second, and Haozhen didn’t look at him, and Big Wu nodded once, to himself, and went to work on the transporter, and didn’t play the radio all day.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fed him.

She did it the way you’d feed a bird that had flown into a window. She brought the soup to the car in the plain mug, the one with HIS on it, and held it out, and waited. For a long time, nothing. Then his hand came up and took it, and held it, and after a while he drank some. She took the mug back when it was empty and brought it again an hour later. At three o’clock Mr. Kwok made congee, plain, with ginger and a little salt, nothing else, and Serafina took that to the car too, with a spoon, and he ate four spoonfuls and gave it back.

At six, Mouse came over from the end of the bench, which she never did. She stood by the passenger window with her headphones round her neck. She didn’t say anything. She took something out of her pocket and put it on the dashboard, through the open window, carefully, beside the brass gauge.

A clementine.

Then she went back to her screens.

He looked at it. It was the first thing he’d looked at all day that wasn’t the whiteboard.

✦ ✦ ✦

At night, she drove him.
