She thought it might help. It always had. She took Nonna out from under the railway bridge at two in the morning and drove the loop, gently, the way she’d driven it all winter, the way you’d rock something. Bridge. Tunnel. Coast road. The ferries and the cranes.

He didn’t sleep.

He sat in the passenger seat with his eyes open and his hands on his knees and looked out of the windscreen at the road coming at them, and at the place on the coast road where his head always slid off the window onto her shoulder, he stayed upright. She drove round three times. Four. The sky started to go grey over the water. He didn’t sleep.

She pulled into the lay-by above the harbour, where the fireworks had been, and turned off the engine.

The engine ticked.

“I’m not going to ask,” said Serafina. She said it to the windscreen. “I want you to know that. I’m not going to ask you where you went, or what happened, or what you did. I’m going to sit here. You talk when there’s something you can say. If that’s tomorrow, it’s tomorrow. If it’s next year, it’s next year.” She swallowed. “I’ve got nowhere to be.”

He didn’t answer.

But on the dashboard, between them, he reached out, slowly, and picked up Mouse’s clementine, and held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday he didn’t speak either.

He got out of the car twice. Once to use the toilet in the back. Once, at four in the afternoon, to stand at the side door to the alley for nine minutes, looking out at the street, with his back to the garage. Then he came back and got in the passenger seat again and closed the door.

Big Wu took the day off from the transporter and rebuilt the grey car’s front suspension instead, which Serafina had already rebuilt in December, very slowly, and very quietly, two metres from Nonna’s passenger window, for eight hours. Mr. Kwok didn’t go home for the evening news. He sat on the stool by the kettle in his cardigan and read the newspaper aloud to nobody, the racing results and the weather and a long story about a dog in a fire station, in Cantonese, in a calm, flat, steady voice, for an hour and a half, the way he said he used to read to his wife at the end.

At eleven, Serafina sent them all home.

At half past four she was sitting in the driver’s seat with her knees up, eating cold congee out of the pot with a spoon, when her phone rang.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was twenty to five on Tuesday morning. It was Aurelia.

Serafina looked at the screen for a second before she answered. Aurelia did not ring at twenty to five in the morning. Aurelia sent messages with full stops at the end of them at reasonable hours.

“Lia?”

“Papà rang me.” Aurelia’s voice was very steady and very far away, the way it went when she was holding something with both hands. “At fourteen minutes past two. From the tower. The fortieth floor. He couldn’t go home. I’m with him now, I’m in the corridor outside his office.” A breath. “It’s going, Sera. The Group. All of it. The banks meet on Friday, all eleven, and if nothing comes by then they call everything in. Four towers in the new zone up the river nobody will buy. The house.” Another breath. “He was crying. On the phone. I’ve never heard him cry. He said Mamma told him not to build them.”

Serafina sat very still in the driver’s seat with the pot of congee in her lap.

Beside her, in the passenger seat, she felt him turn his head.

“The house,” she said.

“If Friday goes the way he thinks, they’ll sell it. In the autumn. Everything with a sticker.” Aurelia was quiet. “I’m going to sit with him till it’s light. I wanted to—I thought you’d want to know before it’s in the papers. I don’t know if you want to come. You don’t have to. You haven’t spoken to him in seven years.”

Serafina looked out of the windscreen at the whiteboard.

“I can’t,” she said. “Not tonight. Lia, I can’t. I’ve got someone in my car who—” Her voice went. She tried again. “I can’t leave him tonight.”

There was a pause on the line. A long one. She heard her sister breathe.

“Then stay with him,” said Aurelia. “Stay with him, Sera. I’ll ring you when it’s light.” Another pause. “Is he all right?”

“No,” said Serafina.

“No,” said Aurelia. “They don’t come home all right. Not always. Not the first time it’s bad.” Very quietly, in the voice from when they were small: “Stay with him. Papà’s got me. And Chen Si’s awake. He’s always awake.”

The line went dead.

Serafina sat with the phone in her hand.

“Your father,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the first thing he had said in two days.

She turned her head. He was looking at her. Not at the whiteboard. At her. In the dim light from the hanging lamp his face was very tired and very pale and something had gone out of it that she had always been able to see before, the thing far back behind the calm, like a light in a house she’d thought was empty.

“The Group’s gone,” she said. “Four towers up the river. He’s selling the house.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I haven’t been in it in seven years. I haven’t spoken to him in seven years.”

“I know,” he said. “You should have gone.”

“I’m not leaving you in a car.”

He looked at her.

Then he looked down at the clementine in his hand, Mouse’s clementine, which he had been holding since Sunday night and which had gone soft and warm in his palm.

“He had a son,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her.

Not all of it. Not the city, or the name, or the building with no map, or the ledgers. She didn’t ask for any of that and he didn’t give it. He told her about a yellow house with blue tiles, and a window box of geraniums, and a man who gave the last bite of his custard tart to a bakery’s dog. He told her about a boy of eleven who practised keepy-ups against the side wall of the house every evening for an hour, trying to get to thirty-two, and how he had counted every one from a chair by a door for twenty-three days without being able to see him. How the boy always dropped it on the even numbers after twenty because he got excited. How on the last night, at half past eight, the boy had got to thirty-one.

He told her about the bins at eleven. And the slippers. And the light coming on in the first-floor window, and the boy on the step in his pyjamas with the football under his arm, looking at him.

“He looked at me,” said Haozhen. “Like I was what’s under the bed.”

His voice didn’t break. That was the worst of it. It stayed level, the east-service-door voice, all the way through, while he told her about the football bouncing off the car window by his face, and the boy in the middle of the road in the light from the bakery, and the geraniums nobody had watered in the morning.

“I did it anyway,” he said. “He threw the ball and I got in the car. I didn’t even slow down.”

Serafina reached across the gearstick and took his face in both hands.

“Look at me.”

He looked at her.

“You did it,” she said. “I know. I’m not going to tell you that you didn’t, or that it wasn’t you, or that it was them. It was you. You did it.” Her thumbs moved on his cheekbones. “And you’ve been sitting in my car for two days because you can’t stand that you did it. That’s what this is. That’s the whole of what this is. Do you understand me? A man who could stand it would be asleep.”

Something happened in his face.

It started at his mouth. A tremor, there and gone. Then his jaw. Then his eyes, which had been dry and fixed and enormous for two days, went bright, and she watched it come up through him like water through a cracked floor, slow at first and then not slow at all.

He made a sound.

It was the low old sound from the night he came back from the twelve days, the one that seemed to come up out of the floor. Only it didn’t stop this time. It went on, and it broke in the middle, and he bent forward in the passenger seat with his face in her hands and his whole body shaking, and he wept. Not the way she’d imagined a man like him might cry, a single tear, contained, filed. He wept the way she had wept in the lay-by in January, with nobody in the seat beside her to hear. Great dragging sobs that hurt to listen to, that sounded as if they were coming out of something that had been locked for ten years and had rusted shut.

She climbed over the gearstick. She banged her knee on the handbrake again and didn’t swear. She got into the passenger seat with him, half in his lap, half on the door, and pulled his head down onto her shoulder and held it there with both arms, and held on while he shook.

The trains went over. The garage shook round them. She counted without meaning to. Three. Four.

“I can’t do it again,” he said, at some point, into her neck, wrecked. “Sera. I can’t. I don’t know how to stop, I don’t know how anyone stops, nobody stops, but I can’t do it again.”

“Rule four,” said Serafina, into his hair.

He went still in her arms.

“Not yet,” he said. “If I say it now they’ll know before I’ve got anything. They’ll know by Thursday.” He drew a breath that shook all the way down. “I need to think. There’s something—I saw something. In a book I wasn’t supposed to read. I need to think about it.”

“Then think,” said Serafina. “I’ll be here. I’ll have the car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept at six.

It happened the way it always used to, in the end, the way she’d been afraid it wouldn’t. She felt it go through him. All at once, from the bottom, like a building coming down. One moment he was breathing against her neck in long torn breaths, and the next his whole weight had gone into her, and his head was heavy on her shoulder, and his breathing had changed. Slow. Even. Down.

She didn’t move.

She sat squashed against Nonna’s passenger door with a grown man asleep in her arms and her knee throbbing where she’d hit it on the handbrake and the grey light coming in under the half-raised shutter, and she didn’t move for six hours.

At nine Big Wu came in with the doughnuts, and stopped, and looked, and went out again, and pulled the shutter all the way down behind him from the outside, very slowly, so it wouldn’t make a noise.

At noon, when he finally woke, the first thing he did was look at the clementine. It had rolled into the footwell. He picked it up.

Then he peeled it, in one long spiral, without breaking it once, and gave her half.

chapters.title: The Song Family Opposes the Match
chapters.desc: A letter in her mother’s handwriting. The house on the Peak, with numbered stickers on everything that can be sold. “A security guard?” Her mother asks him nine questions and he answers every one of them truthfully. They have no idea who he is. Then her mother says the cruellest thing she has ever said, and Serafina walks out of that house for the second time.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody keeps her, madam. I’d like to be wherever she is. That’s all I’m asking for.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
The letter came on the Wednesday, in a cream envelope, in her mother’s handwriting.

It had been seven years since Serafina had seen that handwriting on anything addressed to her. It came to the garage under the railway bridge, which her mother had never acknowledged existed, and Big Wu brought it in with the post and put it on the bench and stood looking at it as though it might go off.

Inside there was a card. One line.

Saturday, four o’clock. Bring him. Before there is no house to bring him to. — V.

Serafina read it standing up. Then she turned it over. Nothing on the back.

“How does she know?” she said.

“The hill climb,” said Mouse, from the end of the bench, very quietly. “You held your hand up to the camera. With the ring. It was in the papers on the Monday. Racer shows off ring on mountain. There was a picture.” She hesitated. “It was quite a big picture.”

“She’d have known before the papers,” said Haozhen.

He was at the kettle. He had been coming in through the side door again for two weeks, at ordinary hours, and picking up his mug, and staying. He looked better. Not well. Better. He slept four hours in the loft most nights and two more in Nonna’s passenger seat in the afternoons, and Big Wu’s mother sent soup every day, and nobody said anything about any of it.

“She’s had someone watching you since you left,” he said. “You told me. Your sister’s husband had a word with him, in 2019. But she’ll have found another. Someone at the circuit. Someone in the series office.” He looked at the card. “She’ll know what I earn. Roughly. She’ll know where I live. She’ll think she knows what I am.”

“What will she think you are?”

“A security guard,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t want to go. She said so for two days.

On Friday night, at three in the morning, in the passenger seat on the coast road, he said, “Your father will be there.”

She didn’t answer.

“You didn’t go in July,” he said. “When your sister rang. Because of me.” He was looking at the sea. “It’s going to be sold in the autumn. All of it. That house. The rooms you grew up in from fourteen. After this, it won’t exist.” A pause. “I’ve walked a lot of people out of a lot of rooms they were never going back to. I’d like you to have the chance to walk out of this one yourself. On your own feet. Not in a photograph in a newspaper.”

She drove for a long time.

“If she’s cruel to you,” said Serafina, “I’ll put her through a window.”

“She’ll be cruel to me,” said Qin Haozhen. “Please don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house on the Peak was yellow, and very large, and it stood at the top of a drive that curved up through old trees with the whole harbour falling away below it, and Serafina had last walked down that drive at nineteen in an evening dress with her shoes in her hand.

She walked up it at four o’clock on Saturday in black jeans and boots and her leather jacket, because she was not going to dress for her mother. He walked beside her in the forgettable suit. Halfway up, without looking at her, he took her left hand, the one with the ruby, and held it, and didn’t let go.

The front door was open. There was nobody to open it. The house had had eleven staff when she was fifteen.

They went in.

There were stickers on everything.

Small white ones, oval, with a number printed on each in black. On the hall table. On the Venetian mirror in its gilt frame at the foot of the great staircase. On the grandfather clock that had come from Milan in a crate in 2011. On the chairs. On a painting of a harbour that Serafina had stared at every morning at breakfast for five years. On the piano, in the music room, through the open door; she could see it from the hall. Lot 212. Lot 213. Lot 214.

She stood in the hall and looked at them and couldn’t move.

“Sera,” he said, very low.

“I’m fine.”

“You’re not.”

“I’m fine,” said Serafina, “I’m absolutely fine, I just didn’t think there’d be numbers—”

His hand tightened on hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was in the morning room.

It was yellow too, the yellow of the walls in the old house in Milan, which Vittoria Conti had had copied exactly when they moved. Tall windows onto the harbour. A small walnut writing desk in the corner by the east window, with a sloping front and brass handles shaped like shells, with a sticker on it. Two sofas facing each other across a low table. A silver coffee pot on the table, with a sticker on it.

Vittoria Song sat on the sofa on the left, in black, with her back very straight.

She was fifty-four. She was still the most beautiful woman Serafina had ever seen, and the coldest, and she looked exactly as she had looked at the bottom of the stairs on the night Serafina left: perfect, and very still, and waiting. Her hair was swept up. There were small diamonds at her ears. There was nothing on her hands at all. No rings. That was new.

Across from her, on the other sofa, in a grey cardigan with leather buttons that was much too big for him, sat Song Weiren.

Serafina had not seen her father in seven years. She had imagined it, sometimes, at three in the morning: that he would be the same, a big warm loud man in a good suit with his hand on everyone’s shoulder. He wasn’t. He had got old. He had got small. He sat on the sofa with his hands between his knees and looked up at his younger daughter as she came in, and his eyes filled, and he didn’t say anything at all.

“Papà,” said Serafina.

Her voice did something she couldn’t stop.

“Sit down,” said her mother, in Italian. “Both of you. There’s coffee. It’s the last of the good coffee. Everything else has gone to a valuer called Mr. Szeto who wears brown shoes with a grey suit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat. He sat on the end of the sofa beside her father, with his back to the window and only the reflection in the silver coffee pot to watch the door by, and Serafina sat beside him, and didn’t let go of his hand.

Her mother looked at him. Not at Serafina. At him.

It was the look Serafina had grown up under. The one that measured. It went over him the way a valuer’s eyes went over a piece of furniture, looking for the sticker. The suit. The shoes. The hands. The face, which gave her nothing, which gave everybody nothing, which slid off her like rain off a windscreen.

“What do you do?” said Vittoria Song, in English.

“I’m in security, madam.”

“What kind?”

“Close protection. Events. Embassies, sometimes.”

“A security guard,” said her mother.

It wasn’t a question. She said it the way she’d once said second place.

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

“What do you earn?”

He told her. A figure. Exactly. Serafina knew it was exactly, because she had seen the bank statement in Da Gianni. Her mother’s face didn’t move.

“Where is your family from?”

“A mining town in the north. You won’t have heard of it.”

“Your father?”

“He died in a roof fall when I was nine.”

“Your mother?”

“She’s a seamstress. She still works. She’s sixty-one.”

“Brothers? Sisters?”

“None.”

“Where do you live?”

“In two rooms above a laundry. In the old harbour streets.”

“Do you own them?”

“No, madam.”

“Do you own anything?”

He considered the question with real care, the way he’d considered the wine on Harbour Road.

“A notebook,” he said. “Some shirts. And half of a clementine, which I’m told I owe someone.”

Serafina made a sound she turned into a cough.

Her mother didn’t smile.

Nine questions. Serafina had counted. He had answered every one of them truthfully and briefly and without the smallest sign of resentment, in the voice from the east service door, and every answer was true, and every answer was the most perfect lie she had ever heard, because her mother sat on her sofa in the yellow room with the stickers on everything and looked at a man who had read the Song family’s file before the banks had, and saw a security guard who lived above a laundry.

They had no idea. None of them. And he wasn’t going to tell them.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You walked out,” said Vittoria, in Italian, to her daughter, at last, “of an engagement dinner. At the Harbour Hotel. In front of two hundred people. Between the soup and the fish.” Her voice was quite calm. “On a boy whose father owned the third-largest construction company in the province. Who would have made you comfortable for the rest of your life. Who would have made us comfortable.”

“He was an idiot, Mamma.”

“He was an idiot with a construction company. Do you know what Li Zhenhua’s company is doing this summer? Very well. He bought two of your father’s sites up the river in June for a third of what they were worth.” She looked at her husband for a moment, then away. “You said you would rather marry a carburettor. And now you bring me this.” She didn’t look at him. “A man who stands by doors.”

“He doesn’t stand by doors.”

“I’ve had a man watching you for seven years, Serafina.” Her mother’s voice didn’t rise. “I know where you sleep. Above a garage. I know where you go on Saturday nights, to a woman in a folding chair, and what they’d give you for it if anybody cared to write it down. I know he drives you there. I know he sleeps in your car.” For the first time, something crossed her face. Distaste, very small, at the corner of the mouth. “In your car.”

“You don’t know anything about him.”

“I know what he is,” said Vittoria Song. “I can see it from here. He’s nothing. He’s a pair of shoes at the edge of a room. You could have had anything, and you chose an engine, and now you’ve chosen a man who’ll still be standing at a door at sixty, waiting for somebody important to come out of it.”

Serafina’s hand had gone white in his.

✦ ✦ ✦

He spoke then. Quietly. In English.

“Madam.”

Vittoria turned her head and looked at him. It was the first time she had looked at his face properly, and Serafina saw her do it, and saw her see nothing there, because he gave her nothing.

“You’re right,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’m not important. I don’t own anything. I’ll probably stand at doors.” He paused. “But I’m not asking you to let me keep her. Nobody keeps her. I’ve watched her for ten months. Nobody’s ever going to keep her.” He looked at Serafina, once, and then back. “I’d like to be wherever she is. That’s all I’m asking for. And I’m not really asking you.”

There was a silence in the yellow room.

On the other sofa, her father put his hand over his eyes.

And Vittoria Song, who had made a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman cry without raising her voice, who had stood at the bottom of the stairs while her younger daughter walked out, who had raised a glass at a birthday party in front of two hundred guests and closed her older daughter’s shop, looked at the man on her sofa. Then she turned her head and looked at Serafina, and said, in Italian, very softly, in the voice she used when she was about to say the worst thing:

“I had two daughters, Serafina. One of them was the best thing I ever made. And the other one was a mistake I made in August.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina didn’t remember standing up.

She remembered the sound the silver coffee pot made when her knee caught the table, and the coffee going over the sticker, Lot 31, and her father saying “Vittoria,” in a voice she had never heard, broken right down the middle. She remembered that her hand was still in Haozhen’s, because when she stood he stood with her, without a sound, as though he’d known half a second before she did.

She remembered looking down at her mother.

She didn’t say anything. She had thought, at three in the morning on the coast road, of a hundred things she would say. She had seven years of things. She found she didn’t need any of them. She looked at her mother on the sofa in the yellow room, in black, with nothing on her hands, with every piece of furniture round her numbered for a man called Mr. Szeto, and she thought, quite clearly: you’re frightened. You’re so frightened you can’t see. And she didn’t say that either.

She turned round and walked out.

Through the morning-room door. Across the hall, past the Venetian mirror with Lot 7 on it, past the clock from Milan. Past the great staircase, at the top of which her sister had stood at twenty and watched her go and said nothing. Out of the front door, which was open, because there was nobody left to close it.

She didn’t run. That was the thing she was proudest of, afterwards. She walked. On her own feet. Down the drive, through the old trees, with the harbour falling away below her and his hand in hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway down the drive she heard someone behind them.

She didn’t stop. He did. He turned his head, and she felt him go still, and then not, and she stopped too.

Her father was coming down the drive.

Slowly, in his grey cardigan that was too big, in house slippers, on the gravel, with one hand out as if he were reaching for a rail that wasn’t there. He was out of breath. He stopped three metres away from them under the trees and stood there with his chest going up and down.

“Sera,” he said.

She couldn’t answer him.

“The hill climb,” said Song Weiren. “In June. I watched it.” He was breathing hard. “On the computer. In the office. I didn’t—I don’t know how to work it, the girl from accounts had to show me. I watched it.” His face crumpled. “You waved. At the top. I thought—for one second I thought—”

He stopped.

He didn’t finish. He stood on the drive in his slippers and looked at his younger daughter with his hands at his sides, and Serafina understood that he had thought, for one second, on a computer in a tower that was about to belong to a bank, that she had been waving at him.

She let go of Haozhen’s hand.

She walked back up the gravel, three metres, and stood in front of her father. He was smaller than she was now. He had always been taller. She put her arms round him, the oily leather jacket and all, and held on, and he made a sound into her shoulder like something breaking, and held on too.

“It was a very good climb, Papà,” she said.

“It was,” said her father, muffled. “It was. You took the hundred and twelfth on the outside. Lau never does that.”

She laughed into his cardigan.

“How do you know about Lau?”

“I asked the girl from accounts,” said Song Weiren, “to find me everything.” He drew back and held her face, the way he had when she was small, and looked at it. Then he looked past her, down the drive, at the man in the forgettable suit standing on the gravel with his hands at his sides where people could see them.

He didn’t say anything to him.

But he nodded. Once. As if he’d been answered.

✦ ✦ ✦

“She’s frightened,” said Haozhen, in Nonna, at the bottom of the hill.

Serafina had her hands on the wheel and the engine running and her face wet and she hadn’t put the car in gear.

“Of what?”

“Of being left with nothing.” He was looking out of the windscreen at the gates. “Nothing in her hands and nobody in the room. I’ve seen it. In a lot of rooms. In a lot of countries. People who’ve had everything, the week before it goes.” He was quiet. “They say the worst thing they can think of. To the person they’re most afraid of losing. So it’ll be their choice.”

She looked at him.

“That doesn’t make it all right.”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “It doesn’t make it anything. It’s just what it is.” He turned his head. “I’m sorry I made you go.”

“Don’t be.” She put the car in first. Her hands were shaking. “My father watched the hill climb. On a computer. The girl from accounts had to show him.”

“I know,” he said. “I heard.”

She pulled out of the gates onto the road down the Peak, and the house went away behind them in the trees, yellow, enormous, with numbers on everything in it.

“Eleven times,” said Serafina, after the first bend, “is still the record,” and he laughed, very low, the dark one with the fear in it, and put his hand on the back of her neck, and kept it there all the way down the hill.

chapters.title: Jinx Builds the Getaway Car
chapters.desc: “Sera, I want out.” Rule four, at last, at the kettle. But they know every car she owns. So it has to be a car nobody knows, built by a woman near the Docks with tattoos on both arms who builds bikes, hates cars, and takes one order at a time with no questions.
chapters.epigraph: “One order. No questions. And you never bring it back here with a hole in it.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
He said it on a Tuesday, at the kettle, at seven in the morning, holding the plain mug.

He said it the way she’d told him to, in January, on the bonnet of Nonna outside the laundry. Before he’d worked it out. Before he had a plan. Before he had even, she thought, said it to himself properly. He just turned round from the kettle with the mug in his hand and steam coming off it and looked at her across the garage, where she was sitting on the bottom stair of the loft in her vest pulling her boots on, and said:

“Sera. I want out.”

She stopped with a lace in each hand.

The garage was very quiet. Big Wu wasn’t in yet. Mr. Kwok wasn’t in yet. Mouse was a shape at the end of the bench with her headphones on, and she didn’t move, but Serafina saw her hands go still on the keyboard.

“Rule four,” said Serafina.

“Rule four.”

She finished tying her boots. Double knots. Then she stood up.

“I’ll have the car,” she said.

“Not your car.”

She looked at him.

“They know your car,” said Qin Haozhen. He put the mug down. “They know all of them. Nonna. Gilded. The transporter. My grey car, obviously, they gave it to me. They’ll know Big Wu’s van and Mr. Kwok’s old taxi and the scooter Mouse rides to the night market. They’ll have every plate.” He said it without any drama at all. “When they come, and they’ll come, the first thing they’ll do is look for a red Lancia. If we’re in it, it’s over before the bridge.”

“So what do we need?”

“A car nobody knows,” he said. “That nobody’s ever seen. That doesn’t look like anything. That nobody in this city would look at twice.” He paused. “And that will do two hundred and sixty on the coast road with four people shooting at it.”

Serafina looked at him for a long moment.

“Two hundred and sixty,” she said.

“If possible.”

“In something that doesn’t look like anything.”

“Yes.”

She picked up her jacket off the stair rail.

“Then we need Jinx,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx’s garage was near the Iron Docks, in a street of chandlers and rope shops and a noodle place that only served men off the container ships, in the part of the city where Zhao Zhendong’s name was said very quietly or not at all. It had a roll-up door painted black and no sign, and inside it was full of motorcycles in every stage of being born.

Jinx was under one.

She came out on a creeper when Serafina kicked the door, three times, the way you did. She was small and fierce and twenty-seven, with her hair shaved at one side and black nails and tattoos on both arms from her wrists to her shoulders, a whole garden of them, peonies and gears and a carp swimming up the inside of her left forearm toward a spark plug. She looked up at Serafina from the creeper and grinned. Then she looked past her at the man standing in the doorway, and stopped grinning.

“No,” she said.

“You haven’t heard what it is.”

“I know what it is. I can see what it is. It’s standing in my doorway.” Jinx sat up on the creeper. “He’s one of the ones Raiden’s father-in-law used to make sure didn’t come into the Walled City. I can see it from here.”

“Lin Jian is Raiden’s father,” said Serafina.

“Then he’s one of the ones Raiden’s father used to make sure didn’t come into the Walled City,” said Jinx. “Stop being pedantic at me in my own garage.” She looked at Haozhen. “You’re Bureau.”

“I can’t tell you that,” said Qin Haozhen.

Jinx looked at him.

Then she laughed. Short and surprised.

“Oh, I like that,” she said. “I can’t tell you that. Not no. Not what’s a Bureau. Just I can’t tell you that.” She stood up off the creeper and wiped her hands. “Elowen says that. To her sisters. About Zhao. Word for word.”

“It’s going round,” said Serafina.

“I’m not building you anything,” said Jinx. “I build bikes. I don’t build cars. Cars are bikes for cowards. Ask Raiden. I’ve told him every day since 2021.”

“I’m not asking you to build a car,” said Serafina. “I’m asking you to help me build one. In your garage. Where nobody’s looking.” She put her hands in her pockets. “You owe me for the gearbox in your sidecar.”

“I paid you for that gearbox.”

“You paid me in a bike,” said Serafina. “Which I love. Which I ride every day. Which is not money.” She tilted her head. “And he wants out, Jinx.”

Jinx went still.

She looked at Haozhen again. Differently. The way she looked at an engine that had come in making a noise she hadn’t heard before.

“Out,” she said. “Of the—” She didn’t say the word. “Out of that.”

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

Jinx was quiet. Then she turned round and walked to the back of her garage, past the bikes, to a wall where a lot of drawings were pinned up with clothes pegs on a line, and stood in front of one of them with her back to them and her arms folded.

It was a drawing of a motorcycle. A beautiful one. In pencil, very fine, every bolt and spring and spoke, and underneath, in someone’s careful architect’s lettering: J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021.

“One order,” said Jinx, to the drawing. “No questions. That’s my rule. I don’t want to know where you’re going. I don’t want to know who’s chasing you. I don’t want to know your name.” She turned round. “And you never, ever bring it back here with a hole in it. That’s the price.”

“Agreed,” said Qin Haozhen.

“And you,” said Jinx, pointing at Serafina, “are washing my floor at the end of every night. With the good soap.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They found the car in a breaker’s yard at the end of the Docks road on the Saturday.

It was a grey 2006 Toyota Crown estate. It had been a taxi company’s, then a funeral company’s, then nobody’s. It had two hundred and ninety thousand kilometres on it and a dent in the rear door and a cracked dashboard and seat covers made of wooden beads, the kind taxi drivers used for their backs. It was the dullest, most ordinary, most invisible car Serafina had ever seen in her life, and when she saw it, wedged between a burned-out van and a pile of tyres, she put her hand over her mouth.

“Oh,” she said. “Oh, it’s perfect.”

He looked at it for a while. Something happened at the corner of his mouth.

“It looks like me,” he said.

“It looks exactly like you,” said Serafina, and paid the breaker four hundred and twenty in cash, and they pushed it onto Jinx’s trailer by hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took five weeks.

They worked at night, in Jinx’s garage, with the black roll-up door down and the bikes pushed against the walls. Serafina and Jinx and, after the first week, Mouse, who arrived one evening without being asked, with a rucksack and two laptops and a soldering iron, and sat in the passenger seat of the stripped-out Crown and began doing things to the wiring that she would not explain to anybody. Haozhen came every night. He held lamps. He passed spanners. He fetched noodles from the place that only served men off the container ships, where they looked at him the first night and then never again.

They took out the engine. It had been tired and honest and had carried a great many people to a great many funerals, and Serafina thanked it before they lifted it out, out loud, in Italian. They put in another one. It came from a car that had never been meant to share a road with a family estate, and it had taken Jinx three phone calls and a favour from somebody in the Walled City she would not name to find. It sat in the engine bay of the grey Crown like a tiger in a dog kennel.

They did the brakes. They did the suspension, very carefully, so that the car still sat at exactly the height a tired old estate should sit, and wallowed a little at walking pace, and only stopped wallowing when you asked it to. They put a different fuel tank in. They did the tyres so that they’d keep going when they shouldn’t. They left the dent in the rear door and the crack in the dashboard and the wooden-bead seat covers, all of them, because Jinx said that was the most important part.

“The beads,” she said, “are the whole point. Nobody who sees the beads ever thinks about what’s under the bonnet. Taxi drivers have been teaching me that for years.”

And on the fourth Saturday, at two in the morning, Raiden came.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in under the black roll-up door in a paint-spattered jacket with a roll of drawing paper under his arm and his most cheerful, slightly useless expression, the one Elowen said she’d been afraid of since he was nine, and said, “Darling, I’ve brought soup, why is there a man from the Bureau in your garage,” in exactly the same tone of voice.

“I can’t tell you that,” said Qin Haozhen, from under the car.

Raiden stopped.

He put the soup on the bench. He looked at the legs sticking out from under the grey Crown, and at Serafina, who was holding a lamp, and at his wife, who was looking back at him with her arms folded and an expression that dared him to ask anything else.

“Right,” said Raiden. “Right. Lovely. I’ll just draw it, shall I.”

He drew it.

He sat on an upturned crate in the corner of the garage with his drawing board on his knees, very quietly, without his silly voice, for four hours, while they worked. And when they finished at six and the grey light came in under the roll-up door, he unpinned a sheet from his board and held it up.

It was the car. The grey Crown estate. Dented, beaded, ordinary, drawn exactly as it looked from the outside, every crease in the bodywork, every chip in the paint. Except that he had drawn it as if the outside were glass. And through the glass you could see what was underneath. All of it. The engine like a tiger. The brakes. The tank. Mouse’s wiring, drawn as a fine silver web. Every bolt and spring, very fine, in pencil, the way he’d drawn Jinx’s bike in 2021.

Underneath, in his careful architect’s lettering: Nobody’s car, as it really is. R. 2023.

“Nobody’s car,” said Serafina.

“That’s what it’s called, isn’t it?” Raiden looked at her. “You name all of them. Jinx told me. What else would you call it?”

Serafina looked at the drawing.

“Nobody,” she said. “Yes. That’s its name.”

Raiden turned to the man who had just come out from under the car, wiping his hands.

“Every building I draw,” he said, “has a door in it that nobody knows about. My brother-in-law taught me that. In a flower shop.” He held out the drawing. “Every car should have one too. This is yours.”

Haozhen took it.

He looked at it. At the plain grey outside, and everything under it.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Don’t thank me,” said Raiden, cheerfully again, already turning away. “Thank my wife. And never bring it back with a hole in it, she’ll kill you, I’ve seen her do it to a carburettor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They took Nobody out for the first time on the last Saturday in October, at three in the morning, on the Docks road.

Serafina drove. He sat beside her on the wooden beads. The roll-up door went up and the grey Crown rolled out into the street of chandlers at walking pace, wallowing a little on its springs, exactly like a tired old estate car going home from a night shift, and turned onto the Docks road, which was four kilometres long and dead straight and empty at three in the morning except for the cranes.

“Ready?” she said.

“Yes.”

She put her foot down.

It was like falling. That was the only way she could describe it to Jinx afterwards. Nobody sat down on its rear wheels and the beaded seat pressed into her spine and the engine made a sound no taxi had ever made, a long rising scream from somewhere deep inside the grey bodywork, and the cranes went past the windows like posts on a fence, and the needle went round the cracked dial to a hundred and eighty, where the taxi company’s speedometer ran out of numbers, and lay there, and Mouse’s little screen under the dash kept counting.

Two hundred and sixty-four.

On the Docks road. In a grey Toyota estate with wooden beads on the seats and a dent in the back door.

She braked at the end of the road and the car stopped like it had hit a wall of feathers, perfectly straight, and she sat with both hands on the wheel and started to laugh, and couldn’t stop.

He was laughing too. He was sitting on the beads with his hand braced on the cracked dashboard, laughing, out loud, the way he had on the coast road in March with the ring on her little finger, and he turned to her and took her face in both hands across the gearstick and kissed her, hard, in the dark at the end of the Docks road with the engine ticking and the cranes standing over them like patient animals.

“Two hundred and sixty-four,” he said, against her mouth.

“You asked for two hundred and sixty.”

“I know what I asked for.”

“I gave you four extra.”

“You always give me extra,” said Qin Haozhen, and kissed her again, and the windows fogged, and her elbow found the horn, which was the original taxi horn and made a noise like a goose, and neither of them stopped until somebody banged on the roof with a spanner.

It was Jinx. She’d ridden down after them on her bike, in her helmet, and she was standing beside Nobody’s driver’s door with the spanner in her hand and her visor up.

“Not in my car,” she said. “I’ve only just done the seats.”

“They’re beads, Jinx.”

“They’re my beads,” said Jinx, and got back on her bike, and rode away up the Docks road toward the garage, and at the far end of it, under the last crane, they saw her stop, and turn round, and sit there on her bike in the dark, watching them. Making sure.

✦ ✦ ✦

They kept it in Jinx’s garage. At the back, behind the bikes, under a canvas sheet, with a pile of old tyres stacked on its roof so that from the door it looked like part of the wall.

Nobody knew it was there. That was the point.

On the bench in the garage under the railway bridge, the next morning, Serafina found a piece of paper by the kettle. It was a sheet from his black notebook, torn out along the perforations. On it, in his small square letters, very neatly, as if it were a list of requirements or a run sheet, there was a single line.

Way out: built.

And under it, smaller, crossed out once and then written again, as if he’d had to think about whether he was allowed:

Way in: also built. (Her.)

chapters.title: The Mission He Didn’t Take
chapters.desc: A grey building in the capital that isn’t on any map. A seventh-floor office with a radiator that knocks. A thin folder about a journalist in Singapore. For the first time in eleven years, he says one word to the state, and it’s the wrong one.
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know what happens to people who say no, Haozhen?” “Yes, Director. I’ve driven them.”
chapters.content:
The building had no name on it.

It stood on a wide grey street in the capital among other wide grey buildings, behind a wall with a gate and a guard box, and it had seven floors and a great many windows, and none of the windows ever had a light on after nine at night, because the people who worked late in it worked in rooms without windows. It did not appear on any map. Taxi drivers who were asked to take you there drove you to the bus stop opposite and let you walk.

He had been coming to it since he was eighteen. He knew the guard on the gate, who was called Old Tsui and had a bad hip and grew chillies in a pot in the guard box. He knew the lift that stuck between four and five and how to kick it. He knew that the radiator in the corridor on the seventh floor knocked three times every twenty minutes, like someone wanting to be let in, and that nobody had fixed it since 2009.

He had never, in eleven years, walked down that corridor not knowing what he was going to say.

He knew now. That was different. He had known since the hotel lobby in Lisbon at six in the morning. He had known since the boy on the step with the football. He had known since the passenger seat, the third night, with her arms round his head.

He just hadn’t said it yet. Not out loud. Not here.

The radiator knocked three times.

He knocked once on the door at the end.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Come,” said Director Duan.

Her office was small and warm and very neat. A desk. Two chairs. A window, the only one on the seventh floor, which looked out at a wall. A kettle, a tin of tea, a photograph on the desk turned away from the visitor’s chair that nobody had ever seen. She sat behind the desk in her grey cardigan with the darned elbow, knitting.

“Sit,” she said. “Hot water’s in the flask.”

He sat. He didn’t pour the water.

“How is she?” said Director Duan.

“Well.”

“She won her class at the endurance round in October, I’m told. Six hours. She and the other driver, the one with the beard. Second overall.” The needles clicked. “And her parents’ house goes to auction on the twenty-eighth. I’m sorry about that. It’s a beautiful house. I saw the brochure.”

He didn’t say anything.

“And how are you, Haozhen?”

“Well, Director.”

“Sleeping?”

“Yes.”

“Liar,” said Director Duan, gently, to the wool. “You’ve never slept in your life.” She turned the scarf on the needles. “Mr. Gong is being very cooperative, by the way. In case you were wondering. He’s been extremely helpful. He’s told us everything he knows about who he showed what to, which is nobody, which is what we thought, which is a great relief to the people upstairs.” A row. “His wife has written to the embassy in Lisbon. Eleven times. And the boy wrote once. In crayon. In Portuguese. Somebody translated it for me.” She looked up over her glasses. “Would you like to know what it said?”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen.

“No,” she agreed. “I didn’t think you would.” She took a folder out of the drawer and put it on the desk between them. “Singapore.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was thin. He didn’t open it.

“A journalist,” said Director Duan. “A woman. Thirty-four. She writes for a magazine in Singapore about money. Where it goes. She’s been writing, recently, about some of ours. She’s very good, which is the problem. She’s found some of the right companies.” The needles clicked. “We’d like her home. She was born in the capital. Her mother’s still here. It would be a homecoming, of a kind.”

“In what condition?”

The needles stopped.

It was the second time. The half-second pause. The row left unfinished, the red wool lying still on the bamboo. She looked at him over the top of her glasses with the same careful attention she’d given him in the tea house in May, the look you’d give a dog you’d raised that had looked at the door, and this time it went on a little longer.

“Alive,” she said. “Of course. We’re not barbarians. Alive, and talking.” She started knitting again. “December. Two weeks, perhaps three. You’ll have Tianyi. He loves Singapore. The chilli crab.”

He looked at the folder.

He looked at it for a long time. The radiator in the corridor knocked three times. Outside the window there was a wall. On the desk, the photograph that faced away from him. In his inside pocket, on the left, there was a sheet of paper torn from his notebook that said Way out: built, and a cream card with a telephone number on it, and nothing else, because he’d given back the brass gauge.

“No,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing happened.

That was what he would remember. He had imagined it, on the plane, a hundred times, and in every version something happened. A door. A hand on a phone. Her face changing. In fact, Director Duan simply went on knitting. Her needles went in and out of the red wool at exactly the speed they always went. She finished the row. She turned the scarf. She started the next row. She did not look up.

“No,” she repeated, eventually, to the scarf. Mildly. As if trying out a word in a foreign language.

“No, Director.”

“You don’t want Singapore. Would you like somewhere else? There’s a man in Prague nobody else wants. It snows in Prague in December. You like snow.”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “Not Prague. Not anywhere.”

The needles went on. In, round, through, off.

“In eleven years,” said Director Duan, “you have never said no to me. Not once. You’ve never said I’d rather not. You’ve never asked to be excused. You went to that hotel in the capital at eighteen and you did what you were asked, and you came back and filled in the form, and you’ve been doing it ever since. You were the best I ever had. You’re still the best I’ve got.” She knitted. “And now you sit in my office and tell me no. Like a child at dinner. Because of a girl who fixes cars.”

“Not because of her.”

“Then because of what?”

He thought about it. He gave it the care he gave everything.

“Because of a boy with a football,” he said. “Who looked at me. And because I’d never let anyone look at me before.”

The needles stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put the knitting down.

He had never seen her do it. Not in the commandant’s office at the academy, not in the tea house, not in a hotel in a country he would not name with a man on the floor. She laid it on the desk, the two bamboo needles and the long red ribbed scarf that had been on them since 2012, and folded her hands on top of it, and looked at him without her glasses.

Her eyes, without the glasses, were small and tired and very dark, and he had the strange thought that she was older than he had ever let himself notice.

“Do you know what happens,” said Director Duan Qiuyan, “to people who say no, Haozhen?”

“Yes, Director,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve driven them.”

She looked at him. The radiator knocked.

Then she put her glasses back on, and picked up her knitting, and found her place, and started again.

“Go home,” she said. “Think about it. You have until the New Year.” In, round, through, off. “Think about your mother, in her little flat, with her sewing machine. Think about Miss Song and her car with the number on it. Think about who you’d be, without us. You don’t have a name without us. You don’t have a file. You don’t have a single thing you didn’t get from this building.” She didn’t look up. “Think about it very carefully. And then come back after the New Year and tell me you’ve changed your mind. And I’ll give you Prague, and we’ll never mention this. I’ll put it down to the strain of the engagement.”

He stood up.

“Thank you, Director,” he said.

“Leave the folder.”

He left the folder.

At the door he stopped.

“The scarf,” he said. “Who is it for?”

The needles didn’t pause.

“Go home, Haozhen,” said Director Duan.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi was in the corridor.

He was leaning on the wall beside the knocking radiator with a stick of cinnamon gum and his hands in his pockets, waiting, as if he’d been there a while. He looked at Haozhen’s face as he came out of the office and closed the door. He didn’t smile.

“She gave you Singapore,” he said.

“Yes.”

“And you said no.”

Haozhen didn’t answer.

Tianyi let out a long breath through his nose. He pushed himself off the wall. He looked up and down the corridor, at the closed doors, the lift that stuck between four and five, the radiator.

“I’ll take it,” he said. “I like Singapore. The chilli crab.” He chewed. “She’ll give it to me this afternoon. She’ll give it to me and she’ll watch my face while I take it to see if I’m going to do what you did.”

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what? Don’t take it?” Tianyi laughed, but there was nothing in it. “Haozhen. I’m not you. I don’t have a racing driver. I’ve got a flat in the east of the city and a fish tank and an ex-wife in the far west who sends me photos of her new dog. I take the folder.” He looked at Haozhen for a moment. “What happened to you? In Lisbon. Before Lisbon. What happened?”

“Someone told me what I was,” said Qin Haozhen.

Tianyi looked at him.

“In a ballroom,” said Haozhen. “In her sister’s dress. She walked across the room and told me.” He paused. “And I’ve been finding out ever since whether she was right.”

They stood in the corridor. The radiator knocked three times. Somewhere below them the lift stuck between four and five and someone kicked it.

“You know what they’ll do,” said Tianyi, quietly. “If you keep saying no. If you don’t come back after the New Year with your hat in your hand.” He wasn’t chewing any more. “They won’t send a stranger. They never send a stranger. You know that. It’s in the training.” He looked at the floor. “They always send the friend.”

“I know.”

“So it’ll be me.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’m sorry.”

Tianyi looked up. For a second his face was very young, the face of a sixteen-year-old in a dormitory of forty boys under a leaking roof, who laughed with his whole face and gave away his window seat to nobody except the quiet boy from the mining town.

Then he grinned, the old grin, and put a fresh stick of gum in his mouth.

“Don’t be sorry,” he said. “Be faster.”

He knocked on the director’s door, once, and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang her from a payphone at the airport, because there was no phone that was his.

It was eleven at night in the capital and eleven at night at home, because it was all one time zone, and she picked up on the first ring. He heard the garage behind her. The radio. A spanner. A train starting, far off, coming toward the bridge.

“It’s me,” he said.

“I know it’s you. Nobody rings me from a payphone except you and the tyre company.” Her voice changed. “Hao. What’s happened?”

He stood in the payphone booth at the end of the departures hall with his forehead against the cold glass.

“I said no,” he said.

There was a silence on the line. Behind it, he heard the train arrive. He heard it go over the bridge. He heard the whole garage shake, and the spanner fall into the bucket, and he closed his eyes and listened to it, eleven hundred kilometres away, the most ordinary sound in the world.

“How did it feel?” said Serafina, when it had passed.

He thought about it.

“Like the fourth lamp post,” said Qin Haozhen.

She made a sound down the line, a laugh and something else together, and he heard her put her hand over her mouth.

“What time’s your flight?”

“Seven. In the morning. I land at half past ten.”

“I’ll be there.”

“Not in Nonna. They’ll be watching—”

“In Nonna,” said Serafina. “In the red car with the dent in the door. At arrivals. In the NO WAITING lane, with the engine running, for as long as I like.” He heard her breathe. “Let them watch. You said no. I want them to see who you said it for.”

He stood with his forehead on the glass.

“I love you,” he said.

“I know,” said Serafina. “You said it through a window. I’m still angry. Get on the plane.”

chapters.title: A File on the Workbench
chapters.desc: A Saturday afternoon. He’s in the north for his mother’s birthday. A woman of fifty-five in a grey coat ducks under the shutter with a shopping bag and her knitting, asks very politely for hot water, and sits on his stool. When she leaves, there’s a file on the bench. Forty photographs. One of them was taken that morning.
chapters.epigraph: “My mother did this with one photograph.” “My director thinks your mother’s an amateur.”
chapters.content:
He had gone north on the Friday.

It was his mother’s birthday on the Saturday. Sixty-two. He had not been home for it in three years, and he told Serafina on the Thursday, at the kettle, that he thought he should go. He said it carefully, the way he said everything now that he had said no to the state. As if each sentence were a step on ice.

“Go,” she said. “Take her something.”

“What?”

“I don’t know. What does she like?”

He thought about it for a long time.

“She sews,” he said. “She’s always liked good thread. The kind she can’t get up there. Japanese. In the little wooden spools.”

So on Thursday night Serafina took him to the haberdasher in the old market district who had been there since before the war, and stood in the doorway while he chose thirty spools of Japanese silk thread in thirty colours with the full, grave attention he’d given the wine on Harbour Road, and the haberdasher’s wife wrapped them in red paper, and he carried them out of the shop held against his chest in both hands.

He took the train on Friday morning. Not a plane. A train, the slow one, eleven hours. He said he wanted to see it come up on the horizon the way it had when he was sixteen, going the other way.

“Ring me from her phone,” said Serafina.

“I will.”

“Tell her I’m sorry I’m not there.”

He’d looked at her at the station barrier.

“She doesn’t know about you yet,” he said. “I’m going to tell her. Tomorrow. At dinner.” He paused. “I’m going to tell her I’m marrying a racing driver who fixes cars and swears in three languages and has never once in her life done what she was told.”

“She’ll hate me.”

“She’ll ask,” said Qin Haozhen, “if you can sew,” and went through the barrier.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday afternoon the garage was empty.

Big Wu was at his mother’s, because it was her mahjong day and she needed him to lose. Mr. Kwok was at the breakwater with his fishing box, catching nothing. Mouse had gone to the night market early for parts. Serafina was under Gilded on the creeper, alone, with the radio on and the shutter half up, because it was December and the air coming in was cold and clean and she liked it.

At ten past three, the radio went off.

She lay very still on the creeper.

She knew it wasn’t him. He was eleven hundred kilometres away eating birthday noodles. And it wasn’t how he turned the radio off. He did it quietly, with one finger on the dial, a quarter turn. This had been switched off at the wall. The plug pulled out. She’d heard it come out of the socket.

“Miss Song,” said a woman’s voice. “I’m so sorry to disturb you. I wonder if I could trouble you for some hot water?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was standing just inside the shutter.

Fifty-five, perhaps. Small. A neat grey bob. A grey wool coat, good but old, buttoned to the neck, and under it the collar of a grey cardigan. Reading glasses on a chain round her neck. Flat shoes. In one hand a canvas shopping bag, the kind you’d take to a vegetable market, with a bag of oranges in the top of it and, poking out beside the oranges, two bamboo knitting needles and a long tail of red wool.

She looked like somebody’s aunt. She looked like the woman who ran the school library. She looked like the most harmless person who had ever walked into that garage, including Mouse.

Serafina rolled out from under the car and sat up.

She’d never seen her. She’d never seen a photograph. He’d never described her, not once, not her face or her clothes or her voice. Serafina had never asked. And she knew exactly who it was the moment she saw the red wool.

“Director Duan,” she said.

“Oh,” said the woman, pleased. “He told you about me.”

“No,” said Serafina. “He told me about your scarf.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She made the tea. She didn’t know why. Her hands did it while the rest of her was standing very still somewhere above them, watching. She filled the kettle at the sink and put it on the camping stove and got down the mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST MECHANIC, and then stopped with her hand on the second one, the plain one that said HIS, and got down the chipped one from 2019 that Big Wu’s mother had brought instead.

Director Duan watched her do it.

She was sitting on the stool by the kettle. His stool. She had sat on it without being asked, with her shopping bag at her feet and her coat still buttoned, and she had taken out her knitting and found her place, and the needles were going. In, round, through, off. Very quiet. Very fast.

“He drinks hot water,” she said. “Still. I’ve never been able to get him onto tea.”

“Neither have I.”

“No.” The needles clicked. “He was like that at eighteen. I remember the first time I saw him. In the commandant’s office at the academy, standing in front of the desk, in a uniform two sizes too big, because they never had the small sizes. They’d told me he never hesitated. I asked him a question. I forget what. Something about a map. He answered it before I’d finished asking.” She smiled at the wool. “I thought, that’s a boy who’s never been allowed to want anything. I could do a great deal with a boy like that.”

Serafina put the chipped mug of hot water down on the bench beside her. Not in her hand. On the bench.

“You did,” she said.

“I did.” Director Duan didn’t look up. “I made him the best there is. He was nobody, Miss Song. A miner’s boy from a town that isn’t on the maps. No father. A mother who sewed. No money. No name. He’d have gone down the pit at sixteen like every other boy in that town and been dead of his lungs at fifty.” The needles went on. “I gave him a name. I gave him eleven years of meaning. I gave him everything he is. He doesn’t have a self without us. I want you to understand that. Not because I’m cruel. Because it’s true.”

“He’s got a self,” said Serafina.

“Has he?”

“He’s got a notebook. He writes lists in it. He’s got a way of folding shirts like envelopes. He sings in the shower when he thinks I’m asleep, and he’s got a better voice than he’ll admit. He likes egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover. He doesn’t like fish either, he just eats it so nobody notices.” Serafina’s voice was rising. She let it. “He takes his watch off when something matters. He sleeps in my passenger seat. He paid for my gearbox. He bought his mother thirty spools of Japanese thread on Thursday night and carried them out of the shop like they were going to break.” She stopped. “You didn’t give him any of that. You don’t even know any of that.”

The needles paused.

Half a second. A row left unfinished.

Then they went on.

“No,” said Director Duan, mildly. “I didn’t know about the singing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drank her hot water. She finished her row. She put the knitting back in the canvas bag beside the oranges and stood up, and buttoned the top button of her coat, which was already buttoned, and looked round the garage once, slowly. The shutter. The side door. The stairs to the loft. The whiteboard, with the postcard of the Monza banking in the middle of it. Gilded on the creeper with its wheel off. The small grey taxi on the driver’s door, under three coats of lacquer.

Her eyes stopped on the taxi for a moment.

Then she reached into the canvas bag, under the oranges, and took out a file.

It was grey. Thick. Tied with a cloth tape. She laid it on the workbench beside the kettle, beside the chipped mug, very precisely, the way he put things down.

“Please give him this,” she said. “When he’s back. And tell him the door is still open. Until the New Year. After that I’m afraid it closes.” She picked up her bag. “It was lovely to meet you, Miss Song. You have a very loud laugh. I’ve only heard it on recordings.”

She walked to the shutter. She ducked under it. On the other side she stopped and looked back.

“He’ll want to know if I read it to you,” she said. “Tell him no. Tell him I thought you’d rather read it yourself.”

Then she was gone. Serafina heard her footsteps go down the street of shuttered workshops, unhurried, flat shoes on the cracked concrete. She didn’t hear a car. Not at the corner. Not anywhere.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t open it for twenty minutes.

She sat on the creeper and looked at it on the bench. Two trains went over. The file didn’t move.

Then she got up and untied the tape and opened it.

Photographs. That was most of it. Glossy, eight by ten, the way the one of her at nineteen had been, the one her mother had sent to Aurelia’s boutique in 2019. Taken at night with a long lens. Granny Shum’s. The paint works, the floodlight, the line. Nonna on the line. Nonna in the S-bends. Nonna at the gas works with the back hanging out. Her own face through the windscreen, laughing. Her hand raised with the white scarf, at the start of somebody else’s race. Each one dated in the corner in small white figures, and numbered, like evidence.

The first one was dated the twenty-sixth of November, 2022. The night he’d lifted at the gas works. In the passenger seat of the grey estate behind her, if you looked very closely, was a black cap and a shoulder.

The last one was dated three weeks ago.

There were forty of them.

Under the photographs there was a copy of her national racing licence, the renewal form she’d filled in in September, with her signature. A photocopy of a page from the road traffic regulations, the section they’d changed in the spring of 2019, with the line about three years marked in yellow highlighter. And a single sheet of paper with nothing on it except the name of the officer in charge of the traffic division’s street-racing unit, and his direct telephone number.

And at the bottom, face down, one more photograph.

She turned it over.

A market. A small one, in a street of low brick houses, in bright cold winter light. Stalls with tarpaulin roofs. Cabbages stacked in pyramids. And at a vegetable stall, with her back half to the camera, a small woman in a padded jacket and a knitted hat, choosing a cabbage. Holding it in both hands. Testing the weight. There was a sewing bag over her arm.

In the corner, in small white figures, the date.

Today. That morning. Nine forty-one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina put the photograph down on the bench very carefully, face up, beside the others.

Then she walked to the sink at the back of the garage and was sick into it.

She stood there for a while afterwards with both hands on the edge of the sink and the cold tap running. Her hands were shaking. Not a little. The way Big Wu’s hands shook the morning after a bad night, before his mother’s soup. She turned off the tap. She turned round.

She looked at the kettle.

The plain mug. His. The one that said HIS in her marker, that she had not taken down, that she had left on the shelf above the kettle where it lived, facing the room.

It was facing the wall.

She hadn’t touched it. She knew she hadn’t touched it. She had reached for it and stopped and taken down the chipped one instead. And at some point in the twenty minutes the director had sat on his stool with her knitting, without Serafina seeing her do it, without Serafina hearing anything, Director Duan Qiuyan had reached up and turned his mug round, the way he used to turn it, at the very beginning, before he let anyone see.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang at nine, from his mother’s phone.

She heard the television behind him, and someone laughing, an old woman’s laugh, high and surprised, and a sewing machine going somewhere, and he said, “She likes the thread. She’s already used the blue. She asked if you can sew,” and his voice was lighter than she’d ever heard it.

Serafina sat on the floor of the garage with her back against Gilded and the file open beside her.

“Hao,” she said.

He heard it. Down eleven hundred kilometres of telephone line, in two syllables. She heard the television go quiet behind him, and the sewing machine stop, and a door close, and then he was somewhere small and dark and alone.

“What happened.”

She told him. All of it, because it was rule one. The radio at the wall. The shopping bag. The stool. The things Director Duan had said about the commandant’s office and a boy who’d never been allowed to want anything. The file. The forty photographs. The licence. The highlighter. The name and number of the officer in the traffic division.

She didn’t tell him about the last photograph. Not yet. She told him about the mug.

He was silent.

“There’s one more,” she said.

“Tell me.”

“It’s a market,” said Serafina. “Up there. Where you are. Cabbages. Brick houses. A woman in a knitted hat. With a sewing bag.” She swallowed. “It’s dated today. This morning. Nine forty-one.”

He didn’t say anything.

She heard him breathe. Once. In. And then she heard, very faintly, down the line, from the other side of the door he’d closed, his mother’s sewing machine start up again, and his mother humming to herself over it, something old and tuneless, while she sewed with thirty colours of Japanese thread.

“Nine forty-one,” said Qin Haozhen. His voice had gone back to the east service door. “I took her to the market at half past nine. I was standing behind her. At the next stall. Buying ginger.” A pause. “They wanted me to know they were standing behind me.”

“Come home.”

“Tomorrow. The first train.”

“Bring her,” said Serafina.

“I can’t. Not yet. If I bring her now they’ll know I’m frightened.” He was quiet. “She’s safe tonight. They don’t want her. They want me to know they can have her. That’s different. It’s in the training.”

“I hate your training.”

“So do I,” said Qin Haozhen, and for a second his voice wasn’t the east service door at all. “Sera. Did she touch you?”

“No.”

“Did she touch anything?”

“The mug.”

He was silent for so long that Serafina thought the line had gone.

“My mother did this with one photograph,” she said, into the silence. “In 2019. To my sister. One photograph of me, at Granny Shum’s. And my sister nearly broke in half.”

“I know.”

“Your director brought a whole file.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “My director thinks your mother’s an amateur.”

“She said so?”

“She’ll have thought so. She always thinks so.” He drew a breath, a long one, and she heard something come into his voice she had never heard before. Not fear. Not the flat one. Something that sounded, very faintly, like her own voice in the hill-climb paddock: can’t be done, is what they said about the Needle.

“Then I need a file of my own,” he said.

She sat on the floor of the garage with her back against the car and the forty photographs spread round her in the light from the hanging lamp.

“How long?” she said.

“A month. Maybe less.”

“Of what?”

“Of everything I know,” said Qin Haozhen, “that she’d rather I didn’t.”

chapters.title: Leverage
chapters.desc: Eleven years of black notebooks in his own code, hidden under a laundry cat’s heated bed. One line in a stolen ledger: two initials and the word “Private”. A month of nights at the workbench, Mouse at the end of it finding companies, and three copies of a file nobody in the capital knows exists.
chapters.epigraph: “Mr. Qin. For what it’s worth. You’re starting to exist.” — Qian
chapters.content:
The notebooks were under the cat.

“Under the cat,” said Serafina.

“Under the cat’s bed. In the laundry. In the back room, by the boiler.” He was standing at the workbench at one in the morning on the second of January with his jacket still on, the first night of the new year, the night after the deadline had passed without his going back. “The bed’s on a wooden box. The box has a false bottom. The cat’s been sleeping on them since 2021. Before that they were in a hollow in a wall in a flat in the capital.”

“Does the laundry woman know?”

“She knows there’s a box under the cat’s bed that she’s not to move,” said Qin Haozhen. “She thinks it’s my grandfather’s ashes. I let her think it.” He put a canvas bag on the bench. “The cat knows. The cat’s never told anyone.”

He opened the bag.

There were twenty-three of them. Black, hardbacked, the same kind he kept in his inside pocket, the kind you could buy at any stationer’s for the price of an egg sandwich. Each one had a year on its spine in white paint, very small, and the years went from 2012 to 2023, and some years had one and some had three. He laid them out on the workbench in a row, in order, under the work lamp, the way she had once laid out parts.

She opened one at random. 2016. The pages were full of his small square letters, every line, both sides. She couldn’t read a word of it. It wasn’t Chinese. It wasn’t anything.

“It’s a code,” she said.

“Mine. I made it up at eighteen, after the hotel. On the train home.” He touched the edge of the notebook. “The first night, I couldn’t sleep, and I thought: I’m going to forget his face. In a year I won’t remember what he was wearing. And I couldn’t stand that. That I’d do it and then forget I’d done it. So I wrote it down. All of it. And I’ve written down every one since.” He was quiet. “Names. Dates. Places. What they were wearing. What they said, if they said anything. Who gave me the folder. Who I handed them to, at which petrol station, at which marina. Every one.”

“For eleven years.”

“I told you,” said Qin Haozhen. “I never forget them. That’s the one thing I never let myself do.” He looked at the row. “It was supposed to be for me. So I’d always know what I was. I never thought it would be anything else.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“What is it now?” said Serafina.

He took off his watch, and laid it face down on the bench beside the notebooks.

“Lisbon,” he said. “The ledgers. The ones I wasn’t supposed to read. I read one line.” He told her. The third ledger, spring 2020. A date, a figure, a company. Two initials in the column for authorisation, very small. D.Q.Y. And in the far-right column, where everything else said section or upstairs or a department number, one word, underlined.

Private.

“Duan Qiuyan,” said Serafina slowly.

“Yes.”

“Private,” said Serafina. “Private as in—”

“As in not for the state.” He was very calm. “As in for someone who paid. Not upstairs. Not the section. Somebody outside, with a reason of their own and the money to have the Bureau take care of it for them.” He looked at the notebooks. “Gong kept the books for nine years. He’d have seen it. He’d have seen all of it. He took the ledgers because of it. That’s why they wanted them back so badly. That’s why it was both of them, him and the books.” He was quiet for a moment. “I think that’s why Gong never showed anyone. He was afraid of who’d believe him.”

“And you think—”

“I think if she did it once,” said Qin Haozhen, “she did it more than once. And I think I drove some of them.” He touched the notebook for 2022. “I think I need to find out which.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took a month.

He worked at night, at the end of the workbench, with the notebooks and a pad of plain paper and a pencil, decoding his own handwriting one line at a time. She’d thought it would be fast. It wasn’t. The code, he said, had been made to be slow, so that if anyone ever found the notebooks they’d give up. He gave up on nothing. He sat on the stool by the kettle from midnight until five every night, with his watch face down beside him, translating eleven years of his own life back into words, and she worked on Gilded two metres away and listened to the pencil.

Some nights he stopped. Just stopped, with the pencil on the paper, and sat there. Once for forty minutes. She didn’t ask. She went on working, and every twenty minutes she brought him hot water in the plain mug, which she had turned back round to face the room the morning after the director left and which had stayed that way, and put it by his hand, and went back to the car.

Once, very late, she came and sat on the bench beside him. Not to read. Just to sit. She put her feet in his lap, boots and all, and leaned back against the wall under the whiteboard, and closed her eyes.

He went on writing. After a while, without looking up, he put his free hand on her ankle.

“Is it in there?” she said, with her eyes closed. “The number.”

The pencil stopped.

“Yes,” he said. “It’s all in here.”

“Don’t tell me.”

He turned his head.

“Not like this,” said Serafina. “Not off a page. Not in pencil. You said you’d tell me when I asked you, in a year. It’s been a year.” She opened her eyes and looked at him. “I’m not asking yet. When you tell me, I want it in your voice. Not out of a book.”

He looked at her for a long time. His hand stayed on her ankle.

“All right,” he said.

“And not tonight.”

“No.”

“You look awful.”

“Thank you.”

“Come to bed,” said Serafina. “Just for three hours. The cat’s been guarding these for three years. She can guard them on the bench till morning.”

He came to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the first one on the ninth of January.

It was 2017. A man in a hotel in a port city, a businessman, a shipping agent. He’d been told, at the time, that the man was carrying documents for a foreign service. He’d taken him at the airport, at a taxi rank, and driven him to a car park, and handed him over. He had written down that the man was wearing a brown suit and had a cough. He had written down the date, and the name of the officer who gave him the folder, which was Director Duan, and the name of the man he’d handed him to.

On the tenth of January, at the far end of the bench, Mouse found the man’s company.

She’d come over without being asked, the second week. She didn’t say anything. She sat down at her screens one night with a list he’d written for her on a single sheet of paper, dates and names, and began looking. She was very good at looking. She found the man’s shipping agency, and the contract it had been about to sign in 2017, and the company that had got the contract instead when the man disappeared, three weeks later. And the director of that company. And his brother-in-law.

Who had been, in 2017, a vice-minister.

“Not Fu,” said Mouse, to Serafina. “A different one. He retired. He lives by a lake.” She turned a screen round. “His company paid a consulting fee. In 2017. To a company in the capital. Northgate Advisory.”

Serafina looked at the name.

“Northgate,” she said.

At the other end of the bench, Haozhen had stopped writing.

“That’s the post box,” said Serafina. “Your post box. The one that bought my gearbox. You called it Northgate.”

“I used the name,” said Qin Haozhen, very quietly, “because it was a name I’d seen on a folder once. In 2017. I didn’t know why I remembered it.” He looked at the screen. “I thought it was just a name.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of January there were four.

The shipping agent in 2017. A woman in 2019, an engineer, who had been told she was selling designs to a foreign company, and whose company had then been bought, cheap, by a man whose wife played bridge with Director Duan. A man in 2020, the line in Gong’s ledger, a lawyer, who had been about to give evidence in a case about a port.

And Lucien Marchal. The twenty-second of October, 2022. Battery Hill. Lot 9.

He’d been told Marchal was carrying information for a foreign service. Marchal had been carrying, Mouse found, a contract. A logistics contract, for the new terminal at the container port, worth more than everything Song Weiren had ever built. Marchal’s company had been about to win it. Three weeks after the Autumn Reception, it had gone to someone else.

The someone else had paid a consulting fee. To Northgate Advisory.

“He was alive,” said Haozhen. He was sitting on the stool with the 2022 notebook open on his knee. “When I handed him over. At the petrol station. He was alive. I’ve always told myself that. They’re alive, mostly, when I hand them over. Somewhere they don’t want to be, answering questions.” He looked at the page. “Marchal didn’t have any answers. There wasn’t anything to ask him. He just had a contract.”

Serafina put down her spanner.

“Where is he?”

“I don’t know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I don’t think anybody’s ever going to ask.”

She came and stood beside him. She put her hand on the back of his neck, the way he put his on hers, driving down the Peak, and kept it there.

“Then we’ll ask,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made three copies.

He did it on the last night of January, on plain paper, by hand, because a printer could be traced and his handwriting could not be faked. An index, first: fourteen pages, every operation that had touched Director Duan’s private account, with dates, places, names, the companies, the consulting fees, the officers involved, his own part in each, written plainly, in Chinese, not in code. Then the four cases in full. Then copies of Mouse’s documents. Then, at the back, one page in his own code, which only he could read, which was the key to all twenty-three notebooks.

The notebooks themselves went back under the cat.

The first copy went into Gilded.

Serafina did it herself. She took out one of the tubes of the roll cage, the rear diagonal, behind the driver’s seat, and Haozhen rolled the fourteen pages and the rest into a tight cylinder in a plastic sleeve, and slid it inside the steel tube, and she welded a cap on the end so neatly that Big Wu, when he came in the next morning and walked round the car twice, couldn’t find it. Number seven would carry it round every circuit in Asia that season. Nobody would ever look inside a roll cage.

The second copy went to Jinx. Under the wooden beads on Nobody’s back seat, sewn into the lining, which Jinx did herself with a curved needle and an expression of great disgust, and then sat back on her heels and said, “No questions,” and didn’t ask any.

The third copy he took up the Coastal High-Rise.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go to the forty-fourth floor. He went to the lobby.

Qian came down. He’d rung, and Qian had answered on the first ring, at eleven at night, and said only “Mr. Qin,” and “Two minutes,” and in two minutes he was standing in the marble lobby in a cardigan over his pyjamas, with the packet of antacids in the pocket of the cardigan, looking at the sealed brown envelope in Haozhen’s hand.

“For Mr. Chen,” said Haozhen. “Not to open. Not unless something happens to me. Or to her.”

Qian took it. He held it in both hands. He didn’t look at it. He looked at Haozhen.
