“Mr. Chen said you’d come,” he said. “He said before the spring. He said, when he comes, Qian, take whatever he gives you and put it in my safe, not hers, and don’t let my wife see you do it, or she’ll want to read it.” He paused. “He was very specific about the safe.”

“Thank you.”

“He also said,” said Qian, “to ask if you needed a door yet.”

Haozhen looked at him.

“Not yet,” he said. “Soon.”

Qian nodded. He put the envelope inside his cardigan, against his chest, the way Haozhen had once carried a brass tyre gauge, and took out his antacids, and took two, and looked at Haozhen for three seconds without blinking.

“Mr. Qin,” he said. “For what it’s worth. You’re starting to exist.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was asleep in Nonna’s driver’s seat when he got back, with the blanket over her and her boots on the dashboard.

He didn’t wake her. He got into the passenger seat. He sat beside her in the dark garage under the hanging lamp, and took the black notebook out of his inside pocket, the one he carried every day, the one with WEDDING on one page and Two hundred on another, and opened it at a new page.

He wrote one line. In Chinese. Not in code.

Then he tore it out along the perforations, and folded it once, and put it in his inside pocket on the left, where the gauge used to go.

She woke at four, and turned her head on the seat, and found him awake beside her, looking at her.

“Done?” she said.

“Done.”

“What did you write? Just now. I heard you tear it.”

“A letter,” said Qin Haozhen.

“To who?”

“To my director,” he said. “It’s one sentence. It’s taken ten years.”

chapters.title: The Resignation Letter That Took Ten Years
chapters.desc: The New Year comes and goes and nobody calls. Lunar New Year comes and goes. So he goes to them, uninvited, on a Monday in February, with one sentence on a page torn from his notebook and the first page of an index. A quiet office, a radiator that knocks, and a woman who doesn’t stop knitting until she reads the word Northgate.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve spent ten years making people disappear, Sera. Don’t ask me to let go of the only person who ever made me feel visible.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
Nobody called.

That was the worst part of January, and February. The deadline came, the first of the year, and went, and he didn’t go back to the capital with his hat in his hand, and nothing happened. No folder. No knock at the side door. No grey estate parked at the end of the street of shuttered workshops with its engine running and no lights on. Director Duan didn’t ring. Tianyi didn’t ring. The Bureau, which had rung him at two in the morning in fourteen countries for eleven years, went completely silent, the way a road goes silent before a lorry comes round a blind bend.

“They’re waiting,” he said, at three in the morning, on the coast road.

“For what?”

“For me to get frightened enough to go back.” He was looking out of the window at the sea. “It’s a technique. You leave someone alone with what they’ve done. Most people come in by themselves. You don’t have to send anyone.”

“Are you frightened?”

He thought about it, the way he thought about everything.

“Yes,” he said. “Not of them.”

“Then of what?”

“Of you deciding,” said Qin Haozhen, “in a month, or a year, that it isn’t worth it. That I’m not.”

She pulled into the lay-by above the harbour and turned off the engine.

The engine ticked.

“Look at me,” said Serafina.

He looked at her.

“I’ve been deciding every day since January last year,” she said. “Every single day. Since the workbench, and the photograph from Antwerp. I wake up in the loft and the trains go over and I look at you asleep and I decide.” She held his eyes. “I’ve decided four hundred times. It’s always come out the same. I’m not going to stop deciding, because that’s how I know it’s real. But it’s always going to come out the same.”

He didn’t say anything for a long time.

“Lunar New Year was nice,” he said finally, very low. “With Mr. Kwok. And the nine dishes. And Big Wu’s mother.”

“It was.”

“I’ve never had two.”

“You’ll have forty,” said Serafina. “Big Wu’s mother’s going to live to a hundred and ten out of spite.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to them on the last Monday of February.

He told her on the Sunday night, in the loft, lying on his back with her head on his chest. He’d written the sentence on the last night of January and carried it in his inside pocket ever since, against his chest, and taken it out every morning to look at it and put it back. He was going to give it to Director Duan himself. In her office. To her face.

“You could post it,” said Serafina.

“I could.”

“You could post it, and we could get in Nobody, and be eight hundred kilometres away by the time it arrives.”

“We could.” He was stroking her hair. “And they’d spend the rest of our lives looking for a grey taxi with wooden beads. And they’d find it. They always find it, Sera. I’ve found it, for them. Every time.” He was quiet. “And my mother would get a visit. And Big Wu. And Mr. Kwok. And Mouse. And your sister.” His hand stopped in her hair. “If I go in by myself, and give it to her, in her office, it’s a resignation. If I run, it’s a defection. Those are different files. Different desks. Different people reading them.”

She lay with her ear on his chest and listened to his heart.

“You could go,” she said. “Somewhere. By yourself. If it’s safer for me. I’d hate it, but if it’s—”

He went completely still under her.

Then he sat up, and took her face in both hands, and looked at her in the orange light from the tracks, and his face was not calm at all.

“I’ve spent ten years making people disappear, Sera,” he said. “For them. For a building with no name on it. I’ve walked them to cars with my hand on their elbow and I’ve never once looked back.” His voice wasn’t steady. “Don’t ask me to let go of the only person who ever made me feel visible. Don’t. I’ll do anything you ask. I won’t do that.”

A train went over. The loft shook. Neither of them looked away.

“All right,” said Serafina, when it had passed. “I won’t ask.”

“Promise.”

“I promise.” She put her hands over his on her face. “Come back from the stairwell.”

“It isn’t a stairwell. It’s an office.”

“Come back from the office,” said Serafina, and pulled him down, and didn’t let him talk again until the alarm went at five.

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Tsui was on the gate. Old Tsui was always on the gate. He came out of the guard box with his bad hip and his chilli plant on the windowsill behind him, flowering, and looked at the man in the forgettable suit standing on the pavement, and his face did something it had never done in eleven years.

“Mr. Qin,” he said. “Nobody told me you were coming.”

“Nobody knows.”

Old Tsui looked at him a moment longer. Then he lifted the barrier.

The lift stuck between four and five. He kicked it. It went on.

The radiator in the corridor on the seventh floor knocked three times, like someone wanting to be let in.

He knocked once on the door at the end.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Come,” said Director Duan.

She was knitting. Of course she was. She sat behind the desk in her grey cardigan with the photograph turned away from him and the window looking out at the wall and the long red scarf coming off the needles in her lap, longer than it had been in November. She didn’t look up.

“Haozhen,” she said. “You’re very late. The New Year was eight weeks ago. I’d begun to think you’d got lost.”

“No, Director.”

“Sit. The flask’s there.”

He didn’t sit.

He took the page out of his inside pocket. Torn from a black notebook along the perforations, folded once. He unfolded it and laid it on the desk in front of her, on top of the papers there, very precisely, the way he put things down. Then he took a second sheet out of the same pocket, folded in three, and unfolded that too, and laid it beside the first.

The needles went on.

She looked at the first page over the top of her glasses. One line. In his small, square, separate letters. In Chinese. Not in code.

I resign. — Qin Haozhen.

In, round, through, off.

“That’s very short,” she said.

“Yes, Director.”

“Ten years, and that’s all you’ve got to say.”

“It took ten years,” said Qin Haozhen, “to make it that short.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t look at the second page at first.

She finished her row. She turned the scarf. She looked at the resignation for a while longer, the one line, with an expression he couldn’t read, and then, almost absently, the way you’d glance at a bill that had come with a letter, her eyes moved across to the other sheet.

It was the first page of the index. Not the file. Not the four cases. Not Mouse’s documents. Just the first page, in his handwriting, in plain Chinese: four dates, four places, four names. 2017. 2019. 2020. 2022. A shipping agent, an engineer, a lawyer, a Belgian. And at the bottom of the page, underlined once, a single word.

Northgate.

The needles stopped.

Not for half a second. Not a row left unfinished. They stopped, and stayed stopped. Her hands lay still in her lap on the red wool and didn’t move again, and the office was so quiet he could hear the radiator in the corridor tick as it cooled between knocks.

She read it twice.

Then she took off her glasses and let them fall on their chain against her cardigan and looked up at him, and he saw her face without anything in front of it for the second time in his life.

“Where’s the rest?” she said.

“In three places.”

“Which?”

“I can’t tell you that, Director.”

She looked at him.

“If anything happens to me,” said Qin Haozhen, “or to her, or to my mother, or to anyone who works in her garage, or to her sister, it goes from those three places to three more. I’ve made sure I don’t know all of them.” He paused. “You taught me that. Never know everything. Then nobody can make you say it. At nineteen. In a car park.”

“I did,” she said. “I did teach you that.”

“You trained me, Director.”

“I trained you very well,” said Director Duan Qiuyan, and for a moment her voice was not gentle at all. It was simply tired. “I trained you to see the right person. I didn’t think you’d ever look at me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She put her glasses back on. She looked at the resignation again, the one line, and then she folded it once along its crease, and put it in the drawer of her desk, on its own, and closed the drawer.

She left the index on the desk. She didn’t touch it.

“It’s not my decision any more, Haozhen,” she said. “You understand that. As soon as you put that word on my desk.” She didn’t look at the word. “It goes upstairs now. Above me. To people who have never met you and never will, who will read a file and look at a photograph and decide.” She picked up her knitting, and looked at it, and didn’t start. “I can’t help you. I wouldn’t, if I could. I want you to know that.”

“I know.”

“They’ll send someone.”

He was quiet.

“They always send someone,” said Director Duan. “Not a stranger.”

“I know.”

“Then go home,” she said. “Go home to Miss Song and her garage with the trains. You’ve got a few weeks. Perhaps two months. It takes them time, upstairs, to read things.” She found her place in the wool. “Enjoy them.”

He stood in front of her desk.

He thought of a dormitory of forty boys under a leaking roof. A uniform two sizes too big. A commandant’s office, and a woman with a red scarf on her needles asking a question about a map, and a boy answering it before she’d finished. A hotel in the capital. A car park at nineteen. Eleven years of folders across this desk, and a flask of hot water, and sit.

“Thank you, Director,” he said.

It was not irony. He meant it, in a way he would never be able to explain to anyone, not even to Serafina, and he saw that Director Duan knew he meant it, and that she couldn’t stand it.

“Go,” she said, to the scarf. “Before I change my mind about not helping.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi wasn’t in the corridor.

He’d been there in November, leaning on the wall by the radiator with his gum. He wasn’t there now. The corridor was empty from end to end. The radiator knocked three times. Every door was shut.

Haozhen stood outside Director Duan’s office for a moment and looked at the empty place on the wall where Tianyi had leaned.

Then he walked down the corridor, and kicked the lift between five and four, and went out through the lobby past the desk where nobody looked up, and across the yard to the gate.

Old Tsui came out of the guard box.

“Going home, Mr. Qin?”

“Yes.”

Old Tsui looked at him. Then he reached back through the window of the guard box, to the pot on the sill, and picked a chilli off the plant. A small one, very red, shiny, the size of a fingertip. He held it out.

“First of the year,” he said. “For luck. You’re supposed to give the first one away.”

Haozhen took it. He looked at it in his palm.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Don’t eat it,” said Old Tsui. “It’ll take your head off.” He lifted the barrier. “Mind how you go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was at arrivals in Nonna, in the NO WAITING lane, with the engine running, for an hour and fifty minutes, because his flight was late and she’d refused to move, and the same traffic warden from June was on duty with his whistle and had recognised the car and come over and looked at her, and she had looked back, and he had gone away again without blowing it.

He got in. He sat down. He closed the door.

“Well?” she said.

He held out his hand. On his palm was a small red chilli.

“I resigned,” he said. “And the man on the gate gave me this. For luck.”

She looked at the chilli. Then at his face.

“What did she say?”

“That they’ll send someone.” He closed his hand round the chilli, gently, so as not to crush it. “In a few weeks. Perhaps two months.” He looked at her. “She said to enjoy them.”

Serafina put Nonna in first.

“Then we’ll enjoy them,” she said, and pulled out of the NO WAITING lane past the traffic warden, who raised his hand, very slightly, as she went by. Not to stop her. Something else.

The season opener at the circuit in the north was on the thirteenth of April. Six weeks and five days.

She didn’t say it. She knew he’d already counted.

chapters.title: They Send Someone
chapters.desc: The season opener at the circuit in the north. Eleven thousand people in the grandstand, a black car with a gold name, and in the pit lane, with a hospitality lanyard and a stick of cinnamon gum, the boy from the next bed in a dormitory of forty, who once gave his window seat to nobody but him.
chapters.epigraph: “They always send the friend. It’s in the training. Better me than someone who doesn’t know you brake at the second lamp post.” — Mo Tianyi
chapters.content:
He saw Tianyi at nine minutes past ten.

He had been looking for him since seven, when the transporter came through the gate. He had walked the paddock twice, the long way round, past the hospitality tents and the series office and the medical centre and the tyre fitters, the way he’d once walked the ballroom on Battery Hill. He’d counted the grandstand from the pit wall with the sun behind it. He had stood in the queue at the noodle stall behind four men who did not eat noodles.

At nine minutes past ten Tianyi walked into the Team AURELIA pit garage through the back, from the paddock side, with a hospitality lanyard round his neck that said GUEST and a paper cup of coffee in his hand and a stick of cinnamon gum in the corner of his mouth, and stopped by the tyre rack, and looked at Gilded on its stands with its wheels off and Big Wu crouched at the front left with the probe, and said, in Mandarin, delighted:

“Oh, it’s much smaller than it looks on television.”

Big Wu looked up.

Haozhen, at the back of the garage by the laptops, put down the clipboard he’d been holding and didn’t move.

“Hello, Haozhen,” said Mo Tianyi.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina saw it from the car.

She was in the driver’s seat already, strapped in, helmet on, visor up, doing the thing she did before every race with her eyes closed and her hands on the wheel and her lips moving, which Mouse called the shopping list and which was in fact the circuit, every corner, every braking point, in order, out loud, in Italian. She opened her eyes in the middle of the Needle. Through the windscreen, past the AURELIA on the bonnet, she saw a man with a lanyard and a coffee standing by the tyre rack, and she saw Haozhen at the back of the garage, and she saw his face.

She’d seen that face once. On the morning of the twenty-third of October, 2022, on page nine of the business section, a paragraph about a man who left on an early flight.

No. That wasn’t true. She’d never seen that face. She’d seen what it did to other people’s.

“Mouse,” she said, into the radio.

Mouse, at the laptops beside him, didn’t look up.

“I know,” Mouse said, very quietly, on the team channel. “Five in the grandstand. Two in the car park. One at the medical centre. He’s the sixth.” A pause. “Haozhen says drive. He says just drive.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Five in the grandstand,” said Tianyi.

They were standing at the back of the garage, by the stack of spare tyres, where the noise from the pit lane was loudest and nobody could hear anything. Tianyi had his back to the wall. So did Haozhen. Two metres apart. Weight on the back foot. Hands where people could see them. Looking at the space just past each other’s shoulder.

“Four,” said Haozhen.

“Five. You missed the one with the camera. In the blue jacket. Block C, row twelve.” Tianyi drank his coffee. “He’s new. He’s very good. He looks like a dad.”

Haozhen looked across the circuit at the grandstand. Block C, row twelve. A man in a blue jacket with a long-lens camera and a small boy beside him, both in Team AURELIA caps.

“The boy?”

“His nephew. He brought his nephew. For cover.” Tianyi chewed. “I told him that was cheap. He said it was a day out.”

The cars began to go out of the pit lane for the formation lap. The noise was enormous. Twenty-four engines, one after another, going past the open front of the garage, and the smell of hot rubber and fuel, and the ground shaking. Gilded went with them, matte black, number seven, the gold name, the small grey taxi on the door under three coats of lacquer, and Haozhen watched it go and didn’t let himself watch it go.

“I asked for it,” said Tianyi, when the noise had gone up the straight.

Haozhen turned his head.

“They were going to send Ruan. You remember Ruan. From the year below. With the hands.” Tianyi looked at his coffee. “I said, send me. I said, I know him. I know how he thinks. I know he brakes at the second lamp post.” A breath. “I read the file, Haozhen. All forty photographs. The garage. The trains. The mug.” He was quiet. “Better me than someone who doesn’t know you.”

“Tianyi.”

“They want you in. Tonight. Quietly. After the race.” His voice had gone flat, the way it went in window seats, when the jokes stopped and the job began. “You walk out of the gate with me, and you get in a car, and you go to the capital, and you sit in a room and you tell them where the rest of that index is. All three places. And whatever three places are behind those.”

“And if I don’t?”

Tianyi looked across the circuit at the cars coming round on the formation lap, weaving to warm their tyres, the black one in fourth.

“Then her licence goes,” he said. “Tomorrow. The officer in the traffic division gets a parcel. Forty photographs. Her name. Three years. The series drops her. The sponsors go. Her sister’s name comes off the car, because her sister can’t be seen sponsoring a criminal. The garage under the bridge gets a visit from the fire department and the tax office in the same week.” He wasn’t looking at Haozhen. “And your mother gets a visit. Not a bad one. A polite one. From someone who’ll sit in her kitchen and drink her tea and admire her sewing and ask how long she’s lived there, and whether she’d ever thought of moving. Somewhere smaller. Somewhere further.”

Haozhen didn’t say anything.

“I’m supposed to bring you in alive,” said Tianyi. “That’s my instruction. Alive, and talking.” He drank the last of the coffee. “They didn’t say anything about her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The lights went out.

The noise came down the straight like a wall falling over, and the field went into the first corner, the long right, twenty-four cars in a river of colour, and in the middle of it a black car went up the inside on the kerb, two wheels on the paint, the way it had in December 2019, and came out third.

The garage went mad. Big Wu shouted. Mr. Kwok banged a saucepan. Mouse, at the laptops, said nothing, but her hands came off the keyboard and pressed flat on the desk.

Tianyi laughed. Out loud, with his whole face, the old way, and shook his head.

“Oh, she’s good,” he said. “Haozhen. She’s really good.”

“Yes.”

“She takes the Needle like you do. I watched the qualifying. She brakes on the marker. To the metre.” He looked at the monitor on the wall, at the black car going down the back straight toward the hairpin. “Did you teach her that?”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “She taught me.”

Tianyi looked at him.

For a moment, in the noise, with the cars going past the front of the garage and the ground shaking under their feet, they were sixteen. Two boys in uniforms that didn’t fit, on a firing range in the north in the snow, and the older one laughing because the younger one had just put five rounds through the same hole and then apologised for it.

“You’ve changed,” said Tianyi.

“You said that in Lisbon.”

“I said it wrong in Lisbon.” Tianyi looked back at the monitor. “In Lisbon I thought you were breaking. You’re not breaking. You’ve just stopped pretending you were never in one piece.” He took out a fresh stick of gum. “I don’t know what to do with that, Haozhen. There isn’t a form for it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The race was three hours.

Haozhen stood on the pit wall for all of it, at the back, behind Big Wu and Mouse, with a headset on that let him hear the team channel and nothing else, and watched her.

She drove the best race of her life. He knew it while it was happening. He’d watched every lap she’d driven since the track day in December 2022, on screens and from pit walls and from the passenger seat, and he’d never seen her like this. She was third for forty minutes. Second for thirty. She did her driver change on lap forty-one, handing the car to the man with the beard, the second driver, Joe Ng, a tyre-shop owner from the coast who drove for nothing because he loved it, and stood on the pit wall in her fireproof suit with the top tied round her waist and her helmet under her arm, steaming in the April sun, and didn’t once look at the back of the garage, where Tianyi was leaning on the tyre stack with his coffee.

She looked at Haozhen instead.

Just once. A long look, over Big Wu’s shoulder, through the noise. He looked back.

Look at the right person.

She got back in for the last stint on lap seventy-two. She came out of the pits fourth. She was second by lap eighty. On lap ninety-one, at the Needle, she went down the inside of the leader under braking, on the marker, to the metre, the way she’d taught him, and came out first.

She won by four seconds.

✦ ✦ ✦

The podium was the safest place in the province.

He’d known that since February. Eleven thousand people. Every camera in the series. A presenter with a microphone, a man from the governor’s office with a trophy, photographers on a stand, the whole grandstand on its feet. Nobody would take anyone off a podium. Not even the Bureau.

She stood on the top step in her suit with champagne in one hand and the trophy in the other, and looked out over the crowd for a long time, the way she had in 2019. Then she found the man in the blue jacket in Block C, row twelve, with the long lens and his nephew.

She pointed the champagne at him.

Most of it went over the photographers.

Then she found Tianyi, at the back of the crowd below the podium, by the medical centre, in his GUEST lanyard with his coffee.

She didn’t point the champagne at him. She looked at him. Straight at him, the way she’d once looked at a guard by a service door on Battery Hill, and held it, and didn’t smile, and didn’t wave, and didn’t look away until he did.

He looked away first.

Haozhen saw it from the pit wall. He’d never seen Tianyi look away first from anybody.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tonight,” said Tianyi, at six, by the transporter, in the long gold light, with the paddock emptying round them and the trucks starting up. “Nine o’clock. The gate on the north side, by the fuel store. I’ll be there. You walk out with me. You get in the car. That’s all.” He looked at Haozhen. “And she goes home and puts her trophy on the shelf and races again in May. And nobody gets a parcel. And your mother keeps her flat.”

“And if I’m not at the gate at nine?”

Tianyi didn’t answer that.

He looked at Serafina instead, who was sitting on the transporter ramp in her suit, with the trophy on the ramp beside her and Big Wu standing over her like a wall. She was looking straight back at him.

“Miss Song,” said Tianyi, in English.

“Mr. Mo.”

He raised his eyebrows.

“He told me your name,” said Serafina. “In February. He tells me things.” She didn’t get up. “He says you laugh with your whole face. He says you were the best shot in the academy. He says you gave your window seat to nobody but him.” Her voice didn’t change at all. “He says you’re his friend.”

Tianyi looked at her in the gold light.

“I am,” he said. “That’s why it’s me.”

“Then you’ll understand,” said Serafina, “when he’s not at the gate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at half past seven. Not at nine. Not by the north gate.

They left by the main gate, in Nonna, in full view, in the queue of team cars and transporters and spectators going home, with the sun going down red over the rice fields and the grandstand empty behind them. She drove. He sat in the passenger seat. Big Wu drove the transporter behind them with Gilded on the back and the first copy of the file welded into the roll cage. Mouse was in the transporter cab, with her laptops. Mr. Kwok had gone back to the city at four on the bus, because Serafina had made him.

They went through the gate. Out onto the road south through the rice fields toward the motorway. Not fast. Like anybody.

In the wing mirror, a kilometre back, a pair of headlights came on.

Then another.

Then a third.

He looked at them. He didn’t say anything. He reached across, and took the brass gauge out of the door pocket where she kept it now, Nonna’s, S.S., A.C., and held it in his palm.

“Look at me,” said Serafina. “Not the mirror.”

He looked at her.

She was driving with both hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, in her fireproof suit with the top half tied round her waist, with a winner’s medal still round her neck on its ribbon and champagne drying in her hair, and her face in the last red light was perfectly calm, the way it was on the grid.

“If we’re going to do this at two hundred an hour tonight,” she said, “I want you looking at the girl driving. Not at the ghosts behind us.”

“Kilometres,” said Qin Haozhen.

She grinned at the road.

“Miles,” she said. “Everything fast sounds better in miles,” and at the junction with the motorway, under the big green sign, she didn’t take the slip road south toward the city. She went straight on, past it, into the dark, onto the old coast road, where the service station was, thirty kilometres away, where a woman with tattoos on both arms was waiting in a grey taxi with wooden beads on the seats and the engine already running.

In the mirror, three pairs of headlights went straight on too.

chapters.title: Shoot the Tyres
chapters.desc: A closed service station on the old coast road, a car wash, and a grey taxi with the engine already running. Three cars behind them, then two, then one. She drives. He shoots out tyres. Nobody dies who didn’t have to, and one man who nearly does is pulled out of the fire by the friend he was sent to bring in.
chapters.epigraph: “You never bring it back here with a hole in it.” “We’ll bring it back, Jinx. I can’t promise about the hole.”
chapters.content:
The service station had been closed since nine. It stood on its own at a bend in the old coast road, a canopy and four pumps and a shop with its shutters down and one light on in the car wash at the back, a long tiled tunnel with brushes in it, the kind you drove into at one end and came out of clean at the other.

Jinx was standing at the far end of the car wash in her helmet with her visor up, beside a grey Toyota Crown estate with a dent in its back door, and its engine was running.

Serafina didn’t slow down for the forecourt. She came off the coast road at ninety with the three pairs of headlights a kilometre behind, and swung Nonna across the empty forecourt between the pumps, and went straight into the car wash tunnel without touching the brakes. The brushes weren’t moving. The tiles went by on either side, white and wet, close enough to touch. At the far end she stopped dead, a metre from Nobody’s back bumper, and was out of the car before it had stopped rocking.

“Go,” said Jinx. “Go, go, go—”

He was already out of the passenger side. She saw him reach under Nonna’s seat and take something out, a dark shape wrapped in a cloth, and put it inside his jacket. Rule two. Not in her garage. Not in her car either; she had never known it was there. She didn’t say anything. There wasn’t time.

Jinx got into Nonna’s driver’s seat. Serafina got into Nobody’s. The wooden beads pressed into her back through the fireproof suit. He got in beside her and pulled the door shut.

“Jinx,” said Serafina, through the window.

“North,” said Jinx. “Over the hill to the reservoir. Lights on. Loud. Like you.” She dropped her visor. “Bring it back, Sera.”

“I’ll bring it back.”

“Without a hole in it.”

“I can’t promise about the hole,” said Serafina, and Jinx laughed inside her helmet, once, and put Nonna in reverse.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car wash had two ways out. Nonna went out the way she’d come in, backwards, very fast, onto the forecourt, and spun round in the light under the canopy with a noise like a scream so that anybody coming round the bend would see a red Lancia with a dent in its door, and went north up the hill road toward the reservoir with her lights on and her turbo howling.

Nobody went out the other end. Into the dark. Lights off. Onto a service track behind the station that went down between two fields to the coast road a kilometre further south.

She drove it blind. She’d walked it on Thursday with a torch, twice. She drove it by memory and the shape of the hedges against the sky, at sixty, on a dirt track in a grey estate with no lights, and he sat beside her on the beads and didn’t say anything, and she felt him not saying anything, all the way down.

At the bottom she stopped at the edge of the coast road with the engine idling.

On the hill to the north, she could see Nonna’s lights going up toward the reservoir. And behind them, a moment later, two pairs of headlights, following.

Two.

“Where’s the third?” she said.

He was looking at the forecourt of the service station, a kilometre back up the road, under its canopy.

A black saloon was sitting on it. Engine running. Lights off. Not following anybody. Waiting.

“Tianyi,” he said.

“He knew.”

“He knew it was a car wash,” said Qin Haozhen. “He didn’t know which end.” A pause. “He does now.”

On the forecourt, the black saloon’s headlights came on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned south onto the coast road and put her foot down.

Nobody sat down on its rear wheels the way it had on the Docks road, and the engine made its sound, the long rising scream from somewhere under the grey bodywork, and the beads pressed into her spine, and the coast road came at them out of the dark, one bend after another, with the cliff on the left and the sea on the right and the white posts going by.

She put the lights on. There was no point now.

In the mirror, the black saloon came off the forecourt and onto the road behind them. It was a long way back. It didn’t stay a long way back.

“He’s quick,” she said.

“He’s very good.”

“Better than you?”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “But he’s not trying to make anybody laugh.”

She went through the first set of bends flat, the way she’d driven the Baizhang Pass, on the edge, a hand’s width from the white posts. Two hundred on the straight past the fishing village. Two hundred and thirty on the long right where the road came out over the water. The black saloon stayed in her mirror. It didn’t close. It didn’t drop back. It sat there, exactly where it was, a length and a half behind, the way the grey estate had sat behind Nonna once through the S-bends by the paint works, as if it were painted on.

“He’s doing what you did,” she said. “At Granny Shum’s.”

“Yes.”

“Why isn’t he trying to pass?”

“Because he doesn’t have to.” He was looking in the wing mirror. “There’s another one coming. From the south. He’s keeping us in the middle.” He was quiet for a second. “The tunnel.”

She knew the tunnel. Four kilometres ahead, through the headland. Six hundred metres long, one lane each way, no hard shoulder. If there was a car waiting at the far end, across the road, and the black saloon behind, there was nowhere to go.

“Look at me,” said Serafina.

He turned his head.

“Not the mirror,” she said. “Me. Tell me what you need.”

He told her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slowed down.

It went against everything she was. She came off the throttle on the long straight before the headland and let the car drop to a hundred and forty, and then a hundred and twenty, and in the mirror the black saloon came up behind them, close, closer, until its headlights filled the back of the car and lit up the beads and the crack in the dashboard and his face, turned away from her, toward his window.

He had wound his window down. The wind came in, cold, off the sea. He had the dark shape out of his jacket. She didn’t look at it. She looked at the road.

“Now,” he said.

She braked. Hard, the way she braked for the Needle. Nobody’s nose went down and the black saloon, a length behind, had to brake too, had to swerve, had to show its side for half a second, its front wheel turned out toward the cliff, lit up in Nobody’s own brake lights, and in that half-second he leaned out of the window into the wind and fired twice.

The noise inside the car was enormous. She felt it in her teeth.

In the mirror the black saloon’s front left tyre came apart. She saw it go: a black ribbon coming off the wheel, spinning away into the dark, and the car lurching, dropping on that corner, the sparks starting from the rim. It slewed. It didn’t spin. Tianyi was too good to let it spin. He held it, on three wheels and a rim, sliding, sparks pouring off the front corner like a welding torch, and dropped back, and back, and she put her foot down again and Nobody went away from it toward the tunnel.

“Is he—”

“He’s fine. He’ll be on the rim. He’ll keep coming.” He pulled his arm in. His face was white. “He’ll keep coming, Sera. He’s like you.”

The tunnel came up out of the dark. A mouth of orange light in the headland. She went in at a hundred and eighty.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a car at the far end.

She saw it as soon as they were inside: six hundred metres of orange tiles and the exit at the end, a small square of dark, and in the middle of the square, side-on across both lanes, a car. A white van. Its lights on. Two men beside it.

She didn’t brake.

“Sera,” he said.

“I know.”

“Sera, there’s nowhere—”

“There’s a gap,” said Serafina.

There was. Between the back of the van and the tunnel wall, on the right, where the van hadn’t quite been able to get all the way across because the tunnel was too narrow. Two metres. Perhaps a little less. The width of a car and a hand’s breadth on either side.

Barely more than a car’s width. Less than the gap on the inside at the first corner in December 2019, two wheels on the kerb.

Don’t watch the car. Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.

“Hold on to the beads,” she said.

He held on.

The two men by the van saw what she was going to do about two seconds before she did it. She saw one of them raise his arm. She saw the flash. She heard something hit the car, somewhere at the back, a flat crack like a stone on glass, and the rear window went white. She didn’t brake. She took Nobody at the gap at a hundred and sixty, and the right-hand mirror went off against the tunnel wall with a bang, and the left side of the car touched the van’s back bumper, a kiss of metal, a long screech, and then they were through, out of the tunnel, into the dark, and the sea was on the right again and the road was empty in front of them.

She was laughing. She couldn’t stop. She was laughing and crying at the same time and her hands on the wheel were perfectly steady.

“Through,” she said. “Through, through, we’re through, Hao, did you see—”

He didn’t answer.

She looked across.

He was sitting on the beads with his left hand pressed flat over the top of his right arm, just below the shoulder, and between his fingers, black in the dashboard light, something was running down his sleeve.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Don’t stop,” he said.

“You’re—”

“It’s my arm. It’s through. In and out. I felt it go.” His voice was very level. “Don’t stop. Not yet. Not on this road.”

She didn’t stop.

She drove with her right hand and reached across with her left and pressed her own hand over his, over the arm, hard, and felt it warm and wet under her palm, and drove like that for two kilometres. The road climbed. The bends tightened. And in the mirror, a long way back, coming out of the tunnel, there was a single pair of headlights.

One headlight. And under it, at the front left, a stream of sparks.

“Oh, you idiot,” said Serafina, to the mirror. “You absolute—”

“He’s on the rim,” said Haozhen. “I told you. He keeps coming.”

The black saloon came up the hill behind them on three tyres and a rim, sparks pouring off it, swaying, much too fast for a car with no front tyre, much too fast for those bends. It wasn’t trying to catch them. Serafina saw that, suddenly. It couldn’t catch them. It was just coming. The way she would have kept coming.

On the bend before the lay-by, where the road went round the head of a gully above the sea, the rim caught on something.

She saw it in the mirror. The sparks went out. The black saloon’s nose dipped, and the car went sideways, and then over. Once. Twice. Off the road on the inside of the bend, into the gully, against the rocks. There was a noise she would hear for a year. And then, a second later, a light. Orange. Growing.

She stopped.

She didn’t decide to. Her foot was on the brake and Nobody was stopped on the side of the coast road and she was looking back down the hill at the gully, at the orange light in it, getting bigger.

“Drive,” said Haozhen. “Sera. Drive.”

She looked at him.

He was looking back down the hill too. His face in the dashboard light was white as paper, with blood all down his right side, and he was looking at the fire in the gully, and she saw his face, and she knew that he was not going to let her drive.

“He gave you the window seat,” she said.

He was already opening the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

She reversed.

Two hundred metres, back down the hill, fast, in a straight line, the way you did on a circuit when you’d overshot your pit box. She stopped at the head of the gully. He was out of the car before it had stopped, with his right arm hanging and his left hand already reaching, going down the rocks into the gully in the light of the fire.

She went after him.

The black saloon was on its roof against a boulder. The fire was at the front, in the engine bay, under the bonnet, the burning smell of oil and plastic and something else, and it was coming back along the underside toward the cabin. The driver’s window was smashed. Inside, upside down, held by his belt, Tianyi was moving. His hands were moving. He was trying to get his belt undone and he couldn’t, because his hands weren’t working right, and his face, upside down in the orange light, was covered in blood.

Haozhen went down on his knees on the broken glass by the driver’s window.

He did it one-handed. She would never understand how. He reached in through the window with his left hand to the belt buckle, and Tianyi’s hands were in the way, and he said something in Mandarin, sharp, and Tianyi’s hands went still, and Haozhen found the buckle and the belt came undone and Tianyi fell, onto the roof of the car, onto his own shoulders, and cried out.

“Sera,” said Haozhen. “His legs.”

She was already there. She got down on the glass beside him. The heat from the front of the car was like an oven door. She got Tianyi under the arms, the way Big Wu had taught her to get a driver out of a wreck in 2020 on a course at the circuit, and Haozhen got his good arm round Tianyi’s chest, and they pulled. Tianyi screamed. His left leg was wrong below the knee. They pulled him out through the window, over the glass, across the rocks, ten metres, twenty, up the gully, and laid him down on the grass at the side of the road, and behind them the fire found the fuel and the black saloon went up with a soft heavy sound like a breath being let out, and the whole gully went orange.

They knelt on the grass at the side of the coast road and watched it burn.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi was laughing.

It was the old laugh, the whole-face one, cracked down the middle with pain. He lay on the grass with his leg bent wrong and blood in his eyes and the burning car lighting up the side of his face, and he laughed up at the sky.

“You came back,” he said. In Mandarin. “You absolute hearse. You came back.”

“You gave me the window seat,” said Qin Haozhen.

Tianyi stopped laughing.

He turned his head on the grass and looked at Haozhen, kneeling beside him with his right arm hanging and blood all down his side, and then at Serafina, on his other side in her fireproof suit with her hands black with someone else’s blood and the winner’s medal still round her neck on its ribbon. He looked at her for a long time.

“Go,” he said. “Both of you. Before the van comes round.”

“Your leg—”

“The van will take me. They’re good at that. It’s in the training.” He shut his eyes. “Don’t go to the bridges. They’ll be at both bridges and the tunnel under the harbour. Go up. Into the mountains. Somewhere with no road on the map.” He opened his eyes again and looked at Haozhen. “I’ll tell them you were faster.”

“Tianyi.”

“I’ll tell them she was faster,” said Mo Tianyi, and grinned, with blood on his teeth. “It’ll be true. Go, Haozhen. Before I remember what I’m for.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove up.

Away from the coast. Up a road with no number on it, into the hills, and then onto a smaller road, and then onto a track between tea terraces that went up and up into the dark with the bushes close on either side, black and wet and smelling of leaves. She drove with one hand. With the other she held his arm, over the sleeve of her own fireproof suit, which she had torn off at the shoulder at the side of the coast road and tied round him above the wound, as tight as she could, while he sat on the beads and told her how.

He was very pale. He kept closing his eyes.

“Talk to me,” she said.

“About what?”

“Anything. The mining town. The winding gear. The keepy-ups. I don’t care. Keep talking.” Her voice was breaking and she didn’t care about that either. “You’re not allowed to close your eyes in my passenger seat unless you’re asleep. That’s the rule. That’s a new rule. Rule five.”

“I’m not asleep.”

“I know you’re not asleep, that’s the problem—”

“Sera.”

“What?”

“Mr. Kwok,” he said, with his eyes closed. “His brother’s house. You’ve got the key.”

She had. Mr. Kwok had pressed it into her hand at four o’clock that afternoon in the paddock, before he got on the bus. An old iron key on a loop of red string. My brother’s house. Yunwu. Above the tea. It’s empty. The neighbours are deaf. The key goes under the stone frog by the door when you leave. He hadn’t asked her anything. He’d just closed her fingers round it, the way Haozhen had closed them round the brass gauge, and got on the bus.

“I’ve got it,” she said.

“Then we’re nearly there,” said Qin Haozhen, and opened his eyes, and looked at her, and in the dashboard light, white as paper, with blood all over Jinx’s beads, he smiled. “I told Jinx we’d bring it back.”

“With a hole in it.”

“Two holes,” he said. “One in the window. One in me.” He closed his eyes again. “She’ll kill us.”

“She’ll have to get in the queue,” said Serafina, and drove on up into the dark, with her hand on his arm, and didn’t take it away again until the track ran out among the tea bushes at the top of the hill in front of a low stone house with a stone frog by the door.

chapters.title: The Safe House in the Mountains
chapters.desc: A stone house above the tea terraces at Yunwu, a dead man’s photograph on the shrine, two deaf neighbours who bring eggs and ask nothing, a stray dog that stops dead in front of you, and rain on a tin roof. A fever, and then fourteen days with nowhere to be. The best two weeks of their lives.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody’s looking for us. For the first time in my life, nobody knows where I am.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
The house had two rooms and a stove and a tin roof, and Mr. Kwok’s brother had died in it in 2019 in his sleep at eighty-four, and nothing in it had been moved since.

There was a bed with a mosquito net in the back room. A table and two stools in the front. A stone sink with a single cold tap that came straight off the hill, and a stove that burned wood, and a shrine on a shelf by the door with a photograph of an old man in a vest squinting at the camera in the sun, a cup of tea in front of him that had dried to a brown ring, and three sticks of incense that had burned down to nothing five years ago. Outside, the tea terraces went down the hill in green steps into the mist, and up the hill into more mist, and there was no other house in sight except one, a hundred metres along the track, with smoke coming from its chimney.

She lit the stove at three in the morning with her hands shaking and boiled water in the only pan.

He sat on the stool by the table with his right arm on the table and the torn sleeve of her race suit still tied round it, and watched her.

“Salt,” he said. “If there’s salt.”

There was salt. In a jar by the stove with a dead moth in it. She made the water salty and let it cool and untied the sleeve, and it had stuck, and she had to soak it off, and he didn’t make a sound, and she did, for both of them.

It was in and out. Like he’d said. A hole at the front of his upper arm, small and neat and dark, and a bigger one at the back, torn, ugly. It had missed the bone. He moved his fingers for her, one at a time, all five, to show her it had missed the nerve too.

“Lucky,” he said.

“Don’t you dare say lucky to me.”

She washed it with the salt water, both sides, the way he told her, again and again, until it ran clean. She packed it with gauze from the first-aid kit Jinx kept under Nobody’s back seat, because of course Jinx kept a first-aid kit under the back seat, and bound it with a crepe bandage, firm, and taped it, and sat back on her heels on the stone floor of a dead man’s house at four in the morning and looked at him.

“Fourteen stitches last time,” she said. “None this time.”

“You don’t stitch these. You leave them open. They heal from the inside.” He looked at her. “You did it right.”

“I don’t care if I did it right.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I just wanted you to know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second day, he got a fever.

She had known he might. He’d told her, at the table, at four in the morning, in the level voice: watch for heat, watch for red lines, watch for the smell. He’d told her what to do. He’d told her where in Jinx’s first-aid kit the antibiotics would be, and they were there, because of course they were, and she gave him two at six in the morning and two at six in the evening. He’d told her he might not make sense.

She hadn’t known what it would be like.

He burned. All day and into the night, on the bed in the back room under the mosquito net, on top of the covers, in his clothes, the way he slept in hotels. His skin was so hot she could feel it from a hand’s width away. He shook. He talked, sometimes, not to her, in Mandarin and in Portuguese and in a language she didn’t know, very fast and quiet, like a radio left on in another room. Once he said a number. Once he said thirty-one. Once, very clearly, in English, in the voice from the east service door, he said, “Please step away from the door, madam,” and opened his eyes and looked straight at her and didn’t see her at all.

She sat on the edge of the bed with a bowl of cold water from the tap and a cloth, all night, and wiped his face, and his neck, and his chest, and talked to him. She didn’t know what about. Everything. Nonna. Monza. The Baizhang Pass. The gas works. Granny Shum’s clementines. She told him the hundred and twelfth corner, out loud, braking point and turn-in and apex, three times, in Italian, the way she did on the grid. She told him she’d wiped the bullet hole out of Nobody’s window with her sleeve so Jinx wouldn’t see it straight away. She told him she loved him, many times, and that he was an idiot, many more, and that if he died in Mr. Kwok’s brother’s bed she would never forgive him and nor would Mr. Kwok.

At four in the morning on the third day, the fever broke.

She felt it go. Her hand was flat on his chest and she felt the heat come out of him all at once, like a car’s engine when you turn the key off, and then sweat, everywhere, soaking the covers, and his breathing changed. Slow. Even. Down.

He opened his eyes.

“Sera,” he said. He knew her. “You’re crying.”

“I’m not.”

“You are,” said Qin Haozhen. His voice was a thread. “You’re crying on my face.”

“Then wipe it off,” said Serafina, “with your good arm,” and lay down beside him on the soaked covers under the mosquito net, in her clothes, and put her face in his neck, and slept for the first time in three days, and so did he.

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept for eight hours.

She woke at noon in the grey light from the window with the rain on the tin roof and he was still asleep beside her, on his back, with his bandaged arm across his chest and his face turned toward her on the pillow. Not calm, the made calm. The other thing. Gone all the way down.

She didn’t move. She lay and looked at him for an hour, until he woke.

“How long?” he said, before he’d opened his eyes.

“Eight hours. Eight hours and nine minutes.”

He was quiet for a long time.

“Not in your car,” he said.

“No.”

“In a bed.”

“In Mr. Kwok’s brother’s bed,” said Serafina. “Under a mosquito net. With the rain.”

He opened his eyes and looked at the roof. At the tin, and the drips coming in at one corner into a bucket, and the mosquito net hanging round them like a mist of its own.

“Nobody’s looking for us,” he said. He said it very slowly, as if testing each word for weight. “They’re looking. But nobody knows where we are. Nobody in the world. For the first time in my life, nobody knows where I am.” He turned his head on the pillow. “Except you.”

“And Mr. Kwok.”

“And Mr. Kwok.”

“And the dog,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dog had arrived on the first morning. It was yellow, and thin, and had one ear that stood up and one that didn’t, and it had appeared out of the tea bushes at seven o’clock while she was at the tap, and sat down on the step by the stone frog, and looked at her, and not left.

It had a habit, they discovered, of running ahead of you on the track and then stopping dead, right in front of your feet, so that you either fell over it or stopped too.

“Brake,” said Serafina, on the fourth day, when she had fallen over it twice. “Its name’s Brake.”

He was sitting on the step in the sun with his arm in a sling she’d made from Mr. Kwok’s brother’s shirt. The dog came and sat beside him and put its chin on his knee.

“You name everything,” he said.

“Everything worth naming.”

He put his good hand on the dog’s head. The dog closed its eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The neighbours were called Mr. and Mrs. Yau, and they were eighty-seven and eighty-five, and they were not, it turned out, deaf.

They came along the track on the second afternoon, in the rain, in matching straw hats, while he was burning in the back room, and Mrs. Yau knocked on the door with a basket of eggs and a bunch of green leaves and looked past Serafina into the house, at the shrine with the old man’s photograph, and then at Serafina’s face, and said, “You’re Ah Wing’s girl. From the city. The racing one, with the garage. He talks about you.”

“Mr. Kwok?”

“Every Lunar New Year. On the phone. The racing one, she’s family now.” Mrs. Yau pushed the basket into her hands. “The leaves are for the fever. Boil them. Make him drink it. It tastes like a shoe.” She looked past Serafina again, toward the back room. “We’re deaf, you understand. We don’t hear cars. We don’t hear anyone asking questions. We haven’t heard anything since 1971.”

“Thank you,” said Serafina.

“Don’t thank me,” said Mrs. Yau, “thank the deafness,” and went back along the track to her husband, who was standing in the rain under his straw hat, carefully not looking at the grey car with the broken rear window parked among the tea bushes.

They came every day after that. Eggs. Greens. A chicken, on the sixth day, already killed. Rice. A bag of last year’s tea. Mrs. Yau taught Serafina to cook the greens in the wok with garlic, and laughed at her for an hour when she burned them, and taught her again. Mr. Yau sat on the step with Haozhen in the afternoons and said nothing at all, for hours, and smoked a pipe, and once, on the ninth day, at the end of a very long silence, said, “The tea’s good this year,” and Haozhen said, “Yes,” and they both seemed satisfied.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fifth day, she took off the bandage and the wounds were clean.

On the sixth day, he stood up for a whole morning.

On the ninth, he walked with her down the terraces into the mist, very slowly, with Brake running ahead and stopping dead in front of them every fifty metres, to where the hill fell away into a gully and a stream came down over the rocks into a pool.

It was cold. It came straight off the mountain. The water was so clear you could see every stone on the bottom, three metres down, green and gold.

She took her clothes off and got in.

She did it before she could think about it, and the cold hit her like a wall, and she shrieked, loud, in three languages at once, so that birds went up out of the tea bushes on both sides of the gully, and came up gasping with her hair plastered flat and her whole body on fire.

He was sitting on a rock at the edge with his arm in its sling, laughing at her.

“Get in,” she said, through her teeth.

“I’ve got a hole in my arm.”

“Keep the arm out. Get the rest in.”

“Sera—”

“Get in, Hao, or I’m coming out to get you, and I’m very cold and very wet and I’ll put my feet on you.”

He got in.

Slowly, with his arm held up out of the water in the sling like a man hailing a taxi, gasping, swearing, in Mandarin, which she had never heard him do. She swam over to him and put her arms round his neck and her cold body against his and he swore again, louder, and then he was laughing too, both of them, in a mountain pool in the mist with a yellow dog barking at them from the rocks and the birds coming back down into the bushes.

She kissed him with her mouth cold and his mouth warm. She kissed him until the cold didn’t matter. His good hand was flat on her bare back under the water and his bad arm was held out of it over her shoulder, and he couldn’t use it, and he couldn’t hold her the way he wanted to, and she could feel him not being able to, feel the control of it go out of him, the whole careful structure of him with nothing to hold it up.

“You can’t do anything,” she said, against his mouth, delighted. “Can you. With one arm. In the water.”

“No.”

“You’ve got no control at all.”

“None,” said Qin Haozhen, and his voice wasn’t steady. “You’re doing this on purpose.”

“I’m doing everything on purpose,” said Serafina. “I’ve got two arms,” and showed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, in the back room, under the mosquito net, with the rain coming down on the tin roof so hard they had to stop talking, she was very careful of his arm, and of nothing else.

It was slow at first. It had to be. She sat astride him on Mr. Kwok’s brother’s bed with the grey light from the window on her skin and the rain roaring over their heads, and took his good hand and put it where she wanted it, and held his bad arm down on the pillow above his head by the wrist, very gently, so he couldn’t move it, so he couldn’t move at all, and kissed him from the notch in his eyebrow down. Slowly. Taking her time over all of it. The white line under his collarbone. The round pucker low on his side. The long pink line she’d stitched. The new bandage. She kissed the edges of the bandage. He lay under her with his eyes closed and his breath going ragged and his hand on her hip shaking, and when at last there was nothing left between them at all, he said her name into the roar of the rain, and then he didn’t say anything, and neither did she.

It wasn’t slow at the end.

It was them. Fast and laughing, the bed creaking under them like an old car on a bad road, the net coming down off its hook and falling over both of them so that they were tangled in it and laughing harder, the dog barking outside at the noise, the rain, and him trying to roll her over and not being able to because of his arm, and her pinning him and not letting him, and the look on his face when he gave up trying. When he let her have it. All of it. Every gram of control he’d ever had, handed over in a dead man’s bed in the mountains, under a fallen mosquito net, with the rain so loud nobody in the world could hear them, not even the deaf.

Afterwards they lay tangled in the net and listened to the rain on the roof.

“Best two weeks,” he said, after a long time, into her hair, “of my life.”

“It’s been nine days.”

“I know how long it’s been,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’m saying it now in case I don’t get the other five.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He got the other five.

They picked tea with Mrs. Yau on the tenth day, in borrowed straw hats, two leaves and a bud, the way she showed them, into baskets on their backs, and Mrs. Yau said Serafina had hands like a man and Haozhen had hands like a monk, and that between them they might make one tea picker. They made congee on the eleventh day, his way, with ginger, and Mr. Yau ate three bowls and said nothing and then said, “A northern congee,” and Haozhen looked so pleased that Serafina had to go outside.

They listened to the radio. Mr. Kwok’s brother’s radio, on the shelf by the shrine, which picked up one station from the valley if you turned it toward the window. On the twelfth day, in the news, between the price of fertiliser and a missing goat, there was a short report about a single-car accident on the old coast road, two weeks ago, near the headland tunnel. The driver had been taken to hospital with a broken leg. Police were not looking for anyone else in connection.

He sat on the stool with his hands round the cup of hot water and listened to it twice, because she turned it back.

“He’s alive,” she said.

“He’s alive,” said Qin Haozhen. “And he told them we were faster.”

He took out his notebook. The black one, from his inside pocket, that had been through a car wash and a tunnel and a fever. He opened it at the page that said WEDDING. Under Venue, where for a year there had been nothing, he wrote something, and turned the notebook round on the table so she could read it.

Venue: the garage. Under the bridge. With the trains.

She looked at it.

“Yes,” she said.

“You didn’t let me finish.”

“I never let you finish,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourteenth morning, at six, Brake stood up on the step by the stone frog and growled.

Serafina was at the tap. She turned round. He was already in the doorway, with his bad arm out of the sling and the dark shape in his good hand, looking down the track between the tea terraces into the mist.

An engine. Coming up the hill. Big, slow, heavy, a car built for weight.

It came out of the mist at the bottom of the last terrace. Black. A long black car, very clean, with tinted windows, coming up the track at walking pace between the tea bushes, and the driver’s window came down as it came, and an arm in a black sleeve rested on the sill.

It stopped twenty metres from the house.

The driver looked at them through the open window for four seconds without blinking.

Then the rear door opened, and a slight man in a camel coat got out, and stood on the track in the mist among the tea bushes in polished shoes, and looked at the stone house, and the dog, and the grey car with the broken window, and at Haozhen in the doorway with the gun lowered at his side.

“I believe,” said Chen Si, “you were looking for a door.”

chapters.title: Chen Si Brokers a Truce
chapters.desc: A black car in the tea terraces. A minister who has tea with Aurelia on the first Thursday of every month. A month of waiting, and then a quiet room in the old town where everything he ever wrote down goes into a stove. Two prices. He pays them both without asking. That night, at last, she asks him for the number, and he tells her.
chapters.epigraph: “There’s a price.” “Yes.” “You don’t want to know what it is?” “No.”
chapters.content:
Zhao Zhendong got out of the driver’s seat and stood by the black car with his hands at his sides and looked at the stone house for four seconds, and at the dog, and at the grey Crown with the broken rear window parked among the tea bushes, and at the man in the doorway with a gun lowered at his side and a bandaged arm, and said:

“Hm.”

Brake, on the step, stopped growling. It went down the track and sat in front of Zhao’s polished shoes and looked up at him. Zhao looked down at it. After a while he crouched, very slowly, and held out the back of his hand, and the dog smelled it, and sat down on his foot.

“Mr. Kwok,” said Chen Si, coming up the track in his camel coat with the mud getting on his shoes, “came to the forty-fourth floor on Wednesday.”

Serafina, at the tap, put down the pan.

“He took two buses,” said Chen Si. “In his cardigan. Qian found him in the lobby at seven in the morning, sitting on the bench by the lifts with a bag of oranges. He said he hadn’t heard from his brother’s house in eleven days, and the deaf neighbours had rung him to say the tea was good this year, which was what they’d agreed they’d say if there was somebody hurt.” He stopped at the foot of the step. “He said, Mr. Chen, my brother’s house has a door that goes nowhere. I think the boy needs one that goes somewhere.” He looked at Haozhen. “So I came.”

Haozhen lowered the gun the rest of the way.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Don’t thank me yet,” said Chen Si. “There’s a price.”

“Yes.”

“You don’t want to know what it is?”

Haozhen looked at him. At the camel coat, and the mud on the polished shoes, and Zhao behind him with a stray yellow dog sitting on his foot.

“No,” said Qin Haozhen.

Chen Si looked at him for a long moment in the mist.

“No,” he agreed, quietly. “I didn’t think you would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He explained it at the table, in the front room, by the shrine with the old man’s photograph, with a cup of last year’s tea from Mrs. Yau’s bag in front of him that he didn’t drink. Zhao stood by the door. Serafina sat on the bed through the doorway in the back room, with Brake’s head in her lap, and listened.

“Qian has your envelope,” said Chen Si. “I’ve read it.”

“You said you wouldn’t.”

“I said I wouldn’t unless something happened to you. A man shot through the arm in a tunnel and hiding in a dead tea farmer’s house for two weeks counts as something.” He turned the cup in his fingers. “It’s very good. It’s the best file I’ve ever read. I’ve been trying to get someone’s name on a document for twelve years with a great deal of money and much less success.” He looked at Haozhen. “You did it with a pencil and a cat.”

“Mouse did the companies.”

“Mouse,” said Chen Si, “is wasted on gearboxes. Don’t tell her I said so.” He set down the cup. “My wife has tea with a minister. On the first Thursday of every month. Mrs. Ling. Last year she signed something for my wife’s family, on a Tuesday, that nobody else in the province would sign. She likes my wife very much. She says she’s the only person in the province who has ever told her the truth about a contract.” He paused. “Mrs. Ling had a teacher, when she was young, in the capital. He’s very old now. He sits on a commission. The kind of commission that reads about people like your director, and decides what happens to them.”

Haozhen didn’t move.

“On Thursday,” said Chen Si, “my wife asked Mrs. Ling for tea. Out of turn. She has never done that before. On Friday, Mrs. Ling rang her teacher. On Saturday, her teacher read the first page of your index. Just the first page.” He paused. “He rang me himself. At home. On Saturday night. He’s ninety-one. He said, Mr. Chen, I have been waiting thirty years for somebody to bring me the word Northgate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took a month.

They came down from the mountains on the fourteenth day, in convoy: the black car first, with Chen Si in the back, and Zhao driving, and no dog, because Brake had lain down across the track and refused, and Mrs. Yau had picked it up and said it would come down to the city when it had made up its mind. Nobody behind, with its broken rear window taped over with a bin bag, and Serafina at the wheel, and Haozhen on the beads with his arm in Mr. Kwok’s brother’s shirt. They put the key under the stone frog. Mrs. Yau stood in her straw hat on the track outside her house and waved until they were out of sight, and Mr. Yau stood beside her and didn’t wave, and smoked his pipe, and nodded once, as if he’d been answered.

Jinx was waiting at the garage near the Docks.

She stood in front of the black roll-up door with her arms folded, every tattoo on them visible, while Serafina got out of Nobody, and looked at the bin bag on the rear window. Then at the dent in the left side where it had kissed the van. Then at the right-hand mirror, which was missing. Then, through the window, at the back seat.

At the wooden beads. Which were black. And stiff. And which had been, two weeks ago, the colour of honey.

“Two holes,” said Jinx.

“I’m sorry—”

“Two holes.”

“One in the window,” said Serafina. “One in him.”

Jinx looked at Haozhen getting out of the passenger side with his arm in a stranger’s shirt. She looked at him. Then she walked past him, past Serafina, to the back of the car, and opened the rear door, and looked at the beads, and touched them, very gently, with her black-nailed fingers.

“I’ll do new beads,” she said, to the car. “I’ll do better beads.” She turned round. Her eyes were very bright. “You absolute idiots. You brought it back.”

“You said bring it back.”

“I said without a hole in it,” said Jinx, and walked straight into Serafina and held on, hard, tattoos and all, and then let go and hit Haozhen on his good arm, quite hard, and went inside and pulled the roll-up door down behind her with a crash, and they heard her crying behind it, and then the radio coming on very loud.

✦ ✦ ✦

The month was the longest of her life. Longer than the twelve days. Longer than the two days in Nonna’s passenger seat.

There was nothing to do. That was the worst of it. Chen Si had said: go home, live in your garage, race in May, don’t go anywhere you don’t usually go, and wait. So she did. She raced in May, at the second round, in the south, with Joe Ng, and came fourth, and didn’t care. Haozhen’s arm healed. He stood on the pit wall with it in a sling and nobody came. Nobody came to the garage under the bridge. Nobody parked at the end of the street with their lights off. Big Wu came in every morning with the doughnuts and looked at him, and every morning said, “Still here, then,” and every morning Haozhen said, “Still here,” and Big Wu went under the transporter.

His mother rang on a Sunday, at eight, on his phone, for the first time, instead of him ringing her. She said a man had come to the flat and bought her a new sewing machine. A good one. Japanese. He’d said it was from her son’s employer, for long service. He’d been very polite. He’d admired her quilts and drunk her tea and gone away again.

Haozhen sat on the stool by the kettle with the phone against his ear after she’d hung up.

“What does it mean?” said Serafina.

“It means,” he said slowly, “that someone upstairs wants me to know they could have done something else instead.”

“Is that good?”

“I don’t know,” said Qin Haozhen. “Nobody’s ever bought anyone a sewing machine before.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Tuesday in May, at eleven in the morning, they went to the Pavilion of Clear Springs.

Up the narrow wooden stair from the lane that smelled of dried fish. The twelve tables. The man who boiled water in the copper kettle and never looked at anyone’s face. It was empty, except for the table at the back by the window with the bamboo blind half down.

Director Duan was sitting at it.

She wasn’t knitting.

Her hands were in her lap. There was no canvas bag at her feet, no oranges, no bamboo needles, no red wool. She was in the grey cardigan with the darned elbow, and her glasses were on their chain against it, and she looked smaller than she had in December, and older, and very tired, and she was looking out of the window at nothing.

Beside her, at the same table, there was a thin grey man of about sixty in a thin grey suit with a briefcase on his knees, who had come from the capital that morning and would go back that afternoon and whose name nobody would ever tell them.

And beside the table there was a stove. A small iron one, on legs, of the kind the tea house used in winter, with its door open and a fire laid inside it, burning low.

Chen Si stood at the top of the stairs in his camel coat. He didn’t come any further. He had said he wouldn’t.

“Go on,” he said, very quietly. “I’ll be here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Haozhen put the canvas bag on the table.

The notebooks. All twenty-three. From under the cat. Black, hardbacked, with the years on their spines in white paint. And on top of them, the three copies. The first, from Gilded’s roll cage, which Serafina had cut out the night before with a hacksaw at the bench, the weld she’d been so proud of, and Big Wu had watched her do it and said nothing at all. The second, from under the new honey-coloured beads in Nobody’s back seat, which Jinx had unpicked with her curved needle and her face set like stone. The third in its sealed brown envelope, which Qian had brought down to the lobby at seven that morning and handed over in both hands, with an expression Haozhen had not seen on him before.

The grey man opened his briefcase. He took out a single sheet of paper, typed, and read it aloud in a flat voice, the way you’d read a delivery note.

The resignation of Qin Haozhen, received on the twenty-sixth of February, was accepted. With effect from that date. His service was concluded. His records would be sealed. There would be no further contact, no further interest, and no further action concerning him, his mother Liang Shufen, Miss Song Serafina, her sister, her sister’s husband, or any person employed at an address under a railway bridge in the industrial district. The material relating to Miss Song held by the traffic division had been withdrawn and destroyed. Mr. Gong Ruiming would be returned to his family in Lisbon within thirty days, with his debts to the state considered discharged. Officer Mo Tianyi had been commended for his conduct on the night of the thirteenth of April and would face no inquiry.

And the director of the section concerned had, that morning, requested early retirement. On grounds of health. It had been granted.

He didn’t look at Director Duan while he read that. Nor did she.

“In return,” said the grey man, folding the paper, “all material.” He looked at the canvas bag. “All copies. All notes. Everything.” He looked at Haozhen. “Destroyed. Now. Here. In front of me. And you will never write it down again.”

Haozhen didn’t answer at once.

He put his hand flat on the stack of black notebooks. Eleven years. Every name. Every date. Every coat and cough and hand on an elbow at a petrol station. The one thing he had never let himself do was forget.

Serafina, beside him, didn’t say anything. She put her hand on his back.

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did it himself. He wouldn’t let anyone else.

One at a time. The three copies first: the roll from the roll cage, the pages from under the beads, the brown envelope, still sealed. Into the stove. The fire took them and they curled and went black and bright and then grey. Then the notebooks. 2012. 2013. He didn’t open them. He put each one in the stove whole, in order, the way he did everything, and waited for it to catch before he put in the next one, and the grey man watched, and Director Duan watched, and the man with the copper kettle stood behind his counter and did not look at anyone’s face.

2016. 2017. The shipping agent with the cough.

2019. 2020.

2022. Three of them. Battery Hill. Lot 9. A man who left on an early flight.

2023. Lisbon. A yellow house with blue tiles.

When he put in the last one he stood in front of the stove with his hands at his sides and watched it burn until it was gone. Then he turned round.

“I don’t need them,” he said, to the grey man. “I remember.”

The grey man looked at him for a moment. Then he closed his briefcase, and stood up, and nodded to Director Duan, a small nod, almost courteous, and walked to the stairs, and past Chen Si at the top of them without looking at him, and down, and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was still sitting at the table by the window.

Haozhen stood in front of her. Serafina stood beside him. The stove ticked as it cooled.

“You saw the right person,” said Director Duan, eventually, to the window. “At the end. You looked at me.” Her voice was very quiet. “I trained you too well.”

“Director.”

“Not any more.” She almost smiled. “I’m a retired civil servant with a bad chest. I shall go to the seaside and grow tomatoes.” She turned her head and looked at Serafina. “Miss Song. You have a very loud laugh. I’m told you also have a very good engine in a very ugly taxi.”

“Nobody,” said Serafina.

“I beg your pardon?”

“That’s its name,” said Serafina. “Nobody.”

Director Duan Qiuyan looked at her. Then she laughed. Once. A small dry sound, the first anyone in the section had ever heard her make, and she put her hand over her mouth as if it had surprised her.

“Of course it is,” she said. “Of course it is.”

She looked back at the window.

“Go home, Haozhen,” she said. “Go home and get married. You’ve got nothing left to write down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si was waiting at the bottom of the stairs, in the lane that smelled of dried fish.

“And yours,” said Haozhen. “The price.”

Chen Si looked at him.

“You haven’t asked what it is,” he said.

“No.”

“In my house,” said Chen Si, “there’s a contract. Clause three. Neither party will lie to the other, about anything.” He looked at Serafina, at the end of the lane, waiting by Nonna, with her hands in her jacket pockets. “You’ve never lied to her. I know. But there’s a sentence in my house. I can’t tell you that yet. And you’ve been saying it to her for a year and a half. About one thing.” He paused. “That’s my price. You tell her. All of it. Everything that was in those books. Before the wedding. In your own voice. Not off a page.”

Haozhen was quiet.

“That’s not a price,” he said. “I was going to do it tonight.”

“I know,” said Chen Si. “That’s why I chose it. I never charge anything a man isn’t already willing to pay.” He turned his collar up against the wind coming down the lane. “It’s the only way to be sure it gets paid.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her that night.

In the loft. On the mattress, sitting up against the wall, with the window open onto the railway and the trains going over, and her sitting facing him with her knees against his, holding both his hands.

“Ask me,” he said.

She’d waited a year and a half. She’d waited since the workbench, and the photograph from Antwerp, and I know the number. I won’t tell you tonight.

“How many, Hao?”

“Thirty-eight,” said Qin Haozhen.

He told her. In his own voice. Not off a page. He told her all thirty-eight, in order, from the teacher in the hotel in the capital at eighteen to the man by the bins in his slippers in Lisbon. Names. Dates. Places. What they were wearing. Who gave him the folder. Who he handed them to. Thirty-four of them had been alive when he handed them over, and he told her what he knew of what had happened to them since, which for some of them was a great deal and for some was nothing. Four, he didn’t know. Two had died in custody. And four had died at the time. Two of those by his own hand.

He told her about those two very slowly.

It took until five in the morning. She didn’t let go of his hands once. She didn’t interrupt him once. When he stopped, sometimes, she waited. When he couldn’t go on, she said, “And then,” and he went on. Twice she cried and he stopped and she said, “Don’t stop,” and he didn’t. The trains went over. She counted them without meaning to. Twenty-nine.

When he’d finished, the sky over the railway was going grey.

He sat against the wall and looked at her. His face was wrecked and open and completely empty, the way it had been in the paddock in December 2022 when she’d shown him a room in his own house he hadn’t known was there. Only this time it was the other room. The one where the people went. He’d opened the door and let her walk through it, all of it, every corner.

“That’s everything,” he said. “That’s what I am.”

Serafina looked at him in the grey light.

“I’ve decided,” she said.

He didn’t breathe.

“I decided again,” said Serafina. “Just now. With all of it. Every one of them.” She was still holding his hands. “It came out the same.”

He made a sound she had heard once before, in Nonna’s passenger seat, on the third night after Lisbon. It came up out of the floor.

She pulled him down against her and held him, the way she had then, with both arms, and the thirtieth train went over and shook the whole building, and he didn’t wake when the thirty-first did, because by then, for the first time since he was eighteen, there was nothing left that he had not said out loud, and he was asleep.

chapters.title: Disavowed
chapters.desc: Nine quiet months: a championship, a prize in Geneva, a man learning to sleep six hours and cook. Then a registered letter from the capital informs him that no person called Qin Haozhen has ever existed, and asks him to sign to confirm he received it. For the first time in years, he laughs until he can’t stand up. And with it comes a parcel, two metres long, in red wool.
chapters.epigraph: “They want me to sign to say I’ve received a letter telling me I don’t exist.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
Nobody came.

That was the summer. And the autumn. And the winter. It was the strangest thing either of them had ever lived through, and it took her until September to understand that the strangeness was simply what other people called ordinary life.

He didn’t have a job. He didn’t have a folder, or a flight, or a phone that rang at two in the morning in fourteen countries.
