He had a stool by the kettle in a garage under a railway bridge, and a mug that said HIS, and a fiancée, and a yellow dog called Brake that Mrs. Yau had sent down from the mountains in June in a basket on the bus, with a label on its collar in Mr. Kwok’s handwriting that said FRAGILE.

He learned to sleep six hours. Not every night. Most.

He learned to cook. Properly, not congee. Big Wu’s mother came on Wednesdays and stood beside him at the camping stove and told him he was doing it wrong, and he wrote down everything she said in a new black notebook, the first notebook he’d ever had that didn’t need a code. Ginger: more than you think. Never wash the wok with soap. Big Wu lies about liking bitter melon.

He learned to be in the pit garage on race weekends without looking at the grandstand. That took longer. Until August. At the round in the south in August, she came in from a stint and pulled off her helmet and looked for him, and he was at the back of the garage, by the laptops, beside Mouse, reading the tyre temperatures off the screen, with his back to the pit lane and the stands and every camera in the series, and he hadn’t looked round once in an hour.

She stood in the pit lane with her helmet under her arm and watched him not looking round for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

She won the championship in November. By four points. Her class, in the Asian series, with Joe Ng and a black car with a gold name on its bonnet and a small grey taxi under three coats of lacquer on the driver’s door.

Aurelia came to the last round in a white coat and every piece of gold she owned and stood in the front row of the grandstand beside her husband and sobbed out loud when the flag came down, the way she had in 2019, and afterwards on the podium Serafina pointed the champagne at her, and this time she didn’t miss.

And in October, before that, in Geneva, in the great hall of the old hotel on the lake, under the chandeliers, Serafina sat in row C and watched her sister win the prize for Seconda, and saw their father stand up at the same second as Chen Si, at either end of the front row, and saw their mother not stand up, and saw why.

Haozhen didn’t come into the hall.

He’d flown to Geneva with her. He’d sat beside her on the plane and slept, which he’d never done on a plane, with his head on her shoulder from somewhere over the sea until the wheels touched the runway. But at the doors of the great hall, with four hundred people going in and photographers on both sides of the red carpet, he’d stopped.

“I’ll wait,” he said.

“Hao.”

“Not yet,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’m not ready for four hundred people. Not with cameras.” He looked at the photographers. “I’ve spent eleven years making sure nobody had a photograph of me. It’s going to take more than five months to stop.”

So he waited in the hotel lobby. In a chair. Not by the door. By the window, with the lake behind him, and his back to the room. When she came out at eleven with her face wet and her mascara everywhere and told him about their mother’s shoulders, he stood up and held her in the middle of the lobby of the best hotel in Geneva, and didn’t look round once to see who was watching.

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter came on the seventeenth of February.

It was a Monday. It came registered, from the capital, to the garage under the railway bridge, and the postman made Big Wu sign for it, and Big Wu looked at the envelope, which was long and brown and stiff and had a seal on the back he didn’t recognise, and carried it to the bench by the kettle holding it out in front of him with two fingers like something that might bite.

“For him,” he said. “From the capital. Registered.”

Haozhen was at the stove with Big Wu’s mother’s wok, making the garlic greens. He turned the gas off. He wiped his hands on the towel. He came and looked at the envelope on the bench for a while without touching it.

Serafina came down the stairs from the loft.

Mouse took her headphones off.

Mr. Kwok, on his stool by the door with the newspaper, put the newspaper down.

He opened it.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were three pages.

He read them standing at the bench, with everybody watching him. He read them once, very carefully, the way he’d read the folder on Lisbon, the way he read everything. His face didn’t change. Then he read them again.

On the second reading, something started to happen at the corner of his mouth.

“Hao?” said Serafina.

“It’s from a department,” he said. “I’ve never heard of it. In the capital.” He looked at the first page. “Further to a review of records,” he read aloud, in a flat voice, the way the grey man had read the delivery note in the tea house, “the department wishes to inform you that no record exists of any person by the name of Qin Haozhen, born the twelfth of January 1994, having served in any capacity in any organ of the state. No record exists of his enrolment at the State Military Academy. No record exists of any salary, pension, or medical file. No record exists of any service.”

He turned the page.

“The department further wishes to inform you that the identity number previously associated with this name was issued in error and has been cancelled. Any documents bearing this number should be considered void.”

He turned the page again.

“Please sign the enclosed form,” he read, “to confirm that you have received this letter. Return it to the department within fourteen days in the envelope provided.”

He held up the third page. It was a form. A small one. A box for a signature and a box for a date, and at the top, printed, Acknowledgement of Receipt.

“They want me to sign,” said Qin Haozhen, “to say I’ve received a letter telling me I don’t exist.”

And he started to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was not the laugh from the glovebox, helpless into his palms. It was not the dark one with the fear in it, at the bench, over the director’s silver pen. It was not anything she had heard from him before.

It started small, at the corner of his mouth, the way the smile had at the track day. Then it got out. It came up through him and he couldn’t stop it, and he put the form down on the bench and leaned on the bench with both hands and laughed, and laughed, out loud, so loud the dog woke up under the workbench and barked, so loud that Big Wu took a step back. He laughed until he couldn’t stand up straight. He laughed until he had to sit down on the floor of the garage with his back against Gilded’s front wheel, the way she had on the night of the photograph from Antwerp, and laughed with his head back against the car and tears running down his face, and every time he tried to stop he looked at the form on the bench above him and started again.

“Acknowledgement of receipt,” he said, and couldn’t finish.

Serafina sat down on the floor beside him.

She started laughing too. She couldn’t help it. She’d never heard him laugh like that, and it was the most infectious thing she had ever heard in her life, and she laughed into his shoulder with her arms round him until her stomach hurt.

Mr. Kwok was laughing. He had his newspaper over his face.

Big Wu was laughing, a huge deep rumble, holding on to the transporter.

And at the end of the bench, very quietly at first and then not quietly at all, with her hands over her mouth and her nose ring catching the light, Mouse was laughing, out loud, at a man sitting on the floor who had just been told he had never existed, and nobody had ever heard Mouse laugh like that before either.

A train went over. The whole garage shook. The spanner fell in the bucket. Nobody stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

“So you’re nobody,” said Serafina, when they could breathe.

They were still on the floor. His head was back against the wheel and his face was wet and he was breathing as though he’d run the length of the Docks road.

“Yes.”

“Officially.”

“Officially. I was never born. I never went to the academy. I never worked anywhere. I’ve never had a salary.” He wiped his eyes with the heel of his hand. “Somebody had better tell the bank. I bought you a gearbox with money I never earned.”

“Like the car,” said Serafina.

He turned his head against the wheel and looked at her.

“Nobody,” she said. “In Jinx’s garage. Under the tyres. Dull, grey, ordinary, a dent in the door. Nobody looks at it twice. Nobody knows what it can do.” She took his face in her hands. “You’re Nobody. You always were. That was the whole point of you. And it isn’t any more.”

“No,” he said.

“So now we’d better make you somebody.”

He looked at her.

“How?”

“I don’t know,” said Serafina. “A driving licence. Your mother’s town. A form, probably. You like forms.” She kissed him, on the mouth, with salt on both of them from laughing. “Sign their stupid receipt first. Then we’ll start.”

He signed it.

He did it at the bench, in his small square separate letters, each one like something typed. Qin Haozhen. Then, after a moment, in the box for the date, the date. And then, after another moment, in very small letters underneath the box, where there was no space for anything, one more line, which she leaned over his shoulder to read.

Received with thanks.

✦ ✦ ✦

The parcel came on the same day, in the afternoon. Not registered. Ordinary post. It had come from a town by the sea three hundred kilometres up the coast that none of them had ever heard of, and it was long and soft and wrapped in brown paper and string, and his name was on it in a neat, small, sloping hand that he recognised from eleven years of folders.

He knew before he opened it. She saw him know.

He untied the string. He folded back the brown paper.

It was red. Ribbed. Wool. Two metres and a little more, folded over and over on itself, and the ends had been cast off at last, both of them, neatly, with a fringe, and the whole thing had been washed and pressed so that it lay flat and soft and warm in the brown paper on the bench like something that had always been meant to be finished.

There was a card. Plain. One line.

It was always for the first one of you who walked out. I didn’t think it would be you. — D.

He stood at the bench with his hands on either side of the scarf and didn’t touch it.

“Who is she?” said Big Wu, very low. “The one who sent it?”

“The woman who made me,” said Qin Haozhen. “Into what I was.”

He picked it up. It was very long. He didn’t know what to do with it. He held it in both hands, the way he’d held the thirty spools of Japanese thread out of the haberdasher’s, as if it might break.

Serafina took it from him.

She shook it out, all two metres of it, and wound it round his neck, once, twice, three times, the way Nonna used to wind scarves round her neck in Milan in the winter, and tucked the ends in, and stepped back and looked at him. A man who didn’t exist, in a red scarf, in a garage, in February.

“It’s cold in garages,” she said. “She was right about that.”

He put his hand up to it.

“I’ll wear it at the wedding,” he said.

“You will not wear it at the wedding.”

“I will,” said Qin Haozhen, “if it’s cold.”

chapters.title: A Man With No File
chapters.desc: A mining town that the maps stopped bothering with, a registry clerk who remembers a boy on the wall by the winding gear, and his mother at her Japanese sewing machine, who has never once believed he was a security guard. Then a driving test he fails for checking his mirrors too often. And Harbour Road, on a Friday afternoon, holding her hand where anyone can see.
chapters.epigraph: “Security guards don’t send that much money home, Haozhen. I’m not stupid. I’m a seamstress.” — Liang Shufen
chapters.content:
The train north took eleven hours, and this time she was on it.

She hadn’t been on a train in nine years. She’d forgotten how slow they were. She sat by the window in her leather jacket with her boots up on the seat opposite until the guard told her to take them down, and watched the province go by, and then the next one, and then the flat brown country beyond that, mile after mile of it under a big grey sky, and in the afternoon the first pithead came up on the horizon, black against the grey, with its winding wheel turning, and he put his hand on her knee.

“That’s not it,” he said. “That’s the next town. Ours is forty minutes more.”

“How do you know?”

“Ours has two wheels,” said Qin Haozhen. “That one’s only got one.”

He was wearing the red scarf. It was March, and cold, and he had wound it round his neck the way she’d shown him, three times, with the ends tucked in, and she had not said anything about it all the way from the city.

✦ ✦ ✦

The town had two streets and a pithead with two winding wheels and coal dust on everything. On the washing. On the windowsills. On the parked bicycles and the steps of the houses and the backs of the old men sitting on them. It was in the air, faintly, a taste on the back of her tongue like a struck match.

His mother’s flat was on the second floor of a building at the end of the second street. Two rooms. A sewing machine by the window, a new one, Japanese, white, with a quilt half-finished on the table beside it and thirty little wooden spools of silk thread lined up along the windowsill in the order of the rainbow.

Liang Shufen was sixty-three. She was very small and very straight and she had his eyes exactly, very dark and much less absent than her face, and she opened the door before they’d knocked and looked at her son in his red scarf, and then at the tall thin woman beside him with short hair cut with kitchen scissors, and an old burn on the back of her right hand, and a ruby on her left.

“So,” she said. “You’re the racing one.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“Can you sew?”

“No,” said Serafina. “I can stitch a forearm.”

His mother looked at her for a long moment. Then she reached out, without asking, and took her son’s left arm, and pushed up the sleeve of his jacket, and looked at the long pale line from his elbow to his wrist, with the pucker at the eighth stitch.

“Who did this?” she said.

“She did,” said Haozhen.

“It’s terrible,” said Liang Shufen. “Look at that one. That one in the middle. She’s pulled it much too tight.” She let go of his arm. She looked up at Serafina again, and something happened to her face that was so exactly the thing that happened to his, the smile’s distant relation from the countryside, that Serafina forgot to breathe. “Come in. You’ll have to learn. I’m not having my son walking about with stitches like that. Take your boots off. Not on my floor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry office was a single room in a concrete building at the end of the first street, with a counter and a window and a clerk behind the counter who was seventy if she was a day and had been the clerk behind that counter since before he was born.

“Qin,” she said, looking at him over her glasses. “Qin Haozhen.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“Old Qin’s boy. From the second street. Whose father was under the roof in 2003.” She looked at him. “You used to sit on the wall by the winding gear. Every day after school. For hours. Watching the wheels go round. Your mother used to come and fetch you for dinner.”

“Yes.”

“I remember you,” said the registry clerk. “And now you come in here and tell me you don’t exist.”

He put the letter on the counter. The three pages from the capital. Issued in error and has been cancelled. She read it slowly, all of it, with her lips moving, and then she read it again, and then she took off her glasses and looked at him.

“Nonsense,” she said. “I’ve got you in the book.”

She had. She got it down from a shelf behind her, a household register, enormous, cloth-bound, the pages gone yellow and soft, and opened it on the counter and turned the pages with a licked finger until she found the page for the flat at the end of the second street. The handwriting on it was old, and blue, and faded. Qin Dahai, head of household, miner. Liang Shufen, wife, seamstress. Qin Haozhen, son. And a date. The twelfth of January, 1994.

“There,” said the clerk, and put her finger on it. “Born. I wrote that. In 1994. In this pen.” She held up the pen, an old blue fountain pen on a chain. “Don’t tell me you don’t exist. I wrote you down.”

He stood at the counter and looked at the line of faded blue handwriting.

Serafina, beside him, put her hand on his back.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three weeks.

There were forms. Of course there were forms. He’d been right about that. A form to say that the identity number previously issued was void. A form to apply for a new one. A form for his mother to sign to say he was her son, which she signed with an expression of great contempt, in front of the clerk, and then signed again because her first signature had gone through the paper. A letter from the headmaster of the primary school, retired now, who came to the registry office on his bicycle to say that he remembered the boy, he’d been very good at maps. A letter from the doctor’s widow, because the doctor who had delivered him was dead, but the doctor’s widow had kept all his notebooks and found the page.

He did them all. Every one. He filled in every box in his small square letters, very slowly, and Serafina watched him do it, at his mother’s table by the sewing machine, under the window with the thirty spools of thread, and she thought she’d never seen him look happier. Not at the track day. Not on the coast road. A man filling in a form to prove that he was born.

“You like forms,” she said, on the fourth evening.

“I like these,” said Qin Haozhen. He didn’t look up. “Every one of these says I’m somebody.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother made dumplings on the second Sunday.

She taught Serafina to fold them. Badly. At the table by the window, with the flour going everywhere, while he sat on the sofa and watched with an expression Serafina had only seen on him in a hotel lobby in Geneva. His mother folded eleven dumplings in the time it took Serafina to fold one, and every one of Serafina’s came apart in the water, and his mother laughed at her, high and surprised, the laugh Serafina had heard down the phone line in December, and said they’d do it again tomorrow, and the day after that, and every day until the girl could fold a dumpling that stayed shut.

Afterwards, washing up, at the sink, with her back to the room, his mother said:

“He told me. In December. On my birthday. He said he was going to marry a racing driver.”

Serafina put down the tea towel.

“He said you fix cars. And swear in three languages. And have never in your life done what you were told.” Liang Shufen rinsed a bowl. “I said, good.” She put the bowl on the rack. “He never did what he wanted. Not once. Not from the day his father died. He did what he was told by me, and then by the school, and then by them. He’d sit on that wall by the winding gear for hours and never say what he wanted. Not even when I asked.”

“He’s learning,” said Serafina.

“I can see.” His mother turned round, with her wet hands, and looked at her son on the sofa, who was pretending to read a newspaper and not listening. “He’s wearing a scarf. A red one. He’s never worn a colour in his life.”

“Ma,” said Haozhen, from behind the newspaper.

“And he’s not in security any more,” said Liang Shufen. “He told me that too. On my birthday. He said he’d stopped. He said he was going to work with cars.” She dried her hands. “I said, good. I said, you were never a security guard.”

Haozhen lowered the newspaper.

“You knew,” he said.

His mother looked at him. It was the look. All the way in. His look, exactly; Serafina saw where he’d got it.

“Security guards,” said Liang Shufen, “don’t send that much money home, Haozhen. Every month. For eleven years. I’m not stupid.” She hung the tea towel on its hook. “I’m a seamstress. I know what things cost.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last night she gave Serafina the quilt.

It was the one from the table beside the sewing machine, the one that had been half-finished when they arrived. It was finished now. She’d sat up three nights doing it, after they’d gone to bed in the back room; Serafina had heard the sewing machine through the wall, very quiet, until two in the morning.

It was blue and grey, mostly, in squares. Ordinary cotton, from the market. But across the middle of it, from one corner to the other, in the Japanese silk thread, in tiny careful stitches, there was a road. Grey, winding, with white lines down the middle. It went up a hill and round a hundred bends. And on it, at the top, near the corner, in red silk so bright it glowed, there was a very small car.

Serafina held it in her arms in the doorway of his mother’s flat and couldn’t speak.

“It’s the mountain,” said Liang Shufen. “The one you went up. He showed me. On his telephone. Eleven times.” She sniffed. “You’re on the outside. At the corner near the top. He said that was the important bit.”

“The hundred and twelfth,” said Serafina, wetly.

“I don’t know what that means,” said his mother. “It looked dangerous. Don’t do it again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He failed his driving test on the twenty-eighth of March.

Not the theory. The theory he passed with a hundred per cent, the first person in the history of the test centre in the industrial district to do so, and the man who marked it came out of his office to look at him. He failed the practical. A thirty-minute drive round the streets near the test centre in a white Honda with dual controls and an examiner in the passenger seat with a clipboard, a heavy, sad man called Mr. Chiu who had been examining drivers for twenty-six years and had seen everything.

“You check your mirrors too often,” said Mr. Chiu, at the end, in the car park, with the clipboard on his knee.

“I check them every four seconds.”

“I know. I counted. Every four seconds. The whole time. Rear-view, left, right, rear-view.” Mr. Chiu looked at the clipboard. “It’s excessive. It suggests anxiety. Anxiety at the wheel is a hazard. I’ve written it down.” He looked up. “Is somebody following you, Mr. Qin?”

Haozhen thought about the question with real care.

“No,” he said. “Not any more.”

“Then stop checking,” said Mr. Chiu, and failed him, and put a red cross in a box.

✦ ✦ ✦

She laughed for an hour. In Nonna, in the car park, with her head on the steering wheel.

“Excessive,” she said. “Excessive mirror checks. You drove a hundred and sixty through a gap in a tunnel with a bullet in your arm and you failed your test for looking in the mirror—”

“I didn’t drive anything through a tunnel. You were driving.”

“I’m putting it on the whiteboard,” said Serafina. “In red. Next to the postcard. Excessive mirror checks. I’m going to have it framed.”

He looked out of the windscreen at the white Honda with its dual controls.

“I’ll do it again,” he said. “In two weeks. And this time I’ll look at the right person.”

“There’s nobody in the car but the examiner.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ll look at the road.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He passed on the eleventh of April. A Friday.

Mr. Chiu again. The same white Honda. The same thirty minutes round the streets of the industrial district, past the paint works and the fish-ball factory and the end of the road where the gas works stood with its two black gasholders against the sky. He checked his mirrors every eleven seconds, which Mr. Chiu counted, and which was, Mr. Chiu said in the car park, about right.

“Pass,” said Mr. Chiu, and ticked a box, and signed it, and tore off a slip of pink paper, and held it out. “Temporary licence. The real one comes by post in six weeks. To your home address.” He looked at the form. “Which is—”

Haozhen gave him the address of the garage under the railway bridge.

Mr. Chiu wrote it down. He looked at the name at the top of the form for a moment. QIN Haozhen. With the new identity number underneath, three weeks old.

“Congratulations, Mr. Qin,” he said. “You exist.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was waiting outside the test centre, leaning on Nonna’s bonnet in the sun, in her jacket, with two egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover in a paper bag going translucent with butter.

He came out with the pink slip in his hand. He didn’t say anything. He held it up.

She shrieked. Loud. In three languages. A woman crossing the road with a pushchair stopped and looked.

“Let’s go,” she said, and threw him the keys.

He caught them. He looked at them. Then he looked at her, and something happened in his face, and he put the keys in his pocket instead.

“Not the car,” he said. “Walk with me.”

“Walk where?”

“Harbour Road.”

She looked at him.

It was three o’clock on a Friday afternoon in April, and Harbour Road was the busiest street in the city. Trams and shoppers and tourists and the boutiques, and the old shops with their glass cases, and photographers. There were always photographers on Harbour Road. People came there to be seen.

“Hao,” she said.

“I’d like to,” said Qin Haozhen. “If it’s not too big.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They took the tram, because he said that was what people did.

They got off at the stop by the wine shop where he’d once spent forty minutes choosing a bottle. They walked. Down Harbour Road, on the side by the harbour, in the sun, in the crowd, past the old shops and the new ones and the Milanese bakery and the noodle place with the queue outside.

And somewhere between the wine shop and the bakery, without saying anything, without looking at her, he took her hand.

Her left one. With the ruby on it.

He held it. In the street. In the middle of the afternoon, with a thousand people round them and a tram going by. And he didn’t check the street. She waited for it, the long sweep, the pause on anyone who moved too fast, the sweep back. It didn’t come. He walked down Harbour Road with his eyes on the pavement in front of him and her hand in his and his red scarf round his neck, and didn’t look round once.

She had to look at the harbour for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside number eighteen, with the gold letters over the door and the broken necklace in the window, a man with a camera was standing on the kerb. He did fashion, mostly, for a gossip site. He photographed the women who came out of the boutiques on Harbour Road with their bags. He saw Serafina Song, the racing champion, the designer’s sister, coming down the street in a leather jacket holding hands with a man in a red scarf, and he lifted the camera.

Haozhen saw him. Serafina felt him see him. Felt his hand tighten on hers, and his whole body go, for half a second, toward the edge of the pavement, toward the tram, toward the doorway of the bakery, toward anywhere out of the line of that lens.

Then she felt him stop.

He didn’t turn his face away. He didn’t put his head down. He walked straight past the man with the camera with her hand in his, at an ordinary pace, with his face in plain view in the April sun, and the shutter went, three times, four, and he let it.

Through the window of number eighteen, at the counter, Aurelia was standing with a necklace in her hands and Lily beside her and Enzo at the bench at the back with his magnifying glasses pushed up on his forehead. All three of them were looking out of the window. Aurelia had put the necklace down.

As they went past, Aurelia put her hand flat on the inside of the glass.

Serafina put hers on the outside. Just for a second. Without stopping.

Then they walked on, down Harbour Road, toward the harbour, in the sun, in the crowd, with the photographer behind them looking at his screen and frowning, because none of the photographs had come out the way he’d meant. In every one of them, the man in the red scarf was looking at the woman beside him, and not at the camera at all.

chapters.title: The Song Family Was Not Invited
chapters.desc: Now that he exists, Mr. Kwok says, there has to be a proper engagement dinner. Six dishes, trestle tables, borrowed chairs, two mothers who have never met, and the trains every eleven minutes. Her parents were not invited. At eight o’clock, they come in under the shutter anyway, and her mother is carrying a folder.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t invited.” “No, Mamma.” “I came anyway. I’m told that’s what people do in this family.”
chapters.content:
“Six,” said Mr. Kwok.

“Six what?”

“Dishes. An engagement is six. A wedding is nine. Everybody knows that.” He was standing in front of the whiteboard with his arms folded, looking at the photograph of Harbour Road that Mouse had printed off the gossip site and stuck up beside the postcard of the Monza banking: a woman in a leather jacket and a man in a red scarf, walking, his face turned toward her, not toward the camera. “You had drinks. Two years ago. With a run sheet. That was not an engagement. That was a man with a clipboard and a duck.”

“It was my mother’s duck,” said Big Wu.

“It was a very good duck,” said Mr. Kwok. “It was still not an engagement.” He turned round. “He exists now. He’s got a pink slip that says so. He’s going to get a licence in the post with his name on it. So now there’s a dinner. A proper one. Six dishes. Round tables. Both families.” He looked at Haozhen, on the stool by the kettle. “Your mother.”

“She’d come,” said Haozhen slowly. “If I asked.”

“Then ask.”

“And mine?” said Serafina.

The garage went quiet.

Mr. Kwok looked at her for a while.

“That’s yours to say,” he said. “Not mine.”

She didn’t say anything for a long time. A train went over.

“No,” she said finally. “Not mine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

So they came on a Saturday in May. Everybody.

Mr. Kwok borrowed three round tables from the noodle shop at the end of the street and the restaurant next to it and the restaurant next to that, and thirty chairs, and three red tablecloths from his daughter in Vancouver by express post. He cooked for two days. Big Wu’s mother came on the Friday to help and they had an argument about the soy sauce that went on for four hours and ended with both of them crying and holding hands. Mouse strung lights along the railway-bridge girders, small warm white ones, hundreds of them, so that the whole ceiling of the garage looked like the harbour at night.

His mother came on the slow train, eleven hours, with a bag of her own dumplings in a cool box and a quilt for Big Wu’s mother, whom she had never met, because she said you didn’t go to a stranger’s house with nothing in your hands. The two old women looked at each other in the garage doorway, both of them very small, both of them very straight. Then Big Wu’s mother took the quilt and Liang Shufen took the arm Big Wu’s mother held out, and they went and sat down together at the end of the first table and didn’t stop talking for four hours.

Mr. and Mrs. Yau came down from the mountains, in their straw hats, on the bus, with a bag of this year’s tea and Brake’s old basket, and Brake lost its mind with joy and ran in circles round Mrs. Yau’s feet and stopped dead in front of them every third circle so that she had to keep stopping too.

Granny Shum came. In her folding chair. With her granddaughter, who had painted her nails gold for the occasion, and her thermos, and her scanner, which she turned off, at the door, very ceremonially, and put in her handbag.

Jinx came, and Raiden, who brought a drawing of the garage, and gave it to Haozhen, and it was the garage as it really was, with every train and every girder and every person in it, and the stool by the kettle, and the mug.

And at seven o’clock, through the side door from the alley, in gold, every piece she owned, with her husband behind her in camel and Qian behind him with his antacids, came Aurelia, carrying a box of pastries from the Milanese bakery on Harbour Road, and behind Qian, unexpectedly, very large, in black, Zhao Zhendong. And on his arm, in green, with a single camellia in her hair and the expression of a woman who had been told this would be a small family dinner, Elowen.

Aurelia stopped just inside the door and looked at Elowen’s camellia.

Elowen looked at Aurelia’s gold.

“That’s a point to me,” said Aurelia.

“For what?”

“For arriving first. With pastries.”

“Then it’s a point to me,” said Elowen, “for not caring where I arrive.”

“Ladies,” said Chen Si, mildly, and Zhao said “Hm,” and the two husbands looked at each other over their wives’ heads with the expression of men who had been having this exact conversation for six years.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat down at half past seven.

Six dishes. Mr. Kwok served them himself, one at a time, the way he said it was done, and announced each one. The roast pork with the crackling, for prosperity. The prawns, which Haozhen ate, conspicuously, while looking at Auntie Chu, who had been invited and was sitting at the third table and who nodded at him, once, with great satisfaction. The chicken, whole, with the head on, so the engagement had a beginning and an end. The noodles, long, for long life. The red bean soup.

And the fish.

Whole. Steamed. With ginger and spring onion and the good soy sauce that Big Wu’s mother had won the argument about. Head and tail. Mr. Kwok put it down in the middle of the first table, in front of Serafina, and stood back.

Serafina looked at it.

The whole garage looked at it. Everybody knew. Big Wu’s mother knew; she’d been eating Serafina’s fish since 2019. Aurelia knew. Haozhen knew; he’d told Chen Si about it at a dinner on the forty-fourth floor two years ago, in front of her sister, and her sister had asked him how long he’d been watching.

Between the soup and the fish, Serafina thought. Two hundred people. The Harbour Hotel. I stood up between the soup and the fish and said I’d rather marry a carburettor, and walked out.

She picked up her chopsticks.

She took a piece of the fish, from the side, the best part, near the cheek, the way Nonna had taught her when she was six and she’d cried. She put it in her mouth. She ate it.

She didn’t make a face. She’d decided she wouldn’t. She ate the whole piece, in front of everyone, and swallowed, and put her chopsticks down, and picked up her glass.

“That,” she said, “was disgusting. Thank you, Mr. Kwok.”

Mr. Kwok put his hand over his eyes.

Beside her, under the table, Haozhen found her knee and held it, very hard, and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight o’clock, between the fish and the soup, somebody came in under the shutter.

She didn’t hear it. Nobody heard it; Mouse had put music on, and there were thirty people talking and laughing and a train going over. She just saw Haozhen turn his head. Not much. A few degrees. The way he’d turned it at the east service door at nine twenty-two when a tray of glasses hit the floor. And she saw his hand come off her knee and lie flat on the table, where people could see it.

She turned round.

They were standing just inside the shutter, under the edge of it, with the street light behind them.

Her father was in a suit that was too big for him. It was dark grey and good and somebody else’s; it hung off his shoulders. He had a bottle of wine in one hand, held by the neck, like a man who didn’t know what you were supposed to bring.

Her mother was in a navy coat. Plain, good, three seasons old, buttoned to the neck. Flat shoes. No jewellery at all. Not a ring. Not a watch. Not the diamonds from the morning room. Her hair was swept up, the way it always was, but there was grey in it now, at the temples, that she hadn’t dyed. She was holding something against her chest with both arms.

A folder. Thick. Grey cardboard, with a cloth tape round it.

The music was still playing. But the garage had gone quiet, table by table, from the shutter inward, the way the ballroom on Battery Hill must have gone quiet once, when a waiter dropped a tray. Aurelia had put down her glass. Big Wu had stood up. Liang Shufen, at the end of the first table, had stopped talking to Big Wu’s mother in the middle of a sentence and turned round in her chair to look.

Serafina stood up.

She hadn’t decided to. Her body did it, the way it had in the yellow room. But this time she didn’t walk out. She stood at the table in front of the fish and looked at her mother across thirty people and three round tables and a garage full of lights.

“I wasn’t invited,” said Vittoria Song.

She said it in Italian. Quite steadily.

“No, Mamma,” said Serafina.

“I came anyway,” said her mother. She looked round the garage, once. The girders and the lights. The round tables with their red cloths. The railway bridge over everything. Big Wu’s mother. Granny Shum in her folding chair. The tarpaulin in the far corner over something long and low. The whiteboard. “I’m told that’s what people do,” said Vittoria, “in this family.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody moved for a moment.

Then Haozhen did. He stood up from his chair beside Serafina at the first table, the chair facing the door, the one with its back to the wall. He picked it up. He carried it across the garage, through the tables, past Granny Shum and Auntie Chu and Raiden, to where her parents stood under the shutter, and set it down in front of her mother, and stepped back.

Vittoria looked at the chair. Then at him.

“Madam,” said Qin Haozhen.

“You lied to me,” said Vittoria, in English. “In the yellow room. In August. You sat on my sofa and told me you were a security guard.”

“No, madam. I told you the truth.” He was very calm. “Every word. You asked me nine questions and I answered them. You didn’t ask the right ones.”

“What should I have asked?”

He thought about it, the way he thought about everything.

“Whether I’d stay,” said Qin Haozhen.

Vittoria Song looked at him, under the edge of the shutter, in her three-season-old coat, with the folder against her chest. Something moved at the corner of her mouth. Not a smile. Serafina had not seen her mother smile in years. But something.

She sat down in his chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

She gave Serafina the folder at the table. Not standing up. Sitting in the chair he’d brought her, which Serafina had carried back herself to the first table and put beside her own, between her and the fish. She laid the folder on the red tablecloth and untied the cloth tape and opened it, and turned it round, and pushed it across.

Cuttings.

Newspapers. Magazines. Printouts from websites, very carefully trimmed with scissors along the edges. Results pages, with a name underlined in pencil. Photographs, not from a long lens at night; from the sports pages, from the series programmes, from the papers. Serafina on a podium in December 2019 with champagne in her hand and her sister in the front row behind her. The page from Italian Vogue. SORELLE. A paragraph from a provincial paper in 2020 about a second place at the circuit in the north. Bahrain, 2021. Japan, 2021. The Baizhang Pass, June 2023, and the photograph of a woman on a mountain holding her left hand up to a camera with something red on it. A tiny result from the back of a sports supplement, four lines long, about a sixth place in the rain in 2022, that nobody but Mouse would ever have found.

Every race. Since the night Serafina walked out at nineteen. Every single one, in order, with the dates written in the corners in her mother’s handwriting.

Serafina turned the pages.

“You said you had someone watching me,” she said, at last. Her voice wasn’t working properly. “For two years. You said you had all the dates. You sent a photograph to Lia. You were going to send me to prison—”

“I had a man watching you,” said Vittoria. “For two years. Until your sister’s husband had a word with him.” She was looking at the folder, not at her daughter. “And then I didn’t. And I kept doing this. By myself. With scissors. At the bureau in the morning room.” She turned a page with one finger. “I didn’t know what else to do with it. You’d gone. I couldn’t stop knowing where you were.”

She stopped on the page with the sixth place in the rain.

“Second places too,” she said. “All of them. And sixth. Even the sixth.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“I said a thing,” said her mother, a little later, very low, in Italian, so that only Serafina could hear. The music was on again. People were talking again, carefully. “In the yellow room. In August. About August.”

Serafina didn’t say anything.

“It wasn’t true,” said Vittoria. “You weren’t a mistake. You were never a mistake.” She looked at her hands on the table, with nothing on them. “You were the one I could never make do anything. Your sister I could make do everything. I made her first. I made her perfect. I made her cry in a bathroom in Vienna at ten years old.” Her voice didn’t change. “You, I couldn’t make do one thing. Not one. From the day you were born. I’d put you in a dress and you’d be under a car in it by lunch.” She drew a breath. “I hated it. I hated it for nineteen years. And then you left, and I sat at the bureau in the morning room with the scissors, and I realised I’d been proud of it the whole time.”

Serafina couldn’t look at her.

“I’m not going to say sorry,” said her mother. “I don’t know how. I’ve never done it. Your sister’s been teaching me, a little, since September before last. I’m a slow student.” She closed the folder. “But I came. I wasn’t invited. And I came.”

“You did,” said Serafina.

“Is that enough?”

Serafina looked at her mother. In the navy coat, with grey at her temples, in a borrowed chair in a garage under a railway bridge, with a red tablecloth from Vancouver in front of her and a half-eaten fish.

“No,” she said. “But it’s a start.”

Vittoria Song nodded, once, the way her daughter’s fiancé nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father made a toast.

Nobody asked him to. He stood up at the end of the meal, after the red bean soup, in his borrowed suit, with a glass of the wine he’d brought, and the garage went quiet again, and he stood there for a while with the glass in his hand and didn’t say anything, and Serafina thought he wasn’t going to be able to.

Then he said, in English, so everyone would understand:

“My daughter went up a mountain.”

He looked at her.

“In 2023. In June. The Baizhang Pass. A hundred and fifty-six corners. I watched it on a computer in an office that belongs to a bank now. The girl from accounts showed me how.” His voice was shaking. “At the hundred and twelfth corner, she went round the outside. Where it’s steepest. Where nobody goes. A hand’s width from the edge.” He lifted the glass a little. “Her grandmother used to say that’s where the brave ones go. Round the top. Never at the bottom.” He looked at the man beside his daughter. “She’s going round the top again. I can see it. I’d like to say—I’d like to say I’m glad it’s with somebody who doesn’t check the mirror.”

“Every eleven seconds,” said Mr. Kwok, from the stove. “It’s on the whiteboard.”

People laughed. Song Weiren laughed too, wetly, and put his hand over his eyes, and then lifted the glass.

“To the top,” he said.

“To the top,” said thirty people, and a train went over the railway bridge and shook every light Mouse had strung along the girders, so that for a moment the whole ceiling of the garage glittered and swung like the harbour in a wind, and nobody, this time, at the soup or the fish or anywhere, stood up and walked out.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight, when everyone had gone except the team, her mother stood in the far corner of the garage in her coat and looked at the tarpaulin.

It was long and low and the shape underneath it was strange, flat, with a tail like a shark.

“What is that?” said Vittoria.

“A car,” said Serafina. “It was in a fire. In 2009. I bought it for scrap two years ago. I’m going to make it go two hundred miles an hour.”

“Three hundred and twenty-two kilometres,” said Haozhen, from the kettle.

Her mother looked at the tarpaulin for a while longer. Then she lifted one corner of it, with two fingers, and looked under it at the burnt black carbon and the melted nose, and let it fall.

“It looks,” said Vittoria Conti Song, “like something that should have been left in the fire.”

“So did I,” said Serafina, “at nineteen,” and her mother turned round and looked at her, and for the first time in years, very slightly, at the corner of her mouth, where it had always been waiting, smiled.

chapters.title: Last Race in the Industrial District
chapters.desc: A works team from Modena wants her for the rest of the season and all of next. Page nine of the contract says she gives up the road. So she goes back to Granny Shum’s for one last Saturday, against a kid in a purple Nissan who was filming from a car roof the night she met the taxi, and a woman from Modena is standing in the crowd.
chapters.epigraph: “Rich girl. You’ll crash by Christmas.” “It’s been nine Christmases, Granny.” “Then you were lucky nine times. Stop now.”
chapters.content:
The woman from Modena came to the garage on a Tuesday in June, in a grey linen suit and white trainers, chewing nicotine gum so hard her jaw clicked.

She was fifty-four. Her name was Donatella Ferri, and she had been a racing driver herself in the eighties, in Italy, in cars with no power steering and very little sense, and then an engineer, and then a team manager, and for the last eleven years she had run Orsini Corse, the works team of a small, old, very fast car maker in Modena that built forty cars a year by hand and raced them all over the world to sell the other thirty-nine. She stood under the shutter and looked round the garage with her hands on her hips. At Gilded. At the transporter. At the whiteboard, with the postcard of Monza and the photograph of Harbour Road and a sheet of paper in red marker that said EXCESSIVE MIRROR CHECKS in a frame. At the tarpaulin in the corner. At Big Wu, under the transporter. At Mouse.

“Allora,” she said, to Serafina. “You are the girl who went round the outside at the hundred and twelfth.”

“Yes.”

“Lau Kam-wing told me. He is a friend. Thirty years. He rang me in Modena in June two years ago and said, Donatella, a girl in a circuit car just broke my record, you should come and look. I said, Kam-wing, nobody breaks your record in a circuit car. He said, I know. Come and look.” She chewed. “I have been looking for two years. I watched your championship. I watched you in the rain in the south. I watched you go up the inside at the Needle in April last year when it was not possible.” She took a folded document out of her linen jacket. “I want you for the rest of this season. And all of next. In our car. On our team. With our engineers and our money and our name on your back.”

Serafina didn’t move.

“A works drive,” she said.

“A works drive,” said Donatella Ferri. “Your sister has already read the contract. She rang me at six this morning about clause fourteen.” She held it out. “She is very frightening, your sister.”

“She gets it from our mother,” said Serafina, and took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a good contract. Aurelia had made it a good contract. It was more money than Team AURELIA had ever seen in a year, and the car was a car Serafina had dreamed about since she was fourteen, and there was a clause, clause six, that Aurelia had written into it herself at six in the morning, that said Big Wu and Mouse came with her, on the team, on salary, as her own crew, or there was no deal.

And there was page nine.

She read it at three in the morning, at the bench, with Haozhen on the stool beside her and Brake asleep on her feet. Page nine was the conduct clause. Every works team had one. The driver will not bring the team or the manufacturer into disrepute. The driver will not take part in any motor sport not sanctioned by the governing body. The driver will not, under any circumstances, take part in any form of racing on public roads.

She read it four times.

“You knew,” she said.

“I read it,” said Qin Haozhen. “At your sister’s. On Sunday. She showed me first. She said you’d want to know I’d seen it.”

“And?”

He was quiet.

“It’s three years, Sera,” he said. “Still. The file’s gone. The traffic division’s photographs are gone. But the law’s the same as it was in 2019. One bad night at the gas works, one boy in a Subaru who doesn’t know how to lose, one police car coming round the paint works the wrong way, and it’s three years and your licence and everything on this page.” He touched the contract. “I’m not going to ask you to stop. I’ll never ask you to stop anything. But I’d like you to know I read page nine.”

She looked at page nine for a long time.

“I haven’t been since December,” she said. “Since the file. Eighteen months.”

“I know.”

“I miss it.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ll drive you.”

She turned her head.

“One more,” he said. “If you want. Before you sign. Saturday. Granny Shum’s. Say goodbye to it properly.” He paused. “I’ll sit in the passenger seat. I’ll stay awake for this one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum knew. Of course she knew. The industrial district knew everything a week before it happened.

She was in her folding chair at the junction by the paint works at a quarter to three, with her thermos and her blanket and her scanner on its string, and when Nonna came down the road from the gas works with its lights on, she stood up out of the chair, which she never did, and there were sixty people standing about in the floodlight, not forty, more than Serafina had ever seen there, and every one of them turned round.

Serafina pulled up at the line. She got out.

Granny Shum looked at her.

“Rich girl,” she said. “You’ll crash by Christmas.”

“It’s been nine Christmases, Granny.”

“Then you were lucky nine times.” Granny Shum sat back down in her chair. “Stop now.”

“I’m stopping,” said Serafina. “After tonight.”

“I know.” Granny Shum looked past her, at the passenger seat. “And your taxi friend. He’s awake?”

“He’s awake.”

“First time,” said Granny Shum, “in two and a half years,” and poured herself some tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

The opponent was a boy called Tsang Ho-yin.

He was nineteen. Everyone at Granny Shum’s called him Ghost Pepper, because he’d once eaten one for a bet on camera and not cried, which was against the rules, and Granny Shum had made an exception because he’d technically not cried. He drove a purple Nissan with a wing the size of a dining table. He had been driving it at Granny Shum’s for a year and he had won thirty-one races in a row, and every one of them he had filmed from a camera on the dashboard and put on the internet.

He came down the line to Nonna and stood in front of her with his hood up and his hands in his pockets.

“I was here,” he said. “The night with the taxi. November 2022. I was on the roof of this car.” He jerked his head at the purple Nissan. “It was my cousin’s car then. I was filming. I’ve got it. The taxi braking at the second lamp post.” He grinned. “It’s got eleven million views. Everyone thinks it’s fake.”

Serafina looked at him.

He was the boy on the roof. She remembered. Sixteen, in a hoodie, panning his phone along the line, getting a cap and a shoulder and nothing else.

“It’s not fake,” said Haozhen, from Nonna’s passenger window.

Ghost Pepper bent and looked in through the window at him. At the red scarf, which it was much too warm for in June, and which Haozhen was wearing anyway, because, he said, it was the last race, and it was a ceremony, and you wore a colour to a ceremony.

“You’re the taxi,” said Ghost Pepper.

“I was,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’m retired.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum dropped the scarf herself.

She hadn’t done it in eleven years. Her granddaughter did it. Her granddaughter, gold nails and all, stood beside the line holding the white scarf and looked at her grandmother, and Granny Shum got up out of her folding chair, very slowly, with the blanket falling off her knees, and held out her hand, and her granddaughter gave it to her.

She walked out between the two cars. Purple Nissan on the left. Red Lancia on the right. She stood between them in the floodlight from the paint works, eighty years old, with her scanner on its string round her neck, and raised her hand with the white scarf in it.

“One run,” she said. “No contact. If the scanner goes, you go home.” She looked into Nonna’s window. “No crying.”

“No crying,” said Serafina.

The scarf came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove it the way she’d driven it at nineteen. And at twenty-one in the Fiat she’d built from two dead ones. And in November 2022, with a grey estate car in her mirror sitting on her bumper through the S-bends like it was painted on.

Off the line. Nonna sat down on her rear wheels and went, the turbo coming in at the top of second with its long rising whistle, and the back of Serafina’s neck went hot. The straight past the container yard. Ghost Pepper beside her for three hundred metres, the purple car’s engine screaming, his wing filling her mirror. Then not beside her. Then behind.

Left at the fish-ball factory.

The S-bends. Left, right, left. The warehouse walls a hand’s width from her mirrors, the corrugated iron flashing past in her lights, and Ghost Pepper behind her, good, very good, as good as she had been at nineteen, staying with her, a length back. She laughed. She couldn’t help it. She laughed all the way through the S-bends, and beside her in the passenger seat he was awake, his hand braced on the dashboard, not looking in the mirror once, looking at her.

“You’re laughing,” he said.

“I know.”

“You always laugh in the S-bends.”

“I know,” said Serafina, and came out onto the gas-works straight with her foot flat and the two black gasholders coming up against the orange sky.

The lamp posts. First. Second.

“Second,” he said, quietly.

She didn’t brake at the second.

Third.

“Fourth,” said Qin Haozhen. “For the noise.”

She went to the fourth lamp post. For the noise. For Nonna. For nine Christmases. She braked, and turned in, and Nonna went round the gas works with the back hanging out and the tyres making the sound they made, the long howl that went up into the night over the gasholders and the factory roofs and the railway, the most beautiful noise she knew, and it cost her a tenth, and she didn’t care. She came up the service road to the line with the purple Nissan two lengths behind and sixty people screaming.

Nine tenths. That was what the granddaughter’s stopwatch said. Nine tenths of a second.

She sat in the car with her hands on the wheel and the engine ticking and didn’t get out.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything. He just reached across and took her hand off the wheel, the left one, with the ruby on it, and held it, and sat with her in the dark car while sixty people banged on the roof.

After a while she said, “That’s it.”

“That’s it.”

“I’m never going to hear that again. The fourth lamp post.”

“You will,” said Qin Haozhen. “In your head. Every time you brake for the Needle.” He held her hand. “And I’ll make it for you. With my mouth. If you ask.”

She laughed, and it came out wet.

“No crying,” she said.

“Granny Shum said no crying at the line,” he said. “We’re past the line.”

So she cried. In Nonna, at Granny Shum’s, at three in the morning, with her face in his red scarf, while Ghost Pepper stood by the window with his hood down and his camera off and his face very young, and Granny Shum sat in her folding chair and drank her tea and did not, for once, make anybody go and stand by the lamp post.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she got out at last, there was a woman in a grey linen suit leaning on the next car.

Donatella Ferri. In white trainers. Chewing nicotine gum. She had been standing at the back of the crowd since half past two, it turned out, between two men eating fish balls, and she had watched the whole thing.

“Allora,” she said. “The fourth lamp post.”

“It costs a tenth,” said Serafina.

“I know what it costs.” Donatella took the gum out of her mouth, looked at it, put it back. “I did this. In 1983. On the road out of Maranello, at night, in a car that was not mine, with a boy who is now a very important man in Bologna and would not like me to say his name.” She looked at Nonna. “I braked at the fourth lamp post also. For the noise. My father found out and did not speak to me for a year.” She took the folded contract out of her jacket. “You want to sign it here? On the bonnet? I think you should sign it here.”

Serafina looked at it.

She didn’t have a pen. She never had a pen. She patted her jacket. Nothing.

Beside her, Haozhen reached into his inside pocket. The left one. And took out a pen.

Silver. Heavy. Beautifully made. With a single numeral engraved on the barrel, just below the clip, very small and very neat.

7.

She stared at it.

“You kept it,” she said.

“It’s a good pen,” said Qin Haozhen. “She had very good taste in pens.” He held it out. “And it should sign something it wasn’t meant for. One more time.”

She took it. She smoothed the contract flat on Nonna’s warm bonnet in the floodlight from the paint works, at the line, at Granny Shum’s, at three in the morning, with sixty people watching and Ghost Pepper filming at last, on his phone, from the roof of his purple car, and she signed it. Serafina Song. Her big, untidy, fast signature, right across the box and out the other side of it, onto the bonnet.

Donatella picked it up and looked at the S going off the edge.

“Brava,” she said. “Now you are mine. No more roads.”

“No more roads.”

“Except,” said Donatella Ferri, “in your head, at the Needle,” and put the contract back in her jacket, and walked away down the line between the cars, chewing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum gave her a clementine.

Then she did something nobody at the Saturday meet had ever seen her do. She stood up out of her folding chair and went to the lamp post beside it and untied, with her old hands, very slowly, the piece of hardboard that had been tied to it since 1979. NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING, in her husband’s paint, gone grey and cracked with forty-six years of rain.

She held it out.

“For your garage,” she said. “Under the bridge. Where the trains are.” She looked at Haozhen. “You’ve broken the first one, I think. Somewhere. Not here.”

“Not here,” said Qin Haozhen. “Never here. I’m sorry.”

“I know never here. I’d have seen.” Granny Shum looked at him. “Men who’ve carried one stand differently. My husband stood like that, for years, after he came home from his service.” She looked at Serafina. “And you’ve broken the last one just now. So it’s yours.”

Serafina held the sign in both hands. She couldn’t speak.

“The middle two,” said Granny Shum, sitting back down, “you’d better keep.” She poured her tea, and drank. “Go home, rich girl. Go and drive for the Italians. Win something. Send me a photograph.”

They hung the sign in the garage under the railway bridge the next morning, over the kettle, above the plain mug that said HIS, where the trains would shake it every eleven minutes for the rest of its life, and Big Wu stood in front of it with the doughnuts, reading it, and then went and put the doughnuts down on the bench without a word and took his emergency whisky bottle down off the shelf, the new one he’d bought after the old one went on a knife cut, and looked at it, and put it back.

chapters.title: Overqualified
chapters.desc: Orsini Corse needs a head of security for its Asian operation. His CV is one line long and says “References: none available.” Donatella Ferri asks why she should hire him. He tells her eleven things wrong with her paddock that he noticed on the walk from the car park. Then the twelfth.
chapters.epigraph: “Your CV is blank, Mr. Qin.” “Yes.” “Why should I hire you?” “Because I noticed eleven things on the way in.”
chapters.content:
The paddock at the circuit in the north was full of Italians on a Tuesday in July, which it had never been before, and every one of them was shouting.

Orsini Corse had arrived on the Monday with two transporters, a motorhome the size of a small house, forty-one people, two cars in dark green with a thin gold stripe, and an espresso machine that needed its own generator. They had set up in the three garages at the end of the pit lane nearest the Needle. They had put up a hospitality tent. They had put a flag on a pole on top of the motorhome, the old Orsini badge, a gold horse’s head on green, and it snapped in the hot wind off the rice fields above the paddock like something that had been there for a hundred years.

Serafina had been in the car since eight. Her first test. Her seat, her pedals, her belts, her steering wheel with forty-one buttons on it, every one of which a man called Kenji Arakawa had explained to her twice in very precise English. She had done sixty laps. She had done the Needle sixty times in a works car. She had got out at noon, soaked through, and stood in the pit lane with her helmet under her arm and her hair in spikes and not been able to say anything at all.

At two o’clock, Qin Haozhen had an interview.

✦ ✦ ✦

Donatella Ferri’s office was the end of the motorhome, behind a sliding door, with a desk, two chairs, a window onto the paddock, a framed photograph of a small dark girl in a helmet in 1983 standing on a podium with her arms up, and a bowl of nicotine gum.

She was sitting behind the desk in a green team shirt with a single sheet of paper in front of her.

“Sit,” she said.

He sat. Facing the door, by the reflection in the window. She noticed. He saw her notice.

She picked up the sheet of paper.

“Your CV,” she said, “is one line.”

“Yes.”

“Security, various, 2012 to 2024.” She looked at him over the top of it. “References: none available.” She put it down. “Mr. Qin. In thirty years in motor sport I have had CVs from men who say they were in the special forces of four countries. From one man who said he guarded the Pope. From a woman who had been head of security for a band I will not name, who were very famous and very badly behaved. They all had references. Pages of them.” She tapped the single line. “Your CV is blank.”

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

“Why should I hire you?”

He didn’t answer straight away. He took off his watch. He laid it face down on her desk beside the bowl of nicotine gum.

“Because I noticed eleven things on the way in,” he said. “From the car park. To this chair.”

Donatella Ferri sat back.

“Go on,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went on.

He did it the way he’d once laid parts out on a workbench, except that he didn’t need the parts. He told her, in order, in the voice from the east service door, and she sat back in her chair with her arms folded and her jaw going on the gum and listened.

“One. The rear flap of the hospitality tent, on the side by the fuel store, is unzipped. It’s been unzipped since nine this morning. Anybody can walk from the fuel store into the tent without passing the girl on the front with the clipboard. I watched two people do it.” He didn’t look at the window. “Neither of them had a pass.

“Two. The data laptop on the pit wall. Your engineer, Mr. Arakawa, leaves it open on the wall between runs with the telemetry on the screen. The screen faces the television gantry. There’s a camera on the gantry with a very long lens. It belongs to a production company that also films for two of your rivals.

“Three. The motorhome key. It’s on a hook beside the door. Inside the door. Which is open. All day.

“Four. On the whiteboard in the second transporter, under Hotel, there’s a list of every driver’s room number.

“Five. The tyre store at the back of garage three is unattended between sessions. For about forty minutes each time. I timed it.

“Six. Your team’s social media went out at eleven this morning with a photograph of Mr. Hart having breakfast. On the terrace of the hotel. With the location switched on. Mr. Hart also went out at eleven-oh-four with the same photograph. With his room number visible in the background on the breakfast card.

“Seven. Your passes are checked by colour. Green for the team. Nobody looks at the photograph. I walked past three of your people with a green pass that says Kenji Arakawa on it. Mr. Arakawa lent it to me in the car park. Nobody stopped me.

“Eight. The espresso machine runs off its own generator. The generator’s fuel line runs under the awning where your guests stand. It’s held up off the ground with a cable tie. The cable tie has gone brittle in the heat.

“Nine. Your VIP guests walk through the garages unescorted. Two of them this morning walked behind the car while it was on the jacks. One of them was eating a sandwich.

“Ten. The kitchen staff in the hospitality tent are agency. Nobody on your team has a list of their names.

“Eleven.” He paused. “Miss Song’s helmet bag is in garage two, on the shelf by the door. Her name’s on it. In gold. Her sister had it made. Anyone walking down the pit lane can see it.”

He stopped.

The motorhome was quiet. Outside, someone was shouting in Italian about tyre pressures. The flag on the roof snapped in the wind.

Donatella Ferri didn’t say anything for a long time.

“Allora,” she said at last. Very slowly. “Eleven.”

“Twelve,” said Qin Haozhen.

“You said eleven.”

“I didn’t say the twelfth.”

She took the gum out of her mouth, looked at it, and put it in the bin.

“Which?” she said.

He nodded at her.

“Your gum is in the same pocket as the key to this office,” he said. “Your left trouser pocket. You’ve taken the gum out nine times since I sat down. Each time the key comes halfway out with it. At about the fortieth time today, it’ll fall on the floor of the paddock, and somebody who isn’t you will pick it up.”

Donatella Ferri put her hand flat on her left trouser pocket.

She looked at him. At his face, which gave her nothing. At the watch face down on her desk. At the single line on the sheet of paper.

Then she laughed. A short loud bark, like Aurelia’s, like a door banging, and put her head back and laughed at the ceiling of her motorhome.

“Madonna,” she said. “Lau Kam-wing said the girl was trouble. He didn’t say anything about the boyfriend.”

“Fiancé,” said Qin Haozhen.

“Fiancé.” Donatella wiped her eyes. “You are very, very overqualified for this job, Mr. Qin.”

“Yes.”

“You know what it pays?”

“Yes.”

“It pays less than the man who drives the second transporter.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’d like it very much.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He started on the Thursday.

They gave him a green team shirt with the gold horse’s head on the chest and his name embroidered under it, small, in white: H. QIN. They gave him a radio. They gave him a desk in the front of the second transporter, under the whiteboard, from which he removed, on his first morning, every driver’s room number, and wrote instead Ask Qin.

And they gave him a pass.

He had to have his photograph taken for it. In the series office, against a white wall, by a bored woman with a camera on a tripod. Serafina went with him. She stood in the doorway of the series office in her race suit and watched him sit down on the stool in front of the white wall, and watched him look at the camera.

For eleven years there had been no photograph of him anywhere in the world that he hadn’t made disappear.

He sat on the stool and looked straight at the lens. He didn’t turn his face. He didn’t put his head down. He didn’t let it slide off. He looked at it the way he looked at her across the garage, all the way in.

“Smile?” said the bored woman.

He didn’t smile. He did something better. She saw it happen in the doorway. The corner of his mouth, the smile’s distant relation from the countryside, which had come to the city two and a half years ago and found a flat and stayed. It was there, very faint, very definite, and the camera clicked, and the woman looked at the screen and said, “That’s nice,” in a surprised voice, as if she didn’t usually say that.

The pass came out of a machine a minute later, warm, on a green lanyard.

ORSINI CORSE. QIN HAOZHEN. HEAD OF SECURITY — ASIA. And his face. In colour. Looking at the camera.

He stood in the series office and looked at it.

Then he gave it to her.

“Hold this,” he said, “for a minute,” and she held it, and he went outside, and she found him round the back of the series office standing by the fence above the rice fields with his hands in his pockets and his face turned away, and she didn’t say anything, and gave him back his pass when he was ready.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu and Mouse started on the same Thursday.

Clause six. Aurelia had written it at six in the morning. Big Wu got a green shirt that didn’t fit and a tool trolley the size of a car and his own bay in garage two, beside her car, and stood in it on the first morning looking at the Orsini mechanics, all eleven of them, all Italian, who looked back at him, and nobody said anything until one of them, a small bald man called Beppe, held out a wheel gun. Big Wu took it. He changed the front left wheel on her car in four point one seconds. Beppe said something in Italian that Serafina did not translate for anybody, and they were friends by lunch.

Mouse got a seat at the end of the pit wall beside Kenji Arakawa, with three screens. She didn’t speak to Kenji. She didn’t speak to anybody. She sat down and put her headphones on and began doing things to the data that Kenji watched over her shoulder for an hour with his mouth slightly open, and at the end of the hour he went and found Donatella and said something to her in Italian that made Donatella come and stand behind Mouse too.

Mr. Kwok didn’t come. He was seventy-four. He said a man of seventy-four had driven his last transporter, and that somebody had to keep the garage under the railway bridge warm, and the kettle on, and Brake fed, and the hardboard sign over the kettle dusted. He said he’d make their lunch on the days they weren’t at the circuit and take it to them on the bus on the days they were.

“You don’t have to,” said Serafina.

“I know I don’t have to,” said Mr. Kwok. “That’s why I’m doing it.”

And Gilded went home. Matte black, number seven, the gold name, the small grey taxi on the door under three coats of lacquer, and a neat round cut in the rear diagonal tube of the roll cage, behind the driver’s seat, that Serafina had welded shut again and never painted. Big Wu drove it back to the garage under the railway bridge on the transporter for the last time and parked it beside the tarpaulin in the corner, and stood beside it, and patted its roof.

On the green Orsini car, on the bonnet, in the same gold serif letters that were painted over the door of 18 Harbour Road, Aurelia had made very sure there was one word.

AURELIA.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday, Callum Hart came and sat on the edge of his desk in the second transporter.

Callum was the other driver. Twenty-six. British. Fair, tall, with a smile that had sold a great many sunglasses, and four hundred thousand followers who wanted to know what he had for breakfast, and he was very fast, and he knew it, and he was perfectly pleasant to everybody, and he had been perfectly pleasant to Serafina, in particular, for nine days.

“So you’re the security,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You took my room number off the whiteboard.”

“Yes.”

“And Donatella says I’m not allowed to post my breakfast any more.”

“Not with the location on,” said Qin Haozhen. “Or the card.”

Callum laughed. He had a good laugh. He swung his foot. “She’s brilliant, isn’t she? Serafina. In the car. I’ve never seen anyone take the Needle like that. Deep. On the marker.” He grinned. “I asked her to dinner on Wednesday. Team dinner. She said she’d think about it.”

Haozhen looked at him.

Not for long. Two seconds. Perhaps three. The look that went all the way in.

Callum stopped swinging his foot.

“Team dinner,” said Qin Haozhen, pleasantly. “That’ll be nice. I’ll check the restaurant.”

He went back to his laptop. Callum sat on the edge of the desk for a moment longer, then got up, and said, “Right. Cheers. Great,” and went out, and Haozhen heard him say to somebody outside, very quietly, in his good British voice, “Christ. Has the security guy ever smiled?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him at his desk at eleven that night, when the paddock was empty and the Italians had gone to the hotel.

She was in her race suit, still, unzipped to the waist, the sleeves tied round her middle, in a black vest. She came up the steps into the front of the transporter and leaned in the doorway with her arms folded and looked at him, at his green shirt with H. QIN on the chest, at his pass on its lanyard lying on the desk face up, at the whiteboard behind him that said Ask Qin.

“Callum Hart,” she said, “has been telling everyone in the paddock that you looked at him.”

“I looked at him.”

“He says you looked at him like a man measuring a coffin.”

“That’s an exaggeration,” said Qin Haozhen. “I was measuring a restaurant.”

She came in. She shut the transporter door behind her. She came round the desk and sat down on it, on his paperwork, right in front of him, with her boots on either side of his chair, and took his pass off the desk and held it up and looked at the photograph.

“You’re smiling in this,” she said.

“Slightly.”

“You’re smiling at me. I was in the doorway.”

“Yes.”

She put it down. She took his face in both hands.

“Are you jealous,” she said, delighted, “of a man who posts his breakfast?”

He looked up at her. He didn’t say anything for a while. Then his hands came up, slowly, to her knees, and stayed there, and his thumbs moved once on the fireproof fabric.

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

She’d never heard him say it. She’d never seen him be it. She sat on his desk in the dark transporter in the empty paddock and looked at the most frightening man she had ever met, in a green shirt with his initial on it, admitting to being jealous of Callum Hart, and she laughed so hard she nearly fell off.

He pulled her off the desk into his lap before she could.

“I’m not going to the team dinner,” she said, into his mouth, when she could.

“Go.”

“I’m not going.”

“Go,” he said, against her throat, “and sit next to me,” and she stopped laughing for quite a long time.

chapters.title: Pit Wall
chapters.desc: Speed traces, brake pressure, throttle, steering angle: four coloured lines on a screen, a thousand times a second. He learns to read them the way he used to read rooms. He finds something in her data nobody else has seen. And at the end of the pit wall, after three years, Mouse finally says a word to him.
chapters.epigraph: “Every driver lies to their engineer. The data doesn’t.” — Kenji Arakawa
chapters.content:
The heat at the circuit in the south came up off the track in sheets. You could see it. It bent the grandstand on the far side of the main straight into a wobbling grey shape like something underwater, and the cars came out of it on the long run down to the first corner as if they were being born from it, one at a time, howling.

Thirty-six degrees in the shade. Fifty-four on the track surface. The tyres were going off in eight laps instead of twenty. The drivers came in from every stint soaked through, the colour of beetroot, with their eyes gone strange, and were made to sit in front of a fan with a cold towel on their neck and drink a litre of something salty before anyone let them speak.

Haozhen was on the pit wall.

Not at the back, the way he had stood behind Big Wu and Mouse for two years with a headset on that let him hear the team channel and nothing else. On the wall. On a stool at the end of the long desk under the awning, with a screen of his own. Kenji Arakawa had put it there on the first Saturday in August without saying anything, and plugged it in, and shown him, very precisely, in English, what everything on it meant.

“Four lines,” Kenji had said. “Speed. Throttle. Brake. Steering. A thousand times a second. Every metre of every lap.” He’d put his finger on the screen. “Every driver lies to their engineer. Every one. They come in and they say the car’s understeering in turn four when what they mean is I was frightened in turn four. The data doesn’t lie. If you can read it, you know what they did. Not what they say they did.” He had looked at Haozhen. “Donatella says you are good at knowing what people did.”

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

“Then learn this,” said Kenji, and went away, and left him with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He learned it in two weeks.

Kenji said afterwards that it took most engineers two years. Kenji said it in the motorhome, to Donatella, with his arms folded, in the tone of a man reporting an accident he had witnessed and still did not quite believe. Haozhen didn’t think it was remarkable. It was only reading. He had spent eleven years reading people from chairs by doors: when they got up, when they sat down, when they went to the window, how long they stood there, what they did with their hands. The four lines were the same. Speed was where she wanted to go. Throttle was how much she believed it. Brake was what frightened her and how much she let it. Steering was what she did about it.

He sat on his stool at the end of the wall with the headset on and watched her go round the circuit in four coloured lines, a thousand times a second, and it was the most intimate thing he had ever done.

He knew when she was happy. The throttle trace came up out of the slow corners in one clean line, no hesitation, no flutter. He knew when she was angry. She braked later, and harder, and let off the brakes in a jagged step instead of a slope. He knew when she was thinking about something that wasn’t driving: there was a corner, the long double-apex left at the end of the back section, where her steering trace went a fraction wider on the second apex, every time, on the laps after she’d come past the pit wall and looked at him.

He didn’t tell her that one.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her the other one.

It was the Saturday, in qualifying, in the heat, on her fourth run. She came in eleventh and furious, and sat in front of the fan with the towel round her neck and her face the colour of beetroot and said, to Kenji, through her teeth, “The rear’s loose at the hairpin. In the braking. It’s moving about. I can’t commit.”

Kenji looked at his screen. He frowned.

“The rear looks fine,” he said. “The car looks fine. It’s the same as yesterday.”

“It’s not fine. I can feel it. It’s stepping out.”

Kenji looked at the screen again, and then at Mouse, at the other end of the wall, who was looking at her own three screens and shaking her head very slightly, which meant the rear was fine.

Haozhen, on his stool, had his finger on his own screen. On the brake trace. On the Needle. He’d been looking at it for twenty minutes.

“Kenji,” he said.

Kenji turned round.

“It’s not the car,” said Qin Haozhen. “Look at lap three of the second run. And lap two of the third. And lap four of this one.” He moved his finger. “The laps after the yellow flag in the first session. When the Ferrari went into the gravel at the hairpin. Every lap since. She’s braking six metres earlier for the hairpin. And then trail-braking deeper to make up for it. That’s what’s moving the rear about. It’s her.”

Kenji leaned over his shoulder and looked.

He looked for a long time.

“Six metres,” he said.

“Six point two. Average.” Haozhen didn’t look up from the screen. “She saw the Ferrari go off. At the hairpin. Into the gravel. On the marker where she brakes.” He was quiet for a second. “She’s never been frightened in a braking zone before.”

Serafina, in front of the fan with her towel, had stopped drinking.

She looked at him down the pit wall. He looked back at her.

“I’m not frightened,” she said.

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “Your foot is.”

She stared at him, with the cold towel round her neck and the sweat running down her face and the heat coming up off the pit lane in sheets. Then she put the bottle down and stood up and pulled her balaclava back on and her helmet over it, and said “Out,” to Kenji, and went.

On her fifth run, she braked for the hairpin on the marker. To the metre.

She qualified fourth.

✦ ✦ ✦

Kenji didn’t say anything to him for an hour after that.

Then he came and stood beside the stool, at the end of the wall, with two cans of cold green tea, and gave him one, and stood there drinking the other one and looking out at the track through the heat.

“Two weeks,” said Kenji.

“Yes.”
