“In Japan, my first engineer, he made me read traces for two years before he let me speak to a driver.” Kenji drank. “He said, Arakawa, the data is a person. You have to learn to listen to them before they know you are listening.” He looked at Haozhen sideways. “Where did you learn to listen like that?”

“Doors,” said Qin Haozhen.

Kenji thought about that for a while.

“Doors,” he said, and nodded, as if it made sense, and went back to his end of the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

The race was three hours, on the Sunday, in the worst of the heat.

She drove the first stint, the third and the last. Callum Hart drove the second and the fourth, in the same car, number seven, and was very fast, and very good, and sat in front of the fan between stints with his eyes shut and said, to nobody, “This is inhuman,” and nobody disagreed.

Haozhen sat on his stool and watched four lines.

At the start of her third stint, on lap fifty-eight, something happened in the data that he didn’t understand.

Not her. The car. In the bottom corner of his screen, where the sensor readings ran in small grey columns down the side, one of them went wrong. Rear-left brake temperature. It had been sitting at about six hundred, climbing in the braking zones, falling on the straights, the way it always did. It jumped to nine hundred and eighty. Then to zero. Then back to six hundred. Then nine hundred and eighty.

He looked at it. He looked at her brake trace, which was perfect. He looked at the rear-left brake temperature again.

He leaned across and touched Kenji’s arm.

“The rear-left temperature sensor,” he said. “It’s flickering. Look. Nine eighty. Zero. Six hundred. It isn’t the brake. Her trace is clean. The brake’s fine.” He pointed. “I think it’s the wire. The sensor wire. The way it’s jumping. It looks like something rubbing through. Like a cable chafing on something every time the suspension moves.”

Kenji looked. Kenji frowned.

At the other end of the pit wall, without anybody saying anything to her, Mouse had already pulled up the same reading on her own screen. She looked at it for about four seconds. Then she put her hand up, flat, without looking round, the way she put it up to tell Serafina to stop talking, and pressed a button on her own radio, and said something very quietly to Big Wu, in the garage, on the crew channel.

Big Wu came out of the garage with a torch and a roll of tape and a face like a storm.

On lap sixty-four, when Serafina came in for fuel and tyres, Big Wu was under the back of the car before it had stopped rolling. Forty seconds. Fuel and four tyres and a man on his back under the rear-left corner with a torch in his teeth. Then the car went, and Big Wu rolled out from under it on the concrete, and sat up, and held up a short length of black wire in his fist, frayed through to the copper at one point where it had been rubbing on the edge of the suspension wishbone for three hours.

“Wire,” he said, to the pit wall. “Chafing. On the wishbone. If it had gone it would have shorted the whole rear loom. She’d have lost the gearbox at the end of the back straight.” He looked at Haozhen. “At two hundred and forty. Into the hairpin.”

Nobody said anything.

Then, at the far end of the pit wall, Mouse took her headphones off.

She turned round on her stool. She looked down the length of the desk, past Kenji, past the four screens and the cans of green tea and the radio, to the man on the stool at the end, in the green shirt with H. QIN on the chest.

She had not said a word to him in three years. Not one. Not in the garage under the railway bridge, not on the night with the clementine, not at the bench through all of January with the companies and the consulting fees, not in the car at the end of the Docks road. She had said things about him, to Serafina. She had never once said anything to him.

“Good,” said Mouse.

To him. Straight at him. One word, very quiet, in the heat, on the pit wall.

Then she put her headphones back on and turned back to her screens.

Big Wu, standing by the garage door with the frayed wire in his fist, dropped his wheel gun. It hit the concrete with a crash that made three Italians jump.

Haozhen sat on his stool at the end of the wall and didn’t move for some time.

✦ ✦ ✦

She finished fifth.

Fifth, in a works car, in her second race for the team, in fifty-four degrees, on a track that was eating tyres in eight laps. The best result Orsini Corse had had in Asia in three years. Donatella Ferri came out of the motorhome and stood in the pit lane in her green shirt and white trainers and shouted something in Italian at the sky and hugged Kenji, who allowed it with an expression of great suffering.

Serafina came in at the end and sat in the car in the pit garage with her hands on the wheel and the engine ticking and didn’t get out for a minute. Then she got out, and pulled off her helmet and her balaclava, and her hair was plastered flat and she was the colour of beetroot and her eyes had gone strange with the heat, and she looked straight past Kenji and Donatella and Callum and the cold towels and the fan and the litre of salty water.

At him. On his stool, at the end of the wall.

He got off the stool.

She walked toward him through the garage in her race suit, unzipping it as she came, peeling it down off her shoulders to her waist, the sleeves flapping, in the soaked black fireproof top underneath, and she didn’t say anything at all. She took his hand. She walked him out of the back of the garage, through the paddock, past the hospitality tent with its rear flap now zipped, past the second transporter with Ask Qin on the whiteboard, to the motorhome.

To the drivers’ room at the back of it. A small room, very small, with a bunk and a basin and a fan and a window with the blind down.

She closed the door. She locked it. She leaned on it.

“You found the wire,” she said.

“Mouse found the wire.”

“You found it first. Big Wu told me on the radio. On the in-lap.” Her breath was going. “Two hundred and forty into the hairpin. With no gearbox.”

“It didn’t happen.”

“I know it didn’t happen,” said Serafina. “That’s the point,” and came off the door at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was fast. It was always going to be fast. She was still running at the speed of the circuit and the heat and fifty-four degrees, and he’d been sitting on a stool for three hours watching her go round in four coloured lines and not being able to touch her.

She kissed him against the basin. Then against the bunk. Her hands were in his hair and his green shirt was coming untucked and she was laughing, out of breath, into his mouth, and the zip of her race suit was caught at her hips and he was trying to undo it and it wouldn’t undo, because the zip on a race suit is built not to undo, and he swore in Mandarin and she laughed harder.

“Fireproof,” she said, gasping. “It’s fireproof. It’s built to stay on. In a crash.”

“I know what it’s built for,” said Qin Haozhen, and got it undone.

He was trained to keep control of everything. She had known that since the paddock in December 2022. She had always made him lose it. That was the game between them, the one that had no rules written down. But that afternoon in the motorhome he didn’t even try to keep it. She felt that. He let go of all of it before she’d done anything. Three hours of watching the brake temperature flicker between nine hundred and eighty and zero, and a frayed wire in Big Wu’s fist, and a gearbox at two hundred and forty into the hairpin, and it all came out of him at once. His hands were shaking on her skin. He pulled her down onto the narrow bunk with him and held her as if the motorhome were going over a cliff, and said her name into her soaked hair, over and over, as if checking she was still there.

The heat. The fan rattling in the corner and doing nothing. The radio clipped to his belt still squawking Italian, which neither of them turned off. The salt on her skin, and the smell of the race suit, fuel and rubber and burnt sugar, and outside, through the blind, the last cars going past on their slowing-down lap, their engines dropping one after another through the gears.

At some point somebody knocked on the door.

“Serafina,” said Donatella Ferri, through it. “The press. They want you. Fifth place. They want—”

“Five minutes,” said Serafina.

There was a pause.

“Allora,” said Donatella. “Ten.”

They heard her walk away down the motorhome, chewing, and the door at the end sliding shut.

Serafina put her face in his neck and laughed until she couldn’t breathe, and he lay under her on the narrow bunk in the heat with his green shirt open and his radio still squawking on his belt and laughed too, his whole chest going under her, the way she’d heard him laugh once, in February, on the floor of the garage, at a form.

“Ten minutes,” she said.

“We’ll need eleven,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve counted.”

chapters.title: The Needle
chapters.desc: The home round. Her parents in the grandstand for the first time. Lap thirty-one, the end of the back straight, a backmarker’s engine letting go a few seconds before she arrives. He sees it in the data before anyone sees it on the screens: brake pressure at maximum, and the speed not coming down.
chapters.epigraph: “The brake line is perfect. The speed isn’t falling. Kenji. The speed isn’t falling.”
chapters.content:
It was a beautiful morning. He would remember that afterwards, and hate it.

September, at the circuit in the north, with the rice in the fields round the valley gone gold and the sky over the grandstand a hard clean blue with nothing in it. Cool for the first time since May. Eleven thousand people in the stands. The home round. The Orsini flag snapping on the motorhome roof, the gold horse’s head on green, and the smell of the espresso machine on its own generator, with its fuel line now in a steel conduit that Haozhen had fitted himself on the Thursday.

Her parents came.

Her father had rung on the Wednesday to ask if it would be all right. He’d rung her, not Aurelia. He’d said, very carefully, on the phone, your mother would like to see it. Properly. Not from a VIP lounge behind glass. From the stands. And Serafina had stood at the bench in the garage under the railway bridge with the phone against her ear and said nothing for a long time, and then said, “Block C. Front row. Lia will get you tickets,” and put the phone down and gone and stood outside in the alley for twenty minutes.

They were in Block C. Front row. Her father in his borrowed suit, with a Team AURELIA cap from 2019 that he’d found in a box of things from the house on the Peak. Her mother in the navy coat, three seasons old, with a pair of binoculars round her neck on a strap that she had bought, Aurelia said, at a shop on Harbour Road on Friday, after asking the man for forty minutes which ones were best for motor racing. Beside them, Aurelia, in gold, and Chen Si, in camel, and Qian, with his antacids.

Serafina waved at them from the pit wall at nine o’clock. Her mother lifted the binoculars and looked at her through them, at sixty metres, and then lowered them and lifted one hand, very slightly, from the rail. Not a wave. Something.

Serafina came back to the garage with her face doing something she couldn’t stop.

“She lifted her hand,” she said.

“I saw,” said Haozhen.

“She bought binoculars.”

“I know. Your sister told me. Forty minutes.” He looked at her. “Go and put your helmet on, Sera. You’ll miss your own race.”

She kissed him. In the garage, in front of Kenji and Big Wu and eleven Italians and Callum Hart, quickly, hard, with her hand on the back of his neck. Then she went and put her helmet on.

That was the last time he saw her face that day before it was the colour of paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove the first stint. Thirty laps. Clean. Perfect. Fourth, then third, then holding third, a car behind her and a car in front of her and nothing between them but tarmac and the long patient business of three hours.

He sat on his stool at the end of the pit wall and watched four coloured lines.

They were happy lines. He knew her happy lines by now. The throttle came up out of every slow corner in one long clean stroke. She was braking on every marker to the metre. At the Needle, on every lap, her brake trace went up in a perfect cliff and came down in a perfect slope, and the speed fell with it, two hundred and forty to seventy-five in a hundred and ten metres, and the steering went round, and the throttle came back, and she was through. Thirty times. He’d watched every one.

On lap thirty, as she came past the pit wall, she looked at him. He saw it on the screen before he saw it through the fence: the steering trace going a fraction wide on the second apex at the end of the back section. The way it always did on the laps after she’d looked.

Lap thirty-one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Kenji saw the backmarker first.

It wasn’t in their race. Not really. There were two classes on the circuit at once, the fast cars and the slower ones, as there always were in that series, the slower ones mostly amateurs in older, smaller cars who paid to race and were lapped every eight minutes. One of them, a silver car with a Japanese name on its doors, driven by a dentist from the coast, came down the back straight on lap thirty-one with a long white plume of smoke suddenly pouring out from under its rear, and then a flash, and then more smoke.

“Engine,” said Kenji, on the team channel, very calm. “Silver car. Back straight. It’s let go. Serafina, smoke on the back straight, smoke, slow car, stay left—”

He heard her. Haozhen heard her, in his headset. One word.

“Copy.”

She was eleven seconds behind the silver car. He watched her go down the back straight on the screen at two hundred and forty, past the smoke, which was already thinning, staying left, the way she’d been told. The silver car had pulled over onto the grass on the right with flames under it. A marshal was running.

He looked at the Needle. On the big screen on the gantry across the pit lane. At the braking zone, the hundred and ten metres of grey tarmac before the hairpin, under the advertising bridge.

It looked grey. It looked dry. It looked like it always looked.

But there was a line on it. A dark line, faintly shining, very thin. From where the silver car had been when its engine let go, at two hundred and thirty, all the way down the last of the straight and into the braking zone for the Needle before it had swerved off onto the grass.

Oil.

The marshal’s post at the Needle was a hundred metres past the start of the braking zone. A man in an orange coat. He had the red-and-yellow striped flag, the one that meant slippery surface, oil, in his hand. He was unrolling it. He was lifting it.

Serafina was at the braking marker.

✦ ✦ ✦

She braked.

He saw it on his screen. The brake trace went up in its perfect cliff, exactly on the marker, to the metre, the way she’d braked for the Needle since 2019, the way she’d taught him in a thirty-year-old Lancia on a track day in December. The brake pressure went to maximum.

The speed didn’t fall.

Two hundred and forty. Two hundred and thirty-eight. Two hundred and thirty-six.

It should have been two hundred. It should have been a hundred and sixty by then. It should have been coming down like a stone.

“Kenji,” he said. His voice was perfectly level. He heard it from a long way off. “The brake line is perfect. The speed isn’t falling. Kenji. The speed isn’t falling.”

Kenji turned round.

On the screen the brake pressure dropped. All at once. She’d come off the brakes. To get the steering back, the way you did when the car wouldn’t turn. He saw the steering trace go, a flick, left, right. He saw the speed. Two hundred and twenty. Two hundred and ten. Coming down now. Too late. Not fast enough. The front tyres were back on the dry tarmac past the oil and biting and it was not enough, there were not enough metres left, there were not enough metres in the world—

Two hundred and one.

One ninety-five.

One ninety-one.

The line stopped.

All four lines. Speed, throttle, brake, steering. They went to zero together, all at once, like someone switching off a light, and stayed there, flat, across the right-hand side of his screen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t see the crash. He never saw the crash. People told him afterwards that it was on the big screen on the gantry, from three angles, and that eleven thousand people saw it, and that it was on the news that night and on the internet for a week. He never looked. He saw four flat lines on a screen at the end of a pit wall. That was all he ever saw.

And then he was moving.

Orsini Corse had the three garages at the end of the pit lane nearest the Needle. He had walked that end of the circuit sixty times since July. He knew there was a gap in the pit wall fence by the last garage, for the fire crew. He knew there was a service road behind the pit-lane exit that ran along the inside of the back straight to the marshals’ post at the Needle. He knew it was four hundred and twenty metres. He had paced it on the Thursday, because he paced everything.

He went through the gap in the fence. He went over the barrier at the end of the service road, the low steel one, with his hand on the top rail. He went across the grass inside the hairpin and down the bank and into the gravel trap.

He did not remember any of it.

He remembered the red flags coming out. All round the circuit, at every post, at once. He remembered that they came out while he was already in the gravel. He remembered a marshal in an orange coat shouting at him and not stopping. He remembered the gravel, deep, grey, dragging at his shoes. He remembered that the gravel had a long deep furrow ploughed through it, from the kerb on the outside of the Needle to the tyre wall, two parallel trenches as if something enormous had been dragged through it on its belly.

And at the end of the furrow, the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had gone into the tyre wall nose first, on the left.

The tyres were stacked six deep, bolted together, bound with conveyor belt, red and white. The car had gone into them so hard that it had pushed the whole wall back a metre and a half and buried its nose in them, and the wall had folded round it. The bonnet was gone. The gold letters were gone. The front of the car on the left side was gone, up to the windscreen. There was a fire at the back, small, under the rear wing, where the oil had got onto something hot, and a marshal was running toward it with an extinguisher.

He got to the driver’s side.

The window net was up. Behind it, in the cockpit, in her seat, held by her belts, she was slumped to the right, toward the centre of the car, with her helmet against the side wing of the seat, not moving.

He knew what you did. He had been taught, at nineteen, in a car park, by a woman with a red scarf, exactly what you did when someone was in a wrecked car and you did not know what was broken. You did not move them. You did not take off the helmet. You did not pull. You did not do any of the things your hands wanted to do.

He knelt in the gravel by the driver’s door, with the fire at the back of the car going out in a white cloud behind him, and put his hand through the window net, and found her hand on her knee, in its glove, and held it.

“Sera,” he said.

Nothing.

“Sera. It’s me. I’m here.” His voice was level. It was the work voice. He heard it from a long way off and hated it and could not make it anything else. “Don’t move. Don’t try to move. They’re coming. I can hear them. I’m not going anywhere. I’m holding your hand.”

Her hand didn’t move in his.

Through the visor, he could see her eyes. They were closed. Her face behind them was the colour of paper. She was breathing. He could hear it, inside the helmet. It was wrong. It was too fast and there was a noise in it, a wet catch on every breath in, and he held her hand through the window net and listened to it and counted, without meaning to, the way he had counted keepy-ups from a chair by a door in Lisbon. Thirty-one. Thirty-two. Thirty-three.

“Please,” said Qin Haozhen.

He had never in his life said that word to anything that wasn’t a person with a folder.

“Please. Sera. Please.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The medical car got there in forty-one seconds. He knew because he counted.

A doctor in a white fireproof suit and two paramedics. They came across the gravel with bags. The doctor knelt beside him and said, in English, very calm, “Sir, I need you to let go of her hand and step back,” and he said, “Yes,” and didn’t move, and the doctor looked at him, and then at his face, and said, much more gently, “Step back one metre, sir. Just one. Where she can hear you. I need the space,” and he let go of her hand, and stood up, and stepped back exactly one metre in the gravel, and stopped.

He didn’t go any further. Not for anything. A marshal took his arm and he looked at the marshal and the marshal let go.

He watched them.

He watched them do everything right. The collar, round her neck, before anything else, through the window. The oxygen. The doctor’s hand inside the helmet’s chin bar, feeling. The doctor saying things to the paramedics, very fast and very quiet, in a language that was English and medicine at once. Reduced GCS. Laboured breathing. Left side. Query chest. Query shoulder. The fire crew coming, the extraction team, six people in orange with a backboard and the special seat that went round a driver’s body and let them lift her out without bending her at all. They cut the roof pillars. They took the roof off. It took eleven minutes. He counted every one of them.

When they lifted her out, she made a sound.

Not a word. A sound, through the helmet, as they moved her. Pain. And then nothing again.

He made a sound too. He didn’t know he had.

They put her on the backboard. They strapped her down. They carried her across the gravel to the medical car, and from the medical car to the helicopter, which had come down on the grass inside the Needle with its rotors going and flattening everything, and they put her in it, and the doctor got in with her.

He walked to the edge of the grass. The rotor wash pushed at him. One of the paramedics stood in front of him with a hand up and said, “Sir, family only,” and he said, “Yes,” and stood there.

He was not family. He was a man in a green shirt with H. QIN on the chest and a pass round his neck with his own face on it, smiling. He had a pink slip in his wallet that said he existed. He had a ring in a box in a glovebox two and a half years ago. He had no paper that said she was his.

The helicopter went up. It went up over the Needle and the advertising bridge and the grandstand, and turned south, toward the city, toward the big hospital on the hill above the harbour, and got smaller, and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was still standing on the grass inside the Needle when the car came.

Not a medical car. A long black car with tinted windows, very clean, that had no business being on a racing circuit, coming along the service road from the paddock at a speed that sent marshals jumping out of its way, and stopping on the grass beside him, and the driver’s window coming down.

Zhao Zhendong looked at him for four seconds.

He reached back without a word and pushed the rear door open from the inside.

Haozhen looked at him.

“Hm,” said Zhao. It was, Haozhen would understand later, the closest Zhao Zhendong had ever come to saying please to anyone who was not his wife.

He got in. In the back seat there was Aurelia, in gold, with mascara all down her face and her hands knotted together in her lap, and beside her, Chen Si, very still, with his phone to his ear, saying, “The ninth floor. Yes. Dr. Ma. Tell him it’s my wife’s sister. Tell him I’ll be there in forty minutes and so will everyone she has,” and in the passenger seat beside Zhao, very straight, in a navy coat three seasons old, with a pair of new binoculars round her neck that she had not taken off, Vittoria Song.

Her father was in the car behind, with Qian.

Nobody spoke. Zhao drove. He drove the way Haozhen had once driven her Lancia round the circuit in the north on a track day in December, with nothing extra. Every corner exactly. Every brake exactly. A hundred and eighty on the motorway south, in a long black car, without anybody in it feeling a single bump.

Somewhere on the motorway, Haozhen realised that he was still holding his hand out in front of him, palm up, the left one, open, on his knee. The way he’d held it through the window net. As if something were in it.

Vittoria Song, in the front seat, turned round and looked at it. Then at his face.

She didn’t say anything. She reached back between the seats. She took his open hand in hers, the one with no rings on it, and held it.

She held it all the way to the city. She didn’t let go once.

chapters.title: Hospital, Night Two
chapters.desc: The ninth floor of the big hospital on the hill. A collarbone, three ribs, a bruised lung, a brain that has been shaken very hard. A machine breathing for her. “Family only,” says the nurse. Her mother says something nobody expected. Thirty hours later, at two in the morning, she opens her eyes and asks about the car.
chapters.epigraph: “He’s family. He’s more family than I am. Let him in.”  — Vittoria Song
chapters.content:
The doctor’s name was Ma, and he had a soft voice and very clean glasses and a way of putting his hands together in front of him when he spoke, as if he were holding something small that might get away.

He had looked after Chen Si, on this floor, in a room with no name on the door, in January 2020. He remembered the family. He looked at them now in the small grey room off the corridor with the box of tissues on the table and the chairs that nobody sat in, and he told them.

The left collarbone was broken in two places. It would need a plate, tonight; the surgeons were already scrubbing. Three ribs on the left side were cracked. Under them, the lung was bruised, badly, where the belts had held her and the car had not stopped. The bruise was filling with fluid. It was making it hard for her to breathe. They had put a tube down her throat in the emergency department and she was on a ventilator now, and they would keep her on it, asleep, at least until tomorrow night, to let the lung rest.

Her head had been shaken very hard against the inside of her helmet. The scan showed no bleeding. That was good. That was very good. But they didn’t know yet what the shaking had done. They wouldn’t know until she woke up.

Her neck was clear. Her back was clear. Her legs were clear.

“The car protected her,” said Dr. Ma. “Very well. Better than I would have believed, from the pictures. The seat, the belts, the helmet, the frame.” He put his hands together. “Whoever built that car built it to keep her alive.”

“Italians,” said Aurelia, in a voice that wasn’t hers.

“Then the Italians,” said Dr. Ma, gently, “did very good work.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The intensive care unit was through two sets of doors at the end of the corridor, and there was a desk inside the second set, and at the desk there was a nurse with a clipboard and a face that had said the same thing ten thousand times.

“Family only,” she said. “Two at a time.”

Her father went in first, with Aurelia. Twenty minutes. They came out and her father sat down on one of the plastic chairs in the corridor and put his face in his hands and didn’t move. Aurelia stood against the wall with her arms round herself, in gold, every piece she owned, and Chen Si stood beside her and didn’t touch her and was so close that his shoulder was against hers.

Her mother went in next. Alone. She didn’t ask anyone to go with her.

She was in there for eleven minutes. When she came out, her face was perfectly composed. Perfectly. Like the face at the bottom of the stairs. She walked to the end of the corridor, to the window, and stood with her back to all of them and looked out at the harbour, and her shoulders, under the navy coat, were not still.

Then Haozhen went to the desk.

The nurse looked at him. At the green shirt with H. QIN on the chest. At the gravel dust on his knees. At the pass round his neck. At his face.

“Are you family?” she said.

He opened his mouth.

He had answered nine questions in a yellow room in August two years ago, every one of them truthfully. He had told a registry clerk that he existed and been shown a line of faded blue ink. He had a pink slip in his wallet. He had a ring in the shape of a ruby on her finger, through there, beyond the second set of doors. He had no paper. He had nothing that said what he was to her.

“No,” he said. “I’m—”

“He’s her husband.”

Vittoria Song had come back from the window.

She stood beside him at the desk. She was smaller than him by a head. She didn’t look at him. She looked at the nurse with the face that had once made a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman cry in a showroom in Milan without raising her voice above a murmur.

“He’s family,” she said. “He’s more family than I am. Let him in.”

The nurse looked at her. At the navy coat, and the binoculars still round her neck on their strap, and the face. Then at Haozhen.

She wrote something on her clipboard. She didn’t ask anything else.

“Through the doors,” she said. “Bed four. Don’t touch the lines.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t touch the lines.

He sat down in the chair beside bed four and looked at her.

She was very small in the bed. She had never been small in her life. She was tall and thin and loud and she took up every room she had ever been in, every garage and paddock and ballroom, and in the bed she looked like a child. Her short hair was flattened and dark with sweat and there was gravel dust in it still, by her ear. There was a tube in her mouth, held with white tape across her cheek, and the tube went to a machine beside the bed, and the machine breathed. In. A pause. Out. A soft clean mechanical sigh, every four seconds. Her chest went up and down with it. Not with her. With it.

Her left shoulder was strapped. Her left arm lay on a pillow. There were lines going into the back of her right hand, beside the old shiny burn, and into her neck. There were wires on her chest, under the gown, going to a screen above the bed.

He looked at the screen.

Four lines. In colour. Moving.

Heart. Oxygen. Blood pressure. Breathing.

He knew how to read lines. He had learned in two weeks. He sat in the chair beside bed four and read hers, the green one going up and down in its small regular peaks, the blue one sitting at ninety-four and dropping to ninety-one and coming back to ninety-four, the yellow one, the white, a thousand times a second, and they were not happy lines. They were not any kind of line he knew. They were the lines of somebody who wasn’t there.

He took her right hand. Carefully. Round the lines going into the back of it.

“Sera,” he said.

The machine breathed.

✦ ✦ ✦

They tried to make him leave at nine.

A different nurse, younger, with kind eyes, who said that visiting hours in the unit ended at nine and that family could wait in the room down the corridor where there were reclining chairs, and that they would call him if anything changed. He said thank you. He didn’t move. She said it again. He said, “I know. Thank you,” and didn’t move. She went away and came back with the nurse from the desk, who looked at him for a long moment, and at his hand on Serafina’s, and at the screen, and said something to the younger nurse very quietly, and they both went away and didn’t come back about it.

At eleven, the surgeons took her down for the plate in her collarbone. He walked beside the bed to the lift. They didn’t let him in the lift. He stood at the lift doors for two hours and fifty minutes until they opened again and she came back out of them, asleep, on the bed, with the machine breathing for her, and a new dressing on her shoulder, and he walked beside her back to bed four and sat down in the chair and took her hand.

At three in the morning he was still there.

He was still there at six, when the light came up grey over the harbour through the window at the end of the unit, and a cleaner came round with a mop and looked at him and mopped round his chair.

He did not sit outside the door. He knew a man who had done that, for fourteen nights, on a plastic chair, outside a room on this floor, for the person he loved. He had read about it in a file. He understood it now. He understood exactly why you would do that.

He wasn’t going to. He was inside. He was holding her hand. If she woke for one second he would be the first thing she saw, not a door.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came in turns all day.

Two at a time. Aurelia, in the same gold as yesterday because she had not been home. She sat on the other side of the bed and talked to her sister for an hour about nothing, about the boutique, about Enzo’s retirement which he had announced again, about a woman who had come in on Thursday and tried to return a ring she had clearly worn to her own wedding. She held her sister’s other hand, the left one, very carefully, on its pillow, below the strapped shoulder. Once she stopped in the middle of a sentence and put her forehead down on the edge of the mattress and stayed there, and Haozhen didn’t say anything, and after a while she sat up and went on with the sentence.

Big Wu, in his green shirt, enormous in the chair, who sat for twenty minutes with his huge hands between his knees and said nothing at all, and then leaned forward and said, very low, “The car’s in bits, Sera. Bits. Best thing that ever happened to it,” and got up and went out very fast.

Mouse, who came in with her laptop under her arm and sat down and opened it and turned the screen to Haozhen. It was the data. Her last lap. Lap thirty-one. Four lines, stopping at one ninety-one. Mouse looked at him. He looked at the screen. Then Mouse closed the laptop and put it on the floor, and took Serafina’s hand from him, and held it, and talked to her. Quietly, fast, the whole time, in a voice nobody had ever heard her use, the voice she must have used once to the only person she talked to.

Mr. Kwok came at noon with a flask of congee that nobody could eat and a flask of soup that nobody could eat, and put them on the windowsill, and went and sat in the waiting room down the corridor and read the newspaper aloud to the room. The racing results. The weather. A long story about a cat in a fire station. In a calm, flat, steady voice, for two hours.

Jinx and Raiden. Donatella Ferri, chewing so hard her jaw clicked, with a card from every one of the forty-one people on the team. Callum Hart, who stood at the end of the bed and looked at her and then at Haozhen and said, “Mate,” and didn’t know what else to say, and Haozhen said, “Thank you for coming,” and meant it, and Callum went out and was found by Mr. Kwok an hour later sitting in the stairwell with his head in his hands.

His mother had rung the night before, at eight, on the Sunday, the hour he always rang her. From the flat at the end of the second street, from the phone by the Japanese sewing machine. He went to the window at the end of the unit and talked to her for four minutes.

“Is she awake?”

“Not yet. Tomorrow night, they think.”

“Is she going to be all right?”

He was quiet.

“They don’t know yet, Ma,” he said.

His mother didn’t say anything for a while. He heard the sewing machine behind her. Then he heard it stop.

“I’m sewing her something,” said Liang Shufen. “A cover. For the arm. For when she comes home.” A pause. “It’s red. With a road on it. Tell her when she wakes up. Tell her I said she’s to do the dumplings properly when she can use her hands.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second day, in the afternoon, they turned the sedation down.

Dr. Ma came and stood at the end of the bed with his hands together and explained it. The lung was better. The oxygen was better. They would let her come up slowly, over hours, and when she was breathing well enough on her own they would take the tube out. She might be confused. She might not know where she was. She might not know who anybody was, for a while. With a head that had been shaken like that, nobody could promise anything.

“Talk to her,” he said. “She’ll hear voices before she knows what they mean. Familiar ones help.”

At seven o’clock they took the tube out.

He wasn’t allowed to watch. He stood outside the curtain and listened. He heard her cough. A terrible sound, raw, dragging. He heard the nurse saying her name, and well done, and keep coughing, and you’re in hospital, you’ve had an accident, you’re safe. He heard her breathe. On her own. Rough and shallow and catching on the bad side, every breath, but hers.

When they drew the curtain back she was lying with an oxygen mask over her face and her eyes closed, and he sat down in the chair and took her hand, and she didn’t wake.

At ten she didn’t wake.

At midnight she didn’t wake.

He sat in the chair and held her hand and read the four lines on the screen above her bed and they were different now. They were moving. They were somebody’s. But she didn’t open her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past two in the morning, on the second night, she opened her eyes.

He didn’t move. He’d been taught, at nineteen, in a car park, by a woman with a red scarf, that you did not move suddenly near someone who was waking up and did not know where they were. He sat absolutely still in the chair with her hand in his and watched her eyes open, very slowly, and look at the ceiling. At the light. At the screen. At nothing.

Then they came down. Across the bed. To the chair.

To him.

She looked at him. Her eyes were dull and dark and swimming and he didn’t know if she knew him. He didn’t breathe.

She moved her mouth under the mask. No sound came out. She tried again.

He leaned in. He lifted the edge of the mask, very gently, away from her mouth, a few centimetres, the way he’d seen the nurse do it.

“Is the car,” said Serafina, in a voice like gravel being dragged across a floor, “all right?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He laughed.

He didn’t mean to. It came out of him before he knew it was there, a crack of a laugh, broken right down the middle, and then the middle went, and it was not laughing any more. He put his forehead down on the edge of the mattress beside her hand, the way Aurelia had, and his shoulders went, and he couldn’t stop it, and he didn’t try.

He felt her hand move in his.

Her fingers. Moving. Slowly. Finding his. Holding on.

“No,” he said, into the mattress, when he could. “No. It’s not all right. It’s in pieces. Big Wu says it’s in bits.”

“Shame,” said Serafina. A long rough breath. “Good car.”

“It was a good car.”

“Did my foot,” she said, and stopped, and breathed, “brake on the marker?”

He lifted his head.

“To the metre,” said Qin Haozhen.

Her eyes closed. Opened again.

“Then it wasn’t me.”

“It wasn’t you. It was oil. From the silver car. The marshal had the flag in his hand. He was lifting it.” He was holding her hand so hard he made himself stop. “It wasn’t you, Sera. You braked on the marker. Your foot wasn’t frightened. You did everything right.”

She looked at him for a while with her dull swimming eyes.

“You’re holding my hand,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You went over the barrier.”

He didn’t ask how she knew. Nobody had told her. She’d been asleep for thirty hours.

“Yes.”

“Before the flags.”

“Before the flags.”

“Idiot,” said Serafina, so softly it was hardly a word at all, and something happened at the corner of her mouth, under the edge of the mask, that was the smile’s distant relation from the countryside, his, that she had borrowed. “You could have been killed. There were cars.”

“There weren’t. They’d stopped.”

“You didn’t know that.”

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “I didn’t.”

Her fingers tightened on his. Very slightly. It was all the strength she had.

“Mamma,” she said. “Did she see?”

He was quiet for a moment.

“She saw,” he said. “She was in the front row, in Block C. With her binoculars.” He swallowed. “She held my hand. In the car. All the way from the circuit to here. And when the nurse asked if I was family, she said I was your husband. She said I was more family than she was.”

Serafina looked at him.

Then her eyes filled, and spilled, and ran sideways down her temples into her hair, into the gravel dust that was still there by her ear, and she didn’t make a sound, and didn’t look away from him once.

“Don’t let go,” she said.

“I won’t.”

“Even if I go back to sleep.”

“Especially then,” said Qin Haozhen, and she went back to sleep, holding on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four, Aurelia came through the second set of doors in her gold from two days ago and found him in the chair, still holding her sister’s hand, looking at the screen.

“She woke up,” he said, without turning round.

Aurelia stopped.

“At ten past two. For six minutes. She knew me.” He was still looking at the four lines. They were happy lines. Not her racing ones. Something else. A sleeping person’s. “She asked about the car first.”

Aurelia Chen, who did not cry in public, who had sobbed out loud in the front row at the circuit in the north in December 2019 and again in November last year, stood at the end of bed four in the intensive care unit on the ninth floor at four in the morning with her hands over her mouth, and laughed, and cried, both at once, so hard that the nurse at the desk got up.

“Of course she did,” said Aurelia, through her hands. “Of course. Of course she asked about the car.”

chapters.title: She Drives Again
chapters.desc: Four months. A plate in her collarbone, headaches that come like weather, a red arm sling with a mountain road on it, and a simulator where she freezes at the Needle every time. Then a January morning at the circuit in the north. He doesn’t stop her. He holds her helmet.
chapters.epigraph: “What if my foot’s frightened?” “Then I’ll tell you. I’ll be on the wall. I’ll read it.”
chapters.content:
She came home on the twelfth day, in Nonna, in the passenger seat.

He drove. Gently. Under the speed limit the whole way, which he had never once done in her car. Out of the hospital car park on the hill and down through the city and along the harbour road past the container terminals, with her in the seat he had slept in a hundred times and the blanket over her knees and her left arm strapped across her chest in a sling. The sling was red. His mother had sent it by express post in a box with eleven bags of dried mushrooms and a note: For the arm. Wear it. Do the dumplings properly when you can use both hands. There was a mountain road stitched across it in grey silk, winding, with white lines down the middle, and at the top, near her collarbone, a very small red car.

She fell asleep before the bridge.

He drove the loop. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. Twice. He didn’t take her home until she woke up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She couldn’t get up the stairs to the loft.

He’d known she wouldn’t. He’d done it before he went to fetch her, on the eleventh night, with Big Wu: they had carried the mattress down the loft stairs and put it on a frame of pallets in the corner of the garage behind Gilded, with the hardboard sign above it and a curtain on a wire round it that Mouse had found at the night market, and a lamp, and the quilt with the silk mountain road on it.

“I’m sleeping in the garage,” said Serafina, from the doorway, in her red sling, looking at it.

“Until you can do the stairs.”

“With the trains.”

“You’ve always slept with the trains.”

“Not on the floor with them,” said Serafina, and then she saw the corner where the tarpaulin had always been, over the long low shape of the burnt prototype. It was empty. Just the oil stain on the concrete in the shape of something long, with a shark’s tail. “Where’s my car?”

“Jinx is keeping it,” said Qin Haozhen. “You need the space.”

She looked at him for a long time.

He looked back. His face gave her nothing. It gave everybody nothing. It had never once, in three years, given her nothing, and she narrowed her eyes.

“You’re lying to me.”

“I’m not lying to you.”

“You’re doing a face.”

“I’m doing,” said Qin Haozhen, “the face for I can’t tell you that yet.”

She stood in the doorway in her sling and stared at him. Then her mouth twitched.

“Rule one,” she said.

“Rule one.”

“You’ll tell me.”

“When I can,” he said. “I promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The headaches came like weather.

That was how she described it to the neurologist, a tall stooping woman with grey hair called Dr. Sato, at the first appointment, in October. Not all the time. Not every day. They came up over her the way rain came up over the harbour, a dark line on the horizon and then everything at once, and when they came she couldn’t stand light, or noise, or the trains, and she lay on the mattress behind the curtain with a cold cloth over her eyes and the quilt pulled up and he sat on the floor beside her in the dark with his back against Gilded’s wheel and held her hand and didn’t say anything.

She forgot things. Small things. Where she’d put her tea. The name of the man at the parts shop she’d been buying from for nine years. Once, in November, the word for spanner, in all three languages, and she stood at the bench with one in her hand and cried, furious, because she couldn’t remember what it was called.

“Spanner,” he said, from the stool.

“I know it’s a spanner—”

“I know you know.”

“Then why can’t I say it—”

“Because your brain hit the inside of your helmet at a hundred and ninety-one kilometres an hour,” said Qin Haozhen, “and it’s very tired, and it’s allowed to be.” He took the spanner out of her hand and put it on the bench. “Dr. Sato said it would come back. It’s coming back. You said spanner yesterday. Twice. In Italian.”

“Did I?”

“Chiave inglese,” he said. “You said it to Brake.”

She laughed, wetly. “That’s not even the right word, that’s the wrong kind of—”

“I know,” he said. “I looked it up. Brake didn’t mind.”

She was angry, a lot. More than she’d ever been. Dr. Sato said that was the head too. She was angry at the plate in her collarbone, and the ribs that hurt when she laughed, and the stairs she couldn’t climb, and the car in bits, and the silver car with the dentist from the coast. She was angry at Big Wu for being careful with her and at Mouse for being careful with her and at Mr. Kwok for making congee every single day, and at him most of all, because he was always there, on the stool, on the floor, in the chair, and never once angry back.

“Shout at me,” she said, in December. At three in the morning. Behind the curtain. “Just once. I’ve been horrible for two months. Shout.”

He thought about it.

“No,” he said.

“Why not?”

“Because I’d have to stop holding your hand,” said Qin Haozhen, “to do it properly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The simulator was in Modena.

Orsini Corse had one in the factory, a full-sized cockpit on hydraulic legs in a dark room with a curved screen round it, and in December Donatella flew them both there, and Serafina sat in it in her race suit for the first time since September.

It was the circuit in the north. Of course it was. They’d built it to the centimetre from laser scans: every kerb, every crack in the tarmac, the advertising bridge, the gravel trap, the tyre wall. She did her out lap. She did the long right and the esses and the back straight.

And at the braking marker for the Needle, she froze.

Not her hands. Her foot. Her foot came off the throttle a hundred metres before the marker, all on its own, and stayed off, and the simulated car rolled down to the hairpin at a hundred and twenty with nobody driving it, and went round it at walking pace, and she sat in the dark cockpit with her hands on the wheel, shaking.

She tried eleven times.

Eleven times her foot came off a hundred metres early. On the twelfth, she braked on the marker, and the sound came through the speakers, the brakes and the tyres at the edge of their grip, exactly the sound it had been on lap thirty-one, and she screamed. Not a word. She ripped off her helmet and screamed in the dark room in Modena with the screen still showing the Needle, the gravel, the red and white tyres, and Kenji Arakawa at the control desk switched it off and the room went black.

Haozhen was at the cockpit before the lights came up.

She was sitting with her helmet in her lap and her face in her hands. He climbed up the side of the simulator, which you were not allowed to do, and got into the tiny space beside the seat, and put his arms round her, round the race suit and the plate in her collarbone and all of it, and held her in the dark.

“I can’t,” she said.

“Not today.”

“I can’t, Hao. Every time. My foot. It knows. It knows what happens at the marker.”

“It does,” he said. “It remembers. That’s what feet do.” He held her. “It’ll learn something else. It’ll take longer than two weeks. It took me two weeks to read your data. It took you three years to stop me checking the mirror.” He put his face in her hair. “We’ve got time. Donatella said so. The season doesn’t start till April.”

“What if it never learns?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“Then you’ll drive something else,” he said. “Or you won’t drive. And I’ll still be here. On the stool.” He was quiet. “But I don’t think that’s what’s going to happen. I’ve watched your foot for three years. It’s the bravest foot I’ve ever seen.”

She laughed, in his arms, in the dark, in Modena. It came out cracked.

“That’s the stupidest thing anyone’s ever said to me.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve been saving it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Sato signed the form on the eighth of January.

Two pages, for the governing body. Cognitive tests: normal. Balance: normal. Reaction times: better than they had been at her last annual medical in 2025, which Dr. Sato said with an expression of mild offence. No headaches for five weeks. The orthopaedic surgeon signed the other half. The plate was solid. The bone had knitted round it. The neck strength, which she had been building back in the gym for six weeks with a physiotherapist and a harness and a great deal of swearing, was within the range.

He drove her home from the appointment with the signed form on her lap, in its envelope, and she held it all the way with both hands, the way he had once carried thirty spools of Japanese thread out of a haberdasher’s.

“Cleared,” she said, at the lights by the flyover.

“Cleared.”

“I could drive tomorrow.”

“You could.”

“Pre-season test’s the twentieth.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve booked the hotel.”

She looked across at him.

“You’re not going to tell me not to.”

“No.”

“Even after Modena.”

“Especially after Modena,” he said. “You screamed. Then you got back in. Twice. Kenji told me. After I’d gone to get you water.” He put the car in gear as the lights changed. “I’m never going to tell you not to, Sera. Not about this. Not about anything.” He was quiet. “I’ll just be on the wall.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The twentieth of January was cold and very clear, with frost on the rice stubble in the fields round the valley and the sky over the grandstand the hard pale blue of a winter morning. The circuit was empty except for the teams. No crowd. Twenty-two cars, a lot of engineers, a man selling noodles.

Her mother was there.

Nobody had told her. Nobody had asked her. She was standing at the fence at the end of the pit lane, at the far end, nearest the Needle, alone, in her navy coat, with her binoculars round her neck, and she had been standing there, the man selling noodles said, since half past seven.

Serafina saw her from the garage at nine. She didn’t wave. She stood looking at her mother for a while, sixty metres away, at the fence, small and straight in her navy coat with her hands on the rail.

Then she went and got changed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was holding her helmet.

He hadn’t planned to. He’d been carrying it from the drivers’ room to the garage because her collarbone was still stiff in the mornings and she didn’t like lifting the helmet bag with that arm, and when they got to the car he just didn’t put it down. He stood beside the green Orsini car in the pit garage, with the gold AURELIA on the new bonnet and a small grey taxi on the driver’s door that Big Wu had cut out of vinyl again, by himself, with a craft knife, and lacquered three times, and he held her helmet in both hands.

She stood in front of him in her race suit with her balaclava on and looked at it.

It was a new one. The old one had gone to the governing body after September, to be examined, and had come back with a report and a crack across the left side that she had looked at once and never again. This one was black, plain, with a thin gold line round it. Aurelia had had it painted. On the back, very small, where only someone standing behind her would see it, there was a white numeral.

7.

“I’m frightened,” said Serafina.

“I know.”

“What if my foot’s frightened?”

“Then I’ll tell you,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ll be on the wall. I’ll read it.” He was holding the helmet very steadily. “Six metres. I’ll see it before you feel it. I’ll tell you on the radio. And you’ll fix it. The way you did in the heat.”

“And if I can’t?”

“Then you’ll come in,” he said, “and I’ll hold this again, and we’ll try tomorrow.”

She looked at him over the helmet.

He didn’t say don’t. He didn’t say are you sure. He didn’t say you don’t have to. She waited for it. More than three years she’d known him and she still waited for it, every time, the thing every other person in her life had said to her since she was nine years old and tried to run up the banking at Monza. He just stood there in his green shirt in the cold January pit garage and held her helmet out to her, steady, in both hands, the way you’d hold out a door.

She took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her out lap was slow. Everybody’s was. Cold tyres, cold brakes, cold track, frost still in the shade under the advertising bridge.

The long right. The esses, where the sun came over the top and got in her visor, and she didn’t lift. The back straight. Nine hundred metres. He watched the speed trace climb on his screen at the end of the pit wall. One ninety. Two hundred. Two twenty. Two thirty-five.

The marker for the Needle.

The brake trace went up.

Six metres early. Six point one. He saw it. He saw it the instant it happened, the brake pressure rising a fraction before the marker, the way it had in the heat in the south after the Ferrari went into the gravel. Her foot. Frightened.

She went round the Needle cleanly, slowly, safely. The throttle trace came up out of it hesitant, fluttering, a line he had never seen her make.

He pressed the radio.

“Six metres,” he said.

Silence on the channel. Kenji, beside him, didn’t say anything. Down the wall Mouse had taken her hands off her keyboard and put them flat on the desk.

The next lap. The long right. The esses. The back straight. The marker.

“Four,” said Qin Haozhen.

The next lap.

“Two.”

He heard her breathe on the channel. Just once. A long rough breath, through her teeth, the kind she breathed at the top of the Baizhang Pass.

The next lap. The back straight. Two hundred and thirty-eight. The marker came up under the advertising bridge, the white board with the black number on it, and the gravel behind the hairpin, and the tyre wall behind the gravel, red and white, rebuilt in October, six deep.

The brake trace went up.

On the marker. To the metre.

And the speed came down like a stone, two hundred and thirty-eight to seventy-five in a hundred and ten metres, and the steering went round, and the throttle came up out of the Needle in one long clean stroke, the way it always had, a happy line, the happiest line he had ever seen her make.

He didn’t press the radio. He couldn’t.

On the team channel, very faintly, under the engine, he heard her laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the far end of the pit lane, at the fence nearest the Needle, a woman in a navy coat three seasons old lowered her binoculars.

She stood there for a moment with her hands on the rail.

Then she turned round, and walked back along the fence to the Orsini garage, slowly, in her flat shoes, and stopped at the back of it, by the tyre rack, where nobody would see her, and stood there with her hands in the pockets of her coat until her daughter came in.

Serafina came in after twelve laps. She stopped the car in the garage and sat in it with her hands on the wheel and the engine ticking. Then she got out, and pulled off her helmet, and her hair was in spikes and her face was red with cold and wet, and she looked round the garage.

She found him first. At the end of the pit wall, standing up, by his stool. She went to him and gave him the helmet back without a word, and he took it, in both hands.

Then she saw her mother, at the back by the tyre rack.

She didn’t go to her. Not yet. She stood with her hand in his and looked at her mother across the garage, and her mother looked back, and Vittoria Song lifted one hand out of her coat pocket, very slightly, the way she had lifted it from the rail in Block C in September.

This time it was a wave.

chapters.title: Just Married, Two Hundred Miles an Hour
chapters.desc: A registry office at ten, where he finally gets a piece of paper that says what he is to her. Nine dishes in a garage under a railway bridge, and the middle of a wedding, at last, from the inside. Then rice, and a grey taxi, and the old military airstrip at dawn, where something red is waiting under a tarpaulin with his handwriting on its nose.
chapters.epigraph: “Two hundred miles an hour.” “You said it in miles.” “It sounds better in miles. Everything fast does. Someone told me.”
chapters.content:
The registry office opened at nine, and they were the first in the queue at a quarter past eight.

She’d said she didn’t care about the paper. She’d said it in March, at the bench, with the spreadsheet open on his laptop and every guest colour-coded and the seating for nine round tables done to the centimetre. I don’t need a form, Hao. I need you at the end of an aisle that isn’t in a stairwell. And he’d looked at her for a long time and said, “I need the form.”

She’d stopped.

“At the hospital,” he’d said. “In September. The nurse asked if I was family. I didn’t have anything. Your mother had to lie for me.” He’d been very calm. “I’d like a piece of paper, Sera. That says what I am. In case anybody ever asks again.”

So they were first in the queue on the twenty-fifth of April, at a quarter past eight, outside the registry office in the old town. She was in a short white dress that Aurelia had made for her, very plain, cut so that it moved, and it stopped two fingers above the top of her boots, which were her own, black, with the heels worn down on the outside the way a driver’s heels wore from working the pedals. He was in a dark suit. Not the forgettable one. A new one, from a tailor on Harbour Road whom Chen Si had sent him to, very good, very plain, and a white shirt, and no tie, and in the inside pocket on the left, folded, a red wool scarf, because it was April and not cold and he had said he would bring it, and he did what he said.

The registrar was a cheerful woman with a lanyard who had married four hundred couples and said so.

They signed at ten past nine. Her signature first. Big, untidy, fast, right across the box and out the other side of it. Then his. Small. Square. Separate letters, each one like something typed.

Qin Haozhen.

The registrar stamped it. She tore off the certificate along its perforations and held it out across the desk.

He took it. He looked at it. His name, and hers, on the same piece of paper, in the same ink, with a red stamp at the bottom and the date.

“Is that what you wanted?” said Serafina.

He folded it once, very carefully, and put it in his inside pocket, on the left, beside the scarf. Against his chest.

“Yes,” said Qin Haozhen.

Outside, on the steps, her sister was waiting, in gold, with her husband in camel, and Chen Si held out his hand, palm up, the way he had once on a circuit, and Haozhen looked at it and laid his own flat on it, his left hand, and Chen Si closed his fingers round it, once, hard, and let go.

“Welcome to the family,” said Chen Si. “It has a contract. I’ll send you a copy.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The garage had never looked like that, and never would again.

Mouse had strung lights along every girder of the railway bridge, thousands, warm white, so that the whole ceiling was the harbour at night. Raiden had drawn the room in October as it was going to look, and Jinx had built it from the drawing: nine round tables, borrowed from every restaurant on the street, with red cloths from Mr. Kwok’s daughter in Vancouver; Gilded at one end, washed and polished, with the small grey taxi on its door and the cut in its roll cage that had never been painted; Nonna at the other, red, with the dent in her door, and a garland of white flowers along her roof from Elowen’s shop. Over the kettle, the hardboard sign, NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING, with a fifth line added underneath in fresh white paint in Granny Shum’s granddaughter’s handwriting: EXCEPT TODAY.

He had stood at the door of eleven weddings in six countries. He’d never been inside one.

He stood inside this one, at a quarter to twelve, under the lights, and looked.

There was Big Wu’s mother at the head of the first table, in red, telling everyone what to eat, and his own mother beside her, in a quilted jacket she’d made herself in grey silk, telling Big Wu’s mother she was wrong. There was Mr. Kwok at the camping stove, which he had refused to give up for a caterer, with Auntie Chu beside him with her prawns, the two of them not speaking to each other in a way that was clearly the beginning of a long friendship. There was Granny Shum in her folding chair in the middle of the floor, with her thermos and her blanket and her scanner, switched off, in her handbag. There were Mr. and Mrs. Yau in their straw hats with a bag of this year’s tea. There was Lau Kam-wing, sixty-five, who had driven down from his valley in his tube-frame special on a trailer and parked it in the alley so everyone could look at it. There was Donatella Ferri, chewing, in a green dress, and Kenji Arakawa, very precise, in a suit, and Callum Hart, who had brought nobody and posted nothing and was sitting next to Mouse being taught, by Mouse, without a word, how to fold a napkin into a rabbit.

There was the Lin family at table three. Lin Jian, grey and quiet and enormous, who had run the Walled City’s cargo for thirty years and now mostly ran his daughters’ errands. Elowen, in green, with a camellia in her hair, and Zhao at the next table, in black, with his back to her chair and the alley door in front of him. Raiden, drawing on a napkin. Jinx, with her tattoos and new honey-coloured beads round her wrist that she had made from the spares. Evangeline, who said nothing at all and beat Aurelia at the toast-glass game in four minutes. Eliana, who had hacked Haozhen’s phone the year before and was hacking it again now, under the table, to change his wallpaper.

And at table one, beside the bride’s place, there were her parents. Her father, in a suit that fitted him, for once, that Aurelia had had made. Her mother, in navy, not three seasons old any more, new, plain, good. With a single string of pearls at her throat that Aurelia had bought back from an auction in Milan.

The trains went over. Every eleven minutes. The lights swung on the girders and the whole ceiling glittered.

He stood in the middle of it and couldn’t move.

Serafina came and stood beside him and took his hand.

“This is the middle,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Is it what you thought?”

He looked round the garage, at all of it.

“No,” said Qin Haozhen. “It’s better. I didn’t know enough people to imagine it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nine dishes. Mr. Kwok announced every one.

The suckling pig, red-skinned, whole on its board, and the groom cut it, very precisely, into exactly the right number of pieces, which made Mr. Kwok cry. The crab claw. The scallops with the green vegetable. The chicken, whole, with the head on, so the marriage had a beginning and an end. The fish. Whole. Head and tail. Steamed with ginger. In front of the bride.

She ate it. The best part, by the cheek. Without a face. In front of everyone, and said, “Disgusting, Mr. Kwok, thank you,” and two hundred people, which was how many there turned out to be, cheered.

The noodles, long, for long life. The fried rice. The red bean soup. The little buns shaped like peaches, for the old people, of whom there were a great many.

Then the toasts. You go round every table with her and drink. Every one. You don’t sit down until you’ve done every table.

They did every table. Nine. With a glass each. Big Wu’s mother made him drink a whole glass of brandy at table one and watched to make sure. Lau Kam-wing told him that if he ever let her go round the hundred and twelfth on the outside again he’d come down from his valley personally. Granny Shum gave him a clementine. Zhao Zhendong looked at him for four seconds and said “Hm,” and Elowen said, “He says congratulations, and that you’re very lucky, and that if you make her cry he’ll put you in the harbour,” and Zhao said, “Hm,” again, and Elowen said, “And that he likes your car.”

At table nine, a parcel was waiting on his chair. Small, square, wrapped in brown paper, posted from the capital. No card. No name.

He opened it.

A box of cinnamon gum. Forty sticks. And inside the lid, in a handwriting he knew from a dormitory of forty boys under a leaking roof, two words in pencil.

Window seat.

He sat down very suddenly on the chair.

“Who is it from?” said Serafina.

“A friend,” said Qin Haozhen. “He kept his promise. He told them we were faster.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight, they left.

That had been in the spreadsheet too. Row two hundred and four. 00:00. Departure. The guests went out into the alley ahead of them and stood in two lines under the railway bridge, two hundred people, with rice in their hands, and somebody had brought sparklers, and the trains went over, and at the end of the alley, at the corner where his brakes had always bitten clean, there was a grey 2006 Toyota Crown estate with a dent in its rear door and honey-coloured wooden beads on its seats and a sign hanging off its back bumper on a string that said, in Jinx’s handwriting, JUST MARRIED, NOBODY KNOWS WHERE.

She drove. Of course she drove.

She came out of the side door with her white dress and her boots and her hand in his, through the rice, through the sparklers, through two hundred people shouting, and got in behind the wheel, and he got in beside her on the beads, and her mother leaned in at her window at the last second, and didn’t say anything, and touched her face, once, with the back of her fingers, and stepped back.

Serafina put her foot down.

Nobody sat down on its rear wheels and went, the engine making its sound under the grey bodywork, the long scream that no taxi had ever made, and the alley and the lights and the two hundred people went backward out of the rear window in a cloud of rice and sparks, and at the end of the street of shuttered workshops she took the corner flat, and the sign on the bumper went off into the night, and he laughed, out loud, the whole thing, with his head back against the beads.

“Where are we going?” he said.

“You know where we’re going.”

“I don’t.”

She looked across at him. He was doing a face.

“You do,” said Serafina. “You’ve been doing that face for seven months. Since the hospital. Since the tarpaulin went.” She looked back at the road. “Rule one, Hao. You said you’d tell me when you could.”

He was quiet for a moment, on the beads, in the dark.

“North,” he said. “Two hours. There’s an old military airstrip at Hengling. Closed since 2008. It belongs to a company in Singapore now that your sister’s banker set up over a bowl of noodles.” He paused. “The runway’s three point two kilometres.”

She didn’t say anything. Her hands were very still on the wheel.

“I can tell you now,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got there at a quarter past two.

A gate in a wire fence, unlocked, with a man she knew standing beside it. Big Wu. In his wedding suit, with the tie gone and the jacket off, holding a torch. He’d left the party at nine. So had Mouse, and Jinx, and Raiden, and Kenji Arakawa, and a small bald Italian called Beppe. She’d noticed them go. She’d thought they’d gone to bed.

They hadn’t.

At the end of the old runway, in the floodlight from a generator, there was a transporter. Orsini green. Its ramp was down.

And on the concrete in front of it, under the light, there was a car.

Long. Low. Flat. With a tail like a shark’s. Not black any more. Not burnt, not blistered, not melted at the nose. Red. Deep red, glowing in the floodlight, the colour of brake lights and old rubies and a 1992 Lancia Delta Integrale with its paint going pink at the edges. Every centimetre of the carbon tub rebuilt. New bodywork, hand-laid, by Jinx and Beppe, from moulds Raiden had drawn off photographs from 1991. An engine in the back that had come from Modena in a crate in November with a note from Donatella that said Do not tell her. Do not tell anyone. Allora. Wheels. Glass. A two-seat cockpit, the way the rules had demanded in 1991, a driver’s seat and, beside it, a second seat, narrower, for a passenger nobody had ever been expected to carry.

On the nose, small, in white, in his own square separate letters, there was a name.

TWO HUNDRED.

She got out of Nobody.

She walked across the concrete in her white dress and her boots, in the floodlight, very slowly, to the red car, and stood in front of it, and didn’t touch it. She stood there.

He came and stood beside her.

“Since September,” he said. “Since the eleventh night. The night before you came home from the hospital. I took it to Jinx’s. Big Wu did the chassis. Mouse did the electronics. Kenji did the data, at night, in Modena, on the simulator, he ran it four hundred times. Donatella found the engine. Raiden drew the body. Jinx and Beppe laid it.” He was looking at the car. “I did the brakes.”

She turned her head.

“You did the brakes.”

“I learned,” said Qin Haozhen. “Big Wu taught me. I’m very slow. I did them four times.” He looked at her. “I wasn’t going to let anyone else do the brakes.”

She looked at the name on the nose.

“You named it a number.”

“It’s a specification,” said Qin Haozhen.

She started to laugh. And then she couldn’t, because she was crying too hard, and she turned round and put her face in his chest, in his new suit, at the end of an old military runway at a quarter past two on her wedding night, and he put his arms round her and held on, and over her head Big Wu looked away at the sky and blew his nose like a ship’s horn.

✦ ✦ ✦

They put race suits on over their wedding clothes. Of course they did. Her rule. She would not get into a car without the suit and the helmet and the belts, not since September, not ever. Hers, the black helmet with the thin gold line and the white 7 on the back. His, her old spare from the track day in December 2022, which he had kept.

She got in the driver’s side. He got in the other. The narrow seat. The passenger nobody had ever been expected to carry. Big Wu did his belts, tight, and checked them twice, and patted the top of his helmet, once, and went away to the transporter.

The engine started.

It wasn’t like Nonna. It wasn’t like Gilded or Nobody or the green Orsini car. It was enormous. It was a sound from 1991 from the long straight at Le Mans in the dark, a deep hard bellow that went down into the concrete and up into the sky and shook the transporter on its springs. Mouse, at a laptop on the transporter ramp with her headphones on, put both hands flat on the desk.

“Ready?” said Serafina, on the intercom.

“Yes.”

“You’re not going to check the mirror?”

“There’s nothing behind us,” said Qin Haozhen, “but a transporter and a man in a suit crying.”

She put it in first.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three point two kilometres.

She’d done the sum on the way up. She’d done it in her head on the motorway with her hands on the wheel of Nobody while he pretended not to know where they were going. Zero to three hundred and twenty-two. Then a kilometre to stop. She’d have about two kilometres to get there. On a runway built for fighter jets, flat, wide, with a white line down the middle going away into the dark like a road to the end of the world.

She let the clutch out.

The car didn’t go. It left. It left everything behind it, the transporter and the floodlight and the generator and Big Wu and the whole of the night, and the white line came at them out of the dark and went under the nose so fast it stopped being a line and became a light. Second. Third. Her back pressed into the seat until she couldn’t have lifted her head. Fourth. The runway lights going past on either side like the lights of the long bridge to the airport, one after another, faster, faster, like something being counted.

“Two hundred,” said Mouse, in her ear. Very calm. Kilometres.

Fifth.

“Two fifty.”

The noise. The noise was everything. It wasn’t outside the car any more. It was inside her. It was her.

“Two eighty.”

Sixth. The last gear. The shark’s tail sat down on the runway and the car stopped feeling like a car and started feeling like something that wanted, very badly, to be somewhere else.

“Three hundred.”

And beside her, in the passenger seat, in her old spare helmet, with his hands loose on his knees, not holding on, he turned his head.

She felt it. She didn’t look. You don’t look, at three hundred, on a runway, with a kilometre to go. She felt him look at her, the way she’d felt it on the long bridge to the airport at five in the morning, on the side of her face, like sun.

Look at the right person.

“Three ten,” said Mouse. “Three fifteen.”

Her foot was flat on the floor.

“Three twenty.”

The marker came up. A white board at the edge of the runway in the floodlight from a second generator, two kilometres from the start. Big Wu had put it there. She saw it. She’d see it in her sleep for the rest of her life.

“Three twenty-two,” said Mouse.

And then, very quietly, in a voice that wasn’t anybody’s but hers, the second word she had ever said to him, on a radio, at three hundred and twenty-two kilometres an hour, at the end of a runway in the dark:

“Haozhen.”

“Two hundred miles an hour,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She braked.

On the marker. To the metre. Her foot didn’t hesitate. The brakes he had done, four times, with Big Wu standing over him, bit, all four at once, perfectly, and the car came down from two hundred miles an hour like a stone falling into deep water, smooth and straight, the weight going forward into the front tyres like water tipped carefully from one cup into another, and it didn’t twitch, and it didn’t pull, and it stopped.

Dead straight. In the middle of the runway. Three hundred metres from the end.

The engine ticked.

Tick. Tick. In the dark at the end of the runway, the metal cooling, like a clock wound too far.

She sat with both hands on the wheel. She couldn’t let go of it. She sat and shook, all over, from her boots to her helmet, and laughed, and couldn’t stop either.

“You said it in miles,” she said.

“It sounds better in miles,” said Qin Haozhen. His voice wasn’t steady at all. “Everything fast does. Someone told me.”

“You did the brakes.”

“I did the brakes.”

“They were perfect—”

“I know,” he said. “I did them four times.”

She got her hands off the wheel. She got her helmet off. She got his off, with her fingers shaking so much she couldn’t find the strap, and he helped her, and his hair was flattened and his face was wet and he was laughing too, in the dark, in the narrow passenger seat of a car he’d rebuilt from a burnt shell for the woman who’d bought it for scrap, and she reached across the cockpit in her race suit over her wedding dress and took his face in both hands and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was them. It was always going to be them.

Fast and laughing, still in gear, in the dark, with the engine ticking. She couldn’t get across the cockpit, there wasn’t room, the belts wouldn’t let her, and she swore at the belts in three languages, and he undid hers and then his, his hands shaking, and the zips of two race suits that were built not to come undone, and they did, and under hers the white dress Aurelia had made, and under his the new suit from Harbour Road, and the red wool scarf fell out of his inside pocket onto the floor of the cockpit with the folded certificate, and neither of them picked it up.

He was trained to keep control of everything. In every room. Always.

She took it. All of it. On the floor of the cockpit of a red car at the end of a runway at three in the morning, with the zips open and her boots still on, she took every gram of control he had ever had, and he gave it to her. He didn’t try to keep any of it. He lay back in the narrow passenger seat with his head against the carbon and her hands on his face and let her drive, and said her name, and then her name again, and then something in Mandarin she had never heard him say, and then nothing at all.

The sky over the end of the runway was going grey when she lifted her head off his chest.

The scarf was round both of them. She didn’t know how. Two metres of red wool, wound round her shoulders and his, because it was April, and it was three in the morning at the end of a runway in the north, and it was cold, and he’d said that if it was cold he’d wear it.

“You wore it,” she said.

“It’s cold,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six, they went north.

Not in the red car. Big Wu put that back in the transporter with Beppe and Jinx, very carefully, as if it were made of glass, and drove it away down the runway in the dawn toward the city, leaning on the horn, two long and a short, for no reason at all except that he could. Mouse went with him, and raised one hand from the cab window as they went, and didn’t put it down until they were out of sight.

They went in Nobody. North. Up into the hills, onto a road with no number on it, and then a smaller road, and then a track between tea terraces that went up and up into the mist with the bushes close on either side, green now, new leaves, two and a bud, the way Mrs. Yau had shown them.

She drove. He sat beside her on the honey-coloured beads, with the certificate in his inside pocket on the left against his chest, and the scarf round his neck, three times, the ends tucked in.

“This is the honeymoon,” she said. “The getaway.”

“Yes.”

“Nobody knows where we are.”

“Nobody,” said Qin Haozhen. “For two weeks.” He looked out of the window at the tea. “Except Mr. Kwok. And Mrs. Yau. And the dog. And your sister, who booked the hotel in Milan for after. And my mother, who sewed the sheets.”

“So everybody.”

“Everybody,” he agreed. “That’s the best part.”

At the top of the track, among the tea bushes, in front of a low stone house with a stone frog by the door, a yellow dog with one ear up, which Mr. Kwok had sent up the day before in a basket on the bus labelled FRAGILE, came running down the path and stopped dead in front of the car.

She braked. On the marker. To the metre.

He was asleep before the engine had finished ticking.

chapters.title: First Podium
chapters.desc: A whole season without one. Fourth, fifth, fourth, sixth. Then the finale at the circuit in the north, a year and a month after the Needle, with two mothers in Block C and a Ferrari in her mirrors on the last lap. Third place. Champagne in his face. He lets it happen.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t move.” “Sera.” “Don’t you dare move. Stand there. Look at me.”
chapters.content:
They didn’t get one all year.
