Not in April, at the opener in the south, in the heat, when she brought the green car home fourth with Callum. Not in May, in Japan, where it rained for three hours and she was sixth and furious. Not in June or July or August. Fourth. Fifth. Fourth again. Once, in Malaysia, she was third with six minutes to go and a tyre went on the last stint and she brought it home on three wheels and a rim in eighth, sparks pouring off the corner like a welding torch, and sat in the car in the garage afterwards and didn’t speak to anybody for an hour, and he sat on the floor of the garage beside the car with his back against the front wheel and didn’t make her.

“Next time,” said Donatella, every time, chewing. “Allora. Next time.”

“You said that in April.”

“I’ll say it until it’s true,” said Donatella Ferri. “I said it for four years in 1987. In 1988 it was true.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The finale was at the circuit in the north. On the third Sunday in October.

A year and a month after the Needle.

She knew. Everyone knew. Nobody said it. Big Wu said nothing all week in the garage under the railway bridge and took the brakes off the spare car twice and put them back on. Mouse said nothing, which was normal, but she said it more. Mr. Kwok made her the noodles with long life in them on the Thursday, the ones he made when someone had died, and then said, crossly, that they were also the ones for luck, and that she should eat them and stop looking at him.

She ate them.

Haozhen didn’t say anything about the Needle at all. On Friday night, in the loft, which she could climb to again since March, with the window open onto the tracks, she lay with her head on his chest and said, into the dark:

“I’m frightened.”

“I know.”

“Not of the corner. I’m not frightened of the corner any more. I’ve done it four hundred times since January.” She was quiet. “I’m frightened of wanting it. This. Third. Anything. I’ve wanted it all year and it keeps going. I’m frightened of how much I want it.”

He was quiet for a long time, stroking her hair.

“I didn’t know how to want anything,” he said, “until I was twenty-eight. You told me to start with a sandwich.” His hand stopped. “Wanting things is very frightening. I still think so. I want things all the time now. It’s terrible.” A train went over. “But I’d rather want them.”

She laughed, into his chest.

“Than what?”

“Than stand at a door,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother came.

She had never been to a race. She had never been to the city before the engagement dinner. She came on the slow train, eleven hours, on the Friday, with a cool box of dumplings and a new quilt for Mr. Kwok, and on Sunday morning Aurelia took her to Block C, front row, and sat her between Vittoria Song and Big Wu’s mother, and the three of them sat there in a row in the cold October sunshine. One in navy, with binoculars. One in a quilted jacket in grey silk. One in red, very small, telling the other two what to eat.

“Three mothers,” said Serafina, in the garage, looking at them through the fence.

“One of them’s Big Wu’s,” said Haozhen.

“Big Wu’s mother is everybody’s mother,” said Serafina. “She told me so in 2019.”

He looked at the front row of Block C for a while. At his mother, who had sewn a road with a red car at the hundred and twelfth corner. At Serafina’s mother, who had kept every race in a folder with scissors and had lied to a nurse. At the binoculars.

“Your mother’s teaching mine to use the binoculars,” he said.

“Is she?”

“Look.”

She looked. In Block C, Vittoria Song had taken the binoculars off her own neck and put the strap over Liang Shufen’s head, very carefully, and was leaning close, showing her the focus wheel. Liang Shufen was looking through them at the wrong end. Vittoria turned them round.

Serafina had to go and put her helmet on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours.

She did the first stint, the third and the last. Callum did the second and the fourth, and was brilliant, and brought the car in at the end of his last stint in fourth, two seconds behind a red Ferrari in third, with forty minutes left, and got out and pulled his helmet off and said to her, in the garage, steaming, “It’s yours. He’s got nothing left in the rears. Go and get him.”

She went.

Haozhen sat on his stool at the end of the pit wall and watched four lines.

Happy lines. All of them. The throttle coming up out of the slow corners in one long stroke, the brake trace a cliff and then a slope, and at the Needle, every lap, on the marker. To the metre. A year and a month. Four hundred times since January. He watched her brake for the Needle and his own foot pressed down on the floor under the desk every time, and Kenji, beside him, noticed, and said nothing.

Two seconds. One point eight. One point four.

“She’s on him,” said Kenji, very quietly, on the team channel. Not to her. To them.

One second. Point eight.

With six minutes left, she was on his bumper. A red Ferrari and a green Orsini, nose to tail, through the long right, through the esses with the low October sun coming over the top of them full into her visor, and she didn’t lift. Down the back straight. Two hundred and thirty-eight. Side by side for a moment, the green car pulling out of the slipstream, and then not, because the Ferrari moved over, the way you were allowed to once, and she had to go back behind.

The Needle. He braked. She braked. On the marker, both of them. Through.

“Last lap,” said Kenji, on her channel, very calm. “Last lap, Serafina. Last lap.”

She didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knew where she’d go.

He’d known since the track day in December 2022, in a thirty-year-old Lancia, when she’d talked him through the circuit on the intercom and said, of the Needle, everybody’s first time, they brake too late; second time they brake too early; third time you thread it. He’d known since lap ninety-one at the season opener in April 2024 with Tianyi leaning on the tyre stack. He’d known since lap thirty-one.

She’d go up the inside at the Needle. On the marker. And she’d thread it.

The long right. The Ferrari ahead, defending, on the inside line. The esses. The sun. She didn’t lift. The back straight. Nine hundred metres. Side by side again, the green car pulling out of the slipstream at two hundred and thirty, and this time she stayed there, on the outside, on the left, and the Ferrari stayed on the right, on the inside line for the Needle, and they went down the straight together, wheel to wheel, toward the advertising bridge and the braking marker and the gravel and the tyre wall behind it, red and white, rebuilt in October last year, six deep.

The outside.

She was on the outside. For the Needle. Nobody passed on the outside at the Needle. Nobody had ever passed on the outside at the Needle. The outside was where the gravel was. The outside was where the tyre wall was. The outside was where—

That’s where the brave ones went, cara. Round the top. Where it’s steepest. Never at the bottom.

He stopped breathing.

The marker. The Ferrari braked, on the inside. She braked. On the marker. To the metre. On the outside. He saw her brake trace go up in its cliff, perfect, and come down in its slope, perfect, and the steering trace go round, wider, further, all the way out to the edge of the tarmac, a hand’s width from the kerb, a hand’s width from the gravel, the outside wheels on the paint—

And the throttle came up.

Early. Earlier than the Ferrari’s. Because on the outside of a hairpin, if you’ve braked on the marker and you trust the car and you trust your foot and you trust the brakes and you take the long way round, you can get the power down before the man on the inside, who is still turning.

She came out of the Needle on the outside a quarter of a car behind the Ferrari, and by the end of the short straight after it, half a car ahead, and by the next corner, three lengths, and the grandstand made a sound like an animal, and Kenji Arakawa, beside him on the pit wall, said a word in Japanese that he would refuse to translate for the rest of his life.

She crossed the line third.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t remember getting off the stool.

He remembered the garage, after. Everybody in it shouting. Big Wu had picked up Beppe, all of him, and was turning in a circle. Mouse was on her feet at the end of the pit wall with her headphones round her neck and both hands over her mouth. Donatella Ferri was standing in the pit lane in her green shirt with her arms up, like the small dark girl in the photograph on her office wall, on a podium in 1983, and she was shouting Allora! Allora! at the sky, and crying, and Callum Hart was hugging Kenji, who allowed it with an expression of great suffering, and then hugged him back.

The car came down the pit lane. Green, filthy, a strip of rubber on the bonnet over the gold letters, with a small grey taxi on the door under three coats of lacquer. It stopped in front of the garage. She sat in it with her hands on the wheel and the engine ticking.

Then she got out, and pulled her helmet off, black, with a thin gold line, with a white 7 on the back. And she looked round the garage, and through the garage, and past all of it.

She found him.

She didn’t say anything. She walked through the whole team to where he was standing, at the end of the pit wall, by his stool, and she put her arms round his neck and her face in his green shirt and held on so hard he couldn’t breathe, and he didn’t care.

“The outside,” he said, into her hair.

“The outside.”

“Nobody goes round the outside at the Needle.”

“I know,” said Serafina, muffled. “That’s why it worked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The podium was in front of the grandstand, under the gantry, a three-step box with the series logo on it and the governor’s man with the trophies and a woman with a microphone, and the photographers on their stand, and eleven thousand people on their feet.

The team stood below it, in a crowd, in green. That was the tradition. The mechanics, the engineers, the team principal, the cooks. Under the podium, looking up, close enough to get wet.

He stood at the front.

He hadn’t meant to. He’d meant to stand at the back, the way he’d stood at the back of every room for eleven years, against the wall, weight on the back foot, hands where people could see them. But Big Wu had put one enormous hand in the middle of his back and pushed, and Mouse had taken his sleeve and pulled, and Donatella had said “Avanti,” and he was at the front, in the middle, directly below the third step, looking up.

She stood on the third step in her race suit with the top tied round her waist and a trophy in one hand and a magnum of champagne in the other.

She didn’t look at the crowd. Not yet. She looked down at him.

Then she shook the magnum.

He saw what she was going to do. He saw it about two seconds before she did it, the way he saw everything, the way he’d seen a tray of glasses start to fall in a ballroom on Battery Hill, the way he’d seen the black saloon’s rim catch on the coast road. Two seconds was a very long time. In two seconds he could have stepped left, behind Big Wu. He could have put his arm up. He could have turned his face away from the photographers on their stand, every one of them with a long lens, every one of them pointing at the third step.

“Don’t move,” said Serafina, from the podium.

“Sera.”

“Don’t you dare move. Stand there.” She was laughing. “Look at me.”

He looked at her.

He didn’t move.

She sprayed the champagne straight down at him.

All of it. The whole magnum. In his face, in his hair, in his eyes, down the front of his green shirt with H. QIN on the chest, on his pass with his own face on it, smiling. It was very cold and very loud and it went everywhere. It went over Big Wu and Mouse and Donatella and Beppe and Kenji. It went over the governor’s man. It went over the photographers, who didn’t care, because they were photographing the man in the green shirt below the third step, standing completely still in the middle of it, with his face turned up toward her, in full view of eleven thousand people and every camera in the series, taking it.

He let it happen. All of it.

And then, standing there soaked, with champagne running off his chin, in front of everybody, he smiled. The whole thing. All the way across his face. The one that had come from the countryside four years ago and found a flat and stayed. In front of strangers. In the October sun. As though he didn’t care in the least who saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

That was the photograph that went on the front of the sports pages the next morning.

Not the woman on the podium. The man below it.

Soaked, in a green team shirt, face turned up, smiling, with his eyes on the third step and champagne in his hair, and behind him a crowd of mechanics in green, laughing, and an enormous man with his hand on his back.

His mother cut it out with scissors at the table by the window in the flat at the end of the second street, beside the Japanese sewing machine, and put it on the wall above it, next to the thirty spools of thread.

Her mother cut it out too, at the kitchen table in three rooms in Mid-Levels, with the view of a wall, and put it in the folder. At the back. After the sixth place in the rain in 2022, and Bahrain, and Japan, and the Baizhang Pass, and a black car on the grid in December 2019. With the date in the corner in her handwriting.

And Granny Shum’s granddaughter sent it to Granny Shum, on her telephone, at seven in the morning, in her kitchen in the industrial district, where she was sitting with her thermos and her scanner turned down low. Granny Shum looked at it.

“The taxi,” she said. “He smiled.”

“He’s smiling at her,” said her granddaughter.

“I can see who he’s smiling at.” Granny Shum gave the phone back. “Send her a clementine,” she said. “To the garage. Under the bridge.” She drank her tea. “Tell her she was lucky ten times. And that’s enough.”

chapters.title: A Garage With Two Names on the Door
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Two years on. The garage under the railway bridge has a sign at last. There’s a team, and a junior driver who used to film from a car roof, and three postcards on the whiteboard. One of them has a football drawn on it, and a number. And at three in the morning, someone different is driving the loop.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s got a sign now. Two names. Nobody’s ever going to walk past it again.” — Big Wu
chapters.content:
For eleven years the garage under the railway bridge had no sign.

That had been the point of it. You found it, or you didn’t. A steel shutter at the end of a street of shuttered workshops, half up, with light coming out from under it and music, very loud, and the smell of petrol and hot metal and something frying. You came because somebody had told you. Granny Shum, or Big Wu’s cousin, or a man under the flyover by the fish market. You ducked under the shutter and you didn’t ask questions.

Now there was a sign.

It went up on a Saturday in October, the third Saturday, two years to the week after the first podium. Raiden drew it. Jinx cut it, from a sheet of steel, with a plasma torch, in her garage near the Docks, and brought it on the back of her bike with Raiden riding pillion holding it over his head like a surfboard. Big Wu and Beppe put it up, on two brackets over the shutter, under the railway bridge, while a train went over and shook the whole street and both of them held on to the ladder and swore.

It was very plain. Black steel. Two names, side by side, in letters that were not quite the same. One set big and untidy and fast, with the S going off the edge. The other set small and square, each letter separate, like something typed.

SONG & QIN.

Big Wu stood in the street and looked at it for a long time with his hands on his hips.

“It’s got a sign now,” he said. “Two names.” He wiped his nose on his sleeve. “Nobody’s ever going to walk past it again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a team.

Not Team AURELIA, though the name was still on the bonnet of every car they ran, in gold, in the same serif letters that were painted over the door of 18 Harbour Road. Aurelia had made sure. Song & Qin Racing. Two cars in the Asian GT series, red, with a small grey taxi on every driver’s door under three coats of lacquer. One for Serafina, who was thirty-one, and three-times a winner in the series since the outside of the Needle, and who still braked on the marker, to the metre, every time. One for whoever was fast enough.

Whoever was fast enough was called Tsang Ho-yin.

He was twenty-two. He had won thirty-one races in a row at Granny Shum’s in a purple Nissan with a wing the size of a dining table, and filmed every one of them, and then one night in 2026 he’d come to the garage under the railway bridge with his hood up and his hands in his pockets and stood under the shutter until somebody noticed him. Serafina noticed him. He said he wanted to stop. He said he’d watched the video of a taxi braking at the second lamp post eleven million times and he didn’t want to be on a road at three in the morning when he was thirty. He said page nine. He’d read about page nine.

So they taught him.

Mouse taught him the data. Big Wu taught him what was under the car. Haozhen taught him the mirrors: every eleven seconds, he said, not every four, and look at the right person. Serafina taught him the Needle. On the marker. To the metre. Third time you thread it.

He was very good. He was, Donatella Ferri said, when she came out from Modena in the spring to look at him, chewing, very nearly as good as the girl had been at his age, and much better behaved, which was not difficult.

They still called him Ghost Pepper. He’d asked them to stop. Nobody had.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mouse ran the engineering.

She had a desk at the back of the garage, by the stairs to the loft, with five screens now instead of three, and a door on her office that she closed, and a sign on the door that said CHIEF ENGINEER that Callum Hart had made for her as a joke in 2027, which she had kept. She spoke to four people. Serafina. Aurelia, in more than single words now. Ghost Pepper, about telemetry, in sentences. And Haozhen.

Not often. Not much. But when she did, it was always the same way. Very quiet. Straight at him. One or two words.

Good. Again. Check the rear. Haozhen.

Big Wu ran everything else. He had a clipboard now. He hated the clipboard. He carried it everywhere.

Mr. Kwok was seventy-seven. He did not drive the transporter. He did not go to the circuits. He came to the garage under the railway bridge every morning at nine, as he always had, with the shopping, and cooked lunch for whoever was there in a wok big enough to bath a child in, and went home at six to see the evening news to be sure he was still alive. On Sundays he went to the breakwater with his fishing box and caught nothing and was very happy about it.

Brake was old. He slept under the workbench on a heated bed that Mouse had wired herself, and when the trains went over he didn’t even lift his head, and every morning at seven he got up, and went to the shutter, and lay down across the doorway, and everyone who came in had to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Haozhen ran the team.

He hadn’t meant to. It had happened the way most things had happened to him since a ballroom on Battery Hill: by somebody else deciding, and him finding, when he looked, that he wanted it. He did the money, and the contracts, which he read the way he had once read folders, all the way through, every line, and then Aurelia read them again. He did the travel. He did the security, which at a two-car team in the Asian GT series meant mostly making sure that nobody’s room number was on a whiteboard and that Ghost Pepper did not post his breakfast with the location on.

And he did the data. On the pit wall. On a stool at the end. With four lines.

He did one other thing. In the far corner of the garage, under the railway bridge, where the tarpaulin had once been, there was a long low red car with a tail like a shark’s and a name on its nose in small square letters. TWO HUNDRED. He kept it. He kept its brakes. Every month, on the first Sunday, he took the wheels off and checked the pads and the discs and the fluid and put it all back, very slowly, by himself, with Big Wu watching from the stool by the kettle and saying nothing at all.

It had done two hundred miles an hour once. At the end of a runway in the north, at three in the morning, on a wedding night.

It had never done it again. It never needed to.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were three postcards on the whiteboard.

They were pinned round the old one, the hand-tinted photograph of the banking at Monza, which was still in the middle where she’d put it in March 2023. Beside the photograph from Harbour Road. Beside the framed sheet of paper that said EXCESSIVE MIRROR CHECKS. Beside a photograph from the front of the sports pages of a man in a green shirt, soaked in champagne, smiling up at somebody you couldn’t see.

The first postcard had come in the spring of 2027.

It was a photograph of a beach somewhere warm, very blue, with a single palm tree and a man in the far distance at the edge of the water, too small to see, with what might have been a walking stick. On the back, in a handwriting from a dormitory of forty boys under a leaking roof, in pencil:

Resigned. One sentence. Took me four years. The chilli crab here is terrible. Window seat’s free if you’re ever passing. — T.

The second had come in the summer of the same year, with no picture at all. Just a plain card in an envelope from a town by the sea three hundred kilometres up the coast, and inside it, taped to the card, a small paper packet of tomato seeds. No note. No name. A neat, small, sloping hand on the envelope that he recognised from eleven years of folders.

He’d planted them. In a pot. On the windowsill of the loft, over the railway. They’d come up. They were very sour.

And the third had come in September. This September. Three weeks ago.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was from Lisbon.

A photograph of a steep street in the old part of the city, going down toward the river, with a yellow tram on it and, on the corner, a narrow yellow house with green shutters and a front faced in blue and white tiles, old ones, a pattern of ships. There were geraniums in the window box on the first floor. They had been watered.

On the back, in an accountant’s small neat hand, in Mandarin:

Mr. Qin. I don’t know your real name. I was told this one by a man from the embassy who said you’d asked for me to come home. I came home. My wife has stopped writing letters to the embassy. My son is sixteen now. He is taller than me. He asked me to send you this.

And under it, in a different hand, a boy’s, in blue biro, in Portuguese, and then, underneath, very carefully, as if copied letter by letter from something somebody had written out for him, in Mandarin:

32.

And a drawing. A football. Round, a little lopsided, with the black patches drawn in very hard so the pen had gone through the card in one place.

He had stood at the whiteboard with it, on the day it came. Three weeks ago. A Tuesday. With his hand flat on his chest, on the left side, over the inside pocket, where once there had been a brass tyre gauge and a cream card and a page torn from a notebook, and where now there was a folded piece of paper from a registry office with a red stamp on it.

Serafina had come and stood beside him.

She’d read it. She’d looked at the number.

“He got there,” she said.

“Thirty-two,” said Qin Haozhen.

She didn’t say anything else. She took his hand, the left one, and turned it over, palm up, and looked at it, the way he’d once looked at hers on the bonnet of a red Lancia outside a laundry, and kissed the inside of his wrist, once, where the pulse was. Then she pinned the postcard on the whiteboard, next to the banking at Monza, where she would have to look at it every day.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had been to Monza. In 2027, in May, between rounds, on the way home from the factory in Modena. She’d walked him up the old banking, the great concrete curve tilted up like a wall, in the rain. She’d run up it. She was twenty-nine. She did not slide down.

He’d stood at the bottom and watched her go up, to the top, where it was steepest, and stand there in the rain with her arms out, and shout something down at him in Italian that he didn’t need translated.

Then he’d walked up after her. Slowly. Checking the mirrors that weren’t there every eleven seconds. All the way to the top.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother came to the garage on Sundays now.

Not every Sunday. Most. In a navy coat, not three seasons old any more, and flat shoes, and a single string of pearls. She sat on the stool by the kettle, his stool, which he gave her without being asked, and drank hot water from the plain mug that said HIS, because she said tea was for people who had something to prove, and she watched her daughter under a car. She didn’t say anything about it. She brought a folder, sometimes, and scissors, and sat at the end of the bench beside Mouse and cut things out of newspapers.

His mother had moved to the city. In the spring. To two rooms above the laundry in the old harbour streets behind the market, where he’d once lived with no curtains. She had curtains. She had made them. She had a Japanese sewing machine by the window and thirty spools of silk thread on the sill in the order of the rainbow, and on Tuesdays and Thursdays she came to the garage and sewed the sponsor patches onto the race suits by hand, very small, very straight, and told everybody they were doing it wrong. The laundry woman’s cat slept on her feet.

The two mothers had met at the engagement dinner, and sat side by side in Block C, and had still never been alone in a room together. That happened on a Sunday in April this year, at the stool by the kettle, when Liang Shufen came in with a race suit over her arm and found Vittoria Song sitting on it. They looked at each other, both of them very small, both of them very straight.

Then Vittoria got up and gave her the stool.

And Liang Shufen said, “Sit down. We’ll share. There’s a box.”

There wasn’t a box. Haozhen went and got one.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning, she couldn’t sleep.

It didn’t happen often any more. It happened sometimes. After a race. After a podium, or a fourth place, or a sixth in the rain. Her body still running at the speed of the circuit while the rest of her lay in the loft over the garage with the window open onto the tracks, counting trains. Seven. Eight.

“Sera,” he said, beside her, in the dark. He was awake. He always knew.

“I can’t sleep.”

He was quiet for a moment.

Then he got up. He got dressed. He went down the stairs. She heard him in the garage, by the kettle; she heard him pick up his mug, and put it down again, exactly where it had been. She heard the shutter go up, very slowly, so it wouldn’t wake the street. She heard an engine start. Old. Italian. A four-cylinder with a turbo that whistled at the top of second and had three hundred and sixty thousand kilometres on it now and a gearbox that had been rebuilt seven times.

She went down the stairs in her vest and shorts with the quilt round her shoulders. The one with the mountain road on it, and the small red car at the hundred and twelfth corner.

Nonna was in the middle of the garage under the hanging lamp, with her engine running and the dent still in her driver’s door, because nobody had ever fixed it.

He was in the driver’s seat.

He’d moved it forward two notches. He’d adjusted both mirrors. He was sitting with his hands on the wheel at a quarter to three. He leaned across, and opened the passenger door, and looked at her.

“Get in,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ll drive.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove the loop.

Gently. The way you’d rock something. No hard braking. No turbo. The engine burbling in third. Out from under the railway bridge, past the sign with two names on it, down out of the industrial district at three in the morning, along the harbour road past the container terminals where the cranes stood up over the water like enormous patient animals. Over the old bridge. Through the tunnel under the harbour and out the other side and round the long empty loop of the coast road, the sea black on one side and the city on the other, every window lit, every tower, and the ferries going back and forth across the dark water like slow lamps.

She sat in the passenger seat with the quilt round her and her bare feet up on the dashboard and watched him drive.

He drove like someone signing his name. No flourishes. Every letter exactly where it belonged.

Somewhere on the coast road, she felt her head get heavy.

She didn’t fight it. She let it go. She felt it tip, slowly, sideways, off the window, toward him, and she felt him feel it coming, and at the place on the coast road where for six years his head had slid off the window onto her shoulder, she felt him drop his right shoulder a fraction, just a fraction, to catch it.

Her head went onto his shoulder.

He didn’t move it by a millimetre. Not on the bends. Not at the lights. He drove the long loop round the harbour, bridge, tunnel, coast road, with the weight of her head on his shoulder and her breath slow and even and warm through his shirt, and the sky beginning, very faintly, to go grey over the water, and he thought that this was harder than anything. Much harder than a door. Much harder than a stairwell, or a tunnel, or a gap a hand’s width wider than a car.

He thought that if he could do this, he could do anything.

“How long?” she said, much later, without opening her eyes, when the sky had gone grey and the ferries had stopped and he’d pulled in under the railway bridge, under the sign, and turned off the engine.

The engine ticked.

“Two hours,” said Qin Haozhen, “and eleven minutes.”

She smiled into his shoulder.

“You timed it.”

“I count everything,” he said. “Someone taught me.” He put his hand on her hair. “Go back to sleep, Sera. We’re home. Nobody’s going anywhere.”

And she did, in the passenger seat, with her head on his shoulder and the quilt round both of them, and he sat in the driver’s seat of a thirty-six-year-old Lancia under a sign with two names on it, with his hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, and didn’t move, and watched her sleep until the first train of the morning went over and shook the whole building, and she didn’t wake, and neither of them wanted anything else at all.

— The End —

chapters.title: Haozhen Learns to Lose at Karaoke
chapters.desc: December 2023. The team Christmas, in a karaoke room above Mr. Kwok’s favourite bar. Big Wu scores forty-one. Mr. Kwok sings for his late wife. And a man who has spent eleven years being forgettable tries very hard to sing badly, and she catches him lifting at the gas works.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re lifting.” “I’m not.” “You’re singing flat on purpose. I can hear it. Sing like yourself.”
chapters.content:
Mr. Kwok’s favourite bar was called the Golden Phoenix and it had been on the corner by the tram depot since 1978, and upstairs, up a staircase carpeted in something red that had once been velvet, it had four karaoke rooms, and the team Christmas had been in the second one every year since 2019.

“Every year,” said Big Wu, on the stairs. “Every year since Sera’s sister paid for the gearbox. Room two. It’s got the good microphone.”

“What happens?”

Big Wu looked at him.

“I sing,” he said, darkly. “And the machine gives me a score. And Mouse records it. And then my mother watches it on Lunar New Year and laughs until she has to lie down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Room two had a sofa round three walls, black leather, split in places and mended with gaffer tape. A low table. A screen the size of a door. A machine on a trolley with a book of songs as thick as a telephone directory, and two microphones, one of which had a crack in it and was the good one. On the wall there was a framed photograph from 1994 of a young Mr. Kwok in a white suit with a woman in a red dress, both holding microphones, both laughing.

“My wife,” said Mr. Kwok, sitting down under it. “She sang better. I sang louder.”

Mr. Kwok’s daughter had sent a box of mince pies from Vancouver by express post, because she said that was what Christmas was in the West, and Mr. Kwok had brought them up the stairs in a plastic bag and put them on the table next to a plate of salt-and-pepper squid and four bottles of beer and a bottle of Chinotto for Mouse. Nobody ate the mince pies. Big Wu tried one and put it down very carefully, the way he had once put down a crate of oil in front of a row of car parts on a workbench.

Big Wu sang first. He always did. He sang a power ballad from the eighties, at the very top of his enormous voice, with his eyes closed and one hand on his chest, and he was so bad that somebody in room three banged on the wall.

The machine gave him forty-one.

“Forty-one,” said Big Wu, with satisfaction. “That’s my best.”

“It’s your worst,” said Serafina.

“It’s my best for honesty,” said Big Wu, and sat down, and Mouse, at the end of the sofa, stopped recording and saved the file in a folder on her phone with no name.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Kwok sang second.

He chose an old Cantonese ballad from 1989, slow, the kind that had been on every radio in every taxi in the city the year he bought his first cab. He didn’t stand up. He sat on the sofa under the photograph of the young man in the white suit and the woman in red, with the good microphone in both hands, and sang it quietly, a little out of tune, in a thin, steady, careful voice, looking at the screen and not at any of them.

Nobody talked.

When he finished, the machine gave him sixty-eight. He put the microphone down on the table, very gently, beside the mince pies.

“She’d have given me eighty,” he said. “She always gave me twenty extra. For trying.”

Serafina, beside him, put her head on his shoulder. He let it stay there, the way nobody in her own family had ever let anybody’s head stay anywhere, until somebody started the next song.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina sang third. She sang everything third.

She sang an Italian song from the seventies that Nonna used to sing in the kitchen in Milan, very fast and very loud, standing on the sofa in her boots, conducting the room with a mince pie, and the machine gave her seventy-nine and she called it a fascist. Then she sang a song by a British band from the nineties, which she did not know the words to and sang anyway, and the machine gave her fifty-two and she called it worse things, in three languages.

Then she held out the good microphone.

“Your turn.”

He was sitting at the far end of the sofa, by the door, with his back to the wall and his hot water in a beer glass, where he had been since they arrived. It was December. It was the twenty-third. Two weeks since a woman in a grey coat had sat on his stool and left a file on the bench. Nine days until the New Year, when a door was supposed to close. He’d been very quiet, for two weeks.

“No,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I don’t sing.”

“You sing in the shower,” said Serafina. “When you think I’m asleep. I told your director. She didn’t know. I’ve been dying to tell somebody else ever since.”

Big Wu turned round on the sofa and looked at him.

“He sings?”

“In the shower. Every morning. Very quietly. With the tap running so I won’t hear.” Serafina pushed the microphone at him. “I hear.”

He looked at the microphone for a while. Then at her, standing on the sofa in her boots with her hair in spikes and a mince pie in her other hand, grinning at him.

He took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He chose the song very carefully. She watched him do it, turning the pages of the thick book slowly, the way he’d turned the pages of the Lisbon folder in a tea house in May. It was a Mandarin song. Old. Slow. Something from before any of them were born, about a moon, and a river, and somebody waiting by a window. The kind of song a seamstress in a mining town might have had on the radio in 1994 while she worked.

He stood up. He held the microphone in his right hand, very correctly, at the right distance from his mouth, the way you’d hold it if you had read about it in a manual.

The music started.

He sang.

And he was terrible.

Not Big Wu terrible. Not loud or wild or out of the room. He was flat. Carefully, exactly, a fraction flat, on every note, all the way through the first verse, in a small dry forgettable voice that slid off the walls of room two like rain off a windscreen. The kind of voice you’d hear in a lift and couldn’t describe to the police five minutes later. Big Wu, on the sofa, winced. Mr. Kwok looked politely at the screen.

On the screen, the little line that showed the right note bobbed along, and the little line that showed his note sat just underneath it, all the way along, perfectly parallel, never once touching.

Serafina, on the sofa, stopped eating her mince pie.

She knew that line. She’d seen it before. Not on a karaoke screen. In a mirror, on a straight past a container yard, at three in the morning: a grey estate car sitting a length behind her, exactly a length, as if painted on, all the way down to the gas works.

At the end of the first verse she stood up on the sofa and pointed the mince pie at him.

“You’re lifting,” she said.

He stopped. The music went on without him.

“I’m not.”

“You’re singing flat. On purpose. Look at it.” She jabbed the mince pie at the screen. “Look at your line. It’s under the right one the whole way. Exactly under it. The same distance under it. Nobody sings flat by the same amount on every note, Haozhen. That’s not bad singing. That’s braking at the second lamp post.”

Mouse, at the end of the sofa, had started recording again.

He stood in the middle of room two with the good microphone in his hand and looked at her for a long moment. Then at the screen. At the two little lines, one exactly under the other, all the way along.

“It’s noticeable,” he said, at last.

“What’s noticeable?”

“If I sing properly,” said Qin Haozhen. “It’s noticeable. People remember a voice.” He looked at the microphone. “I’ve spent eleven years making sure nobody would.”

The room went quiet. The music had reached the second verse. Nobody was singing it.

Serafina got down off the sofa.

She walked across room two, between the low table and the screen, and stood in front of him, and took the microphone out of his hand, and held it, and looked at him.

“Nobody’s taking notes in here,” she said. “It’s Big Wu and Mr. Kwok and Mouse. And me. We already remember you.” She held the microphone out again. “Sing like yourself. Or you never come in my karaoke room again.”

He looked at her.

Then something happened at the corner of his mouth. He took the microphone back.

Mr. Kwok, without being asked, reached over to the machine and started the song again from the beginning.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sang it properly.

She would never be able to describe it. She tried, to Aurelia, at Lunar New Year, and failed, and Aurelia said, show me, and Mouse showed her, on her phone, from the folder with no name, and Aurelia watched it twice and then sat very still for a minute and said, oh.

It was low. That was the first thing. Much lower than his speaking voice, and warm, and very clear, the way the brass gauge had read true when the cheap ones didn’t. He didn’t sing loudly. He didn’t need to. He sang the song about the moon and the river and somebody waiting by a window in a voice that filled room two the way the engine of the grey estate had once filled the S-bends by the paint works, completely, without strain, with nothing extra, every note exactly where it belonged.

On the screen, the two little lines lay one on top of the other, all the way along. Touching. The same line.

Big Wu had his mouth open.

Mr. Kwok had taken off his glasses.

And Serafina stood in front of him in the middle of the room with her hand pressed flat over her mouth, because he was singing it to her. He wasn’t looking at the screen. He’d never looked at the screen. He was looking at her, all the way in, the way he’d looked at her across a ballroom on Battery Hill at nine twenty-two, and he was singing a song about somebody waiting by a window as if he had been waiting by one for a very long time, and had just seen somebody coming up the road.

When it ended, nobody moved.

The machine thought about it. Then a number came up on the screen in gold, with fireworks.

98.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu cried. Of course he did.

Mr. Kwok put his glasses back on and looked at the photograph on the wall of the young man in the white suit and the woman in red, and said, to the photograph, “She’d have given him a hundred and eighteen,” and then got up and went downstairs to the bar.

Mouse saved the file.

And Serafina took the microphone out of his hand, and put it on the table beside the mince pies, and took his face in both her hands and kissed him, in room two of the Golden Phoenix, in front of Big Wu crying, until Big Wu threw a mince pie at them.

“You can sing,” she said, against his mouth.

“No.”

“Ninety-eight.”

“The machine’s broken,” said Qin Haozhen. “It gave Big Wu forty-one.”

“That’s the only number it’s ever got right,” said Big Wu, through his handkerchief.

✦ ✦ ✦

He never admitted it.

Not once. Not at Lunar New Year, when Big Wu’s mother watched the video four times and then made him sing it again at the table. Not at the engagement dinner, when Granny Shum asked. Not at the wedding, when two hundred people banged on the tables and chanted his name and he stood up, very red, and sang it again, the song about the moon and the river, to the woman in the white dress and boots beside him, and the trains went over every eleven minutes, and nobody minded.

“It’s not a good voice,” he said, every time.

“Ninety-eight,” she said, every time.

“The machine was broken.”

But in the mornings, in the shower in the garage under the railway bridge, with the tap running, he went on singing. And he stopped bothering to sing flat. And she lay in the loft with her eyes closed and listened, and didn’t tell him she could hear every note.

chapters.title: Serafina Teaches Him to Change a Tyre
chapters.desc: December 2022, the week after the track day. She decides that any man who sits in her passenger seat should be able to change a wheel. He says he’s never done it. She times him: fourteen minutes. Then, one wet night in the alley, she sees him do it in ninety seconds.
chapters.epigraph: “You lied to me.” “I said I’d never done it in your garage. I’d never done it in your garage.”
chapters.content:
“Can you change a tyre?” she said.

It was the Wednesday after the track day. He was on the stool by the kettle with his plain mug, the one she’d written HIS on in marker two days before and which he had turned round to face the wall, and she was on the floor beside Nonna with the car up on axle stands, because the front left had picked up a nail on the way back from the circuit.

He looked at the wheel.

“I’ve never done it,” he said, “in your garage.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“It’s what I answered.”

She sat back on her heels and looked at him. He looked back with no expression at all, which she was beginning to understand was not the same as having no expression.

“Right,” said Serafina. “Off the stool. Anyone who sits in my passenger seat has to be able to change a wheel. It’s a rule.”

“Since when?”

“Since now. It’s my garage. I make them up as I go.” She held out the wheel brace. “Big Wu made my sister do it. In 2019. In heels. She was terrible. Fourteen minutes. By the end of the week she could do it in four.”

He got off the stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

She taught him properly.

She did it the way Big Wu had taught her at nineteen, on the floor of a different garage, with a Fiat built from two dead ones. Step by step, slowly, every step twice. She was very serious about it. She didn’t often get to teach anybody anything, and she found, kneeling on the cold concrete in her overalls with a wheel brace in her hand and a man she had kissed in a paddock four days ago kneeling beside her, that she liked it far more than she’d expected.

“Handbrake on. Always. Even on stands. Even if it’s on a lift. Even if God is holding it up personally.” She tapped his knee with the brace. “Say it.”

“Handbrake on.”

“Even if God—”

“Even if God is holding it up personally,” said Qin Haozhen.

“Good. Wheel nuts. You crack them before you lift it, not after, or the wheel just spins and you look like an idiot.” She fitted the brace onto the first nut. “Anticlockwise. Lefty loosey. Push down, don’t pull up, use your weight, not your arms. Like this.” She leaned on it. The nut cracked. “Your turn.”

He took the brace. He fitted it onto the second nut.

He did it wrong.

Not very wrong. Just a little. He put the brace on at a slightly awkward angle, so that when he pushed down it slipped, and he had to take it off and put it on again. Then he pushed up instead of down. Then he pushed down, but with his arms, not his weight, and the nut didn’t move, and he stopped and looked at her.

“Use your weight,” said Serafina.

“I am.”

“You’re not. You’re using your arms like a man opening a jam jar.” She took his hands and moved them along the brace, further out, toward the end, and put her own over them. “Here. Lean. Lean on it like it owes you money.”

He leaned. The nut cracked.

He looked at it as if it had surprised him.

“Better,” said Serafina, and didn’t take her hands off his for a little longer than she needed to.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took him fourteen minutes.

She timed it. Of course she timed it. On her phone, propped against the toolbox. Nuts. Jack. Wheel off. Wheel on. Nuts finger-tight, in a star, not round in a circle, because a circle pulls the wheel crooked. Jack down. Torque wrench. In a star again. Every one, to the number. Hubcap.

He did everything she told him, in exactly the order she told him, and he did all of it slightly wrong the first time and exactly right the second, and at the end she looked at the phone and laughed out loud.

“Fourteen minutes,” she said. “Exactly. The same as Lia.”

“Is that bad?”

“It’s terrible. She was in heels.” She took the torque wrench off him. “You’ll get better. Tomorrow you do it again. And the next day. By Friday you’ll be under five.”

“Will I?”

“Lia was,” said Serafina. “And she’s never touched an engine in her life. You drive like you do. You’ll be faster than her by Thursday.”

He looked at her for a moment, kneeling on the concrete beside the red car with oil on his hands and on his trousers, which she’d told him to change and he hadn’t, and something happened at the corner of his mouth.

“Then I’ll need a lot of practice,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came every night that week.

He changed Nonna’s front left every night. Then her front right. Then the rears. Then Gilded’s, which were different, with a single central nut and an air gun, and she had to teach him all over again, and he did it slightly wrong the first time and exactly right the second. Big Wu, who had come in on the Thursday at nine at night to get his jacket, stood in the doorway and watched him for a while with his arms folded.

“He’s slow,” said Big Wu.

“He’s learning.”

“He’s very slow,” said Big Wu, “for a man who drives like that,” and looked at Haozhen for a long time, and Haozhen looked back at him with no expression at all, and Big Wu grunted and took his jacket and went.

By Friday he was down to six minutes.

“Six,” said Serafina, delighted, looking at her phone. “Six. Lia did four by Friday.”

“I’m a slow learner.”

“You’re not a slow learner. I’ve watched you learn the Needle in one lap.” She narrowed her eyes at him. “You’re doing something.”

“I’m changing a tyre,” said Qin Haozhen. “You’re teaching me.”

She sat on the upturned crate and looked at him, at the wheel brace in his hands and the oil to his wrists and his face giving her nothing, and she didn’t know what it was. But she noticed that every time she leaned over him to move his hands along the brace, he let her. And that every time he did a step wrong, she had to show him again. And that he had done a great many steps wrong, all week, in a very particular way, and never the same step twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found out on the Sunday.

It was raining. The first real rain of the winter, cold and heavy, coming down on the railway bridge so hard you could hear it over the trains. He’d been in the garage since midnight. At two he went out to the alley to move the grey estate, because the gutter had blocked and the alley was flooding round its wheels, and she was at the bench with her back to the side door and heard him go out, and heard the engine start, and then heard it stop.

And then a sound she knew. A soft flat hiss.

She went to the side door.

The grey estate was halfway down the alley in the rain with its hazards going and its front right tyre flat to the rim, on something sharp in the gutter. He was already out. He was already at the boot. He had the spare out and the jack out and the brace out before she had opened the door properly.

She stood in the doorway in the light from the garage and watched him.

Handbrake: he’d put it on before he got out. She’d heard it. Nuts: cracked, all five, with the wheel still on the ground, one push each, with his weight, not his arms, without even looking. Jack: under the sill, in exactly the right place, in the dark, in the rain, by feel. Wheel off. Wheel on. Nuts in a star. Jack down. Nuts again, in a star, hard. Brace back in the boot. Flat tyre in the boot. Boot shut.

He stood up and wiped the rain off his face with his forearm.

She looked at her phone. She’d started it without thinking, the moment the hiss stopped.

1:31.

Ninety-one seconds. In the rain. In the dark. In an alley. On a car with four hundred kilos of steel in its doors.

He turned round and saw her in the doorway.

He went completely still.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You lied to me,” said Serafina.

He stood in the alley in the rain. The water was running off his hair into his collar. He didn’t move.

“I said I’d never done it in your garage,” he said. “I’d never done it in your garage.”

“Ninety-one seconds.”

“It’s in the training. Third year. You change them at night under a car park light with someone timing you, and if you’re over two minutes you do it again. If you’re over two minutes in the field,” he said, “you don’t get to do it again.”

“Then why did you let me teach you?”

He looked at her in the doorway, with the light behind her, in her overalls, with her phone in her hand.

“Because you were teaching me,” said Qin Haozhen.

She stared at him.

“You put your hands on mine on the brace,” he said. “Every time I did it wrong. You leaned over me and moved them. You said lean on it like it owes you money. You laughed when I did it in fourteen minutes. You said the same as Lia.” The rain was coming down between them. “I’ve had a lot of people teach me things, Sera. Since I was sixteen. Nobody ever put their hands on mine while they did it.” He paused. “I wanted another week.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she walked out into the rain.

It was freezing. It went straight through her overalls to the skin. She walked down the flooded alley through the water in her boots to where he was standing by the grey car with his hair plastered flat and his face giving her absolutely nothing at all, and she took his hands. Both of them. Black with oil and wet with rain.

She put them on her own face.

“You can just do that,” she said. “You don’t have to do the wheel wrong.”

He looked down at her, with his hands on her face, in the rain.

“I didn’t know that,” he said.

“Well, now you do,” said Serafina, and kissed him, in the alley, in the flood, in the freezing rain, until they were both soaked through and shaking and laughing, and Big Wu’s emergency torch, which she’d left on the bench, rolled off it onto the floor of the garage and lay there shining out of the side door at them, like a spotlight.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning, Big Wu found a new line on the whiteboard, under the number plate, in her large untidy capitals, in red.

Changes a tyre in 1:31. In the rain. LIAR.

He looked at it. Then he took the marker and wrote, underneath, in his own enormous slanting hand:

Told you he was slow on purpose.

chapters.title: The Security Guard Who Smiled Once
chapters.desc: August 2025, the Orsini paddock, as told by Callum Hart. There is a pool. Forty-one people have put money on who can make the head of security smile first. Callum tries jokes, a video of a goat, and an Italian mechanic in a wig. Witnesses are still recovering.
chapters.epigraph: “Has the security guy ever smiled?” “Once. On his pass photo. And we don’t know who at.” — the Orsini team group chat
chapters.content:
The pool was Beppe’s idea.

Beppe was the small bald mechanic who looked after the front of car seven, and had been at Orsini Corse for twenty-two years, and ran the betting on everything: who would crash in practice, how many espressos Donatella would drink before the race, whether Kenji Arakawa would ever be seen eating. He started the pool on the third Saturday in August, at the circuit in the south, in the heat, on a piece of cardboard torn off a tyre box, in the hospitality tent with its rear flap now zipped.

FIRST TO MAKE QIN SMILE, it said, in green marker. 20 EURO. NO TICKLING.

Forty-one people put in. Everybody on the team. The cooks. The other driver’s girlfriend. Kenji put in, which was the first time anybody had seen Kenji do anything that wasn’t data. Donatella put in fifty and said that was so she’d have a reason to fire whoever won.

Callum Hart put in a hundred.

“A hundred,” said Beppe, writing it down. “You are very confident.”

“I’m very charming,” said Callum. “Four hundred thousand people think so.”

“Four hundred thousand people,” said Beppe, “have never met the security.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Callum had been at Orsini for two seasons and he liked everybody, and everybody, mostly, liked him back, and it bothered him that he could not make the head of security like him.

It wasn’t that Qin was unpleasant. Qin was perfectly pleasant. He said good morning. He said thank you. He’d taken Callum’s room number off the whiteboard, and stopped him posting his breakfast with the location on, and once, in July, at three in the morning in a hotel in Japan, he’d knocked on Callum’s door and said, very politely, “Mr. Hart, there’s a woman in the corridor who’s been outside your room for forty minutes with a camera, would you like me to talk to her,” and Callum had said yes, and Qin had talked to her, and she had left, and Callum had never found out what he said.

It was that he never smiled.

Not at jokes. Not at Beppe, who was the funniest man in Modena. Not at Donatella, who was terrifying and hilarious in roughly equal measure. Not at the cooks, who loved him and fed him extra and called him il monaco, the monk. He stood at the back of the garage, or sat on his stool at the end of the pit wall with his four lines, and his face did nothing at all, all day, and when you looked at him he looked back at you for two or three seconds in a way that made you feel he was taking notes.

“There’s a photo,” said the other driver’s girlfriend, who was called Tamsin and was from Bath and did the team’s social media. “On his pass. He’s smiling in that. Slightly.”

“At who?”

“Nobody knows,” said Tamsin. “He won’t say. It was taken in the series office. Serafina was there. She won’t say either.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Callum’s first attempt was a joke.

He’d worked on it. He told it in the garage on the Saturday, after qualifying, to Qin, who was at the back by the laptops reading tyre temperatures, with six members of the team pretending not to listen. It was about a racing driver and a priest and a tyre that went to heaven, and it was quite a good joke, and Beppe laughed so hard at it that he dropped a wheel nut.

Qin looked up from the laptop.

“The tyre wouldn’t go to heaven,” he said. “It’d be recycled. Into playground surfaces, mostly. Or road base.”

He went back to the laptop.

Beppe, picking up the wheel nut, wrote on the cardboard, under Callum’s name: Attempt 1. Fail. Tyre recycled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second attempt was a goat.

Not a real goat. A video of a goat. Tamsin found it. It was a goat in Switzerland that had climbed onto the roof of a car and was standing on it, very proudly, while the car’s owner, a small furious man in shorts, tried to get it down with a broom, and every time he got close the goat jumped onto the bonnet, and then back onto the roof, and the man fell over. It had forty million views. Donatella had watched it eleven times and cried.

Callum showed it to Qin on his phone, on the pit wall, on the Sunday morning, before the race.

Qin watched it. All of it. Two minutes and fourteen seconds. With his full attention, the way he watched the data. At the end, he handed the phone back.

“The goat’s on a Fiat Panda,” he said. “A 2004. The roof’s not rated for that load. It’s denting. Look.” He took the phone back and paused it and pointed. “There. By the aerial. If the goat does that again, it’ll go through.”

Callum looked at the dent by the aerial.

“It’s a goat,” he said. “It’s funny. The goat is funny.”

“The goat is very funny,” agreed Qin, and handed the phone back, and his face did nothing at all.

Attempt 2. Fail. Goat structural.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third attempt was Beppe in a wig.

Nobody was ever entirely clear afterwards whose idea it was. It was a blond wig, long, from a party shop in Kuala Lumpur, and Beppe put it on in the drivers’ room in the motorhome between stints with a pair of sunglasses and a borrowed race suit with HART on the back, and came out into the garage doing Callum. He did Callum taking a selfie. He did Callum posting his breakfast. He did Callum saying “mate.” He did Callum being told by Donatella that he couldn’t post his breakfast any more, and sulking, with his lower lip out, and it was so exactly Callum that Kenji Arakawa had to sit down on a tyre and put his face in his hands, and Donatella laughed until she choked on her gum and had to be hit on the back.

Callum, who was in the car at the time doing the second stint, heard about it afterwards and was not offended, because it was objectively brilliant.

Qin had been on the pit wall.

He had turned round on his stool and watched Beppe do the whole thing, all four minutes of it, with his arms folded. Then he had turned back to his screen.

“Mr. Hart’s braking six metres late for turn four,” he’d said, to Kenji, on the team channel. “Every lap. He’s been doing it since Beppe came out of the motorhome. I think he can see the garage from turn three.”

Beppe took off the wig.

Attempt 3. Fail. Wig noted. Callum told off for turn four.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the Sunday afternoon, everybody had tried.

The cooks had tried: a cake in the shape of a padlock. Kenji had tried, very seriously, with a pun in Japanese that he translated, and then explained, and then translated again, and Qin listened to all three versions and said, “I see,” and Kenji went away looking relieved, as if he’d been let off. Tamsin had tried a photograph of a kitten in a tiny helmet. Donatella hadn’t tried, because she said fifty euro was fifty euro and she wasn’t going to embarrass herself, and then tried anyway, at lunch, by telling a story about 1983 that involved a cow, and a priest, and a Lancia, and was the funniest thing Callum had ever heard in his life, and Qin listened to the whole thing and said, “Was the cow all right?” and Donatella said, “No,” and that was that.

Forty attempts. Forty fails.

The cardboard was full. Beppe had started writing on the back of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened at five past five on Sunday, after the race.

They’d come fifth. The best result Orsini had had in Asia in three years. Callum had done the fourth stint with nothing left in the tyres and the brakes fading and had got out and lain down on the floor of the garage on the concrete in front of a fan with a cold towel on his face and said “inhuman” to nobody, and stayed there.

So he saw it from the floor.

The garage was full. The whole team. Shouting, laughing, Donatella hugging Kenji, Beppe running about with the cardboard. And Serafina came in from the back of the garage, from the paddock, from wherever she’d been after the race. She’d been gone for about eleven minutes. She was still in her race suit, unzipped to the waist, the sleeves tied round her middle, and she was flushed, and her hair was a disaster, worse than usual, flattened at the back and sticking up at the front, and there was a black smear of grease across her nose, and she was looking for somebody.

She found him. On his stool at the end of the pit wall, outside, by the open front of the garage, with his headset round his neck.

She didn’t say anything to him. She didn’t go over. She just stood in the middle of the garage, among forty-one people, and looked at him through the noise, and he looked back at her.

And she said one word. Not even loud. Callum, on the floor, only just heard it.

“Eleven,” she said.

And Qin Haozhen, head of security for Orsini Corse’s Asian operation, who had been unmoved by a tyre in heaven and a goat on a Fiat Panda and Beppe in a blond wig and a cow in 1983, sitting on his stool in a green shirt with his initial on it in the heat of a pit lane in the south, smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

Callum would try, afterwards, to describe it, and fail.

It wasn’t a big smile. That was the thing. It wasn’t a grin, or a laugh. It was quite small. It started at one corner of his mouth and went across his face slowly, the way the sun comes across a track in the morning, and it went all the way, and it stayed. And it changed his whole face. Completely. It took everything that face had been doing all weekend, all season, the nothing, the notes, the two-or-three-second look that made you feel measured, and it simply wasn’t there any more. What was there instead was a man about Callum’s own age, quite young, actually, younger than Callum had thought, looking at a woman with grease on her nose as though she was the only thing in the whole paddock worth the trouble of watching.

The garage went completely silent.

Beppe dropped the cardboard.

Kenji, who had been hugged by Donatella, stopped being hugged and turned round to look.

Tamsin, who did the social media, lifted her phone, and then lowered it, without taking the photograph, and told Callum afterwards that she couldn’t explain why, it just felt like the kind of thing you didn’t.

Then Serafina laughed, and walked out of the back of the garage again, and he got up off his stool and followed her, and the smile was still there when he went past Callum on the floor, and he looked down at him, and said, quite kindly, “Good stint, Mr. Hart. Turn four was better,” and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody won the pool.

Beppe ruled on it that night in the hospitality tent. Nobody on the cardboard had made him smile. Serafina wasn’t on the cardboard. Serafina hadn’t put in twenty euro. So the pool stood. Nine hundred and twenty euro, in a coffee tin, in the second transporter, under the whiteboard that said Ask Qin.

They gave it to Mouse in the end. In December. She’d never put in either. She had never needed to. She had spoken to him once, people said. One word. After the wire.

Callum asked Serafina, much later, at the wedding, in April, at table nine. What eleven meant. Why it had worked.

She looked at him over her glass for a long time.

“Minutes,” she said. “Donatella gave us ten. In the motorhome.” She drank. “He’d said we’d need eleven.”

Callum thought about that.

Then he put his face in his hands at table nine, at the wedding, and laughed until Mouse, who was sitting next to him folding a napkin into a rabbit, reached over without looking up and patted him on the head.

chapters.title: Who Is Faster: Serafina or Jinx’s Bike?
chapters.desc: August 2024. An argument at Lunar New Year that has been going on for seven months. A track day, the main straight at the circuit in the north, a matte black car and a motorbike Jinx built from nothing. Everybody has a bet. Raiden is holding the money, which is the first mistake.
chapters.epigraph: “Off the line, it’s the bike. Over a kilometre, it’s the car. Over a whole lap, it’s whoever’s angrier.” — Big Wu
chapters.content:
It started at Lunar New Year, at the round table in the tall old house in the Walled City, at the Lin family dinner, over the fish.

Serafina hadn’t meant to start it. She’d been invited for the first time. Raiden had asked her, because Jinx had asked him, because Elowen had said that anyone who’d built a getaway car in her sister-in-law’s garage was family whether they liked it or not, and Serafina had come in her red jumper with a box of pastries and sat between Jinx and a silent woman called Evangeline, who had looked at her once and then passed her the vinegar before she’d asked for it.

And Jinx had said, with her mouth full, over the fish, which Serafina was hiding under her rice:

“My bike would beat you.”

“Which bike?”

“The new one. The black one. I finished it in January. It does nought to a hundred in two point eight.”

“Gilded does it in three point one,” said Serafina. “With a driver change and a full tank.”

“So my bike would beat you.”

“Off the line,” said Serafina. “For about a hundred metres. And then I’d come past you on the straight like you were parked.”

Jinx put down her chopsticks.

Raiden, beside her, said “Oh no,” very quietly, and then, louder, cheerfully, to the whole table, “Darling, should we perhaps not do this at your father-in-law’s—”

“Is that a challenge?” said Jinx.

“It’s a fact,” said Serafina.

At the head of the table, Lin Jian put his face in his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on for seven months.

It went on through the spring, and the night in the car wash, and the tunnel, and the two weeks in the mountains, and the tea house in the old town with the stove. It went on in Jinx’s garage near the Docks when they brought Nobody back with two holes in it, through Jinx crying behind the roll-up door with the radio on loud. Every time they met. Every phone call. Every text, which arrived at three in the morning and said things like 2.8 and 3.1 WITH A DRIVER CHANGE and my bike doesn’t need a driver change it has a driver.

In June, Haozhen asked, very reasonably, why they didn’t just find out.

They both looked at him as if he had suggested something indecent.

“Because then it would be over,” said Serafina.

“Because then one of us would have to be wrong,” said Jinx.

“Then don’t,” said Qin Haozhen. “Leave it. It’s very good for the electricity in the group chat.”

In July, Raiden suggested it again. He suggested a date. He suggested a place. He suggested it in the group chat that the wives had and the husbands were not in, which he had somehow got himself added to by Eliana, and which he was removed from by Elowen within forty seconds.

On the first of August, Jinx sent a message to Serafina with no words in it. Just a photograph. The circuit in the north’s calendar for the month, with a track day circled in red on the second Saturday, and, under it, a drawing of a skull.

Serafina replied with a drawing of a car running over the skull.

✦ ✦ ✦

So on the second Saturday in August, at nine in the morning, at the circuit in the north, there were more people in the paddock for a track day than there had been for some race weekends.

Big Wu was there, and Mouse, with her laptop and a pair of timing beams that she had set up herself at the start line and at four hundred metres and at a thousand. Mr. Kwok was there, with the camping stove. Granny Shum’s granddaughter was there, with the white scarf, because Granny Shum had said that if it was a race it would be done properly. Elowen was there in green, with Zhao, in black, who had driven her up and who stood at the pit wall with his arms folded looking at Jinx’s bike for four seconds and said “Hm,” and Elowen said, “He says it’s beautiful and that if she falls off it he’ll be very upset,” and Zhao said, “Hm,” again, and Elowen said, “Very.”

Aurelia came. In gold, every piece, in white, with her husband in camel. She stood at the pit wall with Elowen, the two of them not looking at each other in a way that took enormous effort, and said, “Serafina, obviously,” without being asked, and Elowen said, “Jinx,” without being asked, and then they both said, at exactly the same time, “That’s a point,” and stopped, and looked at each other, furious.

And Raiden was holding the money.

He’d volunteered. He had a biscuit tin, a big round one with a picture of a Scottish castle on the lid, and a notebook, and a pencil behind his ear, and an expression of sunny, total innocence that Elowen had once told Serafina she’d learned to fear when he was nine.

“Bets,” he said, cheerfully, walking up and down the pit wall with the tin. “Bets, ladies and gentlemen. The bike or the car. Off the line, over four hundred, or over a kilometre. Any combination. All money to me.” He shook the tin. “I’ll keep it very safe.”

Chen Si put in a thousand. On the car, over a kilometre.

Zhao put in a thousand. On the bike, off the line.

Aurelia put in two thousand, on the car, over everything, and looked at Elowen.

Elowen put in two thousand and one, on the bike, over everything, and looked back.

Big Wu put in forty, on the car, because he’d built it. Mouse didn’t put anything in, because she was the timing and it would be unethical, she said, to Serafina, in a whisper. Mr. Kwok put in twenty on the bike, because he said that in 1973 he had owned a motorbike and it had been the best year of his life and the car had not been invented yet that could make him feel that way again.

Haozhen didn’t bet.

“Why not?” said Raiden, shaking the tin at him.

“Because I know who’s going to win,” said Qin Haozhen.

Raiden looked at him with great interest.

“Who?”

“I can’t tell you that,” said Haozhen, and Raiden laughed so hard he had to put the tin down.

✦ ✦ ✦

They lined up at nine forty, on the main straight, at the start line, under a hard white August sky.

Gilded, matte black, number seven, the gold name on the bonnet and the small grey taxi on the door. And beside it, Jinx’s bike. Black too. Low, long, and impossibly thin, a single wheel at each end and an engine in the middle like a fist, every centimetre of it built by hand in a garage near the Docks from parts Jinx had made herself, with a carp painted on the fuel tank swimming toward a spark plug, the same as the one on the inside of her left forearm.

Jinx sat on it in black leathers with her helmet on and her visor up and looked across at Serafina in the cockpit of the car.

“Last chance,” she said.

“For what?”

“To say my bike’s faster.”

“Your bike’s beautiful,” said Serafina. “It’s the most beautiful thing on two wheels I’ve ever seen. It’s going to be beautiful in my mirror.”

Jinx dropped her visor.

Granny Shum’s granddaughter walked out between them with the white scarf. She looked at them both. She raised her hand.

“No contact,” she said. “No crying.”

The scarf came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bike won off the line.

Of course it did. It was nought to a hundred in two point eight, with a woman on it who weighed fifty-one kilos and had built every bolt. It left the line like something fired out of a gun, the front wheel lifting a hand’s width off the tarmac and Jinx leaning over it, flat, tucked in, and the noise of it, a scream that went right up the scale and stayed there, and Gilded, beside it, simply couldn’t go as fast as that, not in the first hundred metres, nothing on four wheels could. The bike was a length ahead at fifty metres. Two lengths at a hundred.

At four hundred metres, Mouse’s beam said, the bike was ahead by point three of a second.

On the pit wall, Zhao Zhendong unfolded his arms.

And then the car came.

At three hundred metres the black car had found all its grip and all its gears and all the air it was going to push out of the way, and the bike had found the end of its gearing, short, built for the Docks road, topping out not far past two hundred and forty, with nothing to hold it down but a woman in leathers, and the car began to close. Not fast. Steadily. A metre every second. Half a length at five hundred. Level at six hundred and fifty, the two of them side by side down the long main straight under the grandstand, the black car and the black bike, a hand’s width apart, at two hundred and forty.

At seven hundred, the car went past.

At a thousand metres, Mouse’s beam said, the car was ahead by point six of a second.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came back up the pit lane together, slowly, the bike and the car, side by side, and stopped in front of the pit wall.

Jinx took off her helmet. Her hair was flat and her face was red and she was furious.

“Off the line,” she said. “Off the line. Point three. You saw it.”

Serafina climbed out of the car and pulled off her helmet.

“Over a kilometre,” she said. “Point six. Double. You saw that.”

“Nobody races over a kilometre—”

“Everybody races over a kilometre, that’s what a straight is—”

“The bet,” said Raiden, very loudly and cheerfully, from the pit wall, holding up the Scottish biscuit tin, “was the bike or the car, and as you can see, ladies and gentlemen, it was both. The bike won off the line. The car won over a kilometre. Nobody won over four hundred, because Mouse says that’s technically the bike but she wants to look at the data, and Mouse isn’t betting. So.” He shook the tin. “Since it’s both, and nobody’s entirely right, and everybody’s partly wrong, I’m declaring a draw. And as the holder of the money, in the event of a draw, I’m entitled to a fee.” He tucked the tin under his arm. “For drawing.”

Everybody looked at him.

“Drawing what?” said Elowen.

“The race,” said Raiden. He took a sheet of paper out of his jacket and held it up. It was a drawing. In pencil, very fine, every bolt and spoke. The bike and the car, side by side, at seven hundred metres, at the exact moment the car went past, a hand’s width apart, with the grandstand behind them and the two drivers’ helmets turned toward each other. He’d done it on the pit wall in the forty seconds the race had taken. “That one. It’s very good. It’s worth at least six thousand and sixty-one euro.” He smiled. “I’ll frame it for you.”

There was a pause.

“Raiden,” said Elowen.

“Darling,” said Raiden, to his sister, very lovingly, and ran.

Zhao Zhendong watched his brother-in-law run down the pit lane with a Scottish biscuit tin under his arm full of six thousand and sixty-one euro and a drawing in his other hand, and Jinx running after him in her leathers, screaming, and Serafina running after her in her race suit, laughing. He looked at them for four seconds.

Then he said, “Hm,” and it was, Elowen said afterwards, the closest he had ever come in public to laughing out loud.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You knew,” said Serafina, that night, in the loft, with her head on his chest and the window open onto the tracks. “You said you knew who’d win.”

“I did.”

“Who?”

“Raiden,” said Qin Haozhen. “He’s had the face for I’m keeping the money since Lunar New Year.”

She laughed into his chest until the next train came.

The drawing was framed, in the end. Raiden had it done, and brought it to the garage under the railway bridge in September and hung it over the bench beside the whiteboard, and Jinx came round the next day and hung a second copy of it, exactly the same, beside the first, except that in hers, at seven hundred metres, the bike was a quarter of a length ahead.

Nobody ever took either of them down.

chapters.title: He Checks the Perimeter Before Breakfast
chapters.desc: Spring 2027. Every morning, before the egg sandwiches, he walks the garage: shutter, side door, alley, loft window, the roof hatch, the stairs. Every morning. She starts timing it. Four minutes and twelve seconds on day one. She keeps a chart on the whiteboard for a month. Then one morning he forgets.
chapters.epigraph: “I used to think all I wanted was a long life with you, where I didn’t have to check the perimeter before I kissed you.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
She’d known for four years. She’d just never counted.

Every morning. Before breakfast. Before the egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover, which he still fetched himself every Thursday and which Mr. Kwok fetched on the other days now, because he said a man of seventy-six needed a reason to walk to the flyover. Before the hot water in the plain mug. Before anything.

He walked the garage.

She’d watched him do it since the first winter, half asleep, from the mattress in the loft with the blanket over her head. He came down the stairs, and went to the shutter first, and looked at it, at the bottom edge where it met the concrete, and at the lock. Then the side door to the alley: he opened it, and stood in the doorway for a moment looking up and down the alley, and closed it, and checked the bolt. Then the window over the workbench. Then the back door by the sink. Then up the stairs again, past her, to the loft window, which looked out over the railway, and the hatch in the loft ceiling that went up onto the roof, which he opened, and put his head through, and looked, and closed. Then down again. Then the shutter one more time.

Then he put the kettle on.

Every morning. In four and a half years, she had never seen him miss it once.

✦ ✦ ✦

She started timing it on the first of April.

It wasn’t a joke. She wanted it to be clear, afterwards, to Aurelia, who asked, that it hadn’t started as a joke. It started because on the last night of March she’d been lying awake in the loft at five in the morning, which she did sometimes still, after a race, and had heard him get up and go down the stairs, and had listened to him go round, the shutter and the side door and the alley and the window, and she’d thought: he doesn’t know he’s doing it.

He didn’t. She was sure of it. She’d asked him once, in 2025, and he’d looked at her blankly and said, “Doing what?” He didn’t know any more than he knew he breathed.

So on the first of April she lay in the loft with her phone under the blanket and started the stopwatch when his foot touched the bottom stair.

4:12.

She wrote it on the whiteboard that afternoon, in the bottom corner, small, in red, under the photograph from Harbour Road and the framed sheet that said EXCESSIVE MIRROR CHECKS. 1 Apr — 4:12.

He didn’t notice. That was how she knew she was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

2 Apr — 4:09.

3 Apr — 4:15. (It had rained. He’d stood at the side door for longer.)

4 Apr — 4:11.

Mouse noticed on the fifth. She stood in front of the whiteboard with her headphones round her neck and looked at the column of numbers for a long time. Then she went to her desk and came back with a sheet of graph paper and drew a chart, very neatly, in pencil, with the days along the bottom and the minutes up the side, and pinned it beside the column, and went back to her desk without a word.

Big Wu noticed on the seventh.

“What’s that?” he said.

“Nothing,” said Serafina.

Big Wu looked at the chart. At the dates. At the numbers, all of them about four minutes. At Mouse’s neat pencil line, wandering along at the same height, like a car going round and round a circuit.

“Is that him?” he said. “In the mornings?”

She didn’t answer.

Big Wu was quiet.

“In prison,” he said, eventually, “the first time, there was a man in the next cell who did a thing every morning. He touched the four walls. In order. Left, back, right, door. Before he did anything else. Every morning, for six years. Even on the day he got out.” He looked at the chart. “I asked him once why. He said it was so he’d know where the walls were.”

“Did he stop?”

“I don’t know,” said Big Wu. “I never saw him again.” He put the doughnuts down on the bench. “I hope he did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

10 Apr — 4:06.
