14 Apr — 4:02.

15 Apr — 3:58.

It was going down. Slowly. A few seconds at a time. She didn’t know why. She watched him, every morning, from the loft, and he was doing exactly the same things in exactly the same order, the shutter and the side door and the alley and the window, the loft and the hatch and the stairs. But he was doing them faster. Or he was standing at each one for less long. At the side door, in the first week, he’d stood looking up and down the alley for nearly a minute. By the third week, it was twenty seconds.

18 Apr — 3:44.

21 Apr — 3:31.

Mouse’s pencil line was sloping. Down, toward the bottom right-hand corner of the graph paper, like a car coming down the back straight toward the Needle and braking, a little, every day.

“He’s slowing down,” said Mouse, very quietly, to Serafina, on the twenty-second, standing in front of it. “I mean speeding up. I mean—” She stopped. “He’s stopping, Sera.”

“I know.”

“Does he know?”

“No,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

She thought about telling him. She didn’t.

She thought about it every morning, at five, under the blanket in the loft, with her phone on. She thought about it in Modena, at the simulator, in the last week of April, where they’d gone for three days, and where he walked the perimeter of the hotel room every morning instead, the door and the window and the bathroom and the balcony, in three minutes and two seconds. She thought about it on the plane home.

She didn’t tell him because she was afraid that if she told him he’d notice, and if he noticed he’d do it on purpose, and if he did it on purpose then it would be something he decided, every morning, like her deciding about him every morning in the loft at the beginning. And she didn’t want it to be a decision. She wanted it to just stop. The way the trains stopped shaking the building for him, after the first year. The way the passenger seat had stopped being a place he slept and started being a place he lived.

28 Apr — 3:14.

29 Apr — 3:20. (Ghost Pepper had come in early and startled him.)

30 Apr — 3:05.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first of May, he forgot.

It was a Saturday. She woke at five, as she always did now, and lay under the blanket with her phone, and waited for him to get up.

He didn’t get up.

She lay there. Six minutes. Ten. She turned her head on the pillow. He was awake. He was lying on his back beside her with his eyes open, looking at the ceiling, at the light from the railway moving across it, and he turned his head and saw her looking at him.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing,” said Serafina. “Are you getting up?”

“In a minute.”

She waited. He didn’t get up.

Then he did something he had never done in four and a half years. He rolled over onto his side, toward her, and put his arm over her, under the blanket, and pulled her in against him, and put his face in her hair, and went back to sleep.

She lay absolutely still.

She lay in the loft over the garage under the railway bridge with the window open onto the tracks and his arm over her and his breath, slow and even, going down again, warm against the back of her neck, and the six-ten went over and shook the building, and he didn’t wake. And she didn’t stop the stopwatch, because it had never started.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke at seven.

He woke the way he always woke, all at once, the soldier way, his whole body going from nothing to everything in the space of a breath. She felt it happen. She felt his arm tighten over her. She felt him lift his head and look at the window, at the light, which was wrong, much too bright, two hours too late.

He went very still.

“Sera,” he said.

“Mm.”

“What time is it?”

“Seven.”

He didn’t move. She felt him lie there, with his arm over her, very still, the way he’d been still at the east service door when a tray of glasses fell, and she felt him understand.

“I didn’t,” he said.

“No.”

“The shutter. The door. I didn’t—”

“No,” said Serafina. “You didn’t.”

He sat up. He sat on the edge of the mattress in the grey-gold light with his back to her and his hands on his knees, and she watched the back of his neck, and his shoulders, and waited for him to get up and go down the stairs and do it, all of it, the shutter and the side door and the alley, fast, the way you’d run back into a house you thought you’d left the gas on in.

He didn’t get up.

He sat there.

Then he turned his head and looked at her, over his shoulder, lying under the blanket on the mattress in the loft with her hair flattened on one side and her phone still in her hand.

“You’ve been timing it,” he said.

It wasn’t a question. Of course he knew. He’d always known everything about her a week before she’d told him.

“Since the first of April,” said Serafina. “It’s on the whiteboard. Mouse made a chart.”

“How long?”

“Four twelve. On the first day.” She swallowed. “Three oh five, yesterday.”

“And today?”

She held up the phone. The stopwatch was at zero. It had never started.

He looked at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go down the stairs.

He lay back down. On his side, facing her, on the mattress, under the blanket, in the light that was two hours late. He looked at her face for a while, very close, the way he’d looked at it across a ballroom on Battery Hill, all the way in.

“I used to think,” he said, “that all I wanted was a long life with you. Where I didn’t have to check the perimeter before I kissed you.” He put his hand on her face. “I didn’t think it would ever happen. I thought it was the kind of thing you want so you’ve got something to want.”

“It happened.”

“It happened this morning. And I didn’t even notice.” He was quiet. “I missed it.”

“I didn’t,” said Serafina. “I was here. I saw the whole thing.” She put her hand over his. “You rolled over and went back to sleep. With your arm over me. At five past five. You’ve never done that. Not once. In four and a half years.”

He looked at her.

Then he kissed her. Before the shutter. Before the side door, and the alley, and the window, and the hatch, and the stairs. Before the kettle. Slowly, in the loft, in the late light, with nothing checked and nothing locked and nobody, anywhere, in the whole of the world, at the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they came down at eight, Big Wu was standing in front of the whiteboard with the doughnuts.

He’d read the last line. Serafina had written it at a quarter to eight, coming down the stairs to make the coffee, very small, in red, in the bottom corner, under thirty days of numbers and Mouse’s neat pencil line sloping down toward the bottom of the graph paper.

1 May — didn’t.

Big Wu looked at it.

Then he went to the shutter, very slowly, enormous, and opened it all the way, the whole thing, with a long screech, and let the morning in, and stood in it, in the sun, with his back to them, and blew his nose like a ship’s horn.

Mouse came in at nine. She stood in front of the chart. Then she took out her pencil, and drew the last bit of the line. Down. All the way down. To the bottom of the paper. To zero.

And under it, very small, she wrote one word, and went to her desk.

Good.

chapters.title: The Military Academy at Sixteen
chapters.desc: September 2010. A slow train south from a mining town, a dormitory of forty boys under a roof that leaks onto bed eleven, a firing range in the snow, and a boy who laughs with his whole face and gives away the window seat. Two years later, a woman with red wool on her needles asks a question about a map. The boy they chose because he never hesitated.
chapters.epigraph: “They told me he never hesitated. I asked him a question about a map. He answered it before I’d finished asking.” — Director Duan Qiuyan
chapters.content:
The winding gear stopped being there on the third night.

That was what he would remember about the State Military Academy, at the very beginning, before anything else. Not the gates, which were iron and very tall and had the state’s crest on each one. Not the parade ground, which was the size of the whole of the second street at home and the first street together. Not the uniform, which was two sizes too big because they never had the small sizes, and which he rolled up at the cuffs and the ankles and was shouted at for rolling up, and unrolled, and tripped over.

The quiet.

At home, the winding gear at the pithead had groaned and clanked every four minutes, all day and all night, for every night of his life. He’d slept through it since he was born. He’d thought it was what the night sounded like. In the dormitory at the academy, on the second floor of a long grey building at the end of the parade ground, there were forty boys in forty iron beds in two rows, and forty boys breathing, and somebody crying very quietly at the far end into a pillow, and the rain coming through a crack in the roof onto bed eleven, and nothing else at all. Nothing every four minutes. Nothing big going over.

He lay in bed twelve, beside bed eleven, and didn’t sleep for a month.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was sixteen. He was from a town in the north that the maps had stopped bothering with, and he had a mother who sewed and a father who had been under a roof in 2003, and he had never been further from the town than the county seat, once, on a school trip, to see a museum about coal.

He had come because the man from the county office had come to the school in the spring and given every boy in the top year a test. Maps. Numbers. A page of shapes where you had to say which one came next. A room with a lot of objects on a table, and then the table was covered, and you had to write down everything that had been on it.

He wrote down everything that had been on it. Forty-one objects. And the colour of the cloth they’d been on, and the fact that one of the pencils had been broken, and that the man from the county office had a stain on his left cuff that looked like soy sauce.

The man from the county office had looked at his paper for a long time.

“Your father,” he’d said. “Qin Dahai. The roof fall.”

“Yes.”

“And your mother sews.”

“Yes.”

“Would you like to go to the capital, Qin Haozhen? To a school where they’ll give you everything? Food, a bed, clothes, an education? Where your mother won’t have to pay for any of it?” He’d put the paper down. “Where you’d never have to go down the pit?”

He’d thought about it, the way he would think about everything for the rest of his life, carefully, all the way through.

“Yes,” he’d said. “I’d like that.”

Nobody had asked him what else he’d like. He hadn’t thought anybody would. It hadn’t occurred to him that it was a question.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy in bed eleven was called Mo Tianyi.

He was seventeen, a year older, from a city in the east with the sea in it, and he had been put in bed eleven because he’d arrived last, and bed eleven was the one under the crack in the roof, and the rain came through onto his pillow every night it rained, which in September was most nights.

He didn’t complain. That was the first thing Haozhen noticed about him. Everybody complained about something. The food. The shouting. The cold showers. The boy at the far end who cried. Tianyi didn’t complain about anything. He moved his pillow to the other end of the bed and slept with his feet under the drip, and in the morning he wrung out his socks and laughed about it, with his whole face, and told a joke about a fish.

On the eleventh night, when it was raining very hard and the drip had become a stream, Haozhen got up and moved his own bed. Bed twelve. He pushed it along the floor, very quietly, so that the iron feet didn’t scrape, until it was under the crack in the roof, and the rain came down onto his own blanket instead.

Then he pushed bed eleven along to where bed twelve had been.

Tianyi, in bed eleven, woke up halfway through being moved and lay there looking at him in the dark.

“What are you doing?”

“You’ve been wet for eleven nights,” said Qin Haozhen. “I can’t sleep anyway. It doesn’t matter if I’m wet.”

Tianyi looked at him.

Then he laughed. Quietly, in the dark, delighted, into his blanket.

“You’re very strange,” he said. “What’s your name?”

✦ ✦ ✦

They were friends after that. As much as anybody was, in that place.

Tianyi talked. Haozhen didn’t. Tianyi told jokes at breakfast and at lunch and on the parade ground under his breath while the instructors shouted, and Haozhen listened to all of them and never laughed, and Tianyi said that was the best thing about him, because it meant that when he did laugh, one day, Tianyi would know he’d finally told a good one.

On the train home at the New Year, the slow train north, eleven hours, there were two window seats in their carriage, and Tianyi took one, and then got up and gave it to him.

“You’ve never been on a train,” said Tianyi.

“I came on this one. In September.”

“You came on it in the dark,” said Tianyi. “You’ve never seen it. Sit there. Look.” He sat down in the aisle seat and put his feet up on the seat opposite and closed his eyes. “I’ve seen it. It’s just fields.”

He sat in the window seat for eleven hours and looked at fields. All the way. He’d never seen so many. He’d never seen so much sky. At the end, in the afternoon, the first pithead came up on the horizon, black against the grey, with its winding wheel turning, and then another, and then his own, with two wheels, and he put his hand flat on the glass.

Tianyi opened one eye.

“That’s it?”

“That’s it.”

“It’s very ugly,” said Tianyi kindly, and closed his eye again. “I’m glad you’ve got one.”

He never let anybody else have the window seat after that. Not once. He gave it to Haozhen on every train and every plane and in every car for the next thirteen years, and he never said why.

✦ ✦ ✦

The snow came in December of the second year.

They were on the range. Twenty boys in a line, on their stomachs, in the snow, with rifles, in the cold, with an instructor walking up and down behind them who had been in a war nobody talked about and had a voice like a bucket of gravel. Five rounds each, at a target a hundred metres away, a paper one, on a wooden frame, with rings on it.

Tianyi put five rounds in the centre ring. Five. Everybody stopped. The instructor stopped. Tianyi was the best shot anybody at the academy had seen in ten years, and he knew it, and he lay in the snow and grinned at the target.

Haozhen fired five rounds.

The instructor walked down the line to his target. He looked at it. Then he walked back, and looked down at the boy lying in the snow with the rifle.

“Qin,” he said. “Where are your other four?”

There was one hole in the paper. In the centre of the centre ring. Slightly ragged at the edges.

“They’re there, sir,” said Qin Haozhen.

The instructor went back and looked at the target again. He looked at it very closely, with his face a hand’s width from the paper. He put his finger in the hole.

He came back.

“Five rounds,” he said. “Through the same hole.” He looked down at the boy in the snow. “Do you know how many times I’ve seen that, Qin?”

“No, sir.”

“Once,” said the instructor. “In the war. A man who’s dead now.” He looked at him. “Why did you do that?”

Haozhen thought about the question, the way he thought about everything.

“I’m sorry, sir,” he said. “I didn’t mean to make a mess of the target.”

Beside him in the snow, Tianyi made a noise. A small strangled noise. And then he was laughing, face down in the snow, with his rifle beside him and his whole body shaking, so hard he couldn’t stop, so hard the instructor had to walk away down the range, and Haozhen lay beside him in the cold and looked at him and didn’t understand what was funny.

“You apologised,” said Tianyi, into the snow, when he could breathe. “You put five rounds through the same hole and you apologised to the target—”

Haozhen looked at the target. At the single ragged hole.

Something happened at the corner of his mouth. A long way off. Like a light in a house a long way down a road.

Tianyi saw it. He stopped laughing. He lifted his face out of the snow and looked at it.

“Oh,” he said. “There it is.”

It was gone again almost at once. But Tianyi had seen it. And he told it as a joke at breakfast for thirteen years.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came in June, at the end of the second year.

He was eighteen. He’d been called to the commandant’s office, which nobody was ever called to unless they’d done something very bad or something nobody would tell you about. He stood in front of the desk in his uniform, two sizes too big, rolled at the cuffs, which he had stopped being shouted at for, because the instructors had stopped shouting at him for anything at all by the end of the first year.

The commandant was behind the desk. Beside it, in a chair, there was a woman.

She was about forty-four. Small. A neat dark bob. A grey cardigan. Reading glasses on a chain round her neck. And in her lap, on two bamboo needles, a few rows of red wool. Just a few. A strip a hand’s width long. She was knitting. In the commandant’s office. As though it were a train.

She didn’t look up.

“They tell me,” she said, “that you never hesitate.”

He didn’t say anything. Nobody had asked him a question.

“Let me see.” The needles clicked. “If you were standing on the east side of the parade ground at six in the morning in the winter, and you wanted to leave the academy without anyone on the gate seeing you, which way would you—”

“The drain by the kitchens,” said Qin Haozhen. “It goes under the wall. It’s dry from November to March. The grating’s rusted on the north side.”

The needles stopped.

Half a second. A row left unfinished. The red wool lay still over the bamboo.

The commandant, behind the desk, had gone a strange colour.

The woman looked up at him at last. Over the top of her glasses. With a look he would come to know very well over the next eleven years: a kind of attention, careful, measuring, the way you’d look at something you’d been told was valuable and had just discovered was worth a great deal more.

“I hadn’t finished asking,” she said.

“No, madam.”

“How do you know about the drain?”

“I looked,” said Qin Haozhen. “In September. The first week.” He paused. “In case.”

“In case of what?”

He thought about it.

“In case I ever needed to go,” he said.

The woman looked at him. Then she smiled at her knitting, and began the next row.

“I’m going to take you away from here, Haozhen,” she said gently. “To the capital. To a building with no name on it. I’m going to give you a great deal to do. You’ll be very good at it.” In, round, through, off. “I don’t think you’ll ever need that drain.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went in the July.

He packed in six minutes. Four shirts, folded flat and square like envelopes, which nobody had taught him, which he had simply worked out. A book he didn’t read. Nothing else.

Tianyi sat on bed eleven, which was under the crack in the roof again, because Haozhen had moved it back on the last night so that whoever came next wouldn’t be wet, and watched him pack.

“She asked me too,” he said. “Last week. About a map.”

Haozhen stopped.

“What did you say?”

“I hesitated,” said Tianyi, and grinned, the whole face. “About a second. She said she’d send for me in the autumn.” He swung his feet. “So you’ll have to keep the window seat warm.”

Haozhen picked up his bag.

He looked round the dormitory. Forty iron beds in two rows. The crack in the roof. The window at the end. The quiet. He’d learned to sleep in it, in the end. Four hours. It was enough.

“Tianyi,” he said.

“Mm.”

“Thank you for the window seat.”

Tianyi looked at him, on bed eleven, with his feet swinging.

“Don’t thank me,” he said. “Just take it. Every time.” He grinned. “And one day you’ll laugh at one of my jokes. And I’ll know I finally told a good one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He never did. Not at the academy. Not in the building with no name. Not in fourteen countries, in hotel rooms and window seats and cars at petrol stations. Not on the grass at the side of a coast road at night, in the light of a burning car, with a broken leg in front of him and blood in his own sleeve.

He laughed at one once, years later. In a garage under a railway bridge, in the spring of 2027, standing in front of a whiteboard, holding a postcard of a beach with a single palm tree on it and a man too far away to see.

Resigned. One sentence. Took me four years. The chilli crab here is terrible.

He laughed out loud. Alone, at the whiteboard, with his hand over his eyes. At the chilli crab. At four years. At a boy in bed eleven with his feet under the drip, telling a joke about a fish.

Serafina heard him from under a car, and rolled out on the creeper, and looked at him. Then she took the postcard off him, and turned it over, and found the address in the corner, very small, in pencil. And that afternoon she sent a postcard back. A photograph of the Monza banking, hand-tinted, in colours that had never existed. On the back, in her big untidy capitals, three words.

HE LAUGHED. — S.

Nothing came back. Nothing needed to. But Haozhen knew, the way he knew everything a week before anybody told him, that on a beach somewhere warm a man with a walking stick had read it, and put his head back, and laughed with his whole face, and known at last that it had been a good one.

chapters.title: Forty-Three Songs for the Car
chapters.desc: Nonna’s tape deck has been broken since 2017 and Serafina plays everything off her phone, in the same order, every time: forty-three songs, and she always skips the seventeenth. He doesn’t own a single piece of music. Over a summer he learns all forty-three, by heart, in order. Then he fixes the tape deck.
chapters.epigraph: “Why do you always skip seventeen?” “Because it’s my mother’s.” “Then why is it on there?” “Because it’s my mother’s.”
chapters.content:
He didn’t have any music.

She found that out in March 2023, the week after the glovebox, in Nonna on the coast road at three in the morning, when she handed him her phone and said, “Put something on,” and he held it for a while and then said, “What?”

“Anything. Something you like.”

He looked at the phone.

“I don’t know any,” he said.

She took her eyes off the road for a second to look at him.

“You don’t know any what?”

“Music,” said Qin Haozhen. “To like. I’ve heard it. In hotels. In lifts. In the cars of people I was—” He stopped. “I’ve heard a great deal of music. I’ve never chosen any. I wouldn’t know where to start.”

She drove for a while.

“What did your mother have on? When you were small?”

He thought about it.

“The radio,” he said. “The one station. It played the same forty songs, round and round, for about ten years. She sang along to them while she sewed.” He was quiet. “I don’t know what any of them were called.”

Serafina took the phone back off him without looking and found what she wanted with her thumb and pressed it, and the car filled up with something loud and fast and Italian from 1974 with a great many horns in it.

“Then you’ll have mine,” she said. “All of it. Forty-three songs. In order. You’ll hate half of them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was always the same forty-three. In the same order. Every time.

She’d made it at nineteen, the week she left the house on the Peak, on a phone she’d bought for cash from a man under the flyover by the fish market. She’d sat in a Fiat she was building from two dead ones in somebody else’s garage and put together every song she wanted to have with her, now that she couldn’t go back for anything. And she’d never changed it. She’d added to it, in the first year, up to forty-three. Then she’d stopped. She’d played it in every car she’d driven since. The Fiat. Nonna. Gilded on the transporter, on the long drives to the circuit in the north. She didn’t put it on shuffle. She didn’t skip, except for one.

Track one was the loud Italian one from 1974 with the horns. Nonna had played it in her Alfa in the sixties, too fast, on the road to the lakes. Track two was a Cantonese song from the eighties about a harbour that every taxi in the city had played the year she arrived at fourteen and didn’t understand a word. Track three was something British and angry with guitars that she’d been listening to in her bedroom on the Peak the night before the engagement dinner.

Track seventeen was an aria. Puccini. A soprano singing, very high and very beautifully, an old recording, crackling, from before the war. Serafina skipped it every time. Every single time. Her thumb went to the phone on the dashboard the second the first note started, without her looking, and it was gone.

“Why do you always skip seventeen?” he said, in April.

“Because it’s my mother’s.”

“Then why is it on there?”

Serafina didn’t answer for a long time. They were on the coast road, at the place where his head used to slide onto her shoulder before he’d stopped bothering to rest it on the window first.

“Because it’s my mother’s,” she said.

He didn’t ask again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He learned them.

He didn’t decide to. It just happened, the way most things had started happening to him since a ballroom on Battery Hill. Three nights a week, at three in the morning, the loop. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. Forty-three songs. Forty minutes for the loop, roughly, so she’d get through about eleven songs each time round, and then the next night she’d start where she’d stopped. It took about four loops to get through all forty-three. Then it started again at the horns.

He slept through most of them, at first. Then less. Then, by May, he was awake for all of them, his head on her shoulder with his eyes closed, listening.

By June he knew them.

All of them. In order. What came after what. Which ones she sang to: track nine, loudly, every word, and track twenty-six, very quietly, only the chorus, and track thirty-one, in Italian, under her breath, with her eyes on the road. Which ones she turned up: four, eleven, and twenty-two, all the way, so the windows buzzed. Which one made her drum on the steering wheel at red lights. Which one made her go faster without noticing, on the long straight past the container terminals: track fifteen, every time, so that he’d know they’d reached fifteen before he opened his eyes, just from the way the car leaned.

Which one she skipped.

And which one she never got to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Track forty-three.

He noticed it in June. She never got to it. The loop was forty minutes. Forty-three songs took about two hours and fifty minutes. She’d play eleven, twelve, sometimes thirteen songs in a loop and stop when they got back to the railway bridge, and the next night she’d start at fourteen. And by the time she got to the forties, it would be a race weekend, or a test, or the twelve days, or a stairwell, and something would happen and she’d go back to the start. Back to the horns.

In four months he had never heard track forty-three.

He looked at the list on her phone one night, while she was under Gilded. Forty-three. The title was in Italian. He didn’t know it. The singer was a woman. It was from 1961.

He didn’t ask her. He didn’t play it on his own. It was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to the electronics market behind the tram depot on a Tuesday in September.

It was the first week of September. He had been home from Lisbon for six weeks. He slept four hours in the loft most nights and two more in the passenger seat in the afternoons, and Big Wu’s mother sent soup every day, and the trains went over, and nobody said anything about any of it. He was better. Not well. Better.

He wanted, very badly, to do something with his hands that wasn’t anything he’d been trained for.

So he went to the market. To a stall at the very back, under a sheet of corrugated iron, run by an old man with a magnifying glass on a strap round his head who had been repairing radios since 1968 and who looked at the thing in Haozhen’s hands and laughed.

It was Nonna’s tape deck. He’d taken it out of the dashboard that morning, with her permission, while she watched him with her arms folded. The original. 1992. A radio-cassette, black, with a row of silver buttons and a small green display and a slot for a tape. It had stopped working in 2017, she said. The tape went in and didn’t come out. She’d never had it fixed. She’d been playing everything off her phone through a wire into the back of it ever since.

“Belts,” said the old man. He had it open on his bench in four minutes. “The rubber belts. They go hard. Look.” He pulled one out with tweezers. It snapped. “Thirty years. They all go.” He looked up at Haozhen through his magnifying glass. “I have the belts. You want me to do it?”

“Show me,” said Qin Haozhen.

The old man looked at him for a while.

“Sit,” he said, and pulled out a stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took him eleven days.

Not the belts. The belts took one afternoon, with the old man watching over his shoulder and swearing in Hakka when he dropped a spring. It was everything else that took eleven days.

He bought a second tape deck, a recorder, an old one, from the stall next door. He bought blank cassettes. Two. Ninety minutes each. He took her phone, with her permission, which she gave with her arms folded and her eyes narrowed and the face she made when an engine was making a noise she couldn’t place, and he sat at the end of the workbench every night for eleven nights with Mouse’s headphones on and the recorder and the phone, and recorded them.

All forty-three. In order. Onto the two tapes.

Except seventeen.

Where seventeen should have been, at the start of the second side of the first tape, he left four seconds of silence. Exactly four. So that when it came, in the car, she wouldn’t have to reach for the dashboard. Her thumb could stay on the wheel.

And when he got to the end of the second tape, after forty-three, which he listened to for the first time, alone, at the bench, at two in the morning, with Mouse’s headphones on and his eyes closed, there were still four minutes left on the tape. Four minutes of nothing.

He sat for a while looking at the recorder.

Then he took Mouse’s headphones off. He picked up the recorder. He took it to the middle of the garage, under the hanging lamp, and set it on the bonnet of Gilded, and pressed RECORD.

And waited for the next train.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave her the tapes on a Saturday at the end of September, at three in the morning, in Nonna, in the garage, with the tape deck back in the dashboard.

He didn’t say anything. He put the first tape in the slot. It went in with a soft click, the way it hadn’t since 2017. He pressed PLAY.

The horns. 1974. The loud Italian one, very fast, the one Nonna had played in her Alfa on the road to the lakes. Coming out of the tape deck instead of the phone, warmer, with a faint hiss underneath it, the way it would have sounded in 1992.

She sat in the driver’s seat and didn’t move.

“You fixed it,” she said.

“The belts. They’d gone hard. A man behind the tram depot showed me.” He was looking out of the windscreen. “It’s all of them. In order. Two tapes.”

She took Nonna out from under the railway bridge.

She drove the loop. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. Track two, the harbour. Track three, the guitars. She sang along to nine, loudly, every word. She turned up eleven so the windows buzzed. On the long straight past the container terminals, at fifteen, he felt the car lean.

At the end of the first side, she didn’t turn the tape over. He did. He reached across and took it out and turned it and put it back, without her asking, the way he passed her a spanner.

The second side started.

Four seconds of silence.

He watched her thumb. On the steering wheel. It moved, a fraction, toward the dashboard, the way it had moved every single time for seven years. Then it stopped. In the air. Because there was nothing to skip.

Then track eighteen started, and her thumb went back to the wheel.

She didn’t say anything. She drove without saying anything.

“You left a gap,” she said, at last.

“Four seconds.”

“Why four?”

“That’s how long it takes you,” said Qin Haozhen, “to reach the button. I timed it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t stop at the railway bridge.

That was the first time. She drove past it, at the end of the loop, at about track thirteen, and went round again. And again. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. The sky began to go grey over the water. She put the second tape in herself, at about five, at the lights by the flyover. The thirties. Thirty-one, in Italian, under her breath, with her eyes on the road. The forties.

Forty-three.

He’d heard it once. At the bench, alone, in Mouse’s headphones. A woman’s voice, from 1961, very clear, singing in Italian about something he didn’t understand, slowly, over a guitar.

She heard it in the car, on the coast road, at a quarter to six, with the sun coming up out of the sea.

She’d never heard it in a car. Not in seven years. Not once. She’d put it at the end, she told him afterwards, because it was Nonna’s, the one Nonna sang in the kitchen in Milan when nobody was listening, and she’d thought: I’ll get there one day. When I’ve gone far enough.

She pulled into the lay-by above the harbour, where the fireworks had been, and turned off the engine, and sat and listened to it with her hands on the wheel and her eyes wet, all the way to the end.

Then the tape kept going.

Four minutes of hiss. Then, very faintly, a sound she knew better than any sound in the world. A deep rumble, coming closer, getting louder. The floor of a building beginning to shake. A train going over a railway bridge, enormous, right overhead, every girder ringing. A spanner falling into a bucket with a clang.

And then, somewhere under the noise of the train, very close to the recorder, very quiet, a voice. His.

Not singing. He didn’t sing, then. Not where anybody could hear.

Just two words, said in the dark, in the middle of the garage, at two in the morning, under the hanging lamp, to a tape recorder on the bonnet of a car, when he thought nobody would ever play it.

Come home.

The tape clicked off.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat in the lay-by with her hands on the wheel.

He sat beside her and didn’t say anything. He’d thought, at the bench, recording it, that he’d tell her what it was before she got to it. That he’d warn her. And then he’d thought: no. She’d never got to forty-three. Let her get to the end of something, once, all the way, without anybody telling her what was there.

“That’s forty-four,” she said, eventually.

“Yes.”

“I only had forty-three.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “I thought you’d want one for when you’re away. At a circuit. In a hotel. On a mountain.” He looked at the sea. “So you’d know where the walls were.”

She turned her head and looked at him.

She took the tape out of the deck. She held it in both hands for a while. Then she put it back in, and rewound it, all the way, to the horns, and pressed PLAY, and started the car.

“Again,” she said. “From the start. All forty-four.”

“It’s six in the morning.”

“I know what time it is,” said Serafina. “I’m not stopping at the bridge.”

She didn’t. They went round until nine. Big Wu came in with the doughnuts and found the shutter up and the garage empty and Nonna gone, and stood in the middle of the floor, and then sat down on the stool by the kettle to wait, and at ten past nine he heard a red Lancia coming down the street of shuttered workshops, slowly, with its windows down, playing something very loud and very fast and Italian from 1974, with a great many horns in it.

chapters.title: Wedding Planning With a Spreadsheet
chapters.desc: February 2026. Two hundred guests, nine round tables, one garage, and a laptop open on the long table on the forty-fourth floor. He has colour-coded everyone. There is a column for who must face the door. There is a column called “Score-neutral”. Aurelia reads it for an hour without speaking, and then says the nicest thing she has ever said to anyone who wasn’t her husband.
chapters.epigraph: “Column K.” “What’s column K?” “Whether they need to sit facing a door.”
chapters.content:
“Two hundred and four,” said Aurelia.

“Two hundred,” said Qin Haozhen. “Four are dogs.”

“Four are—”

“Brake. The Yaus’ dog from Yunwu, who’s coming down on the bus with them. And Elowen’s two.” He scrolled. “She asked. I said yes. They’re in column J.”

Aurelia looked at the screen for a long time.

They were at the long table by the window on the forty-fourth floor, on a Sunday afternoon in February, with the whole harbour grey and glittering behind the glass and a pot of coffee between them that neither had touched. Serafina was on the long grey sofa behind them with her boots up, eating pastries from the Milanese bakery out of the box, and Chen Si was in the kitchen making something with a great deal of star anise in it, and had been told, in writing, on a piece of his own paper, that he was not to come out until the seating was done.

On the laptop there was a spreadsheet.

It had two hundred and four rows. It had nineteen columns. Every row was a guest. Every column was something about them. And every cell was coloured, very precisely, in one of eleven colours, according to a key in a separate tab called KEY, which Aurelia had opened first and read for four minutes without saying anything.

“You’ve colour-coded the guests,” she said.

“Yes.”

“By what?”

“Table,” said Qin Haozhen. “That’s the background. Then the text colour is relationship. Family, team, friends, Lin, Song, Orsini, the industrial district.” He pointed. “Bold is who needs to be near the toilets. Italic is who mustn’t sit near Big Wu’s mother.”

“Who mustn’t sit near Big Wu’s mother?”

“Mr. Kwok,” he said. “On a Tuesday. It depends on the soy sauce.”

Behind them on the sofa, Serafina laughed so hard she inhaled a pastry.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia read it. All of it.

She did it the way she read a contract: from the top, every line, both ways, with a pencil behind her ear that she didn’t use, and her lips moving very slightly. She went down the rows. She went across the columns. She opened the KEY tab again twice. Once she stopped and went back up forty rows to check something, and nodded, and went on.

He sat beside her and didn’t say anything.

Column A was the name. Column B was the table, one to nine. Column C was the seat, one to twenty-two, clockwise from the side nearest the shutter, because Mr. Kwok had borrowed the big banquet rounds. Columns D to G were dietary: no pork, no shellfish, no fish (which had one entry, and it was the bride, and she was sitting at the head of table one in front of a whole fish anyway, because it was nine dishes and Mr. Kwok had said so). Column H was who was driving. Column I was who would cry; it had forty-one entries, all highlighted, and Big Wu was at the top in red. Column J was the dogs.

Column K was headed Door?

Aurelia stopped at column K.

“What’s column K?” she said.

“Whether they need to sit facing a door,” said Qin Haozhen.

She looked at it. Most of the column was blank. Seven cells had a Y in them.

Chen Si. Y.

Zhao Zhendong. Y.

Qin Haozhen. Y.

Mo Tianyi (invited, not coming). Y.

Lin Jian. Y.

Granny Shum. Y (scanner).

Vittoria Song. Y.

Aurelia looked at the last one.

“My mother,” she said.

“She sat facing the door at the engagement dinner,” said Qin Haozhen. “In the chair I gave her. And in the yellow room, in 2023, she sat on the sofa on the left. That’s the one facing the door to the hall.” He paused. “And in Block C at the circuit she always sits at the end of the row. Nearest the stairs.” He looked at the screen. “I don’t think she knows she does it.”

Aurelia was quiet for a while.

“She does it at the dinner table in Mid-Levels too,” she said, at last. “In three rooms. With a view of a wall. She sits in the chair facing the front door.” She didn’t look at him. “I’d never noticed. In thirty years.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The problem was the garage.

The garage had two doors. The shutter, at the front, onto the street. The side door, onto the alley. And seven people in column K who needed to face one of them.

Round tables helped. Round tables had no head. But the garage was long and narrow, under the railway bridge, and nine round tables went in it in three rows of three, and the tables in the middle row could see both doors, and the tables at the ends could only see one, and the tables at the back by the sink could see neither unless you sat on the side nearest the shutter, which was where Mouse wanted to put the lights.

And there were two people in column K who could not, under any circumstances, be at the same table, both facing the same door, because they would both go for the same chair, and one of them would have to give way, and it had happened once, on the forty-fourth floor in 2023, and Aurelia had said oh for heaven’s sake and Serafina had bitten her lip.

“Chen Si and Zhao,” said Aurelia.

“Chen Si and Zhao.”

“They’ll both want table three.”

“They’ll both want the seat at table three that faces the shutter,” said Qin Haozhen. “Seat four. Clockwise from the shutter side.”

Aurelia looked at the plan. He’d drawn it in a separate tab. Raiden’s drawing of the garage, scanned, with nine circles on it and two hundred small numbered dots.

“So what did you do?”

He pointed.

Table three. Seat four, facing the shutter: Chen Si. Table four, the next table, directly behind it. Seat nine, facing the side door to the alley: Zhao Zhendong. Their chairs were back to back. A hand’s width apart. Each of them facing a different door. Each of them able to see the other door in the reflection in the steel of Nonna’s bodywork, which would be parked at that end of the garage, and which Big Wu would polish on the Friday until you could shave in it.

“Back to back,” said Aurelia.

“Back to back. They’ll cover each other’s door. They did it in a riot at sixteen. In a cell.” He paused. “I read about it. In a file.”

Aurelia looked at the two dots, back to back, a hand’s width apart.

She didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The other problem was column L.

Column L was headed Score-neutral?

It had two entries.

Aurelia Chen. N.

Elowen Zhao. N.

Aurelia looked at it and closed her eyes.

“I can explain,” she said.

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “Serafina explained. In 2023. It took her forty minutes. There were diagrams.” He scrolled to a third tab, which was called SCORE, and which was a single cell with a question mark in it. “I didn’t know the current number. So I left it.”

“Nobody knows the current number.”

“I gathered.”

“What did you do?” said Aurelia.

He pointed again. Table three. Seat four: Chen Si. Seat five: Aurelia Chen. Facing the shutter. And across the table, directly opposite her, on the other side of the round table, seat nine, with her back to the shutter and facing the side door, beside her husband’s back: Elowen Zhao.

Facing each other. Across one round table. For nine courses.

“You’ve put us face to face,” said Aurelia.

“For the whole of the meal.”

“That’s not score-neutral. That’s the opposite of score-neutral. That’s—”

“That’s the only seat in the garage,” said Qin Haozhen, “where neither of you can be said to have the better one. Same table. Same distance from the bride. Same distance from the kitchen. Same view of Nonna. One of you facing a door, one of you facing the other door. Neither of you near the toilets. Neither of you near Big Wu’s mother.” He looked at her. “I checked it four times. It’s the only seat that’s exactly fair.”

Aurelia looked at seat five and seat nine.

“She’ll say she won,” she said. “Because she’s facing the alley, and the alley’s where the getaway car is.”

“Then you’ll say you won,” said Qin Haozhen, “because you’re facing the shutter, and the shutter’s where everyone comes in.”

There was a pause.

On the sofa behind them, Serafina had stopped eating pastries and was lying with the box on her chest and her hand over her eyes, shaking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia sat back.

She looked at the spreadsheet. All of it. Two hundred and four rows. Nineteen columns. Eleven colours. A KEY tab. A SCORE tab with a question mark in it. Column K. Column L. Two dots back to back a hand’s width apart. Her mother, facing a door.

She took the pencil from behind her ear and put it down on the table, very precisely, the way he put things down.

“I’ve been trying to seat that man and Zhao Zhendong at the same dinner table since 2019,” she said. “I’ve tried eleven times. I’ve used place cards, and diagrams, and once a lazy Susan.” She was quiet. “Every time, one of them sat with his back to the room, and spent the whole night watching the other one’s door in a wine glass.”

“I know,” he said. “I read that too.”

“You did it,” said Aurelia, “in a spreadsheet.”

“I had Raiden’s drawing.”

She turned her head and looked at him. At the forgettable face that she had seen, once, through the window of 18 Harbour Road, walking down the pavement with her sister’s hand in his, in front of a camera, not looking at it.

“I’ve only ever said this to one other person,” said Aurelia Chen. “And I married him.”

He waited.

“You,” she said, “are wasted on security.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si came out of the kitchen at five, with a pot, in an apron, having been told in writing that he could.

He put the pot on the long table. He looked over his wife’s shoulder at the laptop. At table three. At seat four. At the dot behind it, back to back, a hand’s width away, with a name beside it that he knew very well.

He looked at it.

Then he looked at Haozhen.

“Column K,” he said.

“Column K.”

Chen Si picked up a pencil. He leaned over the screen, and with the end of the pencil, very lightly, so as not to scratch it, he touched the dot that was Zhao.

“He’ll want to know,” said Chen Si, “who’s covering his door.”

“You are,” said Qin Haozhen.

Chen Si was quiet.

“Good,” he said. Then, after a moment: “I’d rather there were two of us.”

They looked at each other across the long table on the forty-fourth floor, with the harbour behind the glass and the pot of star anise between them and Aurelia between them too, very still, looking from one to the other.

Then Chen Si put the pencil down, and went to fetch bowls, and on his way past the long grey sofa he took the box of pastries off his sister-in-law’s chest without a word and ate the last one.

“Hey,” said Serafina, through her fingers.

“I’m family,” said Chen Si. “It’s in the contract. Page eleven. Pastries.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The spreadsheet was printed in the end. On A3. In colour. Mouse did it. It was pinned on the whiteboard in the garage under the railway bridge on the Friday before the wedding, beside the postcard of Monza and the framed sheet that said EXCESSIVE MIRROR CHECKS, and on the Saturday, at a quarter to twelve, two hundred people stood in front of it in their good clothes and found their seats, every one of them, without asking anybody, in under four minutes.

At table three, seat four and table four, seat nine sat down at the same moment, back to back, a hand’s width apart, each facing a different door.

Neither of them looked round.

Neither of them needed to.

At the same table, seat five and seat nine looked at each other across the red cloth for nine courses, and at the end of the fish, at exactly the same moment, both of them said, “That’s a point,” and then both of them laughed, which nobody at table three had ever seen happen before, and which column I had not predicted, and which Haozhen, at table one, beside the bride, saw out of the corner of his eye in Nonna’s polished bodywork, and wrote down that night, in his notebook, under What happens in the middle.

chapters.title: Eliana Hacks the Bodyguard
chapters.desc: March 2025. Zhao is in Rotterdam and the youngest Lin sister is giving a talk about a bank that would rather she didn’t. Elowen asks for a favour. He has no identity card, no job and a brand-new phone. She has his phone open in four minutes. He is very impressed. She is very annoyed that he is impressed.
chapters.epigraph: “Four minutes.” “Three minutes and fifty seconds. I was being polite.”
chapters.content:
Elowen rang on the Sunday night, at the garage, on Serafina’s phone.

“Zhendong’s in Rotterdam,” she said. “With Chen Si. Until Thursday. And Eliana’s giving a talk tomorrow. At the university. About a bank.” A pause. “She found something in their system in January. She told them. They said thank you. Then they said they’d sue her. Then somebody started sending her messages.” Another pause. “She says they’re nothing. She says she’s had worse from boys in her year. Zhendong says she’s not going without somebody.”

Serafina looked across the garage at the stool by the kettle.

“How long?” she said.

“One day. Eight till six.”

“He hasn’t got an identity card,” said Serafina. “Officially he doesn’t exist. They sent him a letter.”

“Eliana won’t care,” said Elowen. “Eliana doesn’t exist officially in about four countries.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana Lin was twenty-two and in the last year of a computer science degree at the university on the hill, and her Chinese name was Lin Yu, and her sisters called her Yu-er when they wanted something, and she did not look like anybody’s idea of a person banks were frightened of.

She was small, and pale, and her hair was in a knot on top of her head held with a pencil, and she was wearing a hoodie with a cartoon cat on it and a pair of glasses with thick black frames that she pushed up her nose every eleven seconds. She came out of the tall old house in the Walled City at five to eight on Monday morning with a laptop under one arm and a slice of toast in her mouth, and looked at the man standing at the bottom of the steps in a dark jacket with his hands at his sides where people could see them.

She took the toast out of her mouth.

“You’re the taxi,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Sera’s taxi.”

“Yes.”

“Elowen says you used to be one of the ones my father didn’t let into the Walled City.” She looked at him over her glasses. “She says you were the best one Zhendong ever heard of. He said Hm about you in a voice like he was announcing a death.”

“That sounds like him,” said Qin Haozhen.

Eliana looked at him for a while longer, chewing.

“I don’t need a bodyguard,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’ve had worse messages from boys in my year.”

“I know. Your sister said.” He opened the door of the grey estate car. “I’m not a bodyguard today. I’m a lift.”

She thought about it.

“Can I sit in the front?”

“Yes.”

“Can I change the music?”

“I don’t have any music,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ve got forty-four songs. Forty-three of them aren’t mine.”

Eliana got in the front.

“Sera says you haven’t got a driving licence,” she said, doing up her belt. “Officially.”

“Not yet,” said Qin Haozhen. “I’ll be very careful at the lights.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had his phone open before the end of the street.

He knew she would. He’d known since the steps. He’d put it, very deliberately, in the cup holder between the seats, face up, the new phone. Serafina had bought it for him in February, in her own name, two days after the letter, because the old one had belonged to an identity number that no longer existed. Nobody had his number except Serafina, his mother, Big Wu, Mr. Kwok, Aurelia, Chen Si, Qian, and a man called Mr. Chiu at the driving test centre, about whom he was cautiously optimistic.

He drove. He didn’t look at the cup holder. He felt her look at it.

At the lights by the old market, she picked it up.

“Can I?”

“It’s locked,” he said.

“I know it’s locked,” said Eliana, and pushed her glasses up her nose. “That’s the point.”

He stopped at the lights. He looked at the dashboard clock.

7:58.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:02 she held it up.

The lock screen was gone. In its place, his home screen. Which had been blank. Black, with four icons on it in a row. It wasn’t blank any more. It was a photograph. A mountain road, steep and grey, with rock on one side and nothing on the other, and at the top, in a concrete car park by a temple, a woman getting out of a black car, holding her left hand up to the camera, palm out, with something red on the ring finger.

Underneath, in white letters, small, in the corner, it said: BRING IT BACK.

“I found it on the stream,” said Eliana. “The hill climb. 2023. It’s a screenshot. I cleaned it up a bit.” She scrolled. “I’ve also changed your ringtone. It’s an Italian song from 1974 with a lot of horns in it. Sera’s track one. I got it off her phone in 2023 when she was at dinner. I’ve had it for ages. I’ve been waiting for someone to use it on.”

He looked at the screen.

He looked at it for a long time. The lights went green. The car behind them hooted. He didn’t move.

“Four minutes,” he said, at last.

“Three minutes and fifty seconds,” said Eliana. “I was being polite. I could’ve done it in two, but I wanted to see if you’d look.” She handed the phone back. “You didn’t look. Not once. That’s very annoying.”

“Why?”

“Because everyone looks,” said Eliana. “Everyone looks when I’ve got their phone. They get nervous. They say what are you doing. Zhendong took his off me in 2021 and put it in his pocket and didn’t speak to me for an hour.” She folded her arms and looked out of the window. “You just drove. Like you didn’t care.”

“I cared,” said Qin Haozhen. He put the car in gear. “I wanted to see how long it took you.”

She turned her head and looked at him over her glasses.

“How did you get past the second lock?” he said. “The one behind the screen. It’s not the factory one. Mouse put it on.”

There was a silence in the car.

“You’re impressed,” said Eliana, in a voice of deep offence.

“Very.”

“Nobody’s ever impressed. They’re angry, or frightened. Nobody’s ever—” She stopped. She glared at the windscreen. “There’s a gap in the way it talks to the network on start-up. It’s very small. Mouse would never have seen it unless she was looking for it. It’s not her fault.” A pause. “I’ll show you. At lunch. If you buy the noodles.”

“I’ll buy the noodles,” said Qin Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The talk was at eleven. In a lecture hall on the hill, with two hundred seats, raked, and a lectern, and a screen. There were about two hundred people. Every seat taken. Students, mostly. Some lecturers. A few men in suits at the back who didn’t look like students or lecturers.

He stood at the back. By the door. With his weight on the back foot and his hands at his sides, looking at the space just past the head of whoever was moving.

Eliana talked for forty minutes. He didn’t understand a word. She stood at the lectern in her cat hoodie with the pencil in her hair and talked very fast and very clearly about something called a handshake, and something called a token, and a door in a bank’s system that somebody had left open since 2017, and she showed slides with a great many numbers on them, and at one point the whole hall laughed, and he didn’t know why, and at another point a lecturer in the second row put his head in his hands.

He watched the room.

He watched the men in suits at the back. There were three. Two of them were from the bank; he could tell from their shoes and their lanyards. They wrote things down. They were unhappy, but they were the kind of unhappy that sent a lawyer’s letter.

The third one wasn’t from the bank.

He was sitting at the end of the back row, two seats from the door, in a grey jacket with no lanyard. He didn’t write anything down. He had a phone in his lap, face down. And every eleven seconds, very slightly, he looked up from the lectern at the side door, the one by the stage, that led out to the corridor where the toilets were.

Every eleven seconds. The way a needle comes back to north.

Haozhen watched him for twenty minutes.

Then, while two hundred people were laughing at something about a password, he walked along the back of the hall, unhurried, and sat down in the seat beside the man in the grey jacket, and looked straight ahead at the lectern, pleasantly.

“She’s very good,” he said, in Cantonese.

The man in the grey jacket went very still.

“You’ve been watching the side door,” said Qin Haozhen, still looking at the lectern, “for twenty minutes. Every eleven seconds. You’ve got a phone face down in your lap with the camera end pointing at the stage. You’re not from the bank. The bank sends lawyers.” He paused. “You’re from a firm the bank pays to send people who aren’t lawyers.”

The man didn’t say anything.

“I’d like you to leave now,” said Haozhen. “Through the main door. Not the side one. And I’d like you to tell whoever pays you that the next time somebody sends a message to Miss Lin, it’ll be read by a man who used to work for a building with no name on it, and who knows the name of your firm, and the name of the man who owns it, and the name of the bank that pays him, and what that bank did in 2017 with a door it left open.” He turned his head at last, and looked at the man in the grey jacket for two seconds. Three. All the way in. “Miss Lin’s just told two hundred people about the door. I’ll tell the rest.”

The man in the grey jacket stood up.

He left through the main door. Not the side one.

At the lectern, Eliana, mid-sentence, watched him go. Then she looked at the back of the hall, at the man sitting where he’d been, in the seat by the door, with his hands on his knees. She pushed her glasses up her nose. She went on talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

He bought the noodles.

At a stall behind the library, at a plastic table under a tree, at one o’clock. Beef brisket, for her, with extra radish. Plain, for him. She ate like Serafina, fast, with her whole attention, and when she’d finished she pushed the bowl away and took his phone off the table without asking and turned it round and showed him the gap.

It took her eleven minutes to explain. He understood about a third of it. He said so.

“A third’s very good,” said Eliana grudgingly. “Zhendong understands nothing. Elowen understands nothing and pretends to understand everything, which is worse.” She gave the phone back. “The man in the grey jacket.”

“Yes.”

“You talked to him.”

“Yes.”

“What did you say?”

“I can’t tell you that,” said Qin Haozhen.

Eliana looked at him over her glasses.

“Sera says that’s what you say,” she said. “She says it’s what Chen Si says to Aurelia. She says it saves a great deal of furniture.” She put her chopsticks down. “Was it bad? What he was going to do?”

He thought about it.

“No,” he said. “Not bad. Frightening. He was going to follow you to the toilets and take a photograph of you and send it to you tonight with no message. So you’d know he could.” He looked at her. “That’s all. That’s the whole job, usually. Making someone know you can.”

Eliana didn’t say anything for a while.

“I’d have been fine,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’d have found out who he was by Wednesday. And his firm. And the man who owns it. I’d have put it on the internet.”

“I know,” said Qin Haozhen. “That’s why they sent him. Because you’d have done that, and they wanted to frighten you first.” He picked up his chopsticks. “Now you don’t have to.”

She looked at him across the plastic table, under the tree, behind the library.

“Thank you,” she said. It came out as if it hurt.

“You’re welcome.”

“Don’t tell Zhendong.”

“I’ll have to tell Zhendong.”

“Don’t tell him I said thank you,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six he drove her home.

At the bottom of the steps of the tall old house in the Walled City, a boy was sitting on the kerb beside a bicycle with his elbows on his knees. Twenty-two or so. Tall, thin, in a lab coat with a pen in the pocket, as if he had come straight from somewhere and forgotten to take it off. He stood up when the grey car stopped.

Eliana looked at him through the windscreen. She didn’t say anything. Something happened to her face that Haozhen had seen on Serafina’s, once, in the paddock at the circuit in the north, at four o’clock on a December afternoon, with an engine ticking.

“Who’s that?” he said.

“Nobody,” said Eliana, too fast. “The boy next door. He always waits.”

She got out of the car. She stopped. She bent down to the window.

“I’ve put something else on your phone,” she said. “I forgot to say. An app. It tells you where Sera is. When she’s on track. Live. Her position, her lap time, the gaps.” She pushed her glasses up. “It’s the series’ own data. They don’t know I’ve got it. Nobody else has got it. It’s not exactly allowed.” She thought about it. “It’s mostly allowed.”

He looked at her.

“It’s for when you’re not on the wall,” said Eliana. “So you don’t have to watch it eleven times on a stream.” She straightened up. “Sera told me about that too.”

She went up the steps. The boy with the bicycle went up them beside her, very close, not touching, and at the top, at the door, she turned round and looked at the grey car, and lifted one hand, very slightly. Not a wave. Something.

He sat at the bottom of the steps for a while with the phone in his hand.

On the screen, a woman at the top of a mountain was holding up her left hand.

Bring it back.

He didn’t change it. Not that night. Not ever. And when it rang, at three in the morning, with a lot of horns in it, it was always her.

chapters.title: The Fake Name He Liked Best
chapters.desc: May 2027, a ferry on Lake Como, on the way to see an old man with eleven cars and a parrot and a red Lancia with a forged chassis plate. He has had nineteen names. On the ferry, he tells her about the one he liked best: a deckhand called Ah Sang, on an island boat in a southern sea, whom nobody ever wanted anything from. She calls him by it once.
chapters.epigraph: “Ah Sang.” “No.” “No?” “Say the other one. I like the other one better now.”
chapters.content:
The ferry from Como to the villages along the lake left the pier at ten past nine and stopped eleven times, and she wanted to stand at the front for all of them.

It was May, and the water was very still and very green, and the mountains came straight down into it on both sides, steep, with villages hanging off them in yellow and pink and terracotta, and the old villas along the shore with their gardens going down to the water in steps. The air smelled of wisteria and diesel. A man in a white jacket was selling coffee from a counter in the cabin. A small dog in a basket was barking at a swan.

She stood at the rail at the front, in her leather jacket, with the wind in her short hair, and pointed at things.

“That one’s where Nonna’s cousin lived. With the green shutters. She had a goat. That’s the church where they say the bell rings by itself. That one’s a hotel now, it used to be a convent, Aurelia stayed in it in 2015 and said the nuns’ ghosts kept her awake, which is rubbish, it was the plumbing.” She leaned over the rail. “And that one, at the end, with the boathouse. That’s Signor Bassi’s.”

He stood beside her at the rail and looked at the villa at the end.

“The man with the Stratos,” he said.

“The man with the Stratos. And eleven cars. And the parrot.” She grinned at the water. “He bought it, you know. In 2022. On the Monday after the Reception. For forty per cent less, from the man who was still holding it at eleven o’clock when nobody bid. He rang me. He said, cara, I have the car with the lying plate. I have had the plate taken off and put in a frame. It is the most honest thing in the house.”

He looked at the villa for a long time.

“I was outside,” he said. “On Battery Hill. When the bidding was. In the car park. With the Belgian.”

“I know.”

“I never found out if anyone bought it.”

“Nobody bought it,” said Serafina. “That’s the point. Then Signor Bassi bought it. For less. Because I told him the truth.” She looked at him sideways. “Everything good that’s ever happened to me has started with telling somebody the truth about a car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They were halfway down the lake when he told her about the names.

She hadn’t asked. She’d asked once, in 2023, in Nonna on the coast road, how many, and he’d said nineteen, and she’d said tell me one, and he’d said I can’t tell you that yet, and she’d waited. She’d waited four years. He’d told her the thirty-eight in the loft on the night of the tea house, every one, in order. He’d never told her the names.

He told her now. At the rail. With the water going by green and the mountains on both sides and the dog in the basket barking at another swan.

“There were nineteen,” he said. “Some for a week. Some for a year. A lot of them were the same man, more or less. A guard. A driver. A man at a door.” He looked at the water. “I didn’t like them. I didn’t dislike them. They were clothes. You put them on, you took them off, you folded them.”

“Like envelopes,” said Serafina.

“Like envelopes.” He was quiet for a while. “There was one I liked.”

She didn’t say anything. She’d learned that, in four and a half years. When he was going to tell you something, you let him get there by himself.

“2018,” he said. “The spring. Six weeks. A ferry. An island boat, in a sea a long way south of here, that went between four islands and the mainland every day, twice a day. Old. Rust everywhere. A diesel engine that knocked like someone at a door. I was a deckhand.” He paused. “There was a man who rode it every day. I was supposed to watch him. Who he talked to. Where he got off. What he carried. That was all. I never had to do anything else. They took him in the end, but not on the boat, and not me.”

“What was your name?”

“Sang,” said Qin Haozhen. “Ah Sang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She said it to herself, under her breath, at the rail, trying it. Ah Sang.

“It means alive,” he said. “Or born. Or raw, like raw fish. Depending.” He almost smiled. “They gave it to me off a list. I don’t think anybody thought about it. But I liked it. I liked it from the first day.”

“Why?”

He thought about it, the way he thought about everything.

“Because nobody wanted anything from Ah Sang,” he said. “Ever. Ah Sang scrubbed the deck at five in the morning. He coiled the ropes. He tied the boat up at four islands and the mainland, twice a day. He carried old women’s shopping bags up the gangway and down again. He drank tea with the cook, a woman called Auntie Wan who was seventy and had been on that boat for forty years and swore at the engine like it was her husband.” He looked at the water. “He sang. On the deck, scrubbing. Badly. On purpose. Auntie Wan used to throw things at him.”

“You sang badly on purpose.”

“It’s noticeable,” said Qin Haozhen. “Singing well.”

“I know. I was at the karaoke.”

He did smile then. A little.

“Nobody looked at Ah Sang,” he said. “Nobody wanted him to be anything. He didn’t have to be the best. He didn’t have to be anybody’s tool, or anybody’s scalpel. He didn’t have a file. He had a bunk under the stairs to the wheelhouse, and a locker, and a mug that Auntie Wan had written his name on in marker.” He paused. “He slept. On that boat. Six hours a night. With the engine knocking. It was the only place in ten years, before you, that I slept more than four.”

She didn’t say anything for a while.

“What happened to him?”

“He stopped,” said Haozhen. “When the six weeks were up. He tied the boat up at the mainland on a Friday afternoon and walked off it and didn’t come back on Monday.” He looked at the water. “I never told Auntie Wan. I couldn’t. I’ve wondered, sometimes, what she thought. If she kept his locker.”

“She’ll have kept it,” said Serafina.

“You don’t know that.”

“She wrote his name on a mug,” said Serafina. “In marker. She’ll have kept it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Signor Bassi met them on the jetty at the end of the lake.

He was eighty-six. He was very small and very brown and very bent and he walked with a stick with a silver horse’s head on it, and on his shoulder there was a large grey parrot with a red tail that looked at Haozhen without blinking and then said, very clearly, in Milanese, something Serafina refused to translate.

“Cara,” said Signor Bassi, and held out both hands. “Your grandmother’s face. Exactly. At the bottom of the stairs at the Scala, in 1971, telling a tenor he was flat.” He looked past her at the man beside her. “And this is the guard.”

“Not any more,” said Serafina.

“I know. You told me. On the telephone. In 2025.” He looked at Haozhen, up, from very low down, through very old eyes. “On the night of the Reception, cara, you rang me at five to ten from a car park and told me the truth about a car, and I bought it on Monday for forty per cent less, and I have been grateful to you ever since.” He leaned on his stick. “You did not mention, on that telephone call, that there was also a man in the car park.”

“There was,” said Haozhen.

“With a Belgian,” said Signor Bassi.

Haozhen went very still.

“I read the newspapers, young man,” said Signor Bassi, mildly. “I am eighty-six, not dead.” He turned round on his stick. “Come. I have the car. I have had it out of the garage since Tuesday. The plate is in the hall. In a frame. It is the most honest thing I own.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He let her drive it.

Of course he did. He stood on the drive of the villa in the sun with his stick and his parrot and watched her climb into the red Stratos, a wedge of a car short as a sneeze, drawn by a boy in the back of a maths lesson, with no plate on it at all, just four small neat holes where the rivets had been. And he said, “Along the lake. To Menaggio and back. Do not go faster than the bus.”

She went faster than the bus.

Haozhen sat in the passenger seat. The road along the lake was narrow and very old and cut into the cliff, with tunnels in the rock and the water on one side going by green and enormous, and she took the bends the way she took the Baizhang Pass, on the outside, where it was steepest, and laughed, and the Stratos made a noise like something that had been waiting half a century to be let out.

He didn’t check the mirror once.

On the way back, in the long tunnel before the villa, in the dark, with the engine echoing off the rock, she said it.

Quietly. Not to tease him. Trying it out loud, the way she’d tried it under her breath at the rail. As if she wanted to know what it sounded like in a car, at speed, in the dark, from her.

“Ah Sang.”

He turned his head.

She didn’t look at him. She kept her eyes on the tunnel. On the circle of daylight at the end of it, getting bigger. But she’d felt him turn, and she waited.

“No,” said Qin Haozhen.

“No?”

“Not that one.” His voice was very low, in the noise of the engine off the rock. “I liked him. I liked him for six weeks on a boat in 2018. He was the best name I had, for ten years.” He was looking at her. “He’s not the best one now.”

They came out of the tunnel into the sun. The lake was suddenly there again, all of it, blinding, green and gold, with the mountains on the far side and the villages hanging off them and the old villa at the end with its boathouse.

“Say the other one,” he said. “I like the other one better now.”

She did look at him then. Just for a second. At a hundred and ten, on the road along the lake, in a Lancia with no plate on it, with the sun on his face.

“Haozhen,” said Serafina.

He closed his eyes. Just for a moment. The way he had in the passenger seat of a red Lancia on the coast road on a winter morning in 2022, when he’d woken up and found he had slept, and put his head back against the headrest, and let out a breath he’d been holding since he was eighteen.

“Yes,” he said. “That one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Before they left, in the evening, on the jetty, waiting for the last ferry, Signor Bassi gave her something.

A small flat parcel in brown paper. She opened it on the ferry, at the rail at the front, in the last of the light, with the lake gone dark blue and the villages lighting up one by one on the mountains.

It was the chassis plate.

The lying one. Out of its frame. Small, rectangular, aluminium, with a number stamped on it and four holes at the corners. On the back, in old ink, in an old hand, Signor Bassi had written something in Italian.

She read it and laughed and handed it to him.

“What does it say?”

“It says,” said Serafina, “For the girl who told the truth about a car, and the man who heard her.”

He held the plate in his hand, at the rail, with the dark water going by.

Then he put it in his inside pocket. The left one. Next to a folded piece of paper from a registry office with a red stamp on it, and a pink slip from a driving test centre, two years old, that he had never thrown away.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the island boat in the southern sea, as far as anyone knows, there is still a locker under the stairs to the wheelhouse with a mug in it. Plain, white, chipped at the rim. With a name written on it in marker, gone grey with ten years of salt.

Serafina found it in 2028.

She didn’t tell him she was looking. She spent four months on it, with Mouse, very quietly, at the end of the bench at two in the morning, in single words. Ferry companies. Island routes. A cook called Wan who had retired in 2021 at seventy-three and lived now in a flat above a fish shop on the third island.

She wrote to Auntie Wan.

Auntie Wan wrote back. In pencil. On the back of a menu. One line.

I kept his locker. Tell him to come and sing badly for me before I die.

They went in the spring. He sang. Very badly. On purpose. On the deck of the island boat, scrubbing, at five in the morning, with the engine knocking like someone at a door, and an old woman in an apron threw a shoe at him, and wept, and threw the other one.

And at the end of the trip, when they tied up at the mainland on the Friday afternoon, he walked off the boat. And on the Monday morning, he came back on.
